Upesitom 36 Inch Recessed and Wall Mounted Electric Fireplace, 750/1500W Modern Linear Fireplace Heater, LED Fireplace Insert with Adjustable Flame Colors, Bracket, Timer, Remote Control, Black

Who was using the product(s)?
The fireplace was off. It had not been used in a few weeks. 

How were the product(s) being used?
It was not in use at the time of the explosion.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?
Glass in my face, feet, hands, forearms, hair.
I sprained my wrists. The mantle fell off the wall and landed on me. It was painful and I bruised.
I sprained my ankles
I am still having pain and strugglilng to walk. 
Trauma to my pets.

How did any injuries occur?
I was covered with glass. My pets were covered with glass. When I tried to flee the explosion, and get my cats, I fell to the ground, twisting my ankles. I got glass in my feet, hands and forearms. Glass hit my face and covered my hair. I had to vacuum my hair and my pets fur. Over a week later, I am still stepping on slivers of glass. I sprained my wrists. I sprained my ankles, one of which I just had surgery on. I am still having pain and struggling to walk.  There was damage to my furniture, carpet, cat toys, piano etc, as they were covered in glass and I had to throw them out.
justification: The incident resulted in injuries (glass cuts, sprains, and trauma) but no death, and the occurrence is unlikely given the product was not in use at the time.

incident_description: A hot wire in a Garment steamer melted a hole through the plastic casing.
justification: The incident involved damage to equipment but no reported injury or death.

incident_description: We got home and noticed we didnt have hot water. Upon inspection of the water heater the wiring coming from the water heater was hot and tripped the breaker. After letting it cool off we noticed that the wiring on the water heater was fried.
justification: The incident involved damaged wiring and a tripped breaker, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description: Outdoor ceiling fan, installed 5 years ago, shedded two of five fan blades from fatigue fractures on the blade mounting arm.  The fan blades came off during two separate breezy days about 4 weeks apart while the fan was not being used.  Had the fan been in use, the blades could have separated at high speed.
justification: The incident involved fan blades detaching, but no injury occurred as the fan was not in use. However, the potential for injury exists if the fan had been operating.

incident_description:
I was washing down my Sister's house I had on rubber gloves, protective clothing and  shoes.  Water was running down my body into  my shoes . After I had finished I came home and took a shower immediately.
Woke up the next morning my hands and back were burned and blistered yet, my feet were blistered and some of my skin was eaten off. Mold Armour E-Z House Wash was the product that I used.
justification: The description reports burns and blisters, indicating an injury.

incident_description: I plugged my Hoover twin tank steam mop in to use it. While it was preheating, I started smelling something burning, and then I noticed smoke coming out of the machine. It had already started melting completely in half. I threw the product outside, so my house would not catch on fire and doused it with water. In the process of getting the burning melting machine out of my house, metal pieces fell onto my wood floor and burned my wood floor.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning appliance causing smoke and damage to property, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description: My gas furnace was leaking natural gas from a valve within the furnace according to my gas company.  It is yet to be repaired.
justification: The gas leak is an incident with potential for harm, but no injury or death has occurred yet.

incident_description: We purchased TurtleWax Interior 1 Multi-Purpose Cleaner, which has an attached scrub brush. The instructions on the spray can provide information on removing the attached scrub brush. When removed, the method by which they say to remove it caused my hand to be gouged by the retaining clip on the spray can, resulting in removal of a layer of skin about 1/2" long, and bleeding.
justification: The incident resulted in a minor injury (removal of skin and bleeding), warranting a severity level of 3. The likelihood is possible (3) as such injuries can occur during product use.

incident_description: I purchased an iron on Amazon and it arrived on 5/31/24. Today, 6/1/24 I took it out to use it. I filled it with water below the max fill line, plugged it in, and used it to iron two shirts. It dripped water all over my hardwood floor, it soaked my ironing board, and it sputtered steaming water all over my shirts. Most of the water leaked onto the floor, and I think it was for the most part room temperature, but I did feel some splatters (small droplets of water) from the impact onto the floor, and they felt hot to me (I was barefoot at the time). The iron is also very lightweight, even with water in it. This, coupled with the fact that it does not stand well on the ironing board because its cord is awkwardly placed, means that it feels likely to tip over. Because of the awkwardly placed cord, the only way to sit the iron upright is to place it right on the edge of the ironing board, with the cord draped over the end. This makes it even more likely to fall. If you read some of the negative reviews for this product on Amazon, you will see that at least one person has been burned from trying to catch the iron as it was falling. Their review is titled "Dangerous" and frankly I agree with them. I don't trust this product not to burn me with scalding water and I'm sure it would have eventually fallen off my ironing board had I continued using it, potentially burning my legs or feet.
justification: The incident involved hot water splatters and a risk of the iron tipping over, but no actual injury occurred.

incident_description: Kidde P4010ACS frequently has false alarms even after resetting and cleaning the sensor
justification: False alarms are disruptive but do not cause injury or death, fitting severity level 2. The high frequency of reports suggests occurrence likelihood is almost certain.

incident_description: My brand new Speed Queen DC5003WE electric dryer ran for hours and heated up laundry room/smelled like smoke. This dryer could have burned my home down. Apparently this is a very common issue and the dials are flawed in design. The dials will break if you turn them counterclockwise, which allows the dryer to then run forever. The dial can turn both counterclockwise and clockwise to choose a dryer setting. There is no indication on the dryer to NOT turn the dial counterclockwise.
justification: The incident involved a malfunction that could have led to a fire (potential for severe damage), but no actual injury or death occurred. The issue is described as very common, indicating a high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description: On Sunday, 5/19/2024, the tempered glass in our shower wall spontaneously exploded.  The tempered glass shot out like shrapnel, putting nicks in our tile and the shower floor.  The glass and tile was installed in January 2022.
justification: The incident involved spontaneous glass explosion causing property damage but no reported injuries.

incident_description: House caught on fire due to Lasko ceramic heater. Fire investigation report was given.
justification: The incident involved a house fire caused by a heater, which is a significant event but the description does not mention any injuries or deaths.

incident_description:
I purchased a "Balance-Assist Safety Grab Bar, UPC Code 0007063114045, from Kroger Marketplace,[REDACTED]  about May 27, 2024.
   I tried it out on our master bathtub rim, and the suction was great. On June 2nd I placed it on the wall of my shower/bathtub planning to use it in 10 or 15 minutes.  I soon heard a loud crash, and found the grab bar had come loose and fallen.  I was very surprised, however, I then placed it on the wide tub rim, and again the suction seemed great.  Five minutes later I came back and barely touched it, and it fell over.
   I then thought, if I, or anyone, especially an older person, had relied on it to keep our balance, we could have had a very serious fall and injury.  I then determined to return it, and talk to the manager. Kroger refunded me with no problem, and the manager said he would pull the rest from the shelf.
   I think it should be pulled from every shelf in America, and imagine it has already caused several injuries.
justification: The grab bar failed but no injury occurred, though the potential for serious injury was noted.

incident_description: I had been using my solar inverter for 7-8 months and it all of a sudden start smoking and something inside started burning up.   Before I could reach the unit to shut down all of the circuit breakers parts inside the unit started exploding and spark s shot out. Also a brief flash of flames and then I shut it off, shut off the solar panel input and the backup battery.

incident_description: Hi, I was recently shopping in Home depot, and noticed the product 'Fabuloso' in a large display near the front of the store. Thinking that it might be a summer drink due to its bright purple color in a clear bottle. when I got closer to the items, I hen saw a smaller 2nd line on the label 'multi-purpose cleaner'.  while looking over the product, I thought- this would be quite tempting to a young child looking for a drink of fruit punch (as those drinks come in bright colors, and similar type of packaging).  I thought, ok there must be some type of child resistant cap on the bottle to protect children from drinking the cleaner, thinking they're going to have fruit punch. but no, it's a regular screw on cap, and instead they're drinking a cleaning product.  this was just an observation while I was shopping, no one attempted to open or drink the liquid. I did not purchase the item.  I'm reporting this for your review to help prevent a child's medical issue if they might drink it.
justification: The description reports a potential hazard but no actual incident or injury occurred.

incident_description:
Recently, while shopping at the local grocery store, I noticed what looked like a display of grape and lemon juice, on the endcap of the cleaning aisle.  Plastic bottles, almost identical to [REDACTED] grape juice or [REDACTED], had labels with slices of fruit and Refreshing Lemon in the center. Coming closer, I saw it was Fabuloso cleaning products. The potential dangers of this packaging/labeling are obvious. Looking at the CPSC site, I see that there have been reports going back to 2012, of labeling concerns, including the 2015 report of a woman who went to the ER after having mistaken the product for fruit juice. Yet, in 2024, the product labeling not only remains, but has gotten worse. Fabuloso is now partnering with the Secret Candy Shop and sells a Varity Pack on Amazon, in a pretty pink candy box along with a free Secret Candy Shop magnet (see attached). This is an accident waiting to happen. 
The EPAs Revised August 2017 Label Review Manual states that Unacceptable Graphics and Symbols (for pesticides) include Pictures of candy. Similarly, containers that look like food or candy are prohibited (16-5). Should this not be the same for toxic cleaning products? Please take action before a tragedy occurs.
justification: The description highlights a clear risk of injury due to misleading packaging, with a past incident reported.

incident_description: Speed Queen has a known issue with the knobs on their dryers that leads to timer malfunction, resulting in the dryer remaining on indefinitely. Ive come home to find my dryer running 14+ hours. This is a well-known issue and is a tragedy waiting to happen. I cannot fathom that this dryer has not yet been recalled.

incident_description:
I purchased "UV Dip Resin" manufactured by Crafteka, a Romanian company, through Amazon at the end of November 2023. The product is still sold on Amazon's website, even after I have reported my experience listed below to them, and to Crafteka. On Amazon, this item is listed as "Non-toxic" and "MSDS Approved." On the label, it states "CAUTION! Children should be supervised. Use adequate ventilation. Use the resin only in open-space areas. If you use it for more than an hour, please wear a face mask. Gloves are recommended when using UV resin. Not to be taken internally." I used the item for less than one hour, only ever using it once. There are no "WARNING" labels on the product package or on the website. 

I requested the MSDS directly from Crafteka, and received it on 1/31/24. It states plainly that this chemical has acute respiratory toxicity, and should only be used while wearing a respirator. It also states that prolonged use demands a self-circulating respirator. 

These warnings were known to Crafteka, but were not published on the product or product listing through Amazon. Both companies are aware of my injury, yet they both continue to list the product for sale unchanged. I am furious, and still injured.

Below is a complete accurate timeline of my medical history with this chemical. I can provide medical records if it will help your investigation.

12/3/23  I used the resin in my 2-car garage for under an hour. It was my first and only time
ever working with this material. I was testing the material after viewing other artists use it
successfully on [REDACTED]. I used the material in the late evening, and felt some chest discomfort
by the time I went to bed.
12/4/23  The next day, I had extreme discomfort in my respiratory tract, which coughing could
not resolve. I coughed all day, and the coughing continued chronically from this day onward.
12/29/23  My cough had continued through to this day, and I began to feel sinus pressure as
well. I feared that I now had an infection that I would not be able to clear without antibiotics. I
went to [REDACTED] to be seen by a doctor. She prescribed doxycycline to
combat the infection in both my lungs and sinuses.
1/4/24  I saw my primary care doctor and explained what had happened with the chemical
exposure. I was still suffering with a chronic cough, and some sinus congestion. He prescribed
prednisone to help my lungs fight the infection.
1/26/24  After continuing to suffer with the chronic cough, showing little to no improvement, my
primary doctor referred me to [REDACTED] to be in the care of a
pulmonologist, [REDACTED].
2/1/24  CT Scan of my lungs
2/2/24  Pulmonary function test. Appointment with [REDACTED] to review the scan and
pulmonary function test. I am diagnosed with signs of pneumonia stemming from the exposure
to Dip Resin. The doctor prescribes floxcin (antibiotics), albuterol, and prednisone to help heal
my lungs.
2/13/24  CT Scan of my lungs
2/15/24  follow-up appointment with [REDACTED]. He recommends we perform an
endobronchial ultrasound to clean (lavage) mucous from my lungs, and biopsy granulomas that
have appeared throughout my pulmonary lymph nodes.
2/21/24 - Endobronchial ultrasound is performed under general anesthetic (results are viewable
in the attached documents).
2/29/24  Follow-up appointment with [REDACTED]. My cough is continuing, but has improved
somewhat. He prescribes a nebulizer machine and a 1-week course of medicines to be inhaled
for 15 minutes 4 times per day.

I used the product as directed in my 2-car garage for less than 1 hour. I am an artist, and was
testing the Dip Resin for a new project. I sculpted butterflies out of aluminum wire, dipped the
wire into the resin pot, and activated the resin using a UV light. The resulting fumes from the
resin caused some chest discomfort by later that evening. The next day, I had extreme irritation
in my chest, and was coughing all day. Coughing did not clear the irritation.

The initial injury to my alveoli exposed my lungs to infections. These infections manifested into
uncontrollable coughing throughout the rest of December. I finally sought emergency care when
the infection spread from my lungs to my sinuses, and I began to feel extremely ill. This is when
I was initially prescribed antibiotics on 12/29 at [REDACTED].

I continued to combat the cough and infections throughout January under the care of my
primary doctor. He prescribed prednisone to help bolster my immune system, but this was not
enough for me to heal. I contacted Crafteka the product manufacturer to report my illness and
requested the Material Safety Data Sheet for Dip Resin so that I could research what I had been
exposed to. I was shocked to discover that the material is rated as an acute inhalation hazard
by the manufacturer, and that Crafteka falsely labelled it as safe for use without protection. I
have attached both the reply from Crafteka as well as the MSDS they supplied.

After exhausting my primary doctor's knowledge of chemical exposure, and with a still
deteriorating condition (fever, chills, insomnia, and fear of death) I was referred to [REDACTED]. 
Now in February I was diagnosed with pneumonia
and granulomas attributed to the original exposure to Dip Resin.

Over the past seven months and still to this day I am fighting with a chronic cough. My lung
capacity has been severely impacted by the injury, and I have even had a pulmonary lavage
under general anesthesia to clear the resulting mucous plugs and pneumonia. I was a perfectly
healthy 38-year-old husband and father who never smoked, and now I suffer everyday.
justification: The incident resulted in significant respiratory injury requiring medical treatment, but no death occurred. The likelihood is unlikely as the injury resulted from specific conditions of use not adequately warned against.

On multiple occasions the dryer ran three or more hours before we realized it was still on, the clothes were extremely hot and the whole laundry room had gotten very warm. After some online research we learned this is a known design flaw: the timer knob turns bidirectionally, but turning it counterclockwise will break the timer for that cycle and the dryer will never turn itself off. There is no warning on the machine, and its a huge fire hazard. Speed queen should recall this machine and/or mail out a part that will prevent the timer knob from turning counterclockwise.

The core issue is the Walkoff product comes in spray bottles, and is encouraged to be used in spray bottles. incident_description:
With the light switch in the "off" position, I received a 110V shock while replacing a light bulb in a Zephyr Savona ZSA-M90S range hood.  The shock caused minor injury to my hand.  The circuit was not (nor was it required to be) a GFCI nor AFCI, so the circuit remained online even after I had received the shock.

...

I am the owner of the home and the appliance.

...

During the installation, I was following all labeled instructions on the unit, as well as all warnings in the manual.  I was also practicing basic safety techniques associated with changing a typical household (E26, Edison-base) light bulb.

...

Upon further investigation, I discovered that the circuit controlling the light is switched-neutral.  The same circuit also controls the motor, so the motor is also switched-neutral.  This appliance is thus unsafe by design; any attempt by an end-user to replace the light bulb would require de-energizing the entirety of the circuit at the breaker panel in order to avoid being shocked.  Further, any short to ground on the neutral side would result in, at minimum, the energizing of one or more elements of the appliance without any ability to turn them off, if not also electrical arc/fire hazards.

...

A retrofit kit, consisting of Zephyr part numbers 11000041 and 56210050, is available.  This retrofit kit maintains the switched-neutral configuration.  Figure 1 on Page 2 of the  the document "ZSA-M90S Switch Retrofit", labeled "MAY08.0301", shows a wiring diagram for the kit.  This diagram clearly shows that the intended wiring is that the white (neutral) wire from the AC supply goes to the switch, while the black (hot/line) wire goes directly to the lights.

...

Further, the design of the lampholder itself is problematic.  A [REDACTED]  (phenolic resin) lampholder base is attached to a "trapeze".  This trapeze is bent downwards to enable threading of the bulb, then bent back up so that the bulb fits snugly against the bottom plate of the range hood.  Performing this operation requires the user to place their hands inside the cavity of the range hood, increasing the likelihood of exposure to the live 110V leg of the circuit that is always present.  It also means that a user who wishes to have the lights sit flush as designed must carefully balance between screwing in the bulb further and retracting the trapeze.  These actions increase the likelihood of the E26 threads embedded into the phenolic resin breaking down/apart, as they did in my case; this was a contributing cause of the shock that I received, though in a different configuration, the broken threads could easily have provided a short-circuit path that bypassed the lamp, posing a fire hazard.

...

While rewiring the motor to no longer be switched-neutral is beyond my skills, I was ultimately able to effect a simple retrofit to remedy the issue with the lights.  With one of the traces on the PCB removed, I ran a separate wire for "hot" to the switch for the lights, and then reversed their positioning on the downstream lampholders.  It's probably not realistic to expect an end-user to be comfortable breaking traces on a PCB, but my retrofit demonstrates that Zephyr could at least partially resolve this issue for no more than the cost of a replacement PCB and a wire or two.
justification: The incident resulted in a minor injury from an electric shock, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is high (4) due to the unsafe design of the appliance and the common need for bulb replacement.

incident_description:
Approximately 4 year ago, I purchased 3 SkyTech fireplace remote controls through CJ Bennett Supply in St Charles, MO as part of a home renovation project. The controllers work on a radio frequency similar to a garage door opener. During the summer of 2023, we experienced a situation in which the fireplace started spontaneously. No one was touching, or even near, the controller when it happened. Of concern is that the flues were closed and could have resulted in a soke filled home or a fire. After that event, we had the controllers serviced by a fireplace contractor who changed the frequencies, believing that would solve the problem. Over the ensuing months, the same event happened 3 more times, once in the first fireplace and once each in the other two fireplaces. Fortunately, we were at home during each of these events. The last event was in December 2023. At that point, we notified both the distributor and the manufacturer, SkyTech, and removed the controllers.

When we initially called SkyTech, the representative handling the call told us that they had heard of the problem before and asked for the model numbers for the controllers. I took pictures of the units and called SkyTech about a week later. This time, the representative put me on hold and then returned to the call with an supervisor. I have notes about the call and the names of the SkyTech employees. At that point, the tone of the call changed and the supervisor was insistent that I was doing something wrong and would not even respond when I told her that these spontaneous combustion events occurred when no one was even near the controllers.

At that point, I went back to CJ Bennett and attempted to return the controllers. After several months of negotiation, they could provide an acceptable solution. These products are unsafe and should be investigated before someone's house burns down.
justification: The incident describes spontaneous fireplace activations with potential for serious harm, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
My Klein model CL390 multimeter failed in a manner similar to other models that are subject to CPSC recall. Refer to: 

https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/2016/Digital-Clamp-Meters-Recalled-by-Klein-Tools 

My Klein's AC Voltage meter reads steady 000.0 Volts when exposed to 120 Volts. This is dangerous because the meter indicates a safe situation when it is actually potentially deadly.

No injuries occurred when I used the CL390 because I used a 2nd meter to check the AC Volts. The second meter indicated 120 V when the Klein showed 0. Note that meters typically indicate incorrect measurement conditions by showing a fluctuating display. The Klein shows a steady 0, which potentially gives false-confidence.

I contacted Klein customer support, and they had a tech expert call me back. The tech confirmed my troubleshooting was correct and said there was nothing else that I could do. The warranty has apparently expired, so Klein just gave me information about other products that I could purchase.
justification: The multimeter failed dangerously but no injury occurred due to the user's precaution of using a second meter.

incident_description: Ashley Hearth direct vent wall mounted propane heater is the product; however, the concern is specifically regarding the pilot/igniter assembly. In October of 22 I purchased 3 of these at the same time from Amazon. Subsequently, all 3 have failed. I am a retired Master Mechanic/Machinist for reference. The Pilot Assy fails because of a design flaw in that the brass tube fittings are pressed then swedged into a steel plate. Heat from the burner; expansion and contraction causes the brass fittings to fall out. This misaligns the pilot burner, thermocouple and igniter. One unit simply failed to light because the piezo tip fell out. Another melted the end off the thermocouple as it misaligned directly into the pilot flame and would not light. The third, and most concerning failed as the flame supply tube fell out of the front and continued to remain lit in the heater bottom where it doesn't belong. If the flame tip would happen to come off, there would potentially be an open pilot flame outside the heater creating a very unsafe scenario. The overall function and quality of the rest of the heater seems adequate, although I will also say that when my units arrived, all the tube nuts that secure and seal the gas lines to the gas valve and the pilot assy. were too loose. All three units were like this, and I have done an Amazon review advising customers to check this before putting in service, as it could lead to a gas leak. I was able to loosen the pilot gas line by hand on two units. I suspect this loosening is caused from shipping, and there is little the manufacturer can do. Over tightening the tube nuts at manufacture is not a good option, and shipping always beats everything to death. Especially all the way from China were these heaters are made. In conclusion: At the very least, these heaters need an upgraded pilot assembly. There are two larger BTU sizes of the same style heater plus natural gas versions of all three. Simply search Ashley heater on Amazon to see them all. If they use the same pilot assembly all these products are suspect and need further evaluation to protect consumers. Respectfully submitted: [REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a design flaw leading to potential gas leaks and unsafe flame conditions, which could result in injury or death if not addressed.

incident_description: EMCO/Andersen Fullview interchangeable screen storm door. The product in question has a removable full-size double pane insulated glass insert. This glass insert is very heavy - estimated at more than 30 lbs. It is inserted into the storm door frame from the inside of the door after removing the screen insert. In order swap the screen for the glass insert, a switch needs to be activated on the door so that the door handle lever can be moved into the full vertical position. This lever position disengages the mechanism that holds the insert (glass insert, or screen insert) in place. After inserting the heavy glass insert and returning the door handle to the horizontal position, the switch is supposed to re-engage to prevent the lever from moving into the release position, and the mechanism is supposed to retain the heavy glass insert. However, due to an unknown mechanical defect/failure, the door handle lever can be moved to the full upright and vertical position WITHOUT actuating the switch. This disengages the mechanism that retains the insert in the frame of the storm door, allowing the glass insert to free-fall into the house, potentially falling on people or pets inside the entryway. EMCO/Andersen has not acknowledged the significance this failure and will not provide replacement parts to address the defect that is causing the safety issue.
justification: The heavy glass insert can free-fall due to a mechanical defect, posing a risk of injury to people or pets inside the entryway.

incident_description: On Jan 30th, 2024, I was replacing the low battery in my Kidde Combination Smoke/CO Alarm Model KN-COSM-IB when I noticed the manufacturing date 2013, Oct 17. I started researching if it has a lifespan and if it should be replaced. That is when I learned about a safety recall notice - https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/2017/Kidde-Recalls-Combination-Smoke-CO-Alarms. I learned from the recall notice that after the end of their life, these alarms are supposed to chirp until they are replaced. I contacted customer service, and they refused to replace these units even though they are faulty and have failed to notify me and my family that they should have been replaced after their end of life. I have two of these units installed in my house, and I was under the wrong impression they were working and saving my life. Even though the manufacturing date is later than what is mentioned in the recall notice, they are the same model with the same issue. Clearly, this company hadn't stopped making and selling this faulty model even after the dates mentioned in the recall notice, and my two units prove it so. They were supposed to chirp after the end of their life, and they haven't. I have been replacing the battery whenever there was a chirp for low battery, and they have been quiet after the replacement. It seems even the units made after the date in the recall notice of this model have the same problem. Can something be done about this faulty and dangerous product that fails to notify its owners that it has reached the end of its life and needs replacement? I request you to look into this and help me get them replaced. Thanks...
justification: The incident involves faulty smoke/CO alarms that failed to notify the user of their end of life, posing a potential safety risk, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
The subject device is an adaptor intended to facilitate connection of a device with a NEMA 5-15P 15A 125V grounding type plug to a non-grounding medium-base lampholder.  It's a 3 Prong Outlet Light Socket Adapter purchased on Amazon.

A [REDACTED] member purchased the product and reports that the HOT and NEUTRAL contacts work as intended but there is no ground path for this device representing a clear violation of UL498A (UL Standard for Safety for Current Taps and Adapters) requirements applicable to non-grounding to grounding adapters.  This could explain the lack of third-party safety certification.  Products employing grounding type plugs typically rely on the grounding means as the last line of defense against potential shock and electrocution hazards associated with exposed metal parts.  This last line of defense is defeated when plugged into the subject adapter.   
  
These products do not bear any 3rd party certification mark but there are many readily available through Amazon and [REDACTED].
justification: The device lacks a ground path, violating safety standards, which could lead to potential shock hazards, but no actual injury or incident is reported.

I checked the troubleshooting guide and was able to clear the error by resetting the power to the unit and it continued to run normally for a week or so until the E1 code reappeared. After performing a power reset on the unit a couple more times, I observed signs of overheating as there was evidence of burning paint on the discharge louvers. I immediately disconnected power to the heater and removed the unit from its mounting. Upon further inspection I discovered additional evidence of overheating as the entire top of the unit was discolored from excessive heat and the overheat safety relays on the control circuit board were badly charred. It is my belief that this situation presented a significant fire hazard.

incident_description: I purchased a Safaveih runner rug from Home Depot, Order #[REDACTED] online on 1/11/24. The runner was delivered to the store and I picked it up on 1/18/24. I brought it home, unpacked it and unrolled it. It looked lovely BUT, when I walked on it, I felt  sharp shards (like tacks) poking into my feet.  ( Thankfully, I was wearing socks.)  However, even with socks on, this really hurt and I had two very, very  small bloody cuts on my right foot from this. (Think of stepping on a thumb tack with socks on.) My husband came over and helped me and we realized there were MANY sharp pieces sticking up in this runner rug. At first we attempted to pull/carefully snip the sharp pieces out, but we soon realized there were just too many sharp bits.  (I  have a baggie of some of the small, hard , sharp white pieces we pulled out of the runner.) My husband and I went back to the Home Depot and returned the runner. (We did ask the employee  at the Home Depot to feel the runner and observe the shards and the baggie when we returned the runner.) I contacted Safaveih customer service on Friday 1/19/23 by telephone and was told by the woman I spoke with to expect a call back by the end of the day.  That did not happen so on Monday 1/22/23 I filed an online complaint with their customer service. The very next day, after my asking him to carefully address my complaint, the reply included, " This occurrence is likely due to the production process and is not that common. " They claim to have checked inventory but their factories are overseas and I cannot imagine there was a thorough addressing of this problem in 24 hours. If someone were barefoot walking on this rug , the situation would have been much worse. I don't believe they are taking my concern seriously .

incident_description:
I purchased 7 Kidde smoke detectors and they have a constant problem of false alarms.  They are model P4010ACS which are wired and have a permanent battery.   They first starting false alarming within two months of being installed.   After it happened 3 or 4 times, I started removing the offending detector, thinking that there was a simple defective one.  After removing 4 of them it seemed to be a device wide problem and I replaced them with another brand and no longer have false alarms.  In addition to the false alarms, we would get periodic false alarms where we would get a smoke indication (3 beeps) but only one time, then they would go silent.  Since I replaced them, I have them on the floor in my office, and since they have a 10-year battery they are still active, and still provide both actual false alarms and the short alarm.  It is always only one alarming even though they are all next to each other.  I have made a few inactive as they seemed to be the worst offenders.  
There were no injuries experienced, (other than to my checkbook for replacing them) but they certainly have the potential to cause loss of life if one were to ignore them because of the number of false alarms, or remove them to eliminate the false alarms.  Also, because of the capricious nature of the alarms, one would have to wonder about their resonse in an actual fire.
justification: The incident involves false alarms with no injuries, but potential for serious consequences if ignored.

incident_description:
Used Tide Pods concentrated laundry detergent: three (3) pods for one (1) extra large
load of laundry per package instructions. Part of a pod didn't fully dissolve and wound
up in a pair of my boxer briefs underwear, including bits of the elastic dissolvable
enclosure that contains the liquid detergent and some of the liquid detergent itself. I
didn't notice the detergent and wore said underwear for about two hours before bed
without experiencing any side effects, then went to bed for 7-8hr. When I woke up I
noticed a sensation like I had been cut on my upper inner right thigh and two spots on
my scrotum. Upon investigation I found painful, lightly weepy (like light sweat almost),
red, swollen, inflamed rashes on my thigh and scrotum. Chemical burns as opposed to
rash or scrape. I flushed with warm water in the shower for 10min then applied 1%
hydrocortisone steroid cream per cdc or poison control recommendation (don't
remember). 10hr post-shower and one reapplication of steroid cream
painful rash persists but does not appear to be getting worse, no blistering or open
sores but still very slightly weepy. 24hr post shower wound site is healing, not getting worse, and no longer weeping.
justification: The incident resulted in chemical burns (injury) but no severe or life-threatening effects, and such occurrences are unlikely given proper detergent use.

incident_description:
Product: Crane HS-1932 demineralization filter
Concern: Toxic and harmful

I pre-soaked the filter for thirty minutes and used it to replace the water tank cap according to the instructions then added purified water and turned on the humidifier as usual. Atypically, the dire consequences of this filter quickly became obvious as my [REDACTED] air purifier, upwind ten feet away, unexpectedly reacted with maximum fan speed as the app began issuing alerts about my horrifically polluted indoor air.

Attached are images showing how quickly and astonishingly the air had become toxic:
within twenty minutes, the Air Quality Index (AQI) was an unimaginably extreme 256.1 with equally extraordinary Particulate Matter (PM) levels of 93 PM1, 156 PM2.5, and 180 PM10. Fortunately, the [REDACTED] air purifier quickly alerted me while I was present, awake, and could respond such that one hour after I turned the humidifier off and exhausted the polluted air the PM levels returned to zero.

If anyone has been using this filter and experiencing health problems, particularly cardiopulmonary or cancer, they should be evaluated by a doctor ASAP. Regardless of circumstance, no one should use this filter and should keep children and pets safe from exposure.

The instructions indicate that this filter can be used for thirty to forty fills but any exposure to PM is unhealthy let alone to long-term PM exposure and definitively to long-term PM exposure at such unimaginably extreme levels.

PM1: The most harmfully damaging of invisible microscopic airborne particulate matter (PM) which penetrates the lungs into the bloodstream circulating to the organs and ultimately causing severe cardiopulmonary health problems and death. These minuscule PM are most typically emitted from internal combustion engines (ICEs), power plants, and industrial facilities.

PM2.5: Harmfully damaging invisible microscopic airborne particulate matter (PM) that ultimately causes cardiopulmonary and cancerous health problems and death. Indoor PM2.5 are most typically produced by cooking (broiling, frying, sauting), burning candles or fireplace logs, and using kerosene space heaters.

PM10: A lesser health risk than PM1 or PM2.5 although no amount of exposure to any PM is safe. Generally, these more coarse PM are produced by burning fossil fuels.
justification: The incident describes exposure to toxic particulate matter with potential for severe health impacts, including cardiopulmonary and cancerous conditions, but no immediate injury or death was reported.

incident_description: I bought my BISSELL Powerforce Powerbrush Pet Lightweight Carpet Washer - 2910 from Walmart in May of 2021. I use it a few times a year on our one carpeted room in our house. Last night I was cleaning our carpet as usual after I had just cleaned out the Carpet Washer when I smelled plastic burning. Right away I turned it off, unplugged it, attempted to clean it out again in case there was a clog (there was not). I waited a bit then turned it back on and instantly the burning smell returned, even worse this time so I turned it off and unplugged it immediately. I am an engineer so I proceeded to unscrew the belt access door but it would not come off. My husband took a turn and applied some force and the belt access door finally came off. The rubber belt was dislodged from its track and had FUSED to the plastic housing of the motor. The interior was full of burnt and melted hard plastic. The belt is still melted to the plastic motor housing. Thankfully I turned the cleaner off quickly once I had smelled the burning. Had I not I fear it would have soon caught fire. This is extremely alarming and could have injured me badly and damaged my home. As an engineer who specializes in root cause analysis and design quality I thought there is no way this has happened before or Bissell would have recalled this model. To my alarm I saw on Walmart's website numerous other reviews describing the same thing happening to other users of this model. This device must be recalled until sufficient root cause analysis has been completed with corrective and preventative actions put into place. This device is a hazard and may result in serious injury.ÃÂ It would be absolutely awful if a consumer were injured cleaning their carpets. I must stress that I was using this device as intended and I have cared for it as instructed. It has not been used frequently. Although we've had it for 2.5 years I've only used it a few times a year.
justification: The incident involved a malfunction that could have led to injury or fire, but no actual injury occurred. The occurrence likelihood is high given multiple similar reports.

incident_description: We bought 6 of these alarms in July 2023 in 5 months have had 5 false alarms. It is a dangerous alarm because everyone has started to assume it is a false alarm when they go off. Our neighbors checked on use the first two times but now they assume it is false. Have been woken up and had to come home from work. They go off when no one is cooking and/or is home. I have tried all the suggestions for placement and dust regularly and am still having issues. We have the correct placement for all alarms. I do like the way when one alarm goes off the others go off which is nice  downstairs and our ADU. Since we get so many false alarms it has become unsafe.  The first time I called customer service I was on hold for 30 mins and it took 1 hour to get issue resolved. incident_description:
The pressure switch on my furnace failed, such that it would be stuck open circuit even when the draft inducer was running. However, the furnace still ignited and ran the burners for about a minute before shutting down. It did this a few more times before locking out. The furnace should not have ignited the burners at all in this case, because had the pressure switch been open because of a failure of the draft inducer or an obstruction in the exhaust pipe, it could have released combustion byproducts such as carbon monoxide into the living space.

Additionally, as a troubleshooting step, I temporarily short-circuited the pressure switch, and I discovered that a pressure switch stuck closed does not cause a lockout. If I leave the furnace powered on and remove the short circuit, the furnace starts operation immediately. In this case, the furnace should have recognized a faulty pressure switch and locked out until reset. If instead the pressure switch had failed by being stuck closed, and then suddenly opened for some reason, the furnace could possibly operate with an unreliable pressure switch.
justification: The furnace malfunctioned but no actual harm occurred, though there was potential for carbon monoxide release.

incident_description:
On Sunday, November 5, 2023, while we were having breakfast, we heard a large crash.  What we discovered was one of the glass shower doors purchased and installed in 2020 by a professional contractor had totally "disintegrated".  Glass was everywhere.  There was no apparent reason for this to happen.  We never noticed any chips, scratches or defects in the glass.  The shower is only used by two people, we are the only residents.  Had someone been in the bathroom at the time, they would have been seriously injured, not to mention had they actually been in the shower.
The explosion of glass damaged the frame along the bottom.  (small dents) The tracks were filled with glass shards and fine glass powder that had to be removed.  Glass had blown across the bathroom, under the sink and under shelves.
The contractor purchased the materials, which included the shower doors, from Home Depot and the doors have "Delta" labels on them.  The doors are supposed to be warranted for 5 years.  Apparently, Delta uses Liberty Hardware to supply the doors to Home Depot.  After some difficulty contacting Liberty, we were able to make contact and supply the information they required to make a warranty claim on November 9.  The claim was denied on November 10th citing that a T-strap on the opposite side had been installed incorrectly using an extra screw.
On November 13, we wrote back to Liberty explaining that while the particular T-strap in question indeed had an extra screw, it was of no consequence since the exploding door was installed on the opposite side and did not contact the screw in question.  This was evidenced by the photographs showing the majority of glass on the floor and in the track on the opposite side of the shower.  We asked that the matter be escalated to management.
On November 30th after no answer, we sent a final request for management intervention.  On December 1, the Technical Provider replied that the matter was forwarded to a manager.  As of now there has been no response.  Based upon other similar complaints regarding Delta Shower doors listed on your site, I believe Liberty is supplying a faulty product and hiding behind supposed installation errors.  Again, someone could have been seriously injured by the shards produced when the glass literally exploded had the shower actually been in use at the time.  Photographs are available.
justification: The glass shower door disintegrated without injury, but could have caused serious injury if someone had been present.

incident_description:
Summary: Hot tub / spa steps failed while standing on them.

While I (adult male, 42 years old) getting out of my hot tub (spa), the top platform of my spa steps gave way (fell down). Then I stepped down to the next step and it too gave way.

Upon inspecting the steps that were still in place, I saw that most of them had screws that were very loose. The steps that had given way had screws that had completely come out. So I concluded that the reason the steps failed is that the screws had loosened over time.
 
There is no mechanism to prevent the screws from loosening over time due to normal use and/or due to vibrations from the adjacent hot tub. This seems like a design flaw. The screws should use lock washers, serrated/star washers, and/or thread lock compound to prevent this.

The installation manual also does not specify screw tightening torque, but it should.

I luckily didn't suffer injury because I was able to grab the handrail and prevent myself from falling, but a less agile person could be severely hurt.
justification: The incident involved steps failing but no injury occurred, as the individual was able to prevent a fall by grabbing the handrail.

incident_description:
Before we get to what happened, I think you should know that I am a measurement expert. I am the chair of an [REDACTED] group that just revised [REDACTED], and I am chair of a group revising [REDACTED]. 

Now I want to report an unsafe measurement  device that I came across by chance. It is the voltmeter part of a "3-Piece Technician Test Kit" sold by Home Depot, part number 1004 482 497. It is made by Commercial Electric. The problem is that the reading on the device was zero when there was actually a voltage on the circuit I was testing. The problem is not a fault in the instrument, it is a design error. Home Depot let me test a second sample, and the same problem was present.

A voltmeter has two probes. When switched to measure AC, it should not matter which way round the probes are connected. With this device, it does matter if there is a DC component on the signal. In the case I was measuring. The reading was ZERO with the probes one way round, and not zero the other way round. 

I am aware that the condition of having some DC on an AC circuit is unusual, but that's what there was in my work. (I verified it with my oscilloscope.)

If a user is unaware of the possibility of there being an AC potential even though the meter displays zero, that could be dangerous.

The design error would not be evident in the absence of DC on the circuit, but the fact of a misleading indication could lead to an electric shock. (Frankly, I think Home Depot should pull the meter off the shelf until the design is fixed, but I cannot find a way to contact them that seems likely to achieve that outcome. Home Depot will surely let me return the meter for a refund, but that is scarcely the end of the story.)
justification: The incident describes a design flaw in a voltmeter that could lead to a misleading zero reading, posing a potential risk of electric shock if users are unaware. However, no actual injury or incident has been reported yet.

incident_description:
I am a fire inspector with one of my duties being to inspect smoke alarms in R2 occupancies. Over the last four years I have had repeated experience with First Alert P1210 smoke alarms that cause concern.

1. While California requires battery powered smoke alarms sold in the state to last at least 10 years, I've seen many examples of P1210s dying in as little time as a year or two.
2. Even worse, I've come across many examples that died without providing any warning to the apartment tenant. No chirping warning that the battery is getting low. I go to test them and they are just dead.
3. The installation of the alarm into the bracket can be troublesome, I've seen many examples where the alarm was installed in the bracket but it didn't activate as it was supposed to. The labeling on the diactivation switch is confusing as well.
4. About half of the P1210 alarms I tested would do a chirp chirp chirp instead of the full alarm. At first I thought that was a low battery indication, but finally after coming across so many that did it I called First Alert. Apparently that 3 chirp means the alarm has gone off before. So about half of the P1210s that I've tested have had false alarms. Many of these are in locations away from the kitchen where you might expect a high number of false alarms.

First Alert and other smoke alarm manufacturers need to realize that many of their products get installed into apartments. The tenants didn't buy them, and most often don't have access to the owner's manual. Smoke alarms must be intuitive and simple to install and operate.
justification: The repeated failure of smoke alarms without warning and frequent false alarms pose a significant risk, though no injuries or deaths are reported.

Google Nest Protect Gen 2 Smoke/Carbon Monoxide alarm battery overheating. Second time this has happened in my Nest Protects, I have 7 of them. 

November 2022 issue: Nest Protect reported no issues in regular testing since installed in 2019. Suddenly, it loudly chirped and the app popped up with a low battery warning. I popped it off the ceiling and opened up the battery compartment to swap the batteries and was greeted by the faint smell of what I can only describe as hot plastic/burning rubber. I pulled the batteries out and one of them was BURNING hot. Like boiling water hot - could barely touch it. Battery took hours to cool down outside. Google replaced the device through their safety program. 

November 2023 issue: Same exact issue, different device. Contacted Nest and am awaiting contact from the safety team again. I used a thermal camera and the hot battery, an [REDACTED] Ultimate Lithium AA battery, was around 150 degrees. Other batteries in the device and the other 6 devices I checked as a precaution were only 70 degrees.

Extremely concerning since this is a fire detection device and this could have the potential to cause a fire if the battery got hot enough. After having this happen twice to me and seeing many reports on Google Nest's forum, I felt it appropriate to report to CPSC. See this page for lots of similar reports through the forums: [REDACTED]
justification: The incident involves battery overheating in a safety device, posing a potential fire hazard, but no injury or death has been reported. The issue has occurred twice with the same user and is reported by others, indicating it is likely to happen again.

incident_description:
I purchased the Louisville Ladder Everest Aluminum 10-12 ft Attic Ladder (Model AL228P ) from Home Depot to replace a folding attic ladder in my garage. Louisville Ladder has confirmed that I purchased the correct residential ladder for my ceiling height.


I hired an experienced licensed building contractor to install the ladder with the help of his assistant. To accommodate the new ladder, the ceiling opening had to be enlarged and the trim replaced.


Upon completion of the job, the contractor showed me how difficult opening and closing the folding ladder was and shared that the ladder had scratched his throat while figuring out how to operate it. He noted that the included pole did not help slow down the rate at which the ladder unfolded or folded. 


He showed me the installation instructions, which he had clearly read because it  contained notes about measurements and required clearances that he had written in pencil in provided spaces. On the very last page of the instructions before the appendix, there was a page that was titled ÃÂEverest Aluminum 12ÃÂ Folding Attic Ladder Opening and Closing Instructions.ÃÂ Initially, I didnÃÂt recognize this page as relevant to the ladder I purchased since the page was referring to a fixed length, 12 ft ladder. For the first time, the last page of the instructions noted that 2 people and a separate freestanding ladder are required to safely operate this attic ladder. The contractor was stunned and said heÃÂs never heard of such a thing. Even after being told this late-breaking update, it wasnÃÂt immediately obvious how 2 people would safely operate the ladder and we had to carefully follow the steps to understand how to accomplish this.


I reviewed the instructions again and saw that the first page contains 15 WARNINGS, the first 3 in bold print. Not one of those warnings addressed the safe operation of this ladder and warned that using the ladder would require two able bodied people, one on the ground and one on a separate ladder. I also rechecked the product information on the Home Depot website as well as the Louisville Ladder website, and this material design flaw was not disclosed.


I contacted Louisville Ladders with my concerns. My ac unit is located in the attic above my garage and access to that space is critical. For people like myself who are frequently home alone, this ladder is not suitable. Louisville Ladders failed to disclose upfront critical facts necessary to make that determination.


When I called Louisville Ladders, they asked for additional information and pictures, which I sent - including a photo of my contractorÃÂs scratched throat and two videos showing his efforts to operate the ladder on his own.  [REDACTED], a claims manager for Louisville Ladders, rejected my request for compensation to replace the ladder. She stated (incorrectly) that one of the 15 WARNINGS on the first page instructed the installer to read all the instructions before beginning, so Louisville Ladders was not responsible. This statement is absolutely false - one of the warnings instructed the installer to read all the instructions on the label of the ladder, and the label did not address operating the ladder. 


Even when there is a prominent warning to read all the instructions, this warning is not sufficient. Each ladder comes with an implied warranty from the manufacturer that it is fit and safe for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used. I have found no one, not a single person, who had ever heard of, or would reasonably ever anticipate that, a residential attic ladder would require 2 able-bodied people and a separate ladder to operate. 


I liken this situation to purchasing a car and finding out, after it has been shipped to your house at your great expense, that it can only be operated when there is a driver and a second person in the passenger seat. This car might work for some people some of the time, but that kind of unexpected and extraordinary limitation on use needs to be prominently displayed and made known before the purchase. 


In conclusion, the Louisville Ladder 10-12 ft Aluminum Folding Ladder is unsafe when used in the manner people would expect to use a residential folding ladder, and the manufacturer has provided insufficient warning of this safety concern.
justification: The contractor suffered a scratched throat while operating the ladder, indicating an injury occurred.

We counted our blessings that he had greatly improved, & figured maybe heÃÂd had another episode similar to one heÃÂd had late December, 2022, although it wasnÃÂt exactly the same experience (and we NOW suspect the December episode may have been the first one related to the Bath & Body Works Wallflowers Home Fragrance PlugIns b/c I started using them more regularly around the early winter holidays). After returning back home a few days later (around 7 pm), he again displayed the same sx the next morning (12 hours!). So, I figured, itÃÂs something in this house precipitating these sx. Since then, IÃÂve done a fair amount of reading about these types of products, & IÃÂve learned they contain lots of toxic chemicals. Things like (but not limited to) Formaldehyde, Phthalates, Volatile Organic Chemicals (VOCs), & Propylene Glycol (which is banned in the EU), along with essential oils, many of which are toxic for cats, dogs & birds. And btw, none of this is healthy for humans, either, but I suspect bc they are plugged in at nose height for most pets, they get a stronger dose of the aerosolized chemicals/toxin, & they also likely get it on their feet/fur, which animals then lick.  I feel terrible for using these unnecessary things in our home & putting him though this. We did take our dog to the neurologist & no organic cause was determined to be present. These products are clearly toxic, and had our dog not responded in such a dramatic way, I would still be using them. I worry about  the danger they present to children, too, as they spend fair amounts of time on the floors and also put lots of things in their mouths. These products should not be on the market for us to bring into our very homes!  They compromise the general  publicÃÂs health!

incident_description:
What happened that made you want to report? - I have a small tree service. I recently purchased a Notch branded pole saw from Treestuff.com. It uses a Silky blade which are out standing. I have several Silky saws, but they recently started only selling blades and Notch is who manufacturers the pole and sells it all under their own brand name. I purchased on in May, 2023. It arrived sometime in June. My son and I were working and he was using the new Notch saw. He came to me and said he wouldn't use it anymore because the last extension with the blade popped out twice and nearly cut him. I looked the saw over and didn't see anything loose or damaged. I told him the ferrule latches had to snap into place and the cams had to be locked before using the saw. He said he had done so. So I tried it myself and whether extended or fully collapsed the same thing happened to me. The second time the last extension and blade popped out and came down on me. The razor sharp Silkey blade cut me and tor my shirt. It even ripped through my leather gloves. The only thing that saved my face was that I had my helmet on and eye protection. I notified the manufacturer (distributor). The only response is they wanted a video and if it looked like a problem they would issue a refund if I would find a box (8 feet long) and pay to return it. I will no longer use this saw. It is extremely unsafe and because of the nature of the saw, it could cause significant damage or even death.

What type of product was being used? - 4373-42 20' Notch Nobasu 4 Section Telescoping Aluminum Polesaw

Who was using the product(s)? - My son and I both used the saw and experienced the same results. My son has done trees for 12 years. I have 50+ years experience in arborist work.

How were the product(s) being used? - Pruning trees.
Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product? - Yes, cuts to my arm and shirt and gloves ruined. I could been much worse if I hadn't been using a helmet and eyeprotection.

How did any injuries occur? Using the item number 4373-42 (from Treestuff.com who owns Notch) 20' Notch Nobasu 4 Section Telescoping Aluminum Polesaw - While using the saw, whether extended or fully collapsed withe the ferrule catch engaged and the cams locked, when cutting branches with any pressure at all, the last section pops out and slides down the saw towards the user. It is extremely dangerous because even if it didn't slide down the pole, it is a 5" section with a razor sharp 18" blade falling from as much as 25 feet towards the operator or any other people in the area.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (cuts to the arm) and could have been worse without protective gear. The issue occurred multiple times with different users, indicating a likely recurrence.

incident_description:
Stanley Tools ladder ST677PW manufactured by WernerCo must be recalled. I am not sure if I bought this ladder at [REDACTED]. I am 6'2" and 190-195 lbs; I am not overweight at all. I am an electrical engineer with 35 years of experience. I have a Ph.D.  in Electrical Engineering. I am the author of a book. I am approaching 60. I am a U.S. citizen. 

While on the fourth or fifth step of the ladder, and with the ladder on concrete and level ground, the ladder collapsed and I fell onto the ground. It was so painful that I could have died or gotten paralyzed. With God's help I did not fall onto the ladder itself. If I did, my tissues would have been shredded and my bones and spine broken.

When trying to understand what happened, I could see that one of the two copper spreader braces got weakened and was severely bent (see the pictures I am attaching). It is a pity that I took the pictures after I attempted to straighten the brace. This cannot be reversed now, but the ladder's collapse cannot be disputed whatsoever. The ladder is available for inspection. It can be picked up at my home. The grass in the pictures is just because I was trying to avoid the sun and get the best possible pictures. When I fell the ladder was on level concrete ground. 

Detailed structural analysis and finite element analysis (with calculations of the forces and moments on the two spreader braces) must be done. The report should reveal the weaknesses. This is a 30-minute job if WernerCo / Stanley Tools has a reputable structural analysis software like [REDACTED]. I am an engineer and could easily tell that the two spreader braces are very thin and weak. They need much more strengthening / enforcement. This ladder is neither stable nor reliable nor safe and must be immediately recalled. All customers must be informed of how they can get their ladders replaced. This incident must taken seriously to prevent other people from being killed or seriously hurt.

The correspondence I had with Stanley Tools and WernerCo shows irresponsible, lawless companies that will do anything and everything to slip accountability. WernerCo's CEO did not respond to an email directed to him and sent to his email address. A Claims Administrator at WernerCo offered me $100 to accept by August 17, 2023. The Claims Administrator wrote: "I spoke with our engineering team, and it is their position that the damage shown to your ladder does not indicate a defective product in any way. They are confident that the damage is a result of the accident, not the cause of it. As it was explained to me, a ladder would never sustain such damage under normal circumstances and especially after 15 years of use without any prior incidents.

Please know that all Werner ladders are designed, manufactured, and tested to meet/exceed all Standards maintained by OSHA/ANSI. Your ladder, model ST677PW, Mk 5 has tested and proven to withstand loads well in excess of 900 lbs. Our team also advised that the only purpose of spreader bars is to properly distance the front and rear rails of a ladder. They do not ÃÂholdÃÂ any weight of a person who is working on the ladder. One of their most effective demonstrations to a jury is to overload a ladder, such as yours, with 4-5 men, then have someone physically cut both spreaders to show that the ladder will not fail/collapse."

This is reprehensible. WernerCo's answer is rejected; it is representative of a defiant, irresponsible company that is willing to go the wrong way to avoid responsibility. I am not looking for $100. The accident could have resulted in death or paralysis. The product is defective. This is a safety issue that could hurt or kill others. WernerCo must investigate and conduct structural and finite element analysis. If not, WernerCo commits a huge mistake by disregarding accidents, failures, safety, and quality. WernerCo's case before the jury must be re-opened and investigated anew. 

WernerCo says: "the damage is a result of the accident, not the cause of it". When there was an accident, my questions to WernerCo are: "How did the accident happen? How did the ladder collapse? Why did the ladder collapse? How and why did I fall down?" Isn't this enough for WernerCo to say: "We must understand what happened."

I am not overweight at all. My weight (190-195 lbs) is even a bit below someone with my height (6'2"). What caused the ladder to collapse? This is a question that WernerCo must answer through proper, impeccable engineering analysis.

Millions, even billions, of products around the world are certified and manufactured according to safety and quality standards. Such products are also issued certificates by [REDACTED]. That, however, does not relieve the manufacturer from thoroughly investigating a safety accident when it occurs. That WernerCo demonstrated something to a jury in the past does not relieve WernerCo from responsibility for all future accidents. The same is true for all manufacturers worldwide.

Think of recalls. Aren't [REDACTED], etc vehicles manufactured to safety and quality standards? Do such companies not employ competent engineers? Do such companies not have engineering and design reviews? Aren't their vehicles tested and certified by independent bodies? Do they not have design, safety, and quality certificates? They absolutely do. Still, accidents happen and sometimes people die. Such companies are investigated and charged. They are forced to do recalls if they do not do it voluntarily. That they did a recall in the past does not mean anything and does not relieve them forever from responsibility. When accidents happen, they must be investigated regardless of all the standards that a company follows; regardless of all the certifications that the company has; and regardless of all testing done on the product in the past.

I requested that the case be escalated within WernerCo, but my request was ignored. Action by WernerCo is urgently needed. WernerCo must investigate and must assume responsibility. This is a serious safety issue and a product failure that could result in many others being hurt or even killed.

I could barely walk for a week. I wanted to see if I get better on my own within a reasonable time. I did not go to a doctor because I never like to go to doctors. I had a slipped disk in 2008. Only God and the future will tell if this accident contributed to worsening my situation. My left foot is almost always numb because of the slipped disc pushing against the nerve.

Today, I have no pain. I can say I am OK with the exception of the numbness in the left foot. That, however, does not mean that the accident gets ignored and the case closed. That will be a huge mistake, especially because  the Claims Administrator talked about previous accidents.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (pain and numbness) and could have led to severe consequences like paralysis or death, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is rated 3 (possible) based on the detailed account of the ladder's failure and the potential for similar incidents.

incident_description:
I have 2 American Standard HVAC systems installed at my home (installed in December of 2016), with the furnace units and blower assemblies in the attic.  In September of 2021, one of the blower motors suffered a catastrophic thermal failure and began filling my home with toxic smoke.  In spite of this failure, the HVAC unit did NOT shut down.  I had to shut off power at the breaker box and then guess what the issue was.  It turns out that the electronic control module of the motor was the issue. 

That motor was replaced with a different type of ECM motor back in September of 2021, and that replacement just failed in a similar manner although not as severe.  This time I recognized the smell much sooner and shut the unit down. 

Based on these 2 similar failures and some additional research, I believe that there are tens of thousands or more American Standard/Trane HVAC units installed in homes that pose a toxic smoke hazard and a fire hazard as well.  Thus far Trane has failed to address this safety hazard with me.
justification: The incident involved toxic smoke and a potential fire hazard, but no injury or death was reported.

I am very thankful that I was not using the washer to clean off the siding of my house holding the gun over my head as I could have easily lost and eye or worse if it had hit me in the head with that force.

incident_description:
I am writing to report a serious safety incident that occurred while using a Festool Track Saw, model TS 55 FEQ-F-Plus (No. 576708), on July 8th, 2023. During the use of the tool to trim the edge of a door, a malfunction occurred, which resulted in a dangerous situation leading to severe personal injury.

Description of Incident:
At the time of the incident, I was using the Festool Track Saw as intended to make a cut along the edge of a door. While the tool was in operation, an unexpected issue arose (a resistance in the tool), causing me to remove the saw toward the top of the guide rail. However, the plunge mechanism did not self-retract, leaving the saw blade fully exposed. Subsequently, a kickback occurred, causing the exposed blade to accelerate backwards, resulting in a partial amputation of two fingers on my left hand.

Contributing Factors:

Tool Safety Malfunction: It appears that the malfunction may have originated from the tool's motor, the plunge mechanism or the viewing window, leading to the failure of the automatic blade retraction and exposing the blade during operation.
Kickback Risk: The unexpected blade exposure and subsequent kickback put the operator at a high risk of serious injury, as was evident in my case.
Injuries Incurred:
The incident resulted in the partial amputation of two fingers on my left hand, which required immediate medical attention and subsequent treatment.

Actions Taken:

I am writing to report an unsafe door lock, which is manufactured by a company called Omnia. Under certain conditions, the lock does not open and presents an entrapment hazard.

The lock is an Omnia mortise lockset with these identifying stickers:
Control No. 33L5 Single-Point Lock or Latch
Lock Function F (Lever and LH are checked off)
788N
BM20LH-LB.FIN

The lock is on my front door. When I unlock my door, if I leave the key in the lock and the door closes behind me, it will occasionally lock me inside my condo. It doesn't happen every time, and to date this has happened twice. When it does happen, the key remains inserted on the outside of the door, and the inside door handle and deadbolt knob do not turn. I need to have someone turn the key from outside in order to open the door. This presents an entrapment hazard, as I can't exit my condo under these conditions without someone unlocking the door from the outside.

A locksmith took apart the lock on 6/30/23 and was able to replicate the issue. He said that it was due to a design flaw of the mortise lock itself. He described the issue as: ÃÂWhen the key is oriented to engage the latch, the cam on the mortise cylinder prevents the interior lever from engaging the latch.ÃÂ He said that there was nothing that could be adjusted or cleaned on the lockset to fix the issue. He advised replacing the lockset with a different brand of lock, which would not have this design flaw.

I contacted Omnia on 6/30/23 to inform them of this problem and to ask for a solution. Their response, on 7/5/23, did not provide a solution:
"If the key is left in the cylinder and the key turns at all, the cam of the cylinder could lock up the mortise lock. To prevent the situation you described, we recommend that you not leave the key in the cylinder. Thank you, [REDACTED]"

I am concerned that the manufacturer has apparently acknowledged the entrapment risk that I described and is treating it as the intended behavior for this lock.
justification: The lock presents an entrapment hazard but no injury or death has been reported, and the issue occurs occasionally.

incident_description: In July 2022, I purchased a new DeWalt pressure washer at The Home Depot. I'm quite familiar with using pressure washers as I have used several in the past 35 years. This new pressure washer was working fine as I cleaned the siding on my house. I noticed the engine starting to sputter so I shut the machine off to refill the gas tank. Once refilled, I grabbed the starting cord handle and gave it a pull. Because the starting cord is angled slightly toward the front of the machine, my pulling of it caused the entire machine to lunge forward. What I assume is the hot metal muffler in the front of the machine momentarily came into contact with my left leg and I immediately felt the my leg burning and it turned red. The next day, I had a rectangle-shaped burn mark on my leg with blister bubbles and oozing burns. With the burn being painful, oozing, and blistered, I decided to visit my local Emergency Room. The ER doctor and nurse prescibed medication to apply to the wound and indicated that I had a partial-thickness burn. As it was rather grotesque and somewhat painful, I covered the wound when wearing shorts for the remainder of the summer. Nearly a year later, the scar on my leg is still present and I'm assuming will be there for life. I consider the design of this pressure washer, with the starting cord angled towards the front of the machine, along with its light weight, to be a design flaw. It would have been just as easy for the manufacturer to NOT have the starter cord angled toward the front of the machine. Rather, it should be angled directly to the side of the machine so that the pulling motion does not cause it to easily pull forward on its large rear wheels. I contacted the DeWalt company and their representative insisted that I am the only person to ever injure myself in this manner with one of their pressure washers. They did, however, put me in contact with their lawyer to settle the matter. Although giving assurances that they "want to make this right" and that they would cover my ER bill, cost of bandages, replace the machine with a different model, and account for my injury, the lawyer has stopped all contact with me for the past 4 months. He has not replied to numerous emails requesting resolution.
justification: The incident resulted in a partial-thickness burn requiring emergency room treatment, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is rated as rare (1) since the user is reportedly the only known case of such an injury with this product.

incident_description: We purchased two Homedics ultrasonic humidifiers from Costco this last fall and put both in service in late October. We followed the owners manual and used our tap water which it said you can do. By mid December I was having constant shortness of breath and a very productive cough. My wife experienced only the productive cough but I had one of the units right by my bed in my bedroom at night. Come January 1, 2023 I had to go to the ER, thinking I was having a heart attack with chest pain and difficulty breathing. I was not, and was sent home with instructions to see a cardiologist and a pulmonologist. After those visits I was put on night oxygen, an inhaler, given an EKG, a nuclear stress test, pulmonary function test, sleep study, two week heart monitoring, echocardiogram, and numerous other tests. I had the feeling that I was dying. It continued and on April 4th, 2023 I was again in the ER at the direction of my primary care physician to get a chest CT due to the doctor thinking I was having a pulmonary embolism. In early April I had indoor air quality monitoring done and found the indoor AQI was over 400 and PM2.5 was over 200. Thinking it was from dust we had all our carpets cleaned and no change to the indoor air quality. As the weather became warmer in mid April, we opened windows for the first time since November and the AQI and PM2.5 fell to near zero with the ultrasonic humidifiers off. That night it was cold so we closed the house up again and turned the humidifiers back on, only to see the AQI and PM2.5 climb to oner 100 with just a few hours. Mystery solved. The ultrasonic humidifiers were aerosolizing the minerals in our water to a toxic level indoors even with air filtration purifiers running. The pulmonologist says that my lungs may take up to a year to heal and may never return to what they were before the exposure due to the Homedics ultrasonic humidifiers.
justification: The incident caused significant health issues requiring medical intervention, including ER visits and ongoing treatment, indicating an injury.
