incident_description:
I am a 47 year old mother of two teenage sons, and I have been doing laundry for close to 30 years since being shown by my mother.  For much of that time, I used the old fashioned top load agitator machines, and I was always in the habit of using a full capful of laundry detergent for each large load (I guess it turns out that we have been heavy-handed when adding detergent).

About 8-9 years ago, my husband and I purchased a new [REDACTED] washer without the agitator.  The instruction manual was quite vague, but I didn't think anything of it at the time, and I continued to follow my same laundry routine.

   I didn't think to read the back of the detergent bottles all these years because their overall appearance never changed...I did The laundry as I always had done out of habit, unaware that I was using too much detergent.  The cap sizes never changed, either.  Why are they still so large?  Why are detergents being concentrated (never realized before) without warning customers?  

I became extremely worried a few months ago when I read an article that Tide would be banned in certain states due to presence of carcinogens in its detergent?  What?  I had been using it for years...I thought laundry detergent was safe...it was recommended by [REDACTED] to use in their washers.

It is then that I realized that the default cycle on the [REDACTED] machine I had for the last 8-9 years only did a single 1-2 minute rinse spray.  Even if I hadn't used so much detergent all these years, I still don't know how it could rinse all the clothes properly.  Ironically, all these years, my family and I never noticed.  Our clothes were spun dry so well that I never saw residue, and I think we got used to the strong detergent smell.  Of course, though, as I recently started hand rinsing some of our clothing, I noticed all the detergent built up in the water.

It scares me beyond belief that my sons have been wearing chemically laden clothing since they were little.  My husband has a background in biochemistry and tells me not too worry since my family never had any acute reactions, but I am terrified to hear that laundry detergent could have potential carcinogens.  What if there are long-term health effects from years of wearing clothes with laundry detergent build-up?
 
I have actually reached out to [REDACTED] and Tide about my concerns and waiting to hear back from [REDACTED].  I also wanted to reach out to an organization about this matter because I think laundry detergent use, especially in HE machines needs to be "regulated".  The instructions on bottles and machines are vague.  What exactly defines a large load of laundry?  It's really more about the water amount than the laundry size, isn't it?  Why is it that washing machine manufacturers do not warn customers that they need to use so much less detergent in these high efficiency machines?  Precise instructions and warnings are desperately needed.  There should be clearly labeled warnings and detailed instructions from both the detergent and washer manufacturers on the amount of detergent to use based on the ratio of water per make and model of machine.  There is too much of a discrepancy right now.

I know this may not seem like a big deal,  but I'm sure many consumers are using too much laundry detergent.  It's bad enough to be sending excess detergent down the drain (not to mention the $), but what about potential safety issues?  The date below is an estimation of when I finally became aware of the fact that I was using too much laundry detergent for the past 8-9 years.

I believe that laundry detergent manufacturers should be required to change their bottles and especially cap sizes...they should not be so big because I think it "encourages" consumers to overpour.  The caps also should have clearly labeled measuring marks (horizontal around cap in a different color) so that consumers can actually see them.  Also, HE washers should have warnings on their machines to inform customers to use a minimal amount of detergent (especially for those of us who had been using traditional top-loads).  Furthermore, I think both washer and detergent manufacturers need to provide specific instructions on the dose of detergent to use per amount of water in machine (not just a subjective load size).  There needs to be a particular dilution ratio, and that should be written in the consumer manual of the washer...or better yet, on the machine, in addition to the detergent bottles.  Thank you.
justification: No immediate injury or death reported, but potential long-term health concerns due to prolonged exposure to detergent residues.

incident_description:
To Whom it May Concern,

I am writing to you as a concerned consumer and a professional with a background in Biomedical Engineering, holding a Master's degree and having acquired laboratory safety training from my experience in various chemistry labs. I wish to express my concerns regarding a widely-used product, "Dawn Platinum Powerwash Dish Soap Spray".

I understand that for a product like this to be available on the market, a substantial amount of safety testing and due diligence would typically be performed to ensure it does not pose a significant risk under normal usage conditions. However, my concerns are specifically related to the potential for long-term health impacts due to the inhalation of the very fine mist that is produced by this product's unique spray mechanism.

The Dawn Platinum Powerwash Dish Soap Spray employs a unique spray nozzle that produces a very fine mist, distinct from a traditional spray bottle. This atomization of the soap increases the potential for inhalation exposure. I've observed that this fine mist seems to linger in the air, indicating that particles remain suspended for several minutes. From my personal experience, there is a strong odor associated with the use of this product, and I have experienced noticeable lung irritation after being in the vicinity where it was sprayed.

The product contains several chemicals such as Alcohol Denat., C10-16 Alkyldimethylamine Oxide, Dipropylene Glycol Butyl Ether, Ethanolamine, and Sodium Laureth Sulfate, which are known to potentially cause respiratory irritation upon inhalation. It also includes fragrances, which can trigger allergies and asthma in sensitive individuals. 

Considering the product's widespread use and frequency, there could be a significant health impact, especially for sensitive populations such as children, elderly, and individuals with existing respiratory conditions. Even with moderate exposure, this could potentially lead to chronic respiratory problems, with subsequent increases in medical costs.

Given this unique method of application and potential for increased exposure, it is important to ensure that the safety testing performed adequately addressed the risks associated with inhalation of the fine mist. Specifically, the potential for long-term health impacts of regular, daily inhalation exposure may need further investigation.

Therefore, I kindly request the CPSC to conduct a thorough investigation into this issue, considering the product's unique application method. More comprehensive guidelines may be required for such products to ensure consumer safety, such as clearer labeling about the risks of inhalation and instructions to minimize exposure.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to hearing about the actions that the CPSC might take in response to these concerns to further protect consumer health.
justification: The description reports lung irritation from inhalation, indicating injury, and suggests potential for chronic respiratory problems, which is a known risk with the chemicals involved.

incident_description:
We purchased the PetraTools HD4000 four-gallon battery operated sprayer.  This product is sold by multiple resellers including {REDACTED] Amazon [REDACTED]

This sprayer has an internal 12-volt battery that requires occasionally charged.  The sprayer comes with a proprietary A/C to DC charger that is to be used to charge the sprayer.  This charger is make in China and does not conform to the US electrical code because of the installation of an A/C plug on the DC side of the charger.

The problem is that the electrical receptacle on the sprayer is a 3-pin Shroud female (IEC C13) AC receptacle.  This AC receptacle allows for the insertion of AC plugs into this receptacle that is ONLY designed to have DC power.

After several months of non-use, we used a standard AC cord with this sprayer receptacle.  This resulted in overheating and melting of internal circuitry and posed a fire hazard but luckily the circuit breaker tripped prior to starting a fire.

This is a safety problem and could result in significant damage, fire, injury or death.  This product should be recalled and redesigned to comply with the US electric code and safety requirement.

incident_description: We purchased a Mr. Heater Vent Free 30,000 BTU Radiant Propane Heater (bundle with fan blower) in November 2022.  Twice it has had a propane buildup which cause a flare-up where it basically went "whoomph" and blew a ball of flame 2 to 3 feet out of the front of the unit.  This only occurred when the thermostat was set to under their 2 setting (settings range from 1 to 5).  This is used in our living room as a secondary heat source.  Also note that in our correspondence with Enerco Group (the manufacturer), they state the cause was setting the thermostat to settings that were not whole numbers (i.e. setting the thermostat exactly on 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5).  Nothing in the owners or operators manual indicates the thermostat must only be set on whole numbers.  In our correspondence, Enerco states that even though they know this dangerous flare-up problem can be caused when the thermostat is not left exactly on a whole number setting, they have no plans to replace the thermostat with one that simply clicks into place on the whole numbers.  Enerco states they are changing their owners manual to indicate the thermostat should be set on whole numbers only, but, again, they are still going to leave the thermostat that allows unsafe settings.  This should be a simple hardware fix - replace the thermostat with one that does not cause an explosion of flame.  Enerco refuses.  No one was injured during the times this occurred, but the possibility is very high if someone had been in the wrong place at the wrong time.  I will attach copies of all email correspondence with Enerco representatives, both their emails and mine.
justification: The incident involved a dangerous flare-up but no injuries occurred, and the manufacturer acknowledges the issue but refuses to fix it, indicating a high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
RE: Lochinvar gas boiler Model #KHN110 Serial #1551102312187 . 2 incidents of gas leaks. 
1st was Feb 16, 2022: called my plumber/installer to report my boiler not working and with a strong smell of gas. Was told the gas was leaking - the valve had loosened and that it is now fixed. 
2nd time Oct 13, 2022: very strong smell of gas. I called [REDACTED] to report a gas leak. Technician came to the house with a detector to determine the source of the leak. The detector went crazy when near the boiler, which clearly indicated the leak was coming from the boiler. I took a video with the technician and had him explain verbally and visually show the exact location of the leak inside the boiler. He immediately turned off the gas source, and tagged the boiler. He advised me to open windows and not ignite any flames, etc. until the boiler could be serviced. I immediately called my plumber/installer who came and it was determined that the gas valve was indeed faulty, and it was then replaced.
For months I had been experiencing severe headaches, nausea, tiredness throughout the summer of 2022. As autumn and cooler temperatures approached, I normally closed all my windows and turned on my heat. With windows closed the smell of gas now became obvious. I had not previously associated my symptoms with the presence of gas, but now believe the leaking gas was the cause. Since the replacement of the faulty gas valve, my symptoms began to disappear. 
I have been unable to reach anyone at Lochinvar - they simply do not answer the phone.
THIS IS A DANGEROUS SITUATION AND COULD HAVE RESULTED IN SERIOUS DAMAGE TO MY HOME, AND MORE SO, TO MY OWN WELL BEING!
Lochinvar has numerous registered recalls pertaining to faulty gas valves causing dangerous gas leaks, but my boiler model is not one listed as a recalled model. IT SHOULD BE!
justification: The incident involved gas leaks causing severe headaches, nausea, and tiredness, indicating injury (severity 3). The recurrence of gas leaks suggests a likely occurrence (4).

incident_description: Eccotemp i12-LP tankless hot water heater.  This unit has a product design defect that allows cold air in through the included venting chimney causing the unit to freeze up even when installed within a temperature controlled room.  The cold air enters the chimney vent and sinks down into the heat exchanger causing it to freeze as there is nothing to prevent the air from entering.  This causes the unit to burst, potentially spraying hot water while also flooding the room in which it is installed.  This, in turn, creates other hazards such as potential electrocution and electrical fire.  Manufacturer does not mention in literature that units should not be installed where subject to freezing.  Retailers continue to sell this unit in states where freezing temperatures are common.  Manufacturer's fix is to "winterize" the unit shutting off water to it and draining any time temperatures drop below freezing even though the unit is required to be installed indoors and the structure is heated.  This, in effect, makes the units useless in Wisconsin 8 out of 12 months of the year.  The manufacturer refused warranty on the project, refused to provide a re-engineered product, and offered the solution to fix it using [REDACTED]!.  These units should be recalled and not allowed to be sold for permanent installation in any state that is subject to freezing temperatures.
justification: The defect can cause the unit to burst, potentially leading to injury from hot water, electrocution, or electrical fire, and the issue is likely to occur in freezing temperatures.

incident_description:
I recently purchased 2 containers of Mister Plumber Drain Opener from my local Dollar Tree. Without being opened and still inside of the store bags, one of the containers got tipped over and began leaking onto my living room floor and a [REDACTED] faucet box in the presence of my 4 young children (aged 1 through 10). When I went to assess the situation, I saw that neither container had a safety seal to ensure that product was unable to leak out from the containers. When I went online to contact the AmeriPlus company about this issue I have found nothing but a faulty website, an inoperable phone number [REDACTED], another phone number that is operable but doesn't get answered, and incomplete contact information on the outside of the bottle. As per OSHA regulations, arenÃÂt products required to have some sort of pictogram, and complete street address contact information in the event of accidents? 

After this product got tipped over, my 7-year-old son went to clean the mess up (unknowing that it was hazardous material, he simply saw a mess on the floor). His hands are okay, but when I went to inspect the bottles to see the source of the leak some of the chemical got on my fingers and made them begin to burn. Products that are able to leak out so easily should be not sold to the public without some sort of safety seal on the opening to prevent against leakage. 

I would like to know what the law says about federally regulated products that contain Sodium Hypochlorite and Sodium Hydroxide. Are all consumer labels required to have pictograms and complete contact information in the event of danger?
justification: The incident resulted in chemical burns to the user's fingers, indicating an injury, and the product's lack of safety seals and proper labeling increases the likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description:
GE - General Electric;  Zoneline In-Wall Heat Pump Heater / Air-Conditioning Unit.  
MODEL #: AZ55H09DABM1
SERIAL #:  TF 650149 

Currently, there's an Open recall on limited Serial Numbers of the GE Zoneline HVAC Units listed on the following link's recall notice.       
https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/2016/GE-Recalls-GE-Air-Conditioning-and-Heating-Units

HOWEVER, our particular Serial Number is NOT included in the Recall.  
I called GE's Recall Assistance Line ( 866-723-2697 ) and  GE has advised that they will not do a courtesy repair of the unit similar to the repairs being done on the Recalled Units.  

That being said, I do believe very strongly that the Existing Recall should be expanded to cover similar units.   
Such an expansion could affect tens of thousands of similar GE Zoneline HVAC Units.  
And it's curious as to how and why our unit / similar units are not included in the recall.  

Also noteworthy, is that our unit doesn't appear to have an "indoor-outdoor air vent" option.  Our unit heats and cools INDOOR AIR ONLY.   So there isn't an option to fix the problem by way of shutting a vent or a valve.  

ALSO NOTEWORTHY is how the water pools and puddles indoors, outside the view of most consumers.  
And also where a small child, pet, or adult could come into contact with the water and/or become electrocuted by the water pooling and puddling around higher-than-standard voltage plugs. 
 If the same unit leaked onto carpeting, there could be the creation of mold damage (we don't have carpeting in this area).  
The unit can and does leak into the surrounding wall right around where the electrical components are located.  
(When I noticed it in Summer 2022, I placed a large pan under where the dripping occurred.  But there's clearly signs of long term water dripping, out of view of the home's Senior Citizen Age Occupant - Owners.)   

GE Rep "[REDACTED]" advised that they won't perform a courtesy repair or modification to our unit.  She was also cagey about her location in the US, extension number, etc.  (but given her dialect, I surmised that she COULD be in the Dakotas. )  
800-386-1215
GE Appliance Recall Center 
PO BOX 1780 
RAPID CITY SD 57709

Sincerely, Concerned Homeowner

He then came up to me and wanted me to kiss his finger because he had hurt it. When looking at his finger I noticed two thin slices on it. I then realized it was metal in the measuring tape that had sliced his finger in 2 places and not plastic. The wounds were also black in color because of whatever was on the metal that gave it the black color. It wasn't bad enough to take him to a doctor but it was concerning enough for me to want to report the toy because it is meant for kids and should not contain thin sharp metal capable of slicing skin.
justification: The child sustained minor injuries (two thin slices on the finger) from sharp metal inside the toy, but medical attention was not required.

After calling Kenmore, Sears, and Sears Home Services no one seemed to take action.  I was told by the technician that he wasn't a fire expert and could not determine where it started but probably wiring.  He took pictures and everything inside was melted. Someone in scheduling said they have had many calls and they think there should be a recall. So far no one will help me and the service is awful. incident_description: I had a 6-outlet-wall-tap with a smart plug and space heater plugged-in to it in the bathroom.  Before I went on vacation, I unplugged the smart plug and space heater. I discovered the 6-outlet-wall-tap and smart plug had partially melted and had burn marks, even though they were still working normally.  I suspect the prongs of wall tap receptacle which hold the plug were not tight.  Loose connections could cause arcing and/or a high resistance that can get hot. There are burn marks on the metal prong of the smart plug that suggest arcing occurred.  Even though the 6-outlet-wall-tap had a [REDACTED], it is not safe and should be recalled.  Although the National Electrical Code does require GFCIs in bathrooms, it does not require Arc Fault Circuit Interrupters for bathrooms.  GFCIs do not detect arcing faults.  Had I not incidentally discovered the melted parts which were hidden from view, the condition would have persisted and could have caused a fire and burned down my house.
justification: The incident involved a potential fire hazard with no injury or death, and the likelihood is possible given the described conditions.

incident_description: Purchased a Mr. Buddy propane heater, connecting hose for 20lb. tank and a propane in line hose filter. Pilot light in heater kept shutting off.  Outdoors, I removed the heater from the filter, the filter from the hose, and the hose from the tank. I noted that the filter was quite cold and seemed heavy. By pushing on the coaxial brass stem extending from the center of the filter, I realized that liquid propane gas was squirting out of the filter and did so for over 10 seconds. The filter was not connected to anything; it had become in essence a pressurized lpg hand grenade which if exposed to a flame, would have exploded, probably killing me.
justification: The incident involved a potentially explosive situation with the propane filter, but no actual injury or death occurred.

I unpackaged and went to open the seal to release the fragrance.  The product presents a laceration hazard, and the design should be modified.  It is unsafe. The foil seal hidden within the packaging is actually wider than is visible from the tab at the top, though the consumer would not suspect this going in. When gripping the product from sides, near the exposed tab, I pulled the tab upward from the top to unseal the fragrance.  As I did this, the thick, stiff foil seal sliced through my thumb and forefinger, causing a deep cut in my thumb and a smaller cut on my finger.  First, I did not expect such a large seal, and I certainly did not expect that I would need to hold the product any special way to avoid slicing my fingers open.  I bled quite profusely!  I double checked the package--no warning there either, though again, one should not need safety instructions for an air freshener.  This product packaging is unsafe and needs a redesign. It should not be on the market as currently designed. I can provide photos if needed.
justification: The incident resulted in deep cuts to the thumb and finger, indicating an injury. The likelihood is possible as the design flaw could affect others but may not be universally encountered.

incident_description:
Product: Dewalt Model DCS 438 cut off tool.  Purchased new approximately January 18, 2023.  When I operated the tool I quickly realized that the cutting wheel rotates in a direction opposite to the markings on the tool itself and opposite to what I feel is the intuitive direction of rotation. Specifically, when I press the forward/reverse button to the right (in the direction indicated by the letter "F" on the handle) the cutting wheel rotates clockwise (as seen by an observer looking at the tool from its left side) which is opposite to the direction indicated by the "F" arrow on the guard that shields the user from the cutting wheel.  Sparks generated by cutting metal travel upwards toward the operator. Conversely, when I press the button to the left (in the direction indicated by the letter "R" on the handle, the cutting wheel rotates counterclockwise which is opposite to the direction indicated by the "R" arrow on the wheel guard. Sparks generated by cutting metal travel downwards away from the operator. This does not appear to be a mere labeling problem, because the directions of the "F" and "R" arrows on both the handle and on the wheel guard are as shown in the users' manual.  I reported the problem to Dewalt, and their customer service representative shipped me a replacement tool which, by all appearances, is also brand-new. However the replacement tool suffers from the same problem as the original tool, i.e. it rotates in the wrong direction - in reverse when the switch is set to forward and forward when the switch is set to reverse. 

I believe this is a safety issue for the following reasons:  The cutting tool rotates at 20,000 RPMs.  It can cut through metal and would make short work of flesh and bones.  Because it's a rotating tool it's susceptible to kickback or kick-forward depending on the direction of rotation. Therefore, the tool needs to rotate in a direction indicated by the markings on the tool so that the operator can be keenly aware of what direction of rotation to expect when he squeezes the trigger.  The fact that "wrong-direction" operation occurred on two different tools selected at random suggests to me that the problem is widespread.  Obviously, a user could simply get used to the "wrong direction" operation, however with a dangerous tool such as this one, the operator should not have to make that kind of mental adjustment.

Date below is the date of my trouble ticket to DeWalt.  Actual date of occurrence is probably a day or two earlier.

There are two barcodes on the packaging, the one reported below and X003G8KJRD.

I attempted to upload 14 photos twice (all less than 100 MB) but got error message - something about a proxy server.  Will be glad to try again if someone can fix the problem.

I still have the second replacement tool and will file a second report if you ask me to.
justification: The tool operates in the opposite direction of the markings, posing a potential safety risk, but no injury or incident has been reported yet.

After returning from the Hospital, I evaluated the stool to identify how the stool tipped over resulting in the fall.  I found the stool has a square design where the legs of the stool are completely vertical to the ground and when stepping on the stool causes the stool to tip to the side where the foot is placed.  I have other stools whose legs are angled and distributes the weight and do not tip over.  Unfortunately I did not read the negative reviews of this product on Amazon where others that purchased this step stool had exactly the same problem with the stool tipping over resulting in the person falling and incurring serious injuries.

incident_description: I purchased Everspring Free And Clear Liquid Laundry Detergent from the Lakeville MN Target store. I used it for the first time on January 8, approximately 2 days after purchasing. It was my first experience using this product. The bottle was extremely full, and the way the bottle and the measuring cap are designed, it was impossible to pour without spilling some over the sides and some got on my hand. I washed my hands immediately, but no matter how much I tried, this product left a tacky, gummy, sticky residue which spread to both hands from washing them together. It won't come off. It's been 10 days and I have washed my hands countless times. I've tried hand soap, [REDACTED] dish soap, alcohol wipes, vegetable oil, baby oil, and hand lotion, and nothing has helped. I contacted Target as they are the manufacturer and they told me they had no guidance for this product and advised me to contact my health care provider. When I did so she suggested I call Poison Control. They both suggested the same strategies I mentioned above. I contacted a physician when the problem had not improved within a week and he laughed and then said he'd never heard of something like this, and said I could just keep doing what I'm doing and eventually within a month my skin will replace itself and the problem should go away. In the meantime, my hands are constantly sticky, especially when my skin is warm. This sticky residue also transfers from my hands to other objects or to other areas of my skin. I try not to touch anything at all unless absolutely necessary, but even incidental contact transfers this sticky residue to my arms, my neck, and my face while I am sleeping. It transfers to my phone when I use it, so I am trying not to touch anything if I don't have to. This is causing me a lot of anxiety because I don't know why this is happening or what it is or how to make it go away. I have been doing laundry with various detergents all my life and nothing like this has ever happened before. I've never heard of it happening to anyone else. I'm concerned that this product may have been tampered with but I have no way of knowing. I placed the bottle in a plastic bag and put it out in the garage but I don't want to touch it again. This is not painful but it is extremely annoying and uncomfortable and I interferes with my ability to do everyday activities without compounding the problem. I don't know if this substance is harmful. I had to throw away the towels that I washed with this product. I have health related anxiety and sensory hyper awareness so this issue is very distressing for me. I wish someone would test this product to see what is in it that is causing this bizarre effect. It is like a polymer or a varnish or something that is not water or oil soluble. Getting a splash of laundry detergent on your skin should not be this problematic.
justification: The incident caused persistent discomfort and distress, but no physical injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
Double-hung windows were installed in attic windows. The windows have fake woodgrain which includes a strip of plastic covering the channel where the windows slide up and down. Two months after installation, there was a big windstorm. One of the windows blew in, folding down like they fold when being cleaned. When trying to get the window to latch closed, another gust blew the window in again, hitting me in the face and breaking my nose. 
I had the installer out the following week and asked him to make sure the windows latch. When I pointed out that the latch was not engaging fully in the channel, he removed the latch, shaved some plastic off, and then it worked. 
The following week, an inspector came and when I told him what happened, he told me that it is because of the strip of fake woodgrain over the channel. It makes it so the latch doesn't always catch properly. He told me he often needs to shave some plastic off. 
So this tells me it is a defect in the design, and the installers are using a workaround to make sure the latch sticks. We found this same issue on 6 windows in my house. I have reported it multiple times to the store but they have not stopped selling these windows.
justification: The incident resulted in a broken nose, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The defect is common enough that the inspector frequently encounters it, indicating a likely occurrence (4).

incident_description: I purchased a PowerHorse 13000ES generator in 2020 from Northern Tool to power our home during power outages. The generator worked great for us during power outages until during a very cold power outage prior to Christmas 2022. The temp was at least -20 and we experienced a prolonged power outage. I tried to start the generator but it would not start. That made me examine the system and discovered the fuel valve was leaking. (Turning the valve off stopped the leak) I am very happy that the generator did not start, otherwise I would not have noticed the leak as it was not daylight. The result of a leak on a running generator would not have a happy ending. I had to wait until after Christmas to contact Northern Tool and Powerhorse to report the problem, but they have not yet responded to me. As temperatures warmed to about freezing (32), I checked the valve and it no longer leaked. I then ran the generator to check it all out and the leak did not appear. Fuel tank leak on Westinghouse WH2400i inverter generator.  Notes on problem listed below.  A fire did not occur, fortunately.  I submitted a support request to Westinghouse today with this information and I am awaiting their response.

Notes on fuel leak on Westinghouse WH2400i Generator (inverter style)
Dec. 22, 2022
Serial Number:  10240 A061 513042 0056
Purchased Aug. 22, 2016 from Family Farm & Home in Burton, MI
Generator usage:  Used as residential home backup power when grid power fails.  Used 4 times since purchase, each time less than 4 hours.  Total runtime < 16 hours.
Most recent usage was on Dec. 17, 2022 for about 4 hours.  Previous use was about a year prior.  
After running on Dec. 17, 2022 I let it sit in garage with fuel valve shut off and the fuel fill cap vent closed.  It still had about ÃÂ½ tank of fuel in it.  Next day there was a very strong odor of fuel in garage, and fuel had dripped out of bottom of unit onto concrete floor.  Set unit outside for a few days and it continued to leak.  Exterior plastic housing had become severely deformed and cracked on the air cleaner side of the unit from exposure to the fuel.  Carb drain is on the other side of the unit and was not leaking, and neither was the carb itself.
Disassembled unit on Dec. 22, 2022 and found that the source of the leak is the fuel tank itself.  Fuel leak is in the side of the tank (on the air cleaner side of the unit) at the parting line of the blow molding tool.  Fuel was still weeping out of the leak and wetting the surface of the fuel tank on the side and bottom.  I have pictures and a video of the fuel weeping out of the tank at the parting line seam.  Fuel was covering the inverter electronics and was puddling in the crevices of the plastic bottom housing piece.  Fuel had also soaked the foam noise insulation material that was in contact with the exterior plastic housing and the side of the fuel tank in the area of the leak.  Inner surface of exterior plastic housing also was wetted with fuel.   This explains the exterior housing deformation.  Also noticed that there are 2 plastic locating pins that are part of the bottom of the fuel tank which fit into rubber grommets in the top of the air cleaner surface.  Both of these pins were deformed (bent towards engine), one quite severely.  This was not the source of the leak, but is abnormal.  
This fuel leak is a severe safety hazard!.  This generator has been used very little, and always with low load in non-harsh conditions.  It should not have this kind of problem!  I am requesting that this unit be repaired / replaced at no cost to me.

Product is Cabela's Biometric Personal Gun Safe. This was used by my father to protect his handguns from his grandchildren. He would program the safe for his fingerprint, and it would work for a few weeks and block unauthorized individuals. However, while at his house a few weeks later I tried my own fingerprint and it opened the safe. I had my children try their finger prints and it opened the safe. We thought it was a defective unit so we returned it for a different one. The new unit had the exact same problem, so we returned it for a different brand safe.

I found the following statement in the users manual: "When you first receive your safe there are no recorded fingerprints. Any fingerprint will open the safe until a fingerprint is recorded."

The unit did not work as indicated in the manual, because any fingerprint would work even after the first one was recorded.

We talked to the sales people at the Cabela's store and they said quite a few gun safes had been returned because of this exact same complaint. We called Cabela's phone number tech support, and they said they had never heard of this issue. Either it was a lie or it is not being reported properly.

The safe is not available online, but it is still available in the store. These should not only be removed from sale but there should be a recall and removed from homes. They do not operate as intended and present a hazard to the public because unauthorized people can access guns.

incident_description:
I recently hired a professional handyman to install a newly purchased wired Ring Video Doorbell Pro. The new Ring video doorbell was added to my existing doorbell system. To power the Ring doorbell, a power kit was attached to the existing doorbell chime. Right after the installation was complete, the chime got burnt by electric. If we didnÃÂt find out about the electrical burn or act on it quickly, it would have caused a fire. The professional handyman was not able to figure out what caused the chime to burn.  
After doing some research, I believe that the design of the wired Ring Video Doorbell is flawed, especially the power kit attached to the doorbell chime. When installing traditional doorbells, itÃÂs ok not to turn off the electricity as the circuit would not be complete without pressing the doorbell. However, for the wired Ring doorbell, the power kit adds a parallel circuit in the chime in order to power the wired Ring doorbell 24/7. If we donÃÂt shut off the electricity while installing the Ring doorbell, the chime and the parallel power kit will create a short circuit. 
In the installation manual, Ring indicated that users should turn off the power in the circuit box. However, they didnÃÂt highlight the danger if users donÃÂt turn off the power or distinguish themselves from traditional doorbells. Even my professional handyman was not aware of the differences in the product designs or find out the root cause of the electrical burns in the chime.
This issue seems common among Ring doorbell users. You will find out similar complaints on this Ring community discussion forum: 
[REDACTED]
To protect the safety of consumers, Ring should improve their design to prevent the risk of short circuits and fire hazard. In the meantime, they should emphasize the importance of switching off power before installation and highlight the differences between their product and traditional doorbells.
justification: The incident involved a burnt chime that could have caused a fire, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description: My grandkids ages 4 to almost 2 years old use this step stool. My four year old Grandaughter and almost 2 year old grandson use it to get up on my bed or to use bathroom sink or toilet. Last night my Grandaughter went to get up on my bed using this step stool. Stool collapsed and she hurt her left side of leg falling. After tending to her injury and crying. I picked up stool and there was cracks through the sides below the base. Very upsetting considering it claims it holds up to 300 pounds. This product needs recalled. Fortunately no bones broke or any other injuries! Very traumatizing for her.

incident_description: I heard a popping sound come from the dryer and smoke started coming out of the top rear instrument panel. The dryer was still running and it did not trip the breaker. I unplugged it, the smoke increased and I could smell an electrical fire. The panel then started melting. The Fire department came and removed the dryer from my home. The fire was contained to the dryer control instrument panel. Took off the rear panel and there was a paper Service Manual (by the manufacturer, this dryer has never been opened to be serviced) that was sitting directly on top of the circuit board. The manual had caught fire and the electronics around it were burned. Why would a paper manual be installed inside of a dryer where electronics get hot? Incoming electrical wires coming into the back of the unit was completely fine. There was no lint buildup so was not caused by lint. I couldn't stay in the house because of the smoke and I had already suffered with smoke inhalation while I was waiting for the fire department. I was very lucky that I was standing right there when it happened to be able to unplug it.
justification: The incident involved smoke inhalation and required fire department intervention, indicating an injury occurred.

incident_description:
Our builder installed a number of Kidde FireX smoke alarms in our house in 2020 when we renovated. They are hardwired but have battery back-up. Around February of this year, two of them started emitting a high-pitch chirp that we could not stop - we tried everything including holding down the button and changing the battery. Nothing stopped it so we had no choice but to rip the units out of the ceiling. In August, the same thing happened with a third one. I'm afraid this will continue until we have no choice but to rip all of them out of the ceiling. The chirping noise is maddening. How is this possible? We've never encountered this with any fire alarms we've had in previous houses we've owned in the last 30 years. Driving home owners crazy with a high pitched sound until they have no choice but to rip the unit out hardly seems safe. At this rate, we'll end up with no smoke alarms in the house. I submitted a complaint on Kidde's website on October 2 but have not received a response. It hardly seems fair that we must spend the money to resolve this issue.

Report Updated 1/23/23:
As of January 23, 2023, we have been notified by the customer that Kidde has made no attempts to contact them to rectify the situation.
justification: The incident involves malfunctioning smoke alarms causing significant nuisance but no injury or death, and the issue is likely to recur based on the pattern described.

incident_description:
A residential structure fire that went to a flashover originated in the bedroom of a single-family home. The home was extensively damaged by fire and smoke. fire investigators determined that the point of origin of the fire was the replacement lithium-ion battery pack for a [REDACTED] portable vacuum. The vacuum was hanging on the wall of the room and the charger was plugged into the vacuum and the outlet at the time of the fire. The residents were awake and in another area of the house. They both escaped without any treatable injury. One resident complained of breathing issues from inhaling smoke or vapors. He was not transported by medics.

The Amazon product page for this item included a video and review showing this product was involved in a different fire than this one. We also found at least 6 other reports of this or similar Chinese-manufactured lithium-ion replacement batteries for this vacuum causing fires.
justification: One resident had breathing issues from smoke inhalation, indicating an injury, and there are multiple reports of similar incidents.

incident_description: LG ThinQ Laundry Center (washer-dryer combo washtower) - Model No WKGX201HWA -- purchased Sept 2021 (1 year ago) - Gas Dryer failed to ignite natural gas. Gas dryer did not send out error codes or alarms and failsafe did not activate (unit did not shut down) and dryer continued to inject natural gas into dryer unit. Natural gas smell spread throughout laundry room and could be smelled throughout the floor of the house. Turned off dryer and valve to gas line. Called gas company which sent a tech that tested gas valve, gas hose to dryer and then drye itself. Gas company tech confirmed presence of unburned gas in dryer unit and that it was a gas dryer issue. Unit remained untouched until an LG tech arrived two days later. At that time the unit operated normally. LG tech gave a cursory inspection of unit (opened top and used a flashlight to peer inside - and stated unit was operational. LG tech did state one scenario that could cause such a failure would be an issue with the motherboard. I asked LG tech if he would want a gas dryer in his house (with kids) that had already demonstrated ability to fail with gas continuing to pour into unit - and no cause determined. Tech stated unit works 'now' and it would be the decision LG management if anything further were to be done.

incident_description: I purchased a Mr Heater golf cart heater and was preparing it for use. I installed it into my golf cart cup holder. I followed the instructions to ignite the heater and noticed the start button was hard to push and would not return to it's original position. After several attempts the button loosened up and  seemed to be working properly. I was able to ignite the unit and was making sure it was working properly. After approx. 30 seconds there was a large flame that came out of the side and back of the unit. I quickly removed it from the golf cart a laid it on the ground and the flame went out. I did not try to re-start the unit. There were no injuries and no damage to the golf cart.

incident_description: About two years ago we had a bathroom renovated and the contractor installed a NuTone model 665RP heater/fan/light.  On Wednesday 10/19/2022 I discovered that the plastic grill was partially melted.  Since I had vacuumed dust from the unit the previous week, I knew that this was something new.  I communicated with the manufacturer, providing pictures and a description of the problem.  They insisted that this was not a fire hazard even though enough heat had been generated to melt the plastic grill.  After much back and forth they informed me that problem was because the unit's housing was 1/8" from being flush with the ceiling.  It was supposed to be flush.  There was no indication in the installation instructions that the tolerances were this close and that even the slightest deviation could result in a fire hazard.  Truth be known, I think the unit is either defective or poorly designed, and they simply don't want to stand behind their product.  They offered to send me a new grill but said that it would probably melt also.
justification: The incident involved a melted plastic grill but no injury or fire occurred, and the manufacturer stated it was not a fire hazard.

incident_description: I have five smoke detectors in my house.  After 13 years, I replaced them all with a Kidde brand detector.  After a couple of months, I received a recall notice from Kidde.  They eventually replaced them with a different model.  Soon after I installed the new ones, I started to get false alarms.  I had them all wired together so the false alarms reverberated throughout the entire house and it was impossible to know which one had falsely triggered.  I then adjusted the wiring on each one so that they would not all trigger if one triggered.  Over the next year or so, each one would falsely alarm.  As each one would give a false alarm, I pulled it.  I was left with just one fire detector and that one alarmed the other night, now I have no working detectors.  I've called Kidde twice (once today) and have yet to have a confirmation that they will replace them even though they have a 10 year warranty.  There is certainly a flaw in this model.
justification: False alarms and malfunctioning smoke detectors are inconvenient but did not result in injury or death.

We were able to evacuate the house safely without incident. Once outside our home, we noticed the fire department was at our neighbors house inspecting their home with CO2 detectors as their carbon monoxide detectors had also gone off due to their Generac generator (same size and install type). That particular night there was no wind and the air was very humid. Following that incident and as suggested by the fire department, we taped up the vents in the soffit near the installed Generac generator.

incident_description:
After having several Kiddie wired smoke and carbon monoxide detectors (Model P4010ACS-W) professionally installed costing me a couple of thousand dollars to my 2744 sq ft home less than 6 months ago, I have had half of these alarms randomly go off and on even several times after canceling the alarms to confirm no threat was present. I have had to call the fire department who even they struggled to silence the alarm and only did so after permanently deactivating it. I find this to be a serious threat to my children's safety and my own. Each one of my household members have sensory processing disorder associated with being autistic,one member has PTSD and other an anxiety disorder.  Each time these alarms fault causing my entire household significant distress and scared my 4 year old so bad when the alarm by our stairs went off as we were going up the stairs and she would have fallen down the stairs had I not been behind her to catch her. No physical injuries resulted from any of the 5 occurences that we have experienced with these kiddie alarms. One of the occurrences happened as a result of me blowing of some minor dust from hanging a picture near the device's alarm.

I believe we are risk and that this product is dangerous because these detectors are marketed to warn it's consumors when faced with an applicable threat. At this point  I have zero confidence in these alarms because if they randomly go off what's to say that these will be effective
justification: The alarms caused significant distress and nearly led to a fall, but no physical injuries occurred.

incident_description:
The drain pan under the coil in my gas furnace has now melted twice. In addition to causing water leaks that have damaged the house twice (the pan was replaced once 5 years ago, but has now melted a second time, causing the leak to re-appear). Our furnace is a Goodman and was manufactured around 2011. Our HVAC company re-assessed the problem, and documented the burning/melting in the coil pan. This burn pattern is identical to what appeared 5 years ago, clearly showing that the coils continue to burn/melt the pan.

Our HVAC technician concluded this is the exact issue that resulted in the Goodman/Daikin recall below. However, this recall only includes their furnaces manufactured between 2019-2021. Hence, despite our being a clear fire hazard and displaying the same problem as that covered under the current recall, our model is excluded from the recall. It is apparent that this problem extends to models prior to those manufactured in 2019, including ours. Given that we now know our furnace poses a fire hazard, we would hope this is investigated and the recall extended to cover homeowners like us stuck with these dangerous furnaces. 

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involves a recurring fire hazard with documented damage to property but no reported injuries or deaths.

incident_description:
I sustained several laceration and contusion injuries as a result of what may have been a product failure of my 15.5 ft Ohuhu Telescoping ladder. I was seen and treated at my local ER in Burlington WI where I had both a severe head laceration and a severe elbow laceration stitched. Thankfully there were no breaks or fractures.

The ladder in question had been purchased through Amazon in May 2019 and had worked well until Oct 14. I had extended the ladder to full length and placed in up against the face wall of my garage in order to reinstall a remote security camera. I was maybe 10- 12 feet up when the ladder began to fall to the ground. I'm not sure, but think I rolled out to my left before impacting the driveway - elbow first, then left shoulder, knee and finally my head came into contact with the ladder, and I suffered a significant laceration. At the time I did not realize that I also lacerated my elbow quite badly.

My wife took me to the local ER, where I was attended to by the staff. No broken bones, fractures or head trauma other than the laceration were determined by the X-Rays and CT workups.

Yesterday, Oct 17 I took a good look at the ladder and the area of the driveway where the incident took place. There were no slip marks on the asphalt, but two of the upper ladder rungs showed damage, The uppermost could have been from impact - it is uneven in nature. The lower rung appeared different - a very straight cleaving on both sides of the rung holder.

I contacted the company through their contact us page and offered them the ladder for inspection. I received their reply this morning. It said:

"Dear [REDACTED],

Thanks for contacting us.

We apologize for the fright and inconvenience this has caused you. Is your injury better now? This is kindly to let you know that we have already issued a full refund for your order through amazon. Also, we have recently received feedback from other customer and have picked up their ladder for testing and analysis by our product team, so you do not need to return the ladder. Please stop using this ladder and get rid of it.

We are sorry again for the inconvenience caused and appreciated for your understanding.

Best Regards,
[REDACTED]
Ohuhu Direct"

Based on their response it's possible that my incident may be due to a product failure or safety issue. I note that Ohuhu no longer sells the 15.5 ft version through Amazon, though I do see very similar product under the [REDACTED], [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] names.

Please let me know your thoughts on this situation.

Thanks in advance

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in multiple injuries requiring ER treatment, including severe lacerations, but no fractures or head trauma, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) as the ladder failure appears to be part of a broader product issue, but not all ladders are affected.

incident_description:
Dear [REDACTED]: 
I'm writing about your product STEM. What a horrible product. Your advertising says "safe for kids and pets". Your directions do say "safe anywhere in the home" and warns "slippery when wet" on the front and rear labels. But these don't cover how dangerous this product is. 
Let me start by saying I am handicapped with severe mobility issues and I am at high risk for Covid, so all my groceries are delivered. I bought STEM because the store did not have [REDACTED]. What I wanted it for, was to spray around baseboards and on the exit door steps to get any bugs before they crawl into the house. [REDACTED] is a superior product. 
On Tuesday July 26, I sprayed STEM around the baseboard in my first floor halfÃÂ­bath since I had seen one stray carpenter ant on the ceramic tile floor. The smell is almost overpoweringly offensive, so I left the exhaust fan running for days. On Thursday, I checked the bathroom and saw the STEM had not dried, and I could see wet puddles around the baseboard. I tried soaking those up with paper towels, not an easy task, but I used my cane to push the paper towels along the floor. When I had a visitor on Friday July 29, she thought the floor was too slippery, and she mopped it with a [REDACTED]. The fan was still running as the smell from the STEM was still offensive. By Tuesday August 2, the floor felt dry to the touch but slick. I tried it with the tip of my rubber-soled shoes, and it was still slippery. My friend came to visit again on Friday August 5.  She scrubbed the door with dish liquid - it cuts grease.  The floor is ok now.
That downstairs bathroom was out of commission for over a week. I'm glad I have other bathrooms on the second floor, and a Stairlift to be able to go upstairs, although what used to be a quick trip to the restroom had become a 20 minute journey. I am also very glad I did not use STEM anywhere else in the house. Most of the first floor has ceramic tile floors, particularly at the exit doors, so I would have been trapped. 
In preparing this letter, I looked carefully at the label to try to determine who manufacturers this product. I realized the rear label could be pried up, but I had to use a knife to do this, as it is really glued on tight. I can't imagine how anyone would do that in a store before buying the product, as a knife is necessary. Anyway, after reading the precautions and warnings, I was horrified. To summarize what the instructions say: Do not spray into the air; spray on an insect only when it lands/sits someplace; wipe the wall immediately to avoid staining; if any STEM gets on the floor, immediately wipe it up with a cloth, and wash the area with soapy water; and if you want to get rid of a partially-used bottle, call the local solid waste authority for disposal instructions; never pour down an indoor or outdoor drain.  And it's exempt from the registration with the EPA!!
So this is TOXIC AND HAZARDOUS WASTE ????? You call this safe for kids and pets???? 
I think the reason you hide all these instructions under a label that requires a knife to pry up, is that if a consumer could read them easily, they wouldn't buy the product. I certainly wouldn't have ---1 can do better with a flyswatter, and if the bug is on-the-hoof, I can just squirt it with hair spray. Both are much safer and easier options. 
Someone might be suckered into buying STEM once, but I doubt they'll ever buy it again. I know I won't. You owe me a refund of $8.00 (cash or check, no coupons) for the cost of this garbage. 
STEM is a useless and dangerous product and should be taken off the market.

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a hazardous product causing inconvenience and potential danger, but no actual injury or death occurred.

The voltage difference between the hose fitting and panel was measured to be 84 VDC.  During a wash cycles, up to 160 VDC difference was measured between the hose fitting and rear panel.  The stray current was found to emanate from the thermistor in the water valve and travel through the water in the water valve assembly.  When the thermistor power was disconnected, the voltage difference between the rear panel and water supply hose fitting was measured to be approximately 0 VDC.  This testing demonstrates that a failure within the thermistor housing has allowed water penetration into the thermistor and the passage of leakage current to the water supply hose fitting.  This failure not only represents a shock hazard, but can also result in rapid corrosion and fracturing of the water supply hose fitting itself.

We woke up on the morning of Thursday, September 22nd at about 5:45am to a garage with approximately 7-8 inches of water standing and continuing to fill (though water was escaping through newly broken wall). We immediately noticed that the top of our Pentair Water Softener had exploded off of the unit, gushing water into our garage and kitchen. It was gushing water up toward an electrical outlet (where softener was plugged in) as well almost rising to the level of outlets in garage (completely covering an electrical cord we had running). Had any of us walked into garage, there's a high likelihood we would have been electrocuted. 

As shown in photos obtained by us and the water mitigation company (and also stated by plumber that came out to restore water to our home), it's evident that the top seal of the unit (where electrical component attaches to cylinder shaped water softener) containing the threads split diagonally, causing the electrical component to rupture above the unit and leaving a heavy stream of 75 PSI water running into garage throughout the night. The product had been purchased in March of 2019 through Amazon.com (from third party seller [REDACTED]), and is supposedly covered by a 5-year Pentair warranty.  However, because of the complete loss of faith in the product by Pentair and the tens of thousands of dollars in property damage, we will likely never expose ourselves again to their unsafe product. 

In retrospect, we now realize that we are not the first customers to which this explosion has occurred. There are other Amazon customers who have left product reviews stating a similar story regarding the unprovoked explosion of the top portion of their Pentair Fleck water softener.
justification: The incident involved a water softener explosion causing significant property damage and posing a severe electrocution risk, but no actual injuries or deaths occurred.

incident_description:
Dryer fire.
The accumulated lint in the bottom of an electric LG clothes dryer ignited. 
The resident referred to the dryer as a "steam" dryer. While this event occurred in an LG dryer, it is not a brand-specific problem. It is a design and possibly an installation problem. The dryer was mounted on top of a matching base assembly. The dryer was vented with watertight flexible tubbing, which was attached to the dryer with foil-style tape. The resident stated that the dryer was 4-6 years old, and the lint trap was removed and cleaned after every load.
The dryer had a cold water connection and was connected to the home's cold water system. The dryer was installed in a space which caused the vent hose to drop down from the dryer connection, turn in a 180 degree arc, travel up the wall to the exterior vent point. Additionally, the dryer lint trap was removed and vacuumed on occasion.
It was reported that an overheating light had come on within the last few months and shut down the dryer several times.
On 8/30/2022, while drying a load of clothes, the resident smelled something burning and noticed light smoke escaping from the lint trap. The first arriving engine disconnected the water line and the flexible vent tubbing to remove the dryer from the structure. During this process, they noticed that the flexible vent tubbing contained a large amount of water. 
Fire cause: As the vent discharge point of the dryer was approximately 12-14 inches above the ground (the dryer was mounted on a raised base), the 180-degree bend in the hose (as it went up the wall) formed a "U" shaped "water trap. Over time, steam exiting from the dryer condensed on the sides of the flexible exhaust tubbing and filled the bend to a point where airflow was blocked.   The water filled "horseshoe" bend prevented air from exiting through the dryer vent tube. The foil tape allowed the "trapped" back pressure air to flow into the base of the dryer where a considerable accumulation of lint build up on the floor of the dryer and top of the solid vent pipe inside the dryer. As regular airflow was blocked, back pressure air and "normal" discharge air caused the base of the dryer compartment to overheat. The solid vent pipe inside the dryer was heating from outflow air and from the blocked air that was returning to the base of the dryer. While the specific point of ignition is unknown, fire effects and fire patterns indicated it was on top of the solid vent pipe inside the dryer's back wall.
justification: The incident involved a dryer fire caused by design and installation issues, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description:
To whom it may concern, 
There appears to be a systemic defect with First Alert/BKR 7020BSL smoke detectors. This defect leads to premature end-of-life, failure of the deactivation switch, and possible other malfunctions.

Our family has experienced 4 failures of a First Alert/BKR 7020BSL smoke detectors.  This report documents the 4th failure.  Report No. [REDACTED] discusses the first 3 failures.  For convenience, some of the information in this report is a reproduction from the earlier report. 

On August 18, 2019 I installed five 7020BSL detectors. Now, 4 of the 5 detectors have indicated a failure by sounding the 5-beep end-of-life indication, well before the 10-year listed lifetime. The first 3 failures were reported to First Alert consumer affairs. I chose not to report the 4th failure, as I no longer trust First Alert devices and do not want a replacement device.  Instead, I replaced the 4th failed device with a different brand.

Specific information on the failed units is listed below: 
1st Failure: 
Date of failure: Nov 10, 2020 
Date of Manufacture listed on the back of the unit: Oct 19, 2018 
First Alert Consumer Affairs Case Number for this failure: #[REDACTED]

2nd Failure: 
Date of failure: Nov 22, 2020 
Date of Manufacture listed on the back of the unit: June 14, 2019 
First Alert Consumer Affairs Case Number for this failure: #[REDACTED]

3rd Failure: 
Date of failure: March 16, 2021 
Date of Manufacture listed on the back of the unit: June 14, 2019 
First Alert Customer Support Case Number for this failure: #[REDACTED]

4rd Failure: 
Date of failure: March 28, 2022 
Date of Manufacture listed on the back of the unit: June 14, 2019 
First Alert Customer Support Case Number for this failure: N/A 

All detectors were installed per the manufacturer's requirements, such as distance from vents, ceiling fans etc. After the first failure, we have been cleaning all the smoke detectors monthly per the manufacturer's guidance to help prevent additional failures. 

Secondly, contrary to the product literature, after deactivating the units using the deactivation switch, the 5-beep sequence continues. The failure of the deactivation switch occurred on all the failed units. This further indicates a systemic problem or design flaw. 

To their credit, First Alert did replace the first 3 failed units at no cost. However, this does not address a possible systemic defect, or problems with the other unit we still have installed in our house. Therefore, I am reporting these failures to you, to investigate further. Please contact me if you require further information. 

Below is a description of the risk of harm these defects create.

Firstly, this smoke detector has poor design, which puts the individuals it is intended to protect at risk.  This smoke detector is intended to provide a fire/smoke alarm for individuals who are deaf, hence the strobe light.  However, as designed, the device only indicates end-of-life via 5 auditory beeps - no clear visual signal is provided to indicate end-of-life (e.g. the strobe light does not flash).  Therefore, a deaf individual has no clear indication that the device has failed or reached end-of-life and needs replacement.  This poor design puts the people the device is intended to protect (i.e. deaf individuals) at risk of harm.  There is a high probability that deaf individuals will not promptly replace a failed device and living with a failed smoke detector increases the risk of harm, injury, or death during a fire. 

The risk presented by this poor design is compounded by the device's abnormally high premature failure rate.  As indicated in this report, these smoke detectors tend to fail years before the stated end-of-life.  Therefore, there is a high probability that a deaf individual could be living with a failed device before considering replacing their smoke detectors. Living with a failed smoke detector puts an individual at increased risk of injury or death during a fire.

Secondly, my report indicates there appears to be systemic defects with these devices, causing them to fail prematurely and not be deactivated by the deactivation switch.   There is a risk that there are additional defects, especially in the detection and alarm functions.  It is possible that a defect could cause a device that appears to be in good working order to nonetheless fail to alarm on an actual fire.  Therefore, it is recommended to investigate the extent of the systemic defects in this device and determine if it affects the detection and alarm functions of the device.

As an aside, we installed these smoke detectors in our house because our son was born deaf and we hired a deaf nanny to care for him.  My wife and I are hearing, so we were alerted to the premature failures of these devices and replaced them promptly.

Please let me know if any additional information is needed.
Thank you.
justification: The incident describes a systemic defect in smoke detectors that could lead to failure during a fire, posing a risk of injury or death, especially for deaf individuals. The high premature failure rate and design flaws increase the likelihood of occurrence.

Caller is reporting that she experienced similar problems of the recall#22-021 Hazard:
The molded plastic drain pan located at the bottom of the evaporator coil, when installed with a residential condensing gas furnace in an up-flow configuration, can overheat, melt, and deform, posing a fire hazard.

Caller stated that she noticed water leaking out of the furnace, which a service technician came out and replace which cost $1496.  Caller stated that she would like the company to expand the recall to include her unit.

Report Update:
On August 30th, I received a phone call from [REDACTED].  I am not sure if his last name or company name is correct.  This is what was stated in my voicemail, but the phone number is for Goodman/Amana Homeowners Division.   

[REDACTED] asked me about the problem I experienced and I explained my experience of the leaking of water from the unit when the air conditioner was running in July 2019. I believe my dates and model numbers should be included in the recall and that I should be reimbursed by Goodman for the repair cost that I incurred as a result of Goodman's defective product.

incident_description:
The Carrier Performance Series 2-stage heat pump model # TP-WEM01-A is a health and fire hazard and should be recalled from the market.  Details are as follows.  During a maintenance check performed on May 24, 2022, by Reliant Air Conditioning of Irving, Texas, the technician found the interior insulation on the access panel had been sucked off the panel, leaving only a thin layer of the fiberglass insulation still attached to the panel.  On June 30, a maintenance technician from Reliant Air Conditioning glued the separated part of the insulation to the panel and secured it with tape.  The patchwork repair still leaves some fiberglass insulation exposed.

The failure of the access panel interior insulation is due to either a faulty design or a material defect.  It poses two serious problems for consumers:
 
1.	It is a serious health hazard because the suction generated by the blower motor is strong 	enough to detach the insulation from the panel and can pull fiberglass particles into the air 	stream which can get into a personÃÂs lungs and cause permanent damage.

2.	It is a serious fire hazard because the aluminum foil cover of the fiberglass insulation can 	be sucked into the wiring or into the fan motor and cause an electrical fire.
justification: The incident describes a health and fire hazard due to faulty insulation, which could lead to injury or fire, but no actual incidents or injuries are reported.

incident_description:
We had a whole house generator installed in July, 2021.  The installers walked around our house & asked us questions before installing it.  We agreed to a spot under a garage window with an air conditioner in it, but when we told them it had not been used in years, they said it was ok to put it there.  There were vents in the overhang, but they never mentioned them.  A month later Ida struck with the eye over our house for 4 hours.  We had evacuated several days before, & left our generator running.
Our son was the 1st to return to our area & decided to stay in our house with the generator with his wife & 15 yr old daughter. About 3 in the morning the CO monitor went off.  We had this near our gas fireplace for many years.  Thinking it was a false signal, our son got 2 more CO detectors from the 5th wheel stored in our yard.  All 3 went off an hour later, so they left & went to their own house, without a generator & contacted me about why they left.  I immediately contacted our installer of the generator who told me there were problems with the gas lines being inconsistent with their gas supply.  I immediately contacted our gas company who said there was no problem with the gas supply.  The next morning my son went back to our house & ran into a inspector from the gas company.  Our son brought a CO detector with him & had gone into the house with doors wide open to get readings.  He got a reading of 22 in the front hall (where doors were wide open), a 55 in our living room by the 1st CO detector.  The gas company worker, followed company regulations & did not go into the house, but did hold the detector  in the front hall as far as he could reach & got a reading around 22.  All these readings were at least 50 feet & with several walls in between!
During the next week or 2 the generator motor broke, so we were without power until normal power was reconnected in about 3 weeks.  That is when we returned.
About a month later the generator company came to see about moving our generator.  That side of our house has a 6foot wood fence around it & I think the generator exhaust was directed toward our garage wall.  We had the generator moved to our backyard, outside the fence, with the exhaust pointed to the golf course behind us.  The installers suggested it might be safer to be inside the fence, but we feel no oneÃÂs going to steal it, & that the wood fence might even keep the exhaust contained near our house, that being totally in the open was better.
The company was very cooperative, got a new motor for the generator, moved it 50 feet without charge.
justification: The incident involved CO detector alarms and high CO readings, but no injuries or deaths occurred as the family evacuated in time.

There is an opening, approximately 4ÃÂx3ÃÂ in the chassis of the unit, for the refrigerant pipes.

2.	Wire Harness on Floor (see attachment, ÃÂTrane Wire HarnessÃÂ):
Inside the Trane condenser unit, the wire harness lies on the floor. The other major brands have their wire harness suspended about 8ÃÂ above the floor. Even if a mouse got into the other units, it would be difficult for it to reach and chew on the suspended wires.

incident_description:
No injuries - reporting a hazardous situation I discovered.  I purchased a VEVOR brand electric hoist with wireless remote, capable of lifting 1320 lbs., model #DHL1320lbs from amazon.  During the installation process in my workshop I discovered the system is not electrically grounded.  The unit does come with a 4 foot power cord, containing a three prong electrical plug for a 115 vac outlet, and connects to a control panel that houses the wireless receiver and provides power to the electric motor that drives the hoist.  Because I need something longer that a 4 foot power cord I opened the control panel and discovered that within the control panel the ground wire coming from the plug was cut, removed, and not connected to anything - effectively just sitting unattached in the sealed box.  Despite the pretense of a grounded system that contains a three prong plug, the system does not have a ground path for the electrical motor because the ground wire is cut and not connected to anything (pics available).  This configuration is clearly manufactured this way.  This hoist is just one model in a line of multiple units, and given it comes from China likely comes in other "brand" names.
It is very easy to rationalize a failure within the electric motor that results in an electrical short providing an pathway for current from the host outlet, through the cord, control panel, motor, chassis, down the steel hoist cable (with a steel hook) that would electrify whatever it is connected too.  The steel cable and hook are touch points where an individual can become electrocuted if they came in contact with it during a failed state as well as whatever is likely attached to the hoist (which can also become a hazard if electrified)
Ironically, the documentation provided with the hoist lists several "general safety rules" and the very first two rules state the source sockets must comply with safety rules and the socket plug must be grounded.  Unfortunately any proper grounding of the electrical circuit from the host outlet will not provide the protection it is intended to due to the hazardous wiring inside the hoist's system.
justification: The incident describes a hazardous situation with potential for severe injury or death due to lack of grounding, but no actual incident or injury has occurred yet.

incident_description:
On September 16th and 17th 2021, DeVere Insulation installed Demilec Sealection 500 in three attics of my house in Crownsville, Maryland. 


The first sign of an issue was a lingering odor. The odor was so strong 72 hours after installation that we did not move back into the house. The odor permeated through areas of the house that were near the attics. Ventilators have since been added and maintained for over six months, but the odor remains even in the cold of Winter. After being in the house for ten to fifteen minutes, we have reactions which include headaches, sore throat, watery and burning eyes, congestion, and blurred vision. 


The manufacturer took a foam sample from each of the three areas on October 5th, 2021. The manufacturer has informed me that they will not be providing me the results of the foam test. This was also when the manufacturer informed me that Sealection 500 was installed as opposed to DemilecÃÂs APX and Agribalance that was in the installation contract.


The installer commissioned a VOC test three weeks after installation - October 7, 2021. This test found an amine catalyst from the spray foam in the air. This report concluded that the house should continue to be ventilated, and that further testing was needed before reoccupancy. This report is attached. 


An environmental consultant was commissioned to take a sample of the foam and perform a chamber test. The sample was taken on December 17th, 2021 - three months after the spray foam was applied. The test found Hexamethylcyclotrisiloxane (37 ÃÂµg/m2 -h), Bis (2-(dimethylamino)ethyl) ether (5,300 ÃÂµg/m2 -h), Bis(1-chloro-2-propyl)(3-chloro-1-propyl)phosphate (57 ÃÂµg/m2 -h) among others. Acrolein (23 ÃÂµg/m2 -h) and Propianol (19 ÃÂµg/m2 -h) were among the substances found to be emitting at a rate that would exceed the EPAÃÂs regional screening level for cancer. The chamber analysis was performed at 35 degrees celsius (95 degrees fahrenheit).  The full report is attached which recommends complete removal of the foam, and remediation of the affected areas. According to the EPA, there is no known remediation for Spray Foam. Extensive communication with many sealant companies has confirmed the EPAÃÂs conclusion. 


The manufacturer lists a single compound in the Finished Foam Safety Data Sheet - Urethane Plastics (CAS# 9009-54-5) at 100%. A maximum service temperature of 180 degrees fahrenheit is also noted in the Finished Foam Safety Data Sheet. 


In December of 2021  my wife and I visited our doctors to discuss our symptoms and the results of the VOC test. Each doctor independently directed us to no longer enter the house due to the catalyst in the air, and directed us to wear a respirator if entering the house was absolutely necessary.
justification: The incident caused physical injuries (headaches, sore throat, watery and burning eyes, congestion, and blurred vision) and required medical consultation, indicating a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) given the specific circumstances of the installation and the materials used.

To whom it may concern:
