Two of the pods stuck together which I found to be quite common as they sit under my kitchen sink and acquire moisture. I twisted to get it detached and the chemicals & plastic from the pods blew directly into my left eye. The intense burning and pain was indescribable. I started flushing immediately at my kitchen sink. I immediately contacted [REDACTED] ER to see how I should proceed. I was told to contact poison control of WI. I did and was then told to go immediately into the shower for 20 minutes to start flushing, afterwards to go to dark place to rest the eye. The poison control nurse called me back in 45 minutes from the initial time of my 1st call. Since I was not any better, she advised me to go immediately to the ER. She contacted [REDACTED] in Janesville, WI at which time I immediately went.

I was put directly in the eye room where numbing drops were applied and I was offered pain medication while they continued to check the pH of my left eye. The RN then proceeded to place the Morgan lens into my left eye and 1000 cc of IV fluid was instilled into my left eye due to the chemical burn. The pain was unbearable. I was discharged and told to follow up with ophthalmology. I went to see my optometrist that afternoon. She again checked the pH at which time my left eye was too high alkaline due to the chemical burn & plastic from the pod explosion in my left eye. She told me then to go after the company for this corneal abrasion. She irrigated my eye in the office and prescribed steroid & antibiotic drops. I left the office in tears from the pain.

That night the pain became even worse to the point I was crying out due to the difficulties of light entering my eye and the swollenness and redness I was experiencing. Drainage continued with pus and fluids leaving my left eye. My husband took pictures of both my eyes for documentation. He then proceeded to call the ophthalmologist on call while I was calling the ER back.

My husband took me to [REDACTED] ER immediately. I was again checked for pH, given the vision test where I could only see the big E from my left eye. The ER doctor did a complete evaluation of my left eye. She told me that the pain of chemical exposure and burn to the eye is one of the worst pains seen in the ER. She prescribed narcotics and an antibiotic eye ointment. Both ER visits that day I was told what a familiar occurrence this is in the ER, pods causing chemical burns to the eyes. My husband and I then went to [REDACTED] to get both prescriptions filled while I was in utter tears due to the pain this caused.

We came home and I took 2 narco which gave me sleep from 11pm to 4am.

I followed up the next day with my optometrist where she told me the eye was doing better than the day before but it was going to be a long process. Again, she told me that I should go after the company. She reached out to a corneal specialist and I was asked to follow-up with her on Monday, January 24th. She told me to continue with the drops, the ointment, and the pain mediation at bedtime.

I have [REDACTED] this type of eye injury caused by this product and [REDACTED] is filled with people who have suffered the same problem.

I am asking for the immediate withdrawal of this product from the consumer market.

Sincerely,
[Signed]

[REDACTED]

incident_description:
The customer and the installation technician noticed the problem upon installation in 2014. The gas fireplace insert has a glass front panel. During operation the glass can reach 500 degrees or more. To protect against contact with the glass, the fireplace insert comes with a hinged metal frame door with a metal screen inset. 

The hinged door is attached to hinges on one side and is held closed on the other by a magnet. Because a child or pet could easily open the door, the manufacturer provides a child safety lock. This lock attaches to the door and to the otherwise unused hinge on the right side of the fireplace and makes it impossible to open the door without a screwdriver and some knowledge. 

The technician could not install the child safety lock on this unit. The lock itself is a 1" high L-shaped bracket. The alignment between the door tab and the hinge on the right side of the fireplace is such that the "L" bracket will not fit. The technician gave up trying to install it and said he would check with the service people at the store. There was no further communication from them on this. 

2015: A technician from the same company came out for a customer-paid annual checkup. During his visit, the customer raised the issue again, and again there was no solution. 

2021 December: A technician from the same company came out to replace the fireplace remote controller and the customer again raised the issue. The technician attempted to install the lock but again found it impossible. The technician said he would check with the service department for a solution. No further communication occurred. The customer emphasized the importance of this because of the plan to purchase a puppy. 

2022 February: The customer called the installation company service department, spoke to the service scheduler, explained the problem and the need since the puppy had arrived. The customer offered to send pictures and a detailed writeup, which he did. She forwarded the info to the Service Manager. The Service Manager replied by e-mail: "That lock was always a little tricky to install, but the piece you have is correct and should not be altered. I would either put the slot on the hinge and then put the screw into the bracket and the front or if you are unable to get it that way you can attach the bracket onto the front as you did in the picture and slightly lift and drop the front into the locked position. These were the two common methods to do this." 

The customer responded via e-mail that it was physically impossible to fit the bracket on, as had been evidenced by the failure of the store's technicians. Further, it was not possible to pursue the second idea since it would require the door to be raised 3/16" and still be able to sit securely on the hinge, which is only 4/16" high. 

The service manager did not respond to that e-mail. 
(continued)
justification: The incident involves a potential safety hazard with a gas fireplace insert, but no actual injury or death has occurred.

I had stacked three HeatTrak "Heated Snow Melting Stair Mats" (Residential Heated Stair Mat (10" x 30")) on top of each other, on a PVC/wood deck.   The mats had been turned off by triggering the vendor-provided GFCI.  However, the GFCI apparently was an electronic switch; a neighborhood power outage caused the GFCI to reset, resulting the mats becoming energized.

They overheated, melting through and fusing together; they also damaged and melted the PVC coating on the decking.  The pictures show the result (although the deck picture was taken after I had scrapped off the melted black mat material)

A combination of events combined to result in this failure.  First, I made the erroneous assumption that I could turn the mats on and off by using the GFCI test button.  That had always worked for me; I did not realize that if there was a power outage, it would be reset.  Second, I'm sure the vendor did not expect people to stack the units on top of each other.  However, I had no idea they would get so hot as to self-destruct.   Third, these mats should simply not be used with PVC wood-core decking.
justification: The incident caused property damage (melted mats and deck) but no injuries or deaths.

incident_description:
I am a retail pharmacist who had a patient come to my store after they had mistakenly used a toilet bowl deodorizer in their eye.  This patient believed that this product was an eye drop that they had sitting out on their bathroom countertop.  Immediately the patient knew something was terribly wrong because her eye felt like it was on fire.  She flushed her eye with water as best she could, and then came to my pharmacy along with her husband.  I provided an eye irrigation flush to her and printed out the MSDS Sheet of the product and instructed them to go immediately to her eye doctor.  She went to her eye doctor who also provided eye irrigation as well as medication.  Fortunately, the measures that were taken by the patient, myself, and her eye doctor were enough to preserve her vision.  The patient experienced an extreme amount of pain and discomfort along with inflammation and excessive tearing as a result of using this product.  
The patient does not desire litigation and/or monetary compensation for her experience.  The sole purpose of this complaint is to prevent this from happening to someone else in the future who might not be so fortunate as to maintain their eyesight given this circumstance.  Perhaps their should be a change in the packaging and/or labelling of this product for such a prevention.  As a pharmacist with 14 years experience, I can certainly understand how this simple mistake on behalf of the patient could have happened and believe that it can be avoided in the future with such labelling changes.  The name of the product is called "Just a Drop Odor Eliminator".  It is a small, blue bottle that actually looks like an eye drop once the cap is removed.
justification: The patient experienced extreme pain, discomfort, inflammation, and excessive tearing, which constitutes an injury, but no permanent damage or death occurred.

incident_description: In July 2021 I contacted DC Garage Door Services to replace my existing garage door and garage door opener.  The cost of the door, opener and installation was $3500 and has been paid in full.  Less than a week after the garage door was installed, I went to close the garage door.  From the angle I was standing it looked like my car was not in the path of the garage door.  Unfortunately it was not and the garage door hit my car and continued to attempt to close and it kept trying to close until I hit the reverse button.  Because it kept closing on my car the door and frame crumpled like a cheap suit.  I was stunned and horrified as I watched my new garage door crumple up.  I called the company who installed the door and the same technician that installed it came out and told me I would be responsible for the repairs.  At the time I was so upset I wasn't thinking straight.  I could not afford to spend the money for repairs.  The technician was able to straighten the frame with his hand and we were able to operate it although the new door had dents.  I figured I would have to live with it until I could afford the repairs.  Well a few weeks later as it was shutting the door crumpled again.  I once again called the company that had installed it.  This time I remembered that our old garage door was shut multiple times over 25 years when there was an obstacle in the way and it always auto reversed.  It would auto reverse if a leaf was in it's path.  So I did some research and discovered that it is a federal law that all residential garage doors have 2 sensors to prevent the door from crushing people and cars, a light sensor and pressure sensor.  I even did a test that the article suggested to see if your doors sensors were working.  I put a roll of paper towels in the path of the door and shut and it hit the towels and kept shutting.  The same technician came back to our house.  This time I was not at home so he talked to my son and took absolutely no responsibility.  He said it was all our fault and we would have to pay for repairs.  The technician was gone when I returned so I called the company and I asked for an estimate for the repairs and I also asked that the supervisor call me and explain why this was our fault.  No one ever called me back.   Since then I have sent complaints to the BBB, the NC Attorney General and the Federal Trade Commission.  The letter that they sent to the BBB in response to my complaint stated that my son broke the garage door and that they had told me they would work with me on the cost to make it more affordable.  First of all, my son was not even there when it crumpled the first time and at no time did I even mention my son and they never even responded to my request for an estimate and an explanation, so their response was one big fat lie.  If I have paid a premium to have a garage door and opener installed, then before they leave they better make sure all safety sensors are working properly or inform me that they did not do that.  If the refuse to replace my bent panels, they should at least be responsible for making sure the sensors are in complete order.  That is their responsibility.
justification: The incident involved property damage (car and garage door) but no injuries or deaths, fitting severity level 2. The occurrence likelihood is 4 (likely) due to the repeated failure of safety sensors and the company's negligence.

incident_description: On November 27yh, 2021 I purchased a Soleil Digital Ceramic Heater Model #PTC-915W (date code 0521) from Walmart in Cheboygan, Michigan 49721.  The heater was purchased for supplemental heat in my seasonal cabin.  The heater was used two times, once in late November 2021 and during the evening of January15th, 2021.  The heater was operated on the low setting throughout the night.  At approximately 4am on Sunday January 16th I awoke from sleeping and was a little chilled.  At  this point I changed the heater setting  to High and went back to bed.  I woke up at 7am to the smell of burning plastic and discovered that the heater had stopped working.  I examined the end of the plug which incorporates a GFI and discovered that one of the prongs was melted and that the plastic receptacle was melted and burned on the hot leg (small slot).  The 15amp breaker for this circuit in the load center was tripped.  This heater was brand new and not modified in any way.  I examined the receptacle for correct wiring, making sure there wasn't a loose Hot, Neutral or ground wire.  All wires were wrapped around the attaching screws and all screws were tight.  I replaced the burnt receptacle and cover.  I reset the 15amp breaker and plugged a different non-ceramic heater into the plug.  The prongs on the non-ceramic heater never got hot and the heater performed correctly.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning heater causing a melted plug and receptacle, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
Google Nest Protect smoke detectors  are not sounding the alarm at every smoke detector when smoke is detected.   Google's specifications, as well as fire/building codes in California and other states, require smoke detectors to sound an alarm at every detector when any detector senses smoke.  

This is a serious safety hazard. This functionality is required to ensure that everyone in a house is alerted when a fire is detected somewhere in the building.

Details: My home has 7 Nest Protect smoke detectors. I have tested the system using a blown out match as well as canned smoke at multiple different detectors. In each case, the individual Protect detected the smoke and sounded its alarm (an actual "emergency" alarm--not a "heads up").  In addition, I receive an "Emergency: There is smoke" notification on my phone. However, the alarm did not sound on any of the other 6 Nest Protects.  Nest's built-in test shows that all 7 Protects are correctly interconnected and operating properly. 

I have reported this issue to Google's support on 3 separate occasions with no response:
1) On 10/27/2021, I reported this to Google's chat support.  After escalation, Google told me they do not recommend testing the Nest Protect this way and disconnected.
2) On 10/27/2021, I reported this to Google's phone support.  The support rep agreed this was an issue, escalated the incident to the Nest safety team and told me I should hear back within 24 hours.  I have not yet had a response.
3) On October 31, I posted this incident on Google's Nest Community.  The Product Expert there agreed this was an issue and escalated it to the Google team.  I have not yet had a response.
justification: The incident describes a failure in the interconnected alarm system, which is a safety hazard but no injury or death has occurred.

incident_description: I own a Glowforge laser cutting system. The company is based out of Seattle. After a little over a year of use I have come to the conclusion that these machines appear to be built using very unsafe design practices and their use could lead to catastrophic fire. Electrical faults are rife. The component layout is dangerous. The tube cooling capacity is poor and susceptible to overheating. The main cable that controls the laser head is exceptionally easy to damage during cleaning or maintenance, and the insulation wears off alarmingly quickly, exposing the conductor traces. The main cable also runs very close the stepper motor. These motors run very warm and there is not adequate separation between it and the cable to ensure safety (or reliability). The cable then runs through the drag chain, where it is subject to a great deal of friction and wear. In addition, the machine is advertised as a 'Pro' device that is able to cut wood, acrylic and more. However, the electronics, heat sink and exhaust fan are all located next to each other in the same area of the machine. The accumulation of dirt in fumes in both the fan and over those critical components is alarming. The design reduces cooling capacity over time. Finally, there is a red tension cable that carries around 26,000 volts and feeds the laser tube. This cable is not designed to be flexed or strained at all and is very fragile. However, the high tension cable is installed next to the main ribbon cable (mentioned above) which carry control signs. Mains and high voltage signals should also be separated by a considerable margin for safety - the potential for noise and errors passing between the cables could cause glitches, faults and represent a fire hazard. The final area I am concerned with is the ducting supplied with the system. The ductwork expands every time the machine is in use and the creasing and uncreasing cause punctures in the duct, allowing cutting fumes to vent into the user's work space. The ductwork is not rated for fume extraction. Overall, all of these flaws combined means not only is the machine being falsely advertised as a 'Pro' commercial production unit, it's incredibly unsafe. The vast majority of these lasers are sold and marketed to at-home hobbyists who would not typically be familiar with the threat of electrical failure and fire these design flaws could lead to. The Glowforge Owner's forum (which the company runs) is filled with many comments/tickets about fires in these machines, so the company knows these can lead to life-threatening problems but has done nothing to correct these issues. I feel very strongly there should be a recall on these machines.
justification: The description highlights multiple design flaws that could lead to electrical faults, overheating, and fire hazards, posing a significant risk of injury or death.

The company, W Appliance, Inc. in New York City, has not returned my phone message in which I said I wanted to alert to a potential safety issue with the product. I purchased two of these, both of which have this problem.

ADDITIONAL INFO: The issue is the unit's electronic display shows a single red "plug" icon when the appliance is OFF but connected to a live outlet. It also shows the same icon when the built-in thermostat places the unit in STANDBY because the room temperature has reached the set level. As a result, a user could mistake that red light icon to mean that the appliance is OFF, when in fact it is in STANDBY, able to come on at any time by itself when the room cools down. If the user goes to bed, leaves the room or otherwise leaves the appliance  unattended believing the appliance is OFF when it actually is in STANDBY, this could create a fire hard, especially if the unit is set at 1500 watts and is aimed at a couch, bed or other combustible item. The user manual says: "To shut unit off at any time, press the POWER Button until all indicator lights go OFF. (see attached scan) " But all the indicator light do NOT go OFF. Instead, that one light stays on if the appliance is OFF and connected to live power. (Consumers have an incentive to leave the product plugged because it has a memory function that retains the  thermostat and heat setting unless the product is unplugged.)
justification: The product's misleading display and potential to overheat could lead to a fire hazard, posing a risk of property damage or injury if left unattended.

incident_description: The Knox Safety 7200 CO alarm I bought at Walmart on Oct 14, 2021 (serial #2335), stopped working  11 days after activation on Oct 25 without giving any audio or visual warning--but while still showing 0 ppm constantly, as if it was working fine. This is an extremely dangerous and potentially deadly failure mode that should not occur! It's been stuck like this for a week now: pushing the 3 function buttons has no effect, and neither the display nor the voice messages respond to CO exposure.  It failed while on battery power although the battery appears to still be working and plugging it in again did not fix anything.  Looking at the unit, the only clue it is not working is that the display shows 3 icons next to 0 PPM,  for Danger, Call 911, and Exit. This combination is not described in the manual, which says a trash can icon with the word REPLACE should display when the unit fails for any reason.  I emailed 4 key staff at Knox Safety a pic of the failed display along with a list of over a dozen other problems, asking for a replacement under warranty and urging a nationwide recall, but got no reply.  Among the other problems (which I also found in a 2nd 7200 unit, serial # 2549) are A) they displayed  0 when exposed together (along with a calibrated professional CO detector) under a glass bowl to CO in the range of 30 to 50 ppm for 20 minutes; B) when exposed to CO over 1000ppm, both  displays showed a 4-digit level once, after which they cut off the right digit, so 1234 displays as 123; C) the double beep/flash warning that a "low level" of CO has been detected (before the full alarm with starts) repeats every 60 seconds, not every 10 seconds as the manual says, nor every 30 seconds as the label on back of alarm says; and D) when plugged in, they emit a high pitched whine that is very irritating, and this is still present in the unit that failed.   I have attached a table comparing the Knox 7200 with other UL2034 alarms to how they differ in other important respects.    (Full disclosure: I am a consulting toxicologist who specializes in CO poisoning, but I have no affiliation with any home CO alarm companies and am filing this incident report on my own behalf.)
justification: The CO alarm failed to detect dangerous levels of CO, posing a potentially deadly risk, but no actual injury or death was reported.

We purchased four of these products and sent them to a third party lab, [REDACTED], to be tested. The products were tested over a period of 48 hours and seven days in a chamber with radon levels of 26 pCi/L. The products showed average radon levels of 1.16 pCi/L and 1.17 pCi/L. I reported this to the Illinois Attorney General and to Amazon - to this day, these are still being sold on Amazon and consumers are relying on these to let them know their radon levels in their homes.
justification: The incident involves inaccurate radon detectors being sold to consumers, which could lead to undetected high radon levels, but no actual injury or death is reported.

incident_description:
I own a home with a storm shelter  (FEMA rated Safe Room) built in.  Is is made of filled concrete block with a concrete slab on the top and bottom and a FEMA rated storm shelter door as the only exit.  The door has 3 Medico single cylinder deadbolts and an ASSA passage set for entry and exit.

Yesterday, I found myself locked out of our storm shelter and determined that the latch was not retracting when the handle was turned.  Having had locksmith training, I knew the problem was that the latch had become disengaged from the mechanism that retracts the latch when the handle is turned.  The only way to get the door open was to remove the handle and bezel and cut off the outside flange with an angle grinder since the hardware is only designed to be removed from the inside.  Unfortunately, the paint on the door was damaged a little in the process and the lock was destroyed.

After removing the lockset and getting the door open I was able to confirm  the problem.  When the latch was installed it was not completely perpendicular to the lock mechanism; it was slanted slightly toward the exterior of the door.  The lockset's retraction mechanism has a slot into which the latch retractor fits.  There is a gap on both ends just wide enough for the retractor to slip out of contact with the retractor.  The latch retractor was able to work its way into the gap on the exterior side so the little ears on the retractor were not within the slot.  When the handle awas turned it failed to pull the latch with it, effectively locking the door even though it is a passage set. I do not know why ASSA would leave a gap like that in the retraction mechanism. Making the tab thicker on the latch retractor would prevent this from being able to happen.  The passage set worked fine for the last year or so; it did not happen right away.

This is a  serious problem.  If a family was inside the shelter when it failed like this there would be no possible way to get themselves out; they'd be trapped unless they had tools to remove the handle, bezel, and lock mechanism and retract the latch manually from inside the hole.  In a storm situation when cell towers are down this could result in a life threatening situation, especially if there was extensive damage and emergency response was overwhelmed and it took a long time to check damaged houses. 

I feel very lucky that this happened before we needed it and that we were not inside when it failed.

Thank you

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a life-threatening situation where individuals could be trapped in a storm shelter with no means of escape, potentially leading to death if emergency response is delayed.

incident_description:
I have six Kidde P4010ACS smoke alarms installed in my house.  Kidde sent these to me as a replacement for a recalled version I had previously purchased.  That alarm was recalled because they experienced a high rate of false alarms.  I installed these replacement alarms back in May 2021.

At 1:15am last night all detectors in my house started screaming FIRE! FIRE!   My kids freaked out, everyone ran downstairs, and then after realizing there was no smoke in the house I started checking each alarm.  I disconnected one in a bedroom which was rapidly flashing red/green and silenced it, at which point all the other alarms finally stopped.  This faulty unit immediately went to an amber/red/pause flashing sequence, which the back of the unit indicates either means "faulty alarm, low battery, or end of unit life".

The unit was silent (but disconnected) the rest of the night.  This morning when I picked it up it started screaming FIRE! FIRE! again, and when I tried to silence it, the unit said "CANNOT SILENCE, TOO MUCH SMOKE".  I then broke the safety tab and permanently disabled the alarm and battery (which is built in and not removable).  

My youngest child was in tears last night once this ordeal was over.
justification: The false alarms caused significant distress, especially to the youngest child who was in tears, indicating emotional injury.

I removed the batteries from the detector and put them outside, and have stopped using the detector. This Protect is a second-generation unit manufactured on September 14, 2017, and the serial number is 06AA01AC371703AE. I have four other Nest Protects in my home and am concerned about them having the same issue. I bought these devices to protect my home against fire, not start fires.

incident_description:
My Kwikset 99380-001 Halo Wi-Fi Smart Lock Keyless Entry Electronic Keypad Deadbolt melted and burned the tips of two of my fingers on Sept 23, 2021.
On the late evening of Sept 22, 2021 I was in the laundry room that has a door to the garage and I thought I smelled a faint smell of something odd, like a sort of burnt toast.   I checked all around and could not find the smell and it went away.   The following day the Kwikset door lock in this room alerted us that its battery was dead and needed replacing.   Later on Sept 23, 2021 I removed the battery pack from the lock housing and replaced all three 1.5 volt AA batteries, then reinstalled the battery pack .  I then went to verify the locks operation and the lock would illuminate but would not lock or unlock.  Then I started to smell a strong smell of something burning and I could see smoke emanating from the just installed battery pack.   I tried to remove the battery pack from the lock housing by lifting up on the plastic removal tab, as I had done previously, it is at this point I burnt my finger tips on the molten plastic.   I then went to the garage and got a dental pick to pull the battery pack out.  Once the battery pack was removed the battery pack stopped melting and smoking.   
My fingers were sore but OK, no lasting damage.   
I then notified Kwikset about what just happened and uploaded pictures to them using their online tool.  
I asked Kwikset if there were any recalls on this product and they said no and there were no know issues. They issued me a case number and said they wanted the complete assembly returned to them for analysis using the prepaid label they provided.
They told me they were sending me a identical replacement as soon as they reviewed the pictures.
I am concerned for several reasons:
- My fingers got burned.
- I do not know what would have happened if I was not home and this happened as the door to the garage is a light wood door.  I do not know if the plastic in the battery pack and cover would ignite or just melt.
- I do not know if the plastic just melted could it have melted and jammed the locking mechanism making it impossible to exit or enter via this door.
- At the time I purchased the Kwikset lock that failed I purchased an identical lock, only difference is the color, and installed it in another door.
justification: The incident resulted in minor burns to the fingers, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is rated as 2 (unlikely) since the issue appears to be an isolated incident with no known prior issues reported.

-What happened:
At about 7:45 AM I was preparing to iron a shirt and get ready to leave for work. I stood the iron (Rowenta DW2459 steam iron) on the ironing board and plugged in it to warm it up. Approximately 2 minutes after plugging in the iron, it started smoking with a toxic burning plastic smelling smoke. The smoke immediately filled the closet where I was about to iron. I unplugged the iron and I ran to remove my 4 year old child from the bedroom that was also beginning to fill with smoke, and came back to get the iron and take it outside. It took me only about 10 seconds to return to the room and by that time the iron ignited in flames. I grabbed it by the handle, and ran outside to my back patio and set the iron down vertically. I used a water hose and sprayer to put out the fire. I used my cell phone to capture a few seconds of video while I was putting out the fire and then left the iron there to go tell my wife what happened. She was in a upstairs room with our child, she came into the the closet area with me and we saw that the ironing board was still smoldering and smoking. At that time I noticed that there was a puddle of molten metal about 3 to 4 inches in diameter, sitting on the ironing board and smoking. There were also a few drips of the metal on the floor. We used a water spray bottle to extinguish and cool the metal. I also to a few seconds of video of this and a couple of pictures. We left the room as we were having to hold our breath. I closed the bedroom door to contain the smoke. I returned with a garage fan and set it up in the bedroom window to exhausted the smoke. I also opened a smaller window near the closet to allow cross ventilation. Later, I collected the cooled pieces of metal that spilled from inside the iron. I have also saved the iron.

-Type of product(s) were being used:
 Rowenta Steam Iron for cloths. Model: Rowenta DW2459 Access Steam Iron. Purchased 03/13/2020

-How were the product(s) being used?:
This is a clothing iron, that is used on an ironing board. At the time of the incident, it was standing vertically on the ironing board, and had just been plugged in in preparation for ironing a button-up shirt.  Prior to this incident it has been used normally on an ironing board, and has never had any issues, leaks or damage of any kind.

-Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?:
I was exposed to smoke that smelled noxious. I tried not to breath it, but did breath some. There were no know injuries. I did have a headache for most of the day, but is has subsided.
justification: The incident involved a smoking and flaming iron with no reported injuries, only exposure to smoke and a temporary headache.

incident_description:
FACTS 
On 03/20/21 I purchased a Hyper Tough (corded) circular saw from Wal-Mart in Eufaula, Alabama. Hyper Tough 120 V 12 AMP 7-1/4 inch corded circular saw model # AQ10019G. UPC Code 8952618126.  I did not notice that the protective guard on the Hyper Tough saw leaves a significant portion of the blade exposed in the front (several teeth). My sonÃÂs [REDACTED] circular saw is designed much better, and his blade guard fully covers the cutting blade.
I also did not notice how weak the return spring on the guard cover was on the Hyper Tough saw. It does not snap the blade guard cover back in place like my sonÃÂs [REDACTED] saw.  On 04/02/21 while cutting a board using my Hyper Tough circular saw, I was severely injured. My wife was holding the board. I am extremely dominant right-handed. I was crouched down doing the cutting. I was using two hands to run the saw, with my right hand operating the trigger and safety. The saw made a loud popping sound and kicked backward into the air, with a force hard enough to snatch it completely out of my hands. The saw struck me in the head, and landed on my right thumb, cutting it 95 percent off my hand. The inner skin was all that held my thumb on.  The poorly designed blade cover allowed the injury to happen.  The return spring failed to allow the blade cover to close, even if it did not completely close.
Why was the saw blade still spinning long enough to sever my right thumb if my right hand was completely off the saw trigger and safety?  I was hospitalized due to the injury. Two separate surgeries were required to re-attach my thumb, bones, tendons, and nerves. I had four screws and one pin holding my thumb in place.  On 05/21/21, I had the long push pin in the end of my thumb removed. On 06/18/21, I had the four screws in the side of my thumb removed. The bones, and tendons appear to be healing.  As of today - 08/25/21, my thumb still appears to be swollen, mangled, scarred, and completely numb from the cut line upward. It is essentially a door stop, and I am pretty much right hand disabled, but at least I still have my thumb. I guess that I was somewhat lucky. The saw could have zipped across my face, neck, or cut my right hand off. In any of those three cases, I would likely be dead. That is something the next Hyper Tough customer / victim may face.  I have been using power tools for 51 years (since I was 10) and have never been inured prior to 04/02/21. This ÃÂAccidentÃÂ due to a poorly and negligently designed defective saw has cost me $6,000 out of pocket and much trauma and pain as of today. I have several photos as evidence.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injury requiring multiple surgeries and ongoing disability, but no death occurred.

incident_description: I received a replacement motor, p/n F0512B2506  from Air Vent, Inc. to replace a motor for an Air Vent attic ventilator that failed during the warranty period. Using a old shirt, I moved the batteries onto a shelf, but I'm worried the might catch fire (thinking about all the lithium ion battery problems from a few years ago). Very scary.

I contacted the manufacturer and they sent my case to their safety department. They promised to get back to me.

I screwed in the entire cap and then removed the orange top section, which after reading the instructions later is the correct way to do this.  I knew that the white section was for piercing the tube, but I don't think at the time that I realized that the tube was pierced.  After removing the top orange part of the cap, some super glue spilled out of the tube and got on the middle and lower part of my index and middle fingers, and a very small amount near the tip of my thumb.  I think that the middle and index fingers may have been stuck together very briefly, but I was able to separate them and rinse my fingers under running water and also used liquid soap.  I was not injured, it's more just an annoyance trying to scrape off the dried up glue that is stuck to my fingers.  I'm not fully clear if this was due to my error, but I don't believe that I squeezed the tube and most likely the tube was just pointing down and the glue spilled out.  Even if this was my error, I think that the instructions about how the cap works and to not squeeze the cap when puncturing need to be much more prominent and not just in the small print directions on the back of the package that likely no one reads (I didn't because I've used super glue a few times before and wasn't expecting a problem).  After the fact when I read the instructions there was a paragraph with advice for bonded skin or fingers, so I guess this is a common problem.  What happened to me is very trivial, and I'm only reporting this because I'm worried that someone else could have a much more serious problem than I did if they get this in their eyes or elsewhere.
justification: No injury occurred, only minor annoyance from glue spillage.

incident_description:
I recently purchased an ismartgate pro and two additional sensors for my garage door.ÃÂ ÃÂ When installing the batteries in the sensors, I noticed they immediately started to get warm.ÃÂ ÃÂ Upon closer inspection I realized what was happening but it too me too long and when I tried to get the batteries out they were so hot I got a really bad burn from them.

The batteries are installed into the wireless sensor via two sets of clips.  These clips are one complete metal part to their positive or negative terminal counterparts.  When installing the battery, it is very likely that the metal will score the battery enough so that the positive and negative ends of the battery short itself out.  This will very, very quickly result in the battery getting critically hot-- hot enough to burn you or start a fire.  If you catch this, you have mere seconds to get the batteries out of the device before things get out of hand.  This is an absolutely terrible and unsafe design.  The leads should be completely isolated from the battery clips.  This is sheer engineering laziness and cost-savings measures and someone is going to get hurt or killed because of this.

I emailed the support people at ismartgate and my email was ignored for a week.  Clearly they do not care about this.
justification: The user suffered a really bad burn from the overheating batteries, indicating an injury.

incident_description: I purchased a Hyundai 2000SI Generator, and it failed during recent routine use and was no longer under warranty.  After starting the engine, you could hear arcing/sparking and the Overload light illuminated on the control panel.  This happened, even with nothing connected to the generator.  I am an Aircraft Electrician, so I perform many repairs myself.  Upon disassembling the generator, I discovered that the inverter coils and other components were only installed with plastic zip ties (commonly used for securing wiring harnesses - not in place of correct mounting hardware).  The zip ties ultimately failed, permitting the coils to move, chafe and short out.  There was evidence of burning/overheating, and this component is located directly below the 1 gallon gas tank.  A fire in this area could melt the gas supply hose, and cause a catastrophic fire.  This is manufacturing negligence, not a fair ÃÂwear and tearÃÂ failure.  Upon performing an online search, other videos documenting the same condition were easily located.  I have several photos showing the damaged components.
justification: The generator failure could lead to a fire hazard, posing a risk of injury or death, but no actual injury or death was reported in this incident.

incident_description:
I had a hazardous injury using the Screen Tight Roller Knife product when using the product as intended - rolling spline into the Screen Tight Mini Track system. I purchased the tool because the handle looked more comfortable to grasp when rolling spline, but had purchased a separate knife to use for cutting. I have done screening before, and watched their online video to ensure I was installing it properly. I was working in the left corner of the room, holding the screen and spline in place with my left hand, and rolling with the tool in my right hand. As I was rolling, the bottom of the tool brushed over my left hand. It only took a second to register that I had been cut and now had a long, deep, bloody gash in the back of my left hand and immediately went to seek care. 

When I arrived home after the ER patched me up, I took a look at the tool to figure out why I was injured: The blade had self-deployed. The black latch (intended to be manually deployed by the user to release the blade) had released on its own, without anything touching it (please see video of how easily this blade deploys). Apparently, normal use (rolling spline) or a few quick shakes can cause the blade to unknowingly self-deploy. To add to the agony of the injury, I again had to seek medical care 48 hours later, as my entire hand swelled up and had to be treated for an infection.

It took a long time to work out reimbursement of my medical bills with Screen Tight, and as you will see from my attached correspondence, I was willing to cooperate with the company in any way necessary to ensure others donÃÂt get hurt, but the company designated representative seemingly implied that I was improperly using the tool, and he did not ask for me to send the tool to them for evaluation. Whether it's a defective tool or poor product design isn't something I can opine on, but itÃÂs likely one or the other.

In the weeks while I was waiting for resolution, I read through the online reviews and lost count after seeing at least THREE DOZEN reviews on both Home Depot and [REDACTED] websites that mention blade malfunctions with this product since 2011, and a few reviewers state they had been injured, so it appears as though my injury and experience is not isolated.  Please see my attached documents for more detail.

incident_description:
Hi,

I recently purchased a home built in 2018 and was not made aware by the builder of the home (Lennar corporation) or the manufacturer of the floor joists (Weyerhaeuser) that the joists were coated with formaldehyde.  After we purchased the home I removed the basement ceiling sheetrock in order to start the process to complete the basement.  After we removed the ceiling sheetrock and exposed the defective joists my family and friends that visited the basement became very sick with formaldehyde poisoning symptoms (chest tightness, nose and throat pain).  I reached out to multiple industrial hygienists to learn more about the formaldehyde coated joists.  It is their opinion that the joists off-gassed into the joist cavity and was trapped above the sheetrock.  When I removed the sheetrock a large puff of the toxic gas was released into the home.  There were no warnings or indicators that above the sheetrock there was this dangerous gas or defective floor joists.
I am doing some research on formaldehyde levels in my home and would appreciate your help. My family was recently sick with formaldehyde poisoning symptoms and after having an expert come test our house we found out that our home has HCHO levels that are elevated. Will you please help me understand what are safe and acceptable levels of HCHO in a home where adults and children live essentially 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year?
 
Thank you in advance for any help you may provide.
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in multiple people experiencing formaldehyde poisoning symptoms, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is rated as 4 (likely) due to the described exposure and symptoms.

incident_description: I have a young son who turns 4 in July, my home was built in 1984  and due to our current and future needs I've determined that a electrical sub panel needs to be installed to lighten the load of a few 15 and 20 amp circuits that are close to/at risk of being overloaded if any new devices are added to them. When it comes to my sons young age and the increasing age of my home, 35+ years, advancements in device safety and the laundry list of recommended updates of the past 13 editions of the National  Electric Code since my home was built. Due to my extreme desire to keep my entire family safe, my 3 year old son from doing something really stupid like shoving a metal object into an outlet... Much like his dear ol' dad did around his age, I'm now 32 and remember it vividly but it has led to a lifelong interest in all things electric and I make my living as a day trader and the stock market my degree is in electrical engineering which is great but it was stupid and I don't recommend it and to keep my home not on fire I have a pretty long list updates to get done from install the sub panel to updating the receptacles' to tamper resistant ones as well as adding ones with USB charging and or GFCI/AFCI etc, updated breakers and adding circuits and receptacles' where needed. The main purpose is for my family and I to be safe and if I couldn't do any of these updates safely or to a high enough level where I can guarantee it was done correctly and poses no risk from poor installation or use of the wrong tool etc I would more than happily have a professional handle it and step one of just about any electrical  job is shutting off the power to either the whole home or to the circuit being worked on. Just to be safe I always use my KLEIN TOOLS Circuit Breaker finder tool in the outlet, light fixture or switch being worked on so the correct breaker is turned off, I then would power on one of the 2 now recalled non contact voltage tester, test it on an outlet or fixture that noticeably working then check the device I was going to start working on. I felt that it wasn't really working properly and one day at Home Depot to purchase a KLEIN TOOLS fiberglass fish tape which is kept locked up I had to have an employee in the electrical dept. unlock it for me I asked a few questions about the non contact voltage tester mainly have you had any issues or complaints with it and was told "you turn it on, put it up to your thing and it'll beep or flash or something like that" but said in a manner as if I were an idiot and I am many things but not as dumb as I look. I then asked if it works with DC current knowing that it does not and was promptly told "yeah up to 1000 volts". That confirmed he was not going to be and couldn't be any help I purchased another identical tester which seemed to work fine for several week until replacing an outlet in the garage added by the original owner which happened to be split and serviced by 2 different circuits, no knowing this at the time I turned off only the breaker servicing half of the duplex receptacle, checking on a working fixture and immediately to the one I was replacing, placing the tester at the hot wires, neutral wires then repeating multiple times which I commonly do. I then turned the device to loosen the screws and removed 1 hot wire  moving to the next when I brushed against the first wire I had removed but was still live on a separate 120 volt 20 amp circuit and gave myself a pretty good jolt, good enough to cause the lights briefly dim according to my wife and prompting her to come into the garage from the next room where she was doing laundry. She later told me that I looked a bit dazed which I don't doubt, I've been zapped a few times in my life, not in many years but that one is certainly rather memorable. A days to a week later I was replacing an outlet in our laundry room with a GFCI which is now required the 2008 revision of the N.E.C. I believe, did thing as I normally would testing all wires within the junction box, none appeared to be live or another circuit which was not the case as wire from another circuit other than the one I was working on which I had turn the breaker feeding it off testing before and after but it was live as you or I and gave myself another pretty good jolt. I have been beating myself up about zapping myself a few times because I'm not recklessly just jumping into boxes or doing thing incorrectly or that I'm not capable of doing at a high/professional level because it all about my family and them being safe above all else especially with 2 different testers. 1 okay things happen but 2 the problem most likely is user error usually. I buy KLEIN TOOLS for a reason, yeah I can get tools much much cheaper, they sell entire sets for the cost of my Klein 1000v insulated wire strippers which aren't even the top of the line model I don't think but there is a reason for the higher cost and the same reason KLEIN has been making tools, making great tools since 1857 or something like that which is why I've been really hard on myself for these preventable few zaps recently but since the second I've not used that tester and have been using one made by [REDACTED] that actually built into a clamp multimeter oddly enough but has since worked fine. Sadly I'm actually glad that I haven't been as absent minded as I have been thinking over these past few month's but equally as glad to see the KLEIN TOOLS issued this recall on their own with such few reports of them being a bit wonky but clearly I know for a fact, 2 facts actually  that they were right to do it and will still happily be paying way more for my various KLEIN TOOLS. But [REDACTED] OUCH!!! And hopefully this recall stops any additional weekend warriors, DIYers and or electrical engineering degree holding stock brokers from a good zap and the visual disapproval  from their Mrs... I don't recommend either
justification: The incident describes receiving an electric shock, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The likelihood is possible (3) given the context of DIY electrical work.

incident_description:
Casement windows were installed in our new home.  They are Value Windows (https://www.valuewindowsdoors.com/windows/casement-windows/).  We were given instructions verbally for cleaning the exterior of the windows.  They are 20 feet above the ground.

When we attempting to follow the instructions, the window sash fell out of the window.  I was able to catch it before it fell to the ground, but I had to summon help to put it back into its frame.

Had I not caught the window, it would have fallen to the ground and might have severely injured or killed anyone below.  If a less-strong person had been attempting the cleaning (such as my 82-year-old wife), they might have fallen along with the window when attempting to save the window.  It is much too heavy for her.  Such a fall would certainly have cause extreme injury and possible death.

I will emphasize that we were following the cleaning instructions provided by our contractor.  An extremely dangerous situation resulted.  No one should be attempting to clean the outside of these windows from the inside.

Note that this location is my future home address and is under construction now.
justification: The window sash fell out but was caught, preventing injury, though the potential for severe injury or death was high if not caught.

incident_description: My wife uses a Lakewood Model 5600/7 Oil-Filled Radiant Electric Heater (manufactured by Lakewood Engineering & Manufacturing Company of Chicago) at night to keep her bedroom warm.  She keeps the heater on the first of three power settings and the thermostat set to just a bit less than halfway around its dial between minimum and maximum.  During the night while she was sleeping, the heater started emitting a strong odor of burnt plastic that filled the room, but it did not immediately awaken her.  She eventually woke up with a severe headache and nausea in the morning.  We immediately unplugged the heater and moved it outside, where it continued to emit this foul burned odor.  It was obvious to us that something inside failed, though it was still putting out heat.  We also opened windows in her room for cross-ventillation and put strong fans at the window sills to evacuate the strong odor.  During the removal of the heater and placing of the fan, the smell was so strong, I got nauseous and developed a headache, and my eyes began to sting and water profusely.  It took several hours of circulating fresh air into the room to make it habitable again, and many of the fabrics on my wife's bedding and clothing were saturated with the odor.  There was no obvious smoke, soot or aerosols visible.  This is the SECOND time a similar failure has happened with this exact brand and model of heater, but the first time (two years ago) the appliance was in use and we detected the smell immediately.  In both cases, we'd already been using the appliances for at least two years.
justification: The incident caused severe headaches, nausea, and eye irritation, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The recurrence of the same issue with the same model suggests the likelihood is 'likely' (4).

I called customer service and at first they were going to send out a new blade.  After the second blade fell off they requested the fan back and created a case - [REDACTED]

incident_description: I crushed my big toenail when I went to open the main door into a restaurant. I walked up to the door normally and was about to open it normally by using the handle when my toe in open-toed shoes slammed into something I did not notice that was installed at the bottom of the door.  It was a product called the StepNPull. The restaurant had installed a "StepNPull" at the bottom right corner of the door. The StepNPull is a dangerous metal device that is screwed into the bottom of a door so that the person does not need to touch the handle. Handles are for touching. That's how people open doors. When large metal devices are installed that stick out at the bottom corner of doors, that poses a huge safety risk to people's toes. I lost a lot of blood, and I had to go to urgent care where they had to burn a small hole into my toenail to release the rest of the blood. I am going to need to take 7 days of antibiotics, I am in pain, it is difficult to walk, and the doctor said it would take 2 months to completely heal.
justification: The incident resulted in injury requiring medical treatment, including antibiotics and a prolonged healing period, but no death.

incident_description:
8/2019: The consumer noticed a dirty, burning-like odor in her home.  She had difficulty breathing and consulted her doctor.  The consumer said she has a pre-existing condition, which had not bothered her in 30 years.  The doctor administered medication to assist her with her difficulty breathing.  The consumer said she could not use the medication, because when she tried it, she felt a burning sensation in her chest.  She has a lung disorder.

2020:  The installing company, sent technicians out to inspect the unit, but they told her that they did not notice any odd odors.  Sometime, during the year, they changed the filters on the unit.  This did not help with the quality of air in her home.

10/13/2020:  A different company installed a gas dryer in her home.  However, the gas company had to shut off the gas in her home and they spotted an incorrect connection, which violated code, with the set-up with the consumer's furnace.  The company, who installed the dryer, picked it up and removed it from the consumerÃÂs home.

The consumer called the furnace installing company and they modified the set-up of the pipes in her home.  The gas company technician, pointed out the set-up, could have caused a fire in her home.  The installer's technician adjusted the location of the pipe, in relation to the wood and drywall in the consumer's home.

The consumer still had problems with the air in her home and her health condition got worse.  She could barely walk, became fatigued easily, and experienced a burning sensation in her lungs.
2/2021:  The consumer went to the hospital, because she felt as if her lungs were on-fire.  

When she returned from the hospital, she covered all of the vents in her home and began to feel better afterwards. 

The consumer called the installer several times, but when their technicians came out, they said that they did not notice any problem with the odor in her home.

The consumer called the gas company and the technician who came out, shut of the gas to her home.   She was told that outdoor gas sensor, was needed for proper operation of the furnace in her home.

3/2021:  The consumer called the installer and they came out and installed the sensor.

Afterwards, a local state inspector came out to check the system.  The consumer claims that this inspector, pushed the pipe upwards toward the ceiling and passed the system as working properly.

Later that night, the consumer had to turn off all of the lights in her home, because the lights caused her to feel ill.  Later that night, she called 911 and the Fire Rescue unit came out and turned off the (TXV) gas valve in her home and transported her to the hospital.  

When she returned home, she still experienced worsening health issues, when any lights were ÃÂonÃÂ in the house.  This had been happening, since the furnace was installed and she has been using less lights as possible.

The consumer said that one of the inspector indicated that this TXV valve, was apparently spilling gas in her home.

The consumer still notices an oil based film on the furniture and items in her home.  She tries to clean the film with a vinegar solution.
justification: The consumer experienced significant health issues, including difficulty breathing, burning sensations in the lungs, and hospitalization, indicating injury.

incident_description:
Ceiling Fan Warning ÃÂ Fans made by [REDACTED] and Hubbell Incorporated are being sold by Home Depot and may break apart and seriously injure someone.  I purchased two of HubbellÃÂs 96-inch, indoor/outdoor fans, P250018, from Home Depot and after 1 week of use, one fan lost four of its six blades with the blades falling and damaging two classic cars.  I contacted Home Depot who opened a claim and referred it to the manufacturer, Hubbell, Incorporated.  After phone discussions with Hubbell and almost one year later, they claim no responsibility for the metal arms that hold the fan blades onto the housing breaking apart in the middle.  They claim that the thin aluminum blades hit an obstacle with enough force to break the metal arms yet also said that the leading edges of the blades do not show any sign of hitting an obstacle.  Hubbell has blamed me for improper installation but could not identify how a so-called improper installation could have caused four of six blades to come off the fan.  Interestingly, the so-called improper installation was also used on the second Hubbell fan which did not suffer any failure, and later used with three non-Hubbell fans that have operated fine for almost a year.  It is my opinion that one Hubbell fan experienced some type of metal fatigue possibly due to a bad batch of metal support arms.
I was fortunate that no one was in my shop when the fan blades came off.  Four-foot metal fan blades flying through the air could have caused very serious injury to anyone nearby.  I see reviews of this same fan where people have installed them in their living rooms.  I am sending this message so that anyone who has purchased or is considering purchasing a Hubbell fan will be aware that I experienced an extremely dangerous failure, and neither Home Depot nor Hubbell have offered to refund the purchase price of the returned fans, much less address the damages.
justification: The incident involved fan blades breaking apart and causing damage, but no injuries were reported.

justification: The incident describes a recurring issue with the washing machine cover breaking, which could potentially lead to injury if not addressed, but no actual injury has been reported yet.

incident_description: We were told by an HVAC technician that our six-year-old Trane system is leaking refrigerant.  Now I am reading that this is dangerous and can cause health problems.  I attempted to call Trane, was put on hold and hung up on.  I've emailed them twice with no response.  These units should be recalled.  It is absurd for a newer system to have these issues.
justification: The incident involves a refrigerant leak, which poses potential health risks, but no actual injury or death has been reported yet.

incident_description: Responded to investigate a dehumidifier fire; found a thermally damaged NewAir AD-400 dehumidifier. Owners report that it was in normal use in the basement, they smelled fire and found the dehumidifier on fire. They used an ABC extinguisher to extinguish, but were unable to completely stop the burning process; FD responded and successfully extinguished the fire. No injuries occurred, and the fire was confined to the object of origin. Upon inspection, it appeared that the motor was the source of ignition. The power chord was undamaged and showed no signs of arcing; the electrical breakers inside the panel were un-tripped.
justification: No injuries occurred, but there was a fire incident involving a dehumidifier.

incident_description: While standing on an extended Little Giant ladder, the locking pins let loose? And the ladder sections slid down, pinning my toes between the rails.  This happened to myself while working on the ladder in my house.  I injured my left foot with some minor cuts as well as bruising and swelling due to the smashing between the rails.
justification: The incident resulted in minor cuts, bruising, and swelling, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). Ladder failures are possible but not extremely common, warranting a likelihood of 3.

incident_description: Handle broke while in operation, parts backfired and hit the user, causing scratches, minor bleeding and black & blue.
justification: The incident caused scratches, minor bleeding, and bruising, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description: I was using  my Greenworks GPW1704to power wash a chair outside when the spray gun exploded.  I have multiple bruises and cuts on both thighs and my stomach.  I went to the urgent care for treatment and was told I have a fist sized hematoma on my right thigh along with extensive bruising and cuts.
justification: The incident resulted in multiple bruises, cuts, and a hematoma requiring urgent care treatment, indicating an injury.

incident_description: My Greenworks Pro 2300 Pressure Washer GPW2300 blew apart on die cast aluminum piece on the output of the pressure water side.  The nozzle that attaches to the pressure hose flew the length of the pressure hose I was holding and 'tugged' on me while I was holding it.  Three other metal pieces where blown off the pressure washer when this occurred.  The pressure washer is less than a year old and had been used less than 30 hours of use.
justification: The incident involved the pressure washer blowing apart, causing parts to fly, but there was no reported injury, only a 'tug' on the user.

incident_description: A new Ao Smith 74 gallon hot water heater was placed in my home 4/27/21, it began to produce white smoke and the smell was awful. They sent a replacement burner which was installed 4/30/21 and the same thing happened. Subsequently they replaced the entire hot water heater AGAIN 5/3/21 and the same thing occurred. On this occasion I began to feel ill and called the gas company to make sure there wasn't a gas leak.  The gas company red tagged the unit and now the plumber that was supposed to come out said he believes the call was cancelled bc of the red tag and my health concerns.
justification: The incident caused the individual to feel ill, indicating an injury, and the repeated failures suggest a possible occurrence likelihood.

incident_description:
I had done a home remodel and purchased a what believe high quality Hansgrohe kitchen faucet with spray nozzle.   What has happened is the faucet head has an array of soft rubber which collects black mold.  Not other fixture (mostly [REDACTED] and originally [REDACTED]) in my home has this issue.

I contacted Hansgrohe and their reply is denial of any issue and claim they use mold resistant rubber.
I have requested warnings and maintenance information on their product, however when I was sold the product I was
not told it is more a health hazard than other fixures.
justification: The incident involves mold accumulation on a faucet, posing a potential health hazard, but no actual injury or death is reported.

incident_description: The room deodorizer Sure Scents has a lid with holes that small 'jelly' like beads are in and the beads can come out of those holes and fall to floor.  The beads look like candy.
justification: The beads can fall out and pose a choking hazard, especially to children, but no injury is reported.

incident_description: Toilet burst internally causing tank to shatter and cause minor damage to property and individual.
justification: The incident caused minor damage to property and an individual, indicating an injury occurred.

incident_description: The fan we use in our bedroom turned into a weapon. Thankfully, we were in another room when it happened.  We heard a number of large bangs.  It turns out, one of the two blades tore off,  flew into the ceiling, shot across the bed, and onto a nightstand six feet away.  This was Harbor Breeze fan model LP8294.  The product was being used normally, securely attached to the ceiling and on max speed with the incident occurred.  Thankfully, no injuries occurred.  There was some wall/ceiling damage in the bedroom.
justification: The incident involved a fan blade detaching and causing damage, but no injuries occurred.

justification: The storage box fell onto the vehicle, indicating an incident occurred, but there is no mention of injury or death.

incident_description:
Ez-Flo Eastman water hose connectors for washing machine, leaked and burst water, flooding the laundry room, and damaging my house interior. The water splashed to the nearby power outlet where the washing machine was plugged into, causing a small outlet box fire. The water on the carpet left the carpet smelling musty and moldy from the carpet being soaked wet. 

On May 3, 2021, I called Ez-Flo to try and resolve the problem, but the company attorney, [REDACTED], refused to resolve the problem and he told me to file a class action lawsuit against Ez-Flo instead of resolving. I called back at 2:15pm PST, to talk to somebody else to resolve the dispute, but the customer service rep, [REDACTED], said Ez-Flo [REDACTED] is one of the owners and he told her to hang up on me, she then slammed the phone in my face. 

As a result, I am filing this dispute to try and resolve.
justification: The incident involved property damage and a small fire but no reported injuries or deaths.

justification: The smoke alarm sounding for an extended period indicates a potential fire incident, and the involvement of police suggests a serious situation, though no injury or death is mentioned.

incident_description:
Blades of ceiling fan crack and separate from their mount.

I have 2 identical ceiling fans purchased and installed at the same time: Westinghouse ETL-ES-Comet-WH20 52", Product # 7230100.  Purchased and installed Nov 2020.  Last night, I stopped the fan after it began making a noise and wobbling.  Once stopped a blade separated and fell to the ground.  I inspected both fans and found that 7 of 9 remaining blades across the two fans are visibly cracked and at risk of separating in the same manner.  I have also contacted the manufacturer about the issue.

The fans were professionally installed and have been operating under normal conditions. The one with the failed
blade had been turned on via wall switch. Thankfully no one has been injured. The units are not known to have
been damaged in any way prior to this event.
justification: The incident involved a blade separating from the fan, but no injuries were reported. The likelihood is possible as multiple blades across two fans are cracked.

incident_description: I was in my room walking on my treadmill with the Ceiling fan turned on when I heard a loud crash and noticed the ceiling fan start wobbling erratically and missing a blade.  One of the two large fan blades had snapped off and hit my closet door molding creating an indentation and large dark brown impact stain.
justification: The incident involved a ceiling fan blade breaking off and causing property damage, but no injuries were reported.

No injuries but the product is unusable.

justification: The thermostat malfunction caused discomfort but no injury or death.

incident_description: Purchased a GE electric clothes dryer. Received one  with an opening on its side exposing an electric motor and pulleys, all within easy reach. Apparently, it was shipped with a missing vent "knock out panel." When contacted, GE parts department said they didn't offer any type of cap, plug or cover for that opening. I was told "that's just the way it's made." Other manufacturers do offer caps (e.g., [REDACTED]).
justification: The incident involves a missing panel exposing internal components, posing a potential hazard but no reported injury or death.

incident_description: I am a quadraplegic and I was sold a walk-in tab and assured many times that it would work in my particular home environment. It not only does not work, it is so painful and dangerous as to be a serious risk to my health. The only way I can be moved into and out of the tub is by being hoisted in a sling and moved with a ceiling ramp system - and the measurements from ceiling to top of the tub are shorter than my body in the sling forcing me to bend my neck and legs into an unnatural angle. The salesman repeatedly said this system would work for me; he was standing under the ceiling lift and was shown how it worked and was clearly aware of my significant limitations. Even once in the tub I cannot stay upright as the force of the jets pushs my body risking drowning. I have 60% comprised lung capacity and even a tiny amount of water is life threatening. The salesman and all the marketing by this company strongly advertise this product to disabled customers and they should carefully screen potential customers for potential hazards. All attempts to communicate with senior management of this company have failed. They refuse to listen and appreciate the risk and danger and they refuse to address the situation.  I have experienced days of pain, discomfort and anxiety from having to forced into dangerous positions and inside the tub from the pummeling and jerking in the water.
justification: The incident describes significant pain, discomfort, and risk of drowning due to the unsuitable tub, indicating injury and potential life-threatening conditions.

incident_description:
We have a water heater with a Honeywell gas (LP) control valve (model WV8840B5077) that has been running too hot causing skin burns.  This control valve was having issues in 2017 and was replaced by the installer.  Yet we're again experiencing the same issues.  The installer is planning to replace it again.  The issues we've been having include:
1- Runs too hot causing burns.
2- It shuts off randomly and requires re-start once or twice per week.
In our opinion there should have been a recall by Honeywell as the installer told us that there has been a lot of complaints about the same issues we've been having.
justification: The incident describes burns caused by the water heater running too hot, which qualifies as an injury (severity 3). The issues occur frequently, with burns and random shutdowns happening regularly, indicating a high likelihood (4).

The consumer was not injured however his Roomba was destroyed as it went from one side of the treadmill and spat out the other. 

The consumer contacted the Manufacturer and explained the situation; the representative he spoke to apologized for the incident he encountered and informed him someone would get back with him. 

The consumer states that the unit is used daily for one hour. 

The consumer plans on keeping his treadmill for at least the next thirty days in case an investigation ensues.
justification: The consumer was not injured but the incident caused the treadmill to be thrown and the Roomba destroyed, indicating a clear incident with no injury.

incident_description:
On April 22, 2021, our GE electric clothing dryer, model no. GFDR270EHWW, serial no. RF178370, was operating on a low heat, manual time cycle.  It began to make what sounded like a loud "buzz" sound, so we immediately turned it off.  When we did, a significant amount of black smoke was emitted from the space between the top right of the dryer and the control panel.  We immediately unplugged it and grabbed a fire extinguisher.  Fortunately, while there was a lot of smoke, there was no visible flame.

After giving the machine time to stop smoking and cool, we removed it from the laundry room and, eventually, to the garage due to the noxious smell it continued to emit.  After watching a YouTube video, we removed the control panel to make sure whatever happened stopped.  When we did so, we discovered that one of the harnesses apparently failed, but incredibly, the plug to the harness was held together or secured with what appeared to be masking tape.  We do not know, but strongly suspect, that this haphazard installation or build caused a short, which had we not discovered it so quickly, could have resulted in flame and burned down our house and caused bodily harm or death to any one or all of us.

We purchased the dryer in May or June of 2016.  It had been serviced once, while it was still under warranty, for failing/failed rollers on the drum by a GE authorized or certified technician.  (The warranty claim was made to GE.)  We never serviced the dryer ourselves, as we had no need to.  However, we regularly cleaned the lint trap and the exhaust hose to the exterior of the house.
justification: The incident involved significant smoke emission and potential fire hazard, but no actual injury or death occurred.

Today, I put in new batteries and it didn't work, so I shut it off.   After a few minutes, my wife smelled burning plastic and the fan was hot to the touch.   I quickly removed the very hot batteries.  When I took the case apart, I noticed that the White wire and Negative battery contact were both partially melted
justification: The fan overheated and caused melting of components, but no injury was reported.

The fan fell from the ceiling causing sparks and would have caused great injury to anyone who was standing underneath it, or any property that was underneath it. Fortunately, there was open ground and no one was standing there at the time so no injuries occurred.
justification: The fan fell and could have caused injury, but no one was harmed.

incident_description:
The clothes dryer had been in operation for approximately 10 minute, when it caught fire.  There were no visible flames.  The consumer noticed a burning odor, but was not sure exactly which part presented the problem .  

He called his father, who advised him to remove the faceplate, which he did.  He found that there had been an actual fire inside of the dryer.  It melted some of the wiring, damaged the pilot and some other parts.

The consumer called an electrician to come examine the machine.  The tech. said he had never seen anything like this, but he also could not work on it, because the consumer had dismantled the machine.  The service company's technician on the phone, told the consumer that he thought this might have resulted from lint build-up.  However, this technician, had not physically been out to view the machine.

The dryer was in the home, when the consumer moved in, but he believes that it may have been purchased in 2009/2010.

NOTE:  It has a stamp on it, which indicated that it was converted to LP gas, 1/28/2010, by Dunnett Inc.

The consumer called the manufacturer and reported the incident.  He was initially told that a technician would contact him in within 5- 7 days.  He never heard from them, so he followed up with them several times.  In the end, the manufacturerÃÂs representatives told him that since he modified the machine, they would not work on it.

The dryer is dismantled and being stored in the consumerÃÂs garage.

This could have led to a house fire.
justification: The incident involved a fire inside the dryer with no injuries or deaths, but potential for a house fire.
