incident_description:
On the evening on May 26th, 2018 I was using a Black and Decker Rotary tool to do some light sanding on a wood project. I was using the project for about 5 minutes when it suddenly burst into flames in my hand - There were jets of flames and sparks coming from the vents on the side of the tool. My right hand was severely burnt - second and third degree burns on my palm, thumb, and fingers. Also, as I threw the tool away haphazardly to get it away from me the tool turned and the tool caught the top side of my hand, getting caught momentarily inbetween my fingers and the rotating part of the tool cut very deeply into my knuckles. I contacted Black and Decker immediately via their website, and have yet to receive a response. I reach out two more times, once via their website and a second via their Chat feature. I have provided photos of my injuries as well as photos of the tool showing the burn marks clearly coming from inside the tool. This needs to be addressed as I clearly had a defective tool. Someone is going to get seriously injured or their house is going to burn down - The tool was LITERALLY shooting flames and sparks like a small jet engine. 

I am lucky that I am married to an Emergency room provider, and she was able to dress my injuries. I was unable to use my right hand for 3 days. As anyone knows, burns are very painful. I am extremely upset with Black and Deckers lack of response and interest into looking into this defective product.
justification: The incident resulted in severe burns and deep cuts, requiring medical attention and causing significant pain and temporary disability.

incident_description: First Alert Model No. CO1210 PREMATURE BATTERY FAILURE - this is the second unit that stopped working well within the 10 year advertised life span.  Each unit started chirping indicating "End of Life" the first unit failed before the new year and the second failed this past weekend - during a major power outage resulting from a major wind storm.  I contacted the company on the first unit and they shipped me a replacement at no cost. However a manufacturing defect may exist that has not been brought to the attention of their customers.  Both units were purchased from COSTCO and had a date stamp of "2015 Nov 03" (well short of the 10 year life - that consumers depend on and pay a premium for).  Failure of the product is  a safety issue and requires further investigation and notification to the buying public.  I have contacted First Alert and am waiting for further instruction on what to do with this item. I do not want to return it to COSTCO for a refund since this appears to be an inherent defect that requires further investigation rather than a simple replacement.
justification: The incident involves premature battery failure in smoke detectors, posing a potential safety risk but no reported injuries or deaths.

incident_description: I was vacuuming with my Oreck XL when suddenly a firework-like popping sound and sparks started flying up from the bottom of the handle and then about a 4-inch flame and lots of smoke started coming from the same area.  I quickly unplugged the vacuum and moved it outside (carrying it far below the handle) so that it wouldn't catch my house on fire.  The fire eventually went out.  I don't know how I avoided burns on my hand, but I am worried that someone else could be badly injured.  The repairman at the store said he doesn't see these problems "often," but he has seen it before.  My cord was melted and severed through to the copper wiring underneath due to the fire.
justification: The incident involved sparks, flames, and smoke, but no injury occurred. The repairman mentioned seeing similar issues before, indicating it's not extremely rare.

incident_description:
The submitter is reporting his unit because he believes it produces extremely hot water and it poses a burn hazard. He purchased the unit from Rozga Plumbing and Heating and they also installed the unit on December 8, 2016.

He said around November of 2017 he noticed that the hot water coming from the faucet was extremely hot. He contacted the firm about the issue and they advised him to contact the installer. The submitter contacted the installer and they came out on December 4, 2017 to replace the gas valve. 

However, the issue persisted and the submitter contacted the firm again. The firm sent out a local technician to inspect the unit on January 31, 2018. The technician found that the hot water coming from the faucet was 132.4 degrees Fahrenheit. The technician said he would reach out to the firm and they arranged for another technician to examine the unit on February 7, 2018. The second technician checked the temperature of the water coming from the unit and it was 108 degrees Fahrenheit. The technician then checked the hot water coming from the faucet and it was above 130 degrees for about 5 minutes then it dropped to about 108 degrees.
The submitter was told that this issue is normal and coincides with how the unit should be working. But the submitter is concerned that the hot water can scald his young grandchildren and this issue is a safety defect. The submitter said the hot water is this hot at every faucet and shower in the home.
justification: The incident involves extremely hot water posing a burn hazard, but no actual injury has been reported yet.

incident_description: I have a Samsung Washing Machine model number WA48H7400A that I bought in December of 2014.  It is covering my clothes with mildew and scum during the wash cycle.  The problem is particularly noticeable when I have not used the machine for a few days.  I believe this is because the machine does not drain all the way and when you don't use it the water creates mold and mildew scum that actually washes onto your clothes when you start the machine again.  Cleaning the machine regularly does not help.  Leaving the lid open does not help.  All of the canned responses that Samsung provides to tell you this is your help is ridiculous.  This is a design flaw which leaves water in between two barrels and does not drain completely.  There are 28 pages of peoples comments regarding this issue on the Samsung website and they are doing nothing but tell us this is our fault!
justification: The incident involves a design flaw causing mildew and scum on clothes, but no injury or death is reported.

incident_description: Window inside panes are shattering in the cold weather. Six windows have shattered over the past 6 years. One 6 years ago which was warrantied, 2 last year with no resolution, and 4 within the past 2 weeks. Requests for a company representative to examine the damaged windows gets denied repeatedly. When the first damaged window was replaced several years ago, the technician explained that the glass was no within specifications, and they would remedy any other windows that might implode. The fix for several other windows was to drill a small hole in the inside pane glass to relieve any out of spec glass deflection, then seal the hole. I was told glass replacement was not an option. Emails get dragged on, and when an attempt was made to contact the representative by phone, you get placed in the queue to leave a voice mail. A price break for replacement windows would be a nice gesture from JELD-WEN, however if nothing else, there should be a consumer safety alert issued for these windows due to the violent nature of the failure, and potential for personal injury (lacerations).

Samsung said they could offer a rebate towards a new washer as this is big problem. They offered $36. Disgusting! For my families health. https://us.community.samsung.com/t5/Washers-Dryers/Mold-mildew-dirt-AFTER-washing-in-top-loader-washing-machine/m-p/298797/highlight/false#M5501

incident_description:
Caller is reporting that her boiler overheated and burnt holes which cause CO to escape into her home.  She stated that it seems to have been occurring since she purchased the home in 2011.  Caller stated that she contacted the company and a rep informed her that there was a recall on some of the parts of the boiler.  She stated that a service came out on 2/1 because the unit was not working properly.  She stated that after he was finished she told him that she had smelled gas.  The technician checked and stated that he didn't find anything.  

Caller stated that she called in her contractor who informed her that there were fumes in the house, he then discovered that the exhaust pipe that was attached to the boiler had a hole which was causing the leak.

Caller stated that an emergency call was placed and a service technician came out and placed a patch over the leak, however, there was a 2nd leak which was not attended to.  She stated later that night all the security and CO alarms went off, she immediately turned off the boiler and called the contractor and technician to come back to the home.  (2/2)Caller stated that they came out the following day and tried to repair it, however, this did not resolve the issue. 

Caller stated that the her contractor eventually was able to work on her unit to have it working again.  Caller is concerned that she has been using a boiler that has been part of recall 09-752.

Caller will be contacting the recall firm for assistance as well.

In July 2017 i purchased a Simplisafe alarm system with their smoke detectors (link below). I installed the system and it functioned fine until October 29th, 2017 when i routinely tested the smoke detector in my basement and it did not make any sound and did not trigger an alarm. I reported it to simplisafe that day and they sent a replacement and return shipping tags for the old one. I installed the new smoke detector and it worked find until 2/5/18 when i did a routine test and the detector made no noise and did not trigger an alarm. I called Simplisafe customer service to complain and report the defect as well as the concern for the safety of my entire family. They sent out two free replacements, return shipping tags for the defective unit and apologized for the inconvenience. I have installed the replacement smoke detectors and purchased several stand alone 10 year sealed battery smoke detectors for my home since i am no longer confident that the Simplisafe smoke detectors work properly. I am filing this complaint in fear that someday someone may fall victim to the fault smoke detectors and be injured or killed. Please feel free to reach out to me with any questions or if you need my help to pursue this matter.

https://simplisafe.com/smoke-detector

In 2013 the Department of Aviation provided soundproof windows and doors for my home through their Residential Soundproofing Program. In 2016 I began to get an odor from these windows during the daytime and more noticeably when the sun is directly on my house. The odor was so intense that it made my family physically sick. incident_description:
Honeywell heat/cool thermostat RTH2300B1038

Thermostat fails in heat mode and furnace never shuts off. This is the second time this has occurred each with a different unit. Latest happened today, 02/10/2018, I was wakened by an excessively warm house about 4am and knew immediately the t-stat had failed. LCD screen appeared blank, moving switch from heat to OFF also failed to stop furnace - only removing t-stat from wall stopped furnace.
This is the second time this has occurred, and today's thermostat is a replacement.

The prior was about a month ago. I came home from work and noticed when I unlocked the door the door knob felt warm! Upon entering I found my house at 95 degrees and the furnace actively running. The thermostat LCD was blank and again the only way to stop it was to remove it from the wall.

Changing batteries did not restore thermostat function. These thermostats should never fail in an active heating mode. I don't know how long my furnace ran on the day I was gone, but grant you it was hot and ran longer than it was designed I fear I could have had a fire, or what about my pets? I was fortunate the dogs had been in the shop the house heated to 95. After this failure I bought a the same model as a direct replacement which worked until today.
justification: The thermostat failure led to excessive heating but no reported injury or death, though it posed potential risks to pets and property.

incident_description:
On December 14, 2017, we were informed that the GE Zoneline PTAC heating and cooling unit,  which was installed one year and two months prior in the bedroom of an apartment we rent in the District of Columbia, popped and started smoking.   The company that sold us the unit, Glenmont, inspected it on December 16 and stated the "control panel was burned."   

As several GE Zoneline units have been recalled for risk of fire, we called a GE customer service representative (1-800-386-1215, ext. 5031, Reference No. #[REDACTED]) for help.   The GE recall site states "Moisture from outdoor air can accumulate near the unit's heater when the unit is operated with the vent door continuously open. This, along with two shorted electrical components, can create an electrical ground path and arcing, posing a risk of fire."   

The GE representative stated the unit had not been recalled and therefore, GE would not repair or replace the unit.  He did say, however, the incident was most likely due to moisture.

Glenmont stated the unit did not have a warranty and also refused to repair or replace the unit.  

We decided to purchase another unit a little over one year after purchasing the one that burned and paid the tenants their demand of $1355 for rent credit, damages and for "stress and emotional" impact.
justification: The incident involved a unit smoking and a burned control panel, posing a fire risk, but no injury or death was reported.

Semi-Frameless Sliding Shower Door in Chrome with Clear Glass" from Home Depot (Model # SD2832937 Internet #300499032) on Apr 20, 2018 and a contractor proceeded to install it on April 26. When handling one of the panels, it shattered suddenly with no contact except with the contractor's hands (i.e. he did not bump it against anything). There were no injuries. He purchased a spare panel from Home Depot and finished the installation. I took several showers using the door with no issue. Then my condo manager was addressing an unrelated issue on May 2, 2018 in the bathroom, and the other (original) panel shattered when he opened the shower door. There were no injuries this time either. Both panels that came with the door have now inexplicably shattered, so I believe this to be a manufacturing defect, and one that poses an unreasonable and substantial risk of laceration. Luckily, both incidents happened with fully-clothed individuals present, but that easily might not have been the case since it's a shower door.

incident_description: Firefighter received electrical shock while using junction box fed by generator to power box fan. Firefighter was able to plug 125 Volt 20 AMP twist lock plug in a 250 Volt 20 AMP twist lock receptacle. The 250 Volt 20 AMP L6-20-R twist lock receptacle is made of a material which after use had worn and expanded allowing the plug to be inserted in the wrong orientation. This wrong orientation allowed the ground blade of the 125 Volt 20 AMP twist lock plug to be inserted into the "Phase" blade of the 250 Volt 20 AMP twist lock receptacle. This caused the metal frame of the box fan to become energized. When firefighter touched the metal frame of the box fan and the junction box fed by the generator the shock occurred.
justification: The firefighter received an electrical shock, which constitutes an injury, hence severity level 3. The incident was caused by equipment wear and incorrect plug orientation, making recurrence possible but not certain.

incident_description:
At 11:39 a.m. on April 13, 2015, a water flow alarm associated with the fire sprinkler system in the attic of the Fraser Holiday Inn Express initiated a call to the fire department.  The fire department responded with the first units arriving on scene at 11:45 a.m.  Upon arrival, the fire department observed fire in the roof/soffit area on the back side of the building.  Sprinklers in the attic were containing fire spread, and the responding fire fighters were able to complete fire extinguishment.  Fire, smoke, and water resulted in significant damage to the structure and contents.
The Holiday Inn Express in Fraser had previously provided lodging under another name, but had recently been purchased and renovated, with renovations completed in early October 2014.  The renovation project was executed by general contractor, Superior Builders, Inc. (Superior), with subcontractors Limon Electric Supply, Inc. (Limon Electric), Roofcraft, Inc., and others.  The work included the removal of the existing ice- and snow-melt cables from the roof and replacement of the roof.  A new ice- and snow-melt system was installed on the roof, under the shingles.  The new ice- and snow-melt system was manufactured by Heatwave Systems, LLC, doing business as Heatizon Systems, and the system that was installed is designated as a ZMesh system.  The ZMesh system was installed by the electrical contractor, Limon Electric, after which the shingles were installed by RoofCraft and their subcontractor, G&R Roofing.
The ignition source in the area of origin was the ZMesh system.  Photographs of the point of fire origin showed the presence of the ZMesh material in the area of origin.  In addition, a distinctive oxidation pattern of concentric rings was seen on the sheet metal of the drip edge surrounding a nail hole in immediate proximity to the point of origin (see Figure 6).  This concentric ring oxidation pattern is consistent with extreme heat being generated at the interface between the nail and the sheet metal.  Thus, the burn patterns in and around the area of fire origin were consistent with the ZMesh system providing the energy of fire ignition. A detailed engineering analysis of the Zmesh system determined the product to be unreasonably dangerous.
justification: The incident involved a fire causing significant damage to the structure and contents, but there were no reported injuries or deaths.

incident_description: While using the Whirlpool Duet / Steam electric dryer, Model # WED94HEXR0 , I noticed an electrical burning smell from the dryer. I turned the dryer off and unplugged it. The house electrical circuit breaker did not trip off, No smoke was noticed from the unit, just a heavy acrid electrical burning smell.  The dryer lint screen and the dryer exhaust pipe had little or no lint build up. The dryer tub also had the electrical burning smell. The clothes inside the dryer did not catch fire.  Upon further investigation,  after removing the dryer top cover, I noticed a heavy acrid electrical burning smell. I found that the main electrical harness to the inner to electronic control board was burnt from bare wires where the wire insulation had chaffed away and short circuited the the wires to the dryer metal top cover.  Black soot was noticed in this area and the electrical harness, electrical control board were burned, melted and covered with black soot from the internal electrical fire / short circuit. This dryer has been in normal use for about 8 years.
justification: The incident involved an electrical short circuit and burning smell but no injury or fire occurred, fitting severity level 2. Given the age of the dryer and the described damage, such incidents are possible but not frequent.

incident_description: A recently modified installation of the recalled EMDL with the replacement of the plastic lock with the metal lock has resulted in broken Beryllium Copper spring contacts.  The problem is that the technician never removed the plastic cover of the EMDL to visually verify the engagement distance of the new metal lock into the EMDL.  As a result of incorrect/unadjusted mounting of the EMDL, the spring contacts were pushed way beyond the metal contact plate and actually contacted the underside of the metal lock.  The circuit was closed by the spring contacts touching the metal of the lock rather than the metal contact plate surface at the end of the new metal lock.  Upon opening the door, the metal lock grabbed and distorted the spring contacts to the point where they were dragged back over the end of the metal lock and snapped away from the metal lock when they had clearance to do so.  As a result of repeated cycling in this manner, the contacts broke and fell off, rendering the solenoid circuit inoperable.
justification: The incident resulted in equipment damage (broken spring contacts) but no injury or death, fitting severity level 2. The likelihood is high (4) due to repeated cycling causing the issue.

I am reporting what the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) defines as an ÃÂactual incident and injury involving an unsafe consumer product.ÃÂ  

What happened to prompt my report is the installation of a phenol-urea-fomaldehyde foam insulation product, Tripolymer, in the walls of our Washington, D.C. home in November 2013.  

Once installed in our home, Tripolymer, which was marketed and sold to us as ÃÂUSA Premium Foam,ÃÂ made us sick and put us at risk for future cancer-related health problems by emitting dangerously high levels of formaldehyde, a carcinogen, and phenol in our home.  Both formaldehyde and phenol are listed on the Clean Air ActÃÂs List of Hazardous Air Pollutants.  

Who was using the product and how:  

In 2013 the walls of our three-story Washington, D.C. home had no insulation.  We needed to insulate our house before the winter.  A Gaithersburg, Maryland-based company called MBRS Group LLC (MBRS), doing business as "USA Insulation of Metro DC-West", which was a franchisee of Ohio-based USA Insulation Franchise Corp. (USA Insulation), offered to insulate out home by injecting into our walls a foam insulation product that the salesman called USA Premium Foam (aka Tripolymer).

MBRS offered to install the insulation in our home from the inside, through dozens of small holes that they would drill into the drywall. Given our concerns about toxins while we were trying to have another child and while we had a toddler daughter, we asked MBRS specifically whether the insulation product contained or released any formaldehyde or toxic materials. MBRS assured us during the sales pitch, as well as in the brochure they gave us, which was designed/produced by franchisor USA Insulation, that their foam insulation was ÃÂnon-toxicÃÂ and "formaldehyde-free".  We signed the contract, and within about a month they arrived at our house to do the job.    
 
We asked the salesman during the sales presentation (in October 2013) whether he needed to see any architectural blueprints or drawings.  He said he only needed to drill a few holes in the walls to check the depth (which we later learned was Tripolymer, manufactured by a company named C.P. Chemical).  Later we learned that the manufacturer (in its specs sheet) instructed all of the dealers/installers, including MBRS, that the foam insulation should be applied in a thickness that is in accordance with architectural drawings.  However, MBRS never checked or obtained our architectural drawings.  Per the Washington, D.C. building code, insulation that is not installed in adherence with manufacturer's instructions is a violation of the code.  

We also later learned that the installer or franchise operational manual (on page 18) for USA Insulation franchisees instructs installers that USA Premium Foam is "strictly to be used as cavity fill insulation." It notes that when installed, USA Premium Foam "must be supported and enclosed on all sides in order to insure proper curing."  It also instructs the installer technicians not to inject the foam into horizontal spaces such as ceilings, and that "USA Premium Foam should not be installed in wood or steel-stud partitions or walls in basements..."  All of that is relevant because our wall cavities were not enclosed on the top where the foam ended up flowing over into the horizontal ceiling cavities.  Also, MBRS did not follow the instructions about the basement and proceeded to foam multiple basement walls in our house. Those are examples of the misapplication of the insulation by MBRS.  

Moreover, the contract we signed with USA Insulation/MBRS Group in October 2013 was for "up to 600 square feet" of insulation.  However, according to our retired EPA expert who did the volume calculations by adding up the walls that were foamed and the space in those walls, MBRS put three times that amount in our house.  They even injected insulation into walls they were not supposed to insulate, including one in the basement in between the back basement door and the bathroom. No wonder the crew told me during the installation "we've never put this much foam into a house this size."  

When MBRSÃÂ technicians came to install Tripolymer/USA Premium Foam on November 6, 2013, I asked if I needed to get out of the house and/or open up windows and crank up the exhaust ventilation to ensure good ventilation.  The installers said not to open windows, as it would make their job tougher due to potential drafts, wind, and temperature change (and the effect on the foam injection process), and they told me I didnÃÂt need to leave or go outside, as it was perfectly safe to be there for and watch the installation process.  By the time they finished, the smell was overpowering and sickeningly sweet.  I got a migraine that very evening.  We immediately started using exhaust ventilation and opened numerous windows to try to air the house out and get rid of the overpowering sweet chemical smell (this is something we continued to do for months).  Nothing worked to remediate the problem ÃÂ not coffee beans, the purchase of big plants, activated carbon, etc.  

By December 2013, the smell had not gotten better or dissipated, and we were sick with various symptoms detailed elsewhere in this write-up.  We asked what was in the foam that was making or could make us sick, but the owner had no answer.  We asked if it there was any formaldehyde or other toxic chemicals in the insulation or potentially off-gassing, but he said no.  The owner declined to provide us with the Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) for the insulation and its resin and other components for several days; he eventually shared one for the product, but not for the resin or other components.  At first he offered to come test the air quality in our home but changed his mind.  He then sent an email offering to send a crew to demolish the walls and tear out all the insulation and replace it with traditional batt insulation.  But he would not provide alternative housing for us amid the demolition, and he conditioned the offer on us not going to his insurance company, and under no circumstances could we posting anything negative about the experience on [REDACTED] or similar sites.  We declined the offer and were not able to reach an agreement on how to handle the problem.  At no time during those negotiations in November-December 2013 did the owner volunteer that the MSDS for the resin warned that in the event of contamination, persons affected should immediately consult a doctor and get out of the contaminated area (we learned that later on our own).   

The Companies Manufacturing and Selling/Installing Tripolymer:

During the time it was installed in our home in late 2013, Tripolymer was manufactured by C.P. Chemical, Co. Inc, based in White Plains New York, and owned at that time by [REDACTED]  However, around 2016, after our house was insulated with Tripolymer (aka USA Premium Foam), the owner of USA Insulation Franchise Corp., [REDACTED], used an LLC called FDI Enterprises, LLC, based in Cleveland, Ohio, to acquire or purchase the intellectual property rights for Tripolymer and the resin and foaming agent elements that comprise it.  This is according to public court records that are currently involved in an ongoing trademark lawsuit against C.P. Chemical and [REDACTED]/FDI Enterprises.  The lawsuit was filed by Florida-based ÃÂTripolymer, IncÃÂ, which claims in the lawsuit that it was the exclusive nationwide distributor of Tripolymer.

Multiple Complaints Filed with the CPSC: Tripolymer has been the subject of multiple complaints filed with the CPSC, including as recently as 2017 (report # [REDACTED]).  Another complaint dates to 1994.  These complaints have been filed by consumers claiming to have been harmed by formaldehyde emissions from Tripolymer installed in their homes.  C.P. Chemical and FDI Enterprises may have violated the CPSCÃÂs requirement that a manufacturer must report to the CPSC alleged product defects and risk of harm to consumers within a few days of becoming aware of those defects or risks of harm.  C.P. Chemical, FDI Enterprises, and their distributors/installers/sellers would have been aware of those defects for some time.  In 2016 we filed a legal complaint regarding these defects in D.C. Superior Court, against USA Insulation Franchise LLC, USA Insulation Enterprises , Inc., USA Insulation Franchise Corp, MBRS Group LLC, and [REDACTED], owner of MBRS.  MBRS then filed a third-party suit against C.P. Chemical.

We allege that the companies named in our legal complaint have committed violations of laws and regulations governing the manufacture and installation of Tripolymer (see attached law suit). 

Health effects: In the very first hours and days following the installation of Tripolymer (aka USA Premium Foam) in our home, and continuing for almost two months after that, up until we moved out of the house in late December 2013, we experienced migraines, nausea, skin rashes, blurred vision, sleep disturbances, memory loss, anxiety, a burning sensation in our throats and noses, and respiratory, sinus, and gastrointestinal (diarrhea) problems, among other negative health effects.

Most of the negative health effects we experienced after the exposure to the toxic insulation faded or went away soon after we moved out of the house in late December 2013. Our toddler daughter was too young for some of the relevant tests recommended by our doctors around the time of our exposure to the toxic insulation, but we will seek health monitoring/tests in the years to come.  The risk of cancer and asthma will be something that requires continued medical monitoring for all of our family.  Following consultations with medical professionals, my wife, my daughter, and I plan to be screened annually for nasopharyngeal cancer (by having either an indirect or direct nasopharyngoscopy or an Epstein-Barr virus serology/test), leukemia (by conducting regular blood count exams), and regular pulmonary function tests. 

Tripolymer made us so sick that we had to move out of our house at the end of 2013 and use alternative (rental) housing for several months, on the advice of medical professionals and industrial hygienists, until we had the insulation removed in September-October 2014. 

Several other people (those who entered our house between November 2013 and late 2014) were exposed to the aforementioned health risks of Tripolymer/USA Premium Foam. 

The type of product being used was Tripolymer, though it was being marketed/sold under the name USA Premium Foam.  Tripolymer is a phenol-urea-formaldehyde tripolymer foam insulation product.  This Tripolymer product (or an earlier iteration) was banned nationwide for about a year under action taken by the CPSC against urea-formaldehyde foam insulation products (UFFIs) in the early 1980s.  

Although the CPSC ban was eventually overturned by a judge, by 1982 the New York Times reported that there were an estimated 700 lawsuits against manufacturers, installers, and sellers of UFFIs, as well as a 2 billion dollar class action lawsuit, and many more suits were filed after 1982.

Some manufacturers have asserted in recent years that there have been advances in the production of this type of injection foam to reduce formaldehyde emissions.  However, in 2009, the Massachusetts state government and the government of Canada notified the manufacturer/owner of Tripolymer that they had tested Tripolymer 105 (the same one installed in our home).  They relayed to C.P. Chemical that they considered Tripolymer to be a urea-formaldehyde foam insulation product that was not safe for consumersÃÂ health due to its history of and potential to emit or off-gas formaldehyde (per the attached documents and our outreach to those governments).  In 2011 the Connecticut government also tested Tripolymer 105 and then notified C.P. Chemical that Connecticut also prohibited the use, sale, and marketing of UFFIs, including Tripolymer.  (A few years later, around 2015, Connecticut changed its law by loosening restrictions.)

Testing Results Reveal the Danger of Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam: 

Between January 2014 and April 2015, we hired multiple licensed specialists and labs to conduct scientific tests and analysis of the air quality in our home, as well as tests of the toxic foam insulation itself.  We did this in part to help medical professionals determine in early 2014 exactly what had made us sick, whether the exposure we experienced exceeded safety guideline levels established by regulatory agencies, and whether the house was safe and inhabitable again following the removal of the insulation product from September-October 2014.  

Following the installation of Tripolymer in our home, the average levels of formaldehyde measured in our home during three sets of tests between January and May 2014 by an industrial hygienist (and former EPA expert) were 158.7 parts per billion of air (ppb) during January 2014, 254 ppb during April 2014, and 225 ppb during May 2014.  The levels of phenol were 19.7 ppb during January 2014, 33 during April 2014, and 15 during May 2014. 

These levels were on the borderline between what experts deem ÃÂpolluted indoor conditionsÃÂ and extreme conditionsÃÂ (per ÃÂFormaldehyde in the Indoor Environment,ÃÂ a widely cited 2010 study by [REDACTED]).

These levels meant we were exposed to higher formaldehyde levels than professional funeral directors/embalmers are typically exposed to during an average month in an OSHA-regulated work place (and for more hours than they are typically exposed to formaldehyde), per a 2011 New York Times expose and a study published by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine in 2007.  It also meant we were exposed to more than the average level of formaldehyde (77 ppb) in the infamous and defectively constructed toxic trailers that were provided by the Federal Emergency Management Association (FEMA) and used to house Gulf Coast victims of Hurricane Katrina, which the CDC identified as potentially causing respiratory illnesses in the residents of those trailers. 

In the spring of 2014, air quality tests of the two adjoining row houses on either side of our home showed that those houses had normal levels of formaldehyde and phenol (nothing like the levels recorded in our home).  Tests of the air outside our home also showed normal levels outside.

Furthermore, inside the wall cavities of our home, where the foam insulation had been installed, testing of the cavity air by experts revealed that the level of formaldehyde exceeded 2000 (two thousand) ppb.

In June 2014, further testing of our homeÃÂs air quality revealed the average level of formaldehyde in our home to be 240 ppb.  The average level of phenol was 45 ppb.  

Samples of Tripolymer insulation from our homeÃÂs walls were also tested during these months.  The experts found that the Tripolymer foam insulation contained a significant quantity of formaldehyde.  

In addition, in June 2014, testing of a sample of insulation foam from our homeÃÂs walls proved to be a match with the infrared (IR) chemical fingerprint for urea formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI).  UFFIs were banned nationwide by the CPSC for a time in the early 1980s and remain banned today by multiple state governments and Canada.  

In September-October 2014, 10 months after Tripolymer was installed in our home, we paid over $30,000 to have experts carefully remove the extremely brittle and often powder-like Tripolymer from the walls of our home.  The specialists meticulously filmed and photographed the removal of the foam.  Along with the retired EPA expert and other environmental engineers, they found it to be extremely friable, often crumbling into a baby powder-like substance in several of the walls (see attached photos).  

Following the removal, experts tested the air quality again twice, in November 2014 and one last time in April 2015. The levels of formaldehyde dropped dramatically, to 76.2 ppb and finally to 23 ppb.  The levels of phenol also dropped dramatically, to 2 ppb (in November 2014) and then to 1 ppb (in April 2015).  

The Meaning of the Test Results for Consumer Safety: The testing demonstrated the following:

ÃÂ	Our Home was contaminated by high levels of formaldehyde and phenol;

ÃÂ	The Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam installed in our home contained formaldehyde and phenol;

ÃÂ	The levels of formaldehyde recorded in our homeÃÂs air, prior to the removal Tripolymer in late 2014, far exceeded residential safety levels established by the World Health Organization (80 ppb), the Canadian government (40 ppb), and other regulatory agencies;

ÃÂ	Prior to the removal of the insulation product, the air inside the wall cavities of our home (where the foam was installed), had formaldehyde levels that exceeded occupational safety levels established by the Department of LaborÃÂs Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), for long-term and for short-term exposure.  (Note: Per OSHA, the American Industrial Hygiene Association, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), it would be inappropriate to apply occupational safety guidelines for formaldehyde exposure to residential settings because occupational guidelines were designed for adults, not children (such as our then-toddler daughter), and they were not intended for non-monitored exposures in a home, where exposure can far exceed the typical eight- or 10-hour workday upon which occupational guidelines are based.)

ÃÂ	Over several months, until the Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam was removed in September/October 2014, the levels of formaldehyde continued to increase, not decrease, following the installation of the insulation in November 2013 (the levels increased from January to April 2014, and they increased from May to June 2014);

ÃÂ	Other internal formaldehyde and phenol sources were negligible; 

ÃÂ	External formaldehyde and phenol sources were negligible and the formaldehyde was not coming from the adjacent row houses or from outside; 

ÃÂ	The testing of phenol in our home further demonstrated that the foam insulation was emitting phenol because phenol was distributed just like the formaldehyde in our home.  Also, the phenol concentration was much was much higher in the foamed wall cavities compared to the rooms of our home; and by May 2014 phenol levels in the living spaces of the home were averaging 10 times the U.S. government health standards for chronic inhalation of phenol.

ÃÂ	The Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam installed in our home contained free formaldehyde as shown in testing in the spring of 2014; 

ÃÂ	The Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam in our HomeÃÂs walls was the source of the formaldehyde contamination.  This was evidenced by the fact that the wall cavities of our home had much higher formaldehyde concentrations than the rooms.  Also, after removing the Tripolymer insulation in the fall of 2014, the levels of formaldehyde and phenol dropped sharply to normal (safe) levels;

ÃÂ	Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam is capable of emitting formaldehyde at levels over 0.1 parts per million (or 100 ppb) of air.  Our testing documented emission levels far above that level.  Therefore, as required by OSHAÃÂs Formaldehyde standard, 29 CFR 1910.1048(m)(3), the product label must include a statement that the product has formaldehyde in it.  (At the time we purchased the insulation, the sellers, distributors, and installers of Tripolymer/USA Premium Foam claimed the product was ÃÂformaldehyde-freeÃÂ and did not emit any toxic chemicals.  The product brochures and advertising continue to make those formaldehyde-free claims today.)

ÃÂ	Tripolymer/USA Premium Foam is also capable of emitting formaldehyde at levels over 0.5 ppm (or 500 ppb), since our air quality testing documented formaldehyde emissions of over 2000 ppb.  Therefore, as required by OSHA, the product label must also have a list of all product health and safety hazards, and the phrase ÃÂPotential Cancer HazardÃÂ; and

ÃÂ	The website (as of April 8, 2018) for Tripolymer insulation (now owned by FDI Enterprises LLC, which is owned by [REDACTED], the owner of Ohio-based USA Insulation) should delete or correct the following claims that mislead consumers about the safety, content, and health risks of this product: 

ÃÂSafeÃÂthe foam is non-toxic.ÃÂ

ÃÂNo, per current federal regulations, Tripolymer Foam Insulation does not use or contain VOCsÃÂ. ((Formaldehyde is a VOC, and our testing showed the foam itself contained significant amounts of formaldehyde.))

ÃÂTripolymer Foam Insulation has been tested for toxic materials as recommended by the United States Environmental Protection Agency. All tests show conclusively that Tripolymer Insulation does not contain or has undetectable levels of these substances.ÃÂ ((Our testing showed the foam insulation contained detectable and even significant amounts of a toxic material -- formaldehyde.))

Key Information on the Product:

The TripolymerÃÂ® 105, used at our residence for house insulation, is a Phenol-Urea-Formaldehyde foam. The foam consists of two components, (A) the resin in aqueous solution and (B)the foaming agent/catalyst. The starting resin used for the foam is made by reacting phenol to a solution of urea-formaldehyde, as evident from the patent published by C. P Chemicals Inc. in 1980 and in 1982 (see the report by [REDACTED] attached, which contains the patent).

The resin is mixed on site with the foaming agent, component B, containing acidic catalyst and surfactant (phosphoric acid and dodecyl benzenesulfonate) [3,4] in aqueous media, and compressed air. The catalyst facilitates molecular cross-linking/Curing. The initial foaming is very fast, but the foam continues to cure for 48-72 hours [5] and hardens in the places of installation. 

According to TripolymerÃÂs Material Safety Data Sheet filed in 2013 by C.P. Chemical with the Department of LaborÃÂs Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), the name of the product that was installed in our home was Tripolymer Foam G Series # 105; it has also been referred to as Tripolymer 105 G-7, and Tripolymer 105.  It was marketed and sold to us as ÃÂUSA Premium FoamÃÂ by Maryland-based MBRS Group, LLC and its Ohio-based franchisor USA Insulation as ÃÂUSA Premium Foam G Series # 105ÃÂ.  [REDACTED], who owns MBRS confirmed for us that USA Premium Foam is the same as Tripolymer 105.  Owners, salesmen, and other personnel working at multiple franchisees (in various states) under the USA Insulation umbrella also confirmed for us over the phone that Tripolymer 105 is what was installed (as USA Premium Foam) in our home. 

In an article from 2013 entitled ÃÂFormaldehyde-based Foam Insulation Back from the Dead,ÃÂ author [REDACTED], the founder of BuildingGreen.com, identifies Tripolymer as a formaldehyde-based foam insulation product that is made, distributed, and installed by companies that are actively trying to hide the fact that formaldehyde is a key intentional ingredient in their insulation product.  [REDACTED] writes:

ÃÂBack in the late 1970s and early 1980s [formaldehyde-based foam insulation] was the ultimate bad guy of the insulation worldÃÂCanada banned the product, as did the Consumer Products Safety Commission in 1982 in the U.S.ÃÂthough the latter later reversed the ban a year later.ÃÂ

ÃÂThe UFFI industry shrank to just seven manufacturers by 1981, then two large producers, Borden and Ciba-Geigy, ceased production. But the remaining five companies have continued to produce UFFI, though under different names.  Most of those companies have gone to significant effort to avoid any association with UFFI.  Among the five manufacturers of UFFI today, you will variously see the material referred to as ÃÂinjection foam,ÃÂ ÃÂamino foam,ÃÂ ÃÂaminoplast foam,ÃÂ ÃÂtri-polymer foam,ÃÂ ÃÂdry-resin foam,ÃÂ and various combinations thereof.  The only reference youÃÂre unlikely to see is ÃÂurea-formaldehyde,ÃÂ and if you ask manufacturers what the stuff is most will go to great lengths to obfuscate their response.ÃÂ

In 1977 the National Bureau of Standards (now the National Institute of Standards and Technologies), a federal agency, issued a landmark report that featured C.P. ChemicalÃÂs insights on what can make insulation foam defective and a health threat.  The report, ÃÂUrea-Formaldehyde-based Foam Insulations: An Assessment of their Properties Performance,ÃÂ includes a focus on factors that increase the likelihood that the products will off-gas formaldehyde into a home and threaten the health of the residents.  In the report, C.P. Chemical, the company that manufactured the Tripolymer / USA Premium Foam that was installed in our Home in November 2013, looms large.  The report cites C.P. Chemical in Annex A as one of four major U.S. manufacturers of urea-formaldehyde foam insulation that were consulted extensively in order to write the report.  Under section 8 on ÃÂFormaldehyde GasÃÂ the report concludes:

ÃÂFormaldehyde odors are caused by the presence of free formaldehyde gas. There are two sources of the formaldehyde. First, formaldehyde is present in the urea-formaldehyde-based resin and may be liberated upon foaming. Secondly, formaldehyde is liberated during hydrolysis of urea-formaldehyde-based foams which may occur under conditions of high temperature and high humidity. Factors which would increase the likelihood of liberating formaldehyde from either source will contribute to an odor problem. The major manufacturers of urea-formaldehyde based foam insulations have outlined a number of these factors which are in general related to improper manufacture or improper application of the resin. The relative significance of these factors is not known. The factors contributing to formaldehyde odor problems as described by the manufacturers [the four manufacturers consulted, including C.P. Chemical] are: 

an excessive amount of formaldehyde in the resin
an excessive amount of catalyst in the foaming agent an improper ratio of resin to foaming agent excess foaming agent
foaming at high humidities 
foaming with cold chemicals
dry density of the foam exceeding manufacturers' specifications 
application against recommended practice; e.g. in an air plenum or ceilings 
improper use or lack of vapor barriers improper venting on some constructions.ÃÂ

The report also found the following: ÃÂThe foams should not be applied in attics and ceilings. This recommendation is based on properties of the foams dealing with shrinkage, resistance to high temperature and high humidity, and odor. Excessive shrinkage may occur when the foams are applied to an open cavity and dried too rapidly.  Preliminary laboratory data indicate degradation of the foams when exposed to high temperature and high humidity. If free formaldehyde gas is present, being denser than air, it may tend to settle in inhabited areas.ÃÂ  

It is worth noting that MBRS installed several feet of insulation in our ceilings even though we did not request that.

Key Health Information on Formaldehyde and Phenol:

Per the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSD), part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), ÃÂformaldehyde is a highly toxic systemic poison that is absorbed well by inhalation.ÃÂ  Per OSHAÃÂs formaldehyde fact sheet, ÃÂacute exposure is highly irritating to the eyes, nose, and throat and can make anyone exposed cough and wheeze.  Subsequent exposure may cause severe allergic reactions to the skin, eyes, and respiratory tractÃÂand long-term exposure to low levels in the air or on the skin can cause asthma-like respiratory problems and skin irritationÃÂÃÂ  

Under the ÃÂDelayed EffectsÃÂ section, the Medical Management Guidelines for formaldehyde, published by the CDCÃÂs ATSDR, note that ÃÂformaldehyde poisoning can cause permanent alterations of nervous system function, including problems with memory, learning, thinking, sleeping, personality changes, depression, headache, and sensory and perceptual changes.ÃÂ  Per the CPSCÃÂs ÃÂAn Update on Formaldehyde,ÃÂ one of the "affected areas/systemsÃÂ is the neurological system, and ÃÂpotential adverse health effectsÃÂ include ÃÂimpairments in dexterity, memory, and equilibrium."  The EPAÃÂs guide on VOCsÃÂ effects on indoor air quality also lists ÃÂmemory impairmentÃÂ as one of formaldehydeÃÂs health effects.  Under the section entitled ÃÂFollow-up,ÃÂ the ATSD recommends that ÃÂPatients with symptoms of seizures, convulsions, headache, or confusion need to be followed for permanent central nervous system dysfunction with neurobehavioral toxicity testing, with particular attention to problems with memory, personality changes, and perceptual dysfunction.ÃÂ  Per the Toxicology Data Network of the NIH, the odor threshold of formaldehyde is between 0.05-1.0 ppm (or between 50 ppb and 1000 ppb).

Formaldehyde is classified as a known human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the CDC, and others.  The IARC concluded, based on human exposures in the workplace, that formaldehyde can cause nasopharyngeal cancer (cancer of the nose and throat).  It also found limited evidence that formaldehyde may cause other respiratory tract cancers, and a possible link with leukemia.  According to the National Cancer Institute (NCI), a component of the NIH, following a series of studies conducted by the NCI, ÃÂNCI investigators have concluded that exposure to formaldehyde may cause leukemia, particularly myeloid leukemia, in humans.ÃÂ

Both formaldehyde and phenol are listed on the Clean Air ActÃÂs List of Hazardous Air pollutants.  In addition, the CDC warns that exposure to formaldehyde ÃÂmay increase your chances of fertility problems or a miscarriage.ÃÂ   

Per the Toxicology Data Network of the NIH, ÃÂphenol is an acutely hazardous substance due primarily to its toxicity.ÃÂ  Designated as "Poison B" by the U.S. Department of Transportation, phenol containers are labeled "Poison".  Per the CDC, inhalation symptoms for phenol include: Sore throat, burning sensation, cough, dizziness, headache, and nausea; ÃÂthe substance may have effects on the liver and kidneys.ÃÂ  Per the ATSDR, ÃÂshort-term exposure to phenol in the air can cause respiratory irritation, headaches, and burning eyes. People who had skin exposure to high amounts of phenol had skin burns, liver damage, dark urine, irregular heart beat, and some died.  In animals, breathing air with high levels of phenol resulted in irritation of the lungs. Repeated exposures induced muscle tremors and loss of coordination. Exposure to high concentrations of phenol in the air for several weeks caused paralysis and severe injury to the heart, liver, kidneys, and lungs, and in some cases, deathÃÂPhenol has caused minor birth defects and low birth weight in animals generally at exposure levels that also were toxic to the pregnant mothers.ÃÂ  Warning of potential phenol exposure can come from its sickeningly sweet, acrid odor, detectable at 0.047 ppm (or 47 ppb), per the Toxicology Data Network of the NIH.
justification: The incident involved significant health effects including migraines, nausea, skin rashes, and respiratory issues, consistent with injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is rated as 3 (possible) given the documented history of similar incidents and regulatory violations.

After my electric power was lost, then restored, the unit ignited on its own while in the OFF position. I notified the seller of this problem and suggested that they notify the manufacturer about this danger. In the manual, it states not to leave it plugged in as it might ignite on its own. I had accidentally left the unit plugged in the night before. Since many do not even read these fine print manuals it poses a significant danger to all. As far as I know, the eBay seller has not informed the manufacture of this incident. Regardless of what it says in the manual, this is very unsafe, potentially causing a significant fire, loss of property and loss of life.

The seller is [REDACTED]. The item is a factory reconditioned Procom Kerosene Forced Air Heater generating between 160 and 220 thousand BTU's. In my opinion, this item needs to be recalled and taken off the market.
justification: The heater ignited on its own while in the OFF position, posing a fire hazard, but no injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
I'd like to call your attention to a product that 1 recently purchased which I believe has a 
dangerous design feature. In August 2017 I purchased a Kenmore 26132 top loader washing machine. After 
leveling machine, doing hook up, and following instructions I ran a couple of loads of clothes 
successfully. However at end of week I attempted to run another load and the machine froze up 
intermittently and sounded like the gears were coming apart.

Immediately called Sears trouble shooter and after going thru their check off process was asked to 
hold phone up to machine so rep. could hear sound. Upon hearing noise, Sears advised to stop using & 
scheduled a Service Tech. call. Two technicians  responded the following a.m. As soon as Tech pushed the
power button, he quickly shut it off and without even pulling the machine out to check for problem 
advised us that he already knew what had happened.  He proceeded to tell us the motor in this 
machine is very close to floor, that it had overheated and caught up in carpet underneath and 
burned the carpet. Sure enough as soon as he moved machine that was exactly what had happened.  The 
plastic casing around motor had come off in dozens of hot pieces and were thrown all around  carpet 
melting into the carpet wherever it touched.      
                                                  
He also told us he had another call wherein the owner had a plastic drip pan beneath the washer 
(which was designed for that purpose) & that the motor had melted a hole thru the pan. The second Tech.
further advised us that once water is added the weight from the water pushes the motor even lower
making it dangerous to have on any type of flooring, carpet, tile, plastic, etc. I assume they would be 
ok on concrete. Nothing is mentioned in any literature about this issue.

This machine is located in a small populated rural area so we knew if the technicians had already
experienced this problem more than once that this was a serious matter. We advised Sears to that 
effect but got no reaction.  We had the dealer check all his other machines.  We did not want 
another model unless it was designed differently.  The dealer advised that all current models no 
longer have a protective metal bottom panel on them and further that this model had the motor 
closest to the floor. We ended up with an LG which was a little higher than the Kenmore but even so 
the Tech. recommended that we raise all 4 legs to the maximum level before using. It certainly looks 
odd but we have done so.

In filing a claim, the company's position is that this is a manufacturing error and they will be 
sending our claim on to the manufacturer once they determine who made this model. I am enclosing two 
pics....one which shows the multiple white pieces of casing burnt into the carpet and with the imprint of the 
motor burnt into the carpet.  The other picture has the washer laying down (the motor casing has 
already been removed by the tech) and shows just how close this entire mechanism is to the floor.   
I hope you can convince Sears a recall is in order. Luckily I was inside when the washer malfunctioned but this 
could have been much worse situation.

Sincerely,
[REDACTED]

Consumer Protection Agency
Re: Report No.20171120 0692C 17 14049 addendem
In response to your letter of Nov. 21, 2017 I have made a correction to copy. After my report, Whirlpool contacted me on Nov.9, 2017.    My complaint had been transferred to them as Sears Rep. deemed the problem a manufacturing error.  Their agent asserted the following:
-We didn't level washer. I advised him that was inaccurate.  The washer was leveled at time of installation. The rep. then said that we must have tried to line it up to dryer?? I advised that we did not do that and doing so would defeat the necessity for leveling. No reason for his assertion was given.
-He then asserted that the carpet pad must be "guishy". I advised him that we had carpet in this property for 40 yrs or so and the pad is not "guishy". Further that we have had numerous appliances and washers in this area without any incident over that time. None were off balance or rocked and the washer sat firmly where placed.
-He also stated the washer was designed to shut down if the motor malfunctioned. Clearly this didn't happen and I reminded him that the washer was shut down manually after Sears troubleshooter listened to the motor noise and advised us to do so. This is one of the design flaws in addition to the location of motor.
--Lastly, he stated that instructions were to not place washer on carpet.   I refuted that assertion as none of the installation or user documents contained that requirement.  We still have our copy of those documents. In fact, a company rep. installed our previously replaced washer in this same location without incident or concern. The rep. indicated he would research the documents and call me again. To date that has not occurred.
My overall impression was that Whirlpool was not concerned about correcting the design to eliminate the danger of this machine and was more interested in making this about something that we as consumers did wrong. He had no reason for any of the above assertions and none of them were true. Very frustrating.
justification: The incident involved a dangerous design flaw causing property damage (burned carpet) but no reported injuries or deaths.

incident_description:
I have one of these units, (Model FA110G,) and contacted Kidde about it. They agreed to send me a new one
with a metal handle/valve/nozzle, which they did. However, I have an identical unit, (Model SM110,) that
doesn't have the model name listed in the recall notice. Odd thing is, the SM110 seems to have leaked out all of
its charge gas even though it has ever been used and it has been stored next to the other one since I got it. The
FA110G still carries a full charge.

Since the recalled model numbers essentially refer to the very same units sold by different entities through
many different channels, could KIDDE be playing games with the model numbers on this recall to limit their
liability?

BTW, one of these extinguishers was given to me by my employer during Fire Prevention Week many years
ago, and the other was purchased at my front door from a person raising funds for a volunteer fire
department. They were both new-in-box and I don't remember which one is which.

Attached are a few photos:

The trio of extinguishers is L-R,
Kidde SM110, Kidde FA110G, and he replacement sent by Kidde the PRO 110-2, PRO2.5TCM-8, (both of
those model designators are listed on its label.)

As you can see, the plastic-handled models are pretty much identical with the only discernable difference being
a small difference in the length of the nozzle.

Perhaps you may want to get with Kidde and see if they've "overlooked" a few models.

Thank you,
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a potential product issue with no reported injury or harm, focusing on model discrepancies and a leaked charge.

incident_description:
This product is way too dangerous!
Bought a can of SprayWay ammonia-free glass cleaner on sale...tried using it on my bathroom mirror--sprayed less than a second and started wiping.  Strong chemical-smell fumes immediately caused me severe coughing--by the time I got to the bathroom door, my eyes were blurring and itchy.  I turned on exhaust fan and left.  Fumes still apparent after 5 min!  After bathroom was "normal" I returned to finish wiping mirror...small section I had wiped before leaving was not particularly clean.  I then used my ammonia cleaner and had spotless mirror in about a minute, with no adverse effects.

They do have warnings on the can (which I, of course, didn't read until afterwards!)  It does say in tiny print not to get the product in contact with eyes or skin.  How could one clean a window or mirrow without spraying the product?

I sent a complaint to the manufacturer and I will take the SprayWay back for refund, but this is not a safe product and should be taken off the market.
justification: The user experienced severe coughing, blurry and itchy eyes, indicating injury from chemical exposure. The likelihood is high as similar incidents can occur if warnings are not followed.

incident_description:
I live in a new sub-division built by Pulte Homes. We have gas fireplaces made by Heatilator. According to their owners Manual the fireplace can be used with a battery back up in the event of power loss. Here in our neighborhood we have had 2 power outages in the last 45 days once of which lasted 26 hours and the other though shorter was when the outside temperature was 11 degrees. On these occasions all of us used the battery back-up....Thus far 3 neighbors including myself have had these D size batteries explode leaking battery acid. My batteries leaked on my fingers causing much discomfort and required me to call Georgia Poison Control. I contacted  [REDACTED] the makers of the batteries. They send me a letter which reads in part "Don't put batteries in very warm places. Extreme temperatures reduce battery performance and may also cause leakage." Again, the owner's manual from Heatilator recommends using batteries in the event of a power outage. The battery sleeve is at the base of the fire place unit. It gets very warm there....
I have contacted Heatilator with a terrible response from them that I should contact my local dealer. My local dealer was less than helpful. I have contacted Pulte Homes and have not had a response yet. I am furious
justification: Battery explosion caused discomfort and required contact with poison control, indicating an injury.

incident_description:
I own a SoleusAir dehumidifier and had it located in the basement. I went into basement back in September of 2017 and heard a loud noise coming from the unit. When I checked the unit, I found the motor area to be VERY hot to the touch and the unit was blowing very hot air. I unplugged the unit and figured the motor had seized. I started to do research on line and found the recall information. My unit was affected by the recall. I was very lucky to have heard the noisy unit when I went into the basement. My wife is in the basement daily for a workout and did not know the difference in sound.

I contacted Gree and completed the recall information. I received the recall package weeks later and promptly sent it in with all required information. It was explained to me at that time that I would receive my refund within 2-6 weeks. It is now January 12, 2018 and I have not received my refund as of yet. I just spoke to Gree and was told they did not receive the return package from me until October 16, 2017 and did not start to process the refund until December 1, 2017. Are you kidding me??? That is ridiculous. They stated they will get the refund to me as soon as possible.

If a company is involved with a recall such as this, they should be a little more attentive and ambitious to satisfy ALL customers in a timely fashion. This is NOT timely. Furthermore, they won't even refund the purchase price that I have on my receipt. They will only refund $229. Why?????
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning dehumidifier that could have posed a fire hazard, but no injury or death occurred. The likelihood is possible as recalls and delays in refunds are not uncommon.

incident_description:
On March 26, 2018, a homeowner observed a flame emanating from the bottom of a Homedics humidifier,Model UHE-CM25TGTA. She immediately unplugged the unit. The home owner's husband, a fire chief for the local fire department, contacted this writer, (fire Marshal), re the incident. I advised him to bring it to the office, (fire marshal's office), and that I would examine it.

I disassembled the unit and observed burn/soot marks in the units interior. I removed a circuit board that was secured in place via two screws. When I lifted the circuit board off of its mounts, I observed a scorched wire in the two wire power cord, that was directly beneath the circuit board. I traced the shorted wire and found that it was the hot side of the power cord. The underside of the circuit board possessed many sharp edges. These edges were formed by the penetrations of the components that were soldered (bottom side)and mounted on the topside of the board.
The pointy projections sat directly on top of the power cord There was no protection afforded to the power cord. Without any buffer material to protect the cord from being abraded or penetrated by the circuit board components, the underside of the circuit board shorted out to the power cord.

I believe the home owner's presence in the room and quick action, prevented the event from growing into a larger problem.
justification: The incident involved a flame and potential fire hazard, but no injury or death occurred due to quick action.

This single unit (unitize) Frigidaire dryer/washer model number is:  FFLG2022MW3, serial number:  4E43913102.  We have had this dryer/washer unit since December 2014.  We do laundry about twice a week and made sure the lint trap was lint free and the unit is level.

The dryer/washer is located in our garage.  We were in bed asleep upstairs when the dryer fire started.  We heard an alarm go off but thought that it was outside the house.  Seconds later, I smelled smoke inside the house.  I ran out to the backyard and saw lots of smoke coming from the dryer exhaust vent.  As soon as I opened the dryer door, it was still spinning with flames that look like a crematorium.

I extinguished the flames and immediately turned off the gas supply.  It was the garage smoke alarm that saved our lives.

The Kenmore Dryer has a safety hazard allowing metal coins to come in contact with exposed thermal fuse leads and built up lint.

On  29 November 2017 Above model dryer quit heating. I checked on Youtube for the causes... a major cause is a blown Thermal Fuse.  I checked the dryer inside the dryer cabinet.  The dryer was purchased from Kenmore/Sears in approximately 2014. It came with the house that I just purchsed.

When I removed the front housing cover, I could see that the lint accumulates inside the main dryer housing. One quarter dropped onto the thermal fuse crossing both contacts, creating a fire hazard with the lint inside the dryer housing.
The quarter had an electrical burn  on each end where it shorted out  across the bare metal electrical clips connecting the thermal fuse. We were fortunate that the lint did not combust, the dryer just stopped heating.  There was a one inch layer of lint inside the dryer housing covering the thermal fuse and other components. After vacuuming out the inside dryer cabinet and removing layers of lint build up, replacing the thermal fuse and recovering about 6 coins,  I found that the dryer works great. A few minutes later, my wife and I looked at each other and she said, ÃÂDo you smell that?ÃÂ I said, ÃÂYep, smoke!ÃÂ.

We both jumped out of bed and ran to check the kid's room. Seeing no issues there, we continued up the hallway to the common living areas. I could see from the kitchen into the utility room where the breaker panel is located. There was an orange glow of fire in the bottom 1/4 of the panel.

The product was a Pelonis space heater, model# HF-0063, date code 1508; serial# appears to be 20215109Z.  I bought this product @ Home Depot on or shortly before 2016-Feb-1.  

I've used this product in winter only.  This (winter 2017-2018) would be the 3rd winter in which I used the product (the heater is less than 2 years old).  

I've always used this fan-forced heater in its oscillation or swing mode, in which the body of the heater automatically rotates left & right using a motor.  

Today the heater turned off unexpectedly; its display was completely blank, and pushing the power-on button did nothing.  

I unplugged the heater & plugged it back in; the heater still didn't work.  

Thinking that the problem might be where the power cord enters the heater, I flexed the cord somewhat.  Soon the heater started beeping intermittently; it normally beeps when it's turned on.  

A few seconds later, with an arcing sound, a jet of flame, about 3 inches long, shot out of the point where the power cord enters the heater.  That flame might have caught something else on fire if there had been any such object close enough.  

After a couple of seconds, the flame seemed to extinguish itself the moment before I pulled the plug from the wall.  

This heater's predecessor, a similar unit by DeLonghi, also failed due to the power cord flexing, but didn't emit any flame.  Apparently it's possible to design this kind of heater so that it doesn't emit flame even if the power cord does fail.

incident_description: I had just put a load of wet laundry into my 18mo old, GE front loading, electric dryer.  The appropriate settings were chosen, and the unit was turned on.  Approximately 10 mins later, acrid smoke began to emanate from the front-right of the control panel, which set off my home fire alarm.  The unit was still running, and I quickly turned the unit off via the panel, as well as unplugged the unit from the wall outlet.  After the smoke cleared, I checked the vent to ensure it wasn't a lint fire (it wasn't).  I subsequently hired an appliance repair company to come out and diagnose/repair the unit.  Upon inspection and removal of the control panel from the dryer, significant damage was obvious on the control panel.  Several electrical wires from the electrical harness were melted at their connectors, several panel relays were charred and melted.  There was melted and burnt plastic and wiring in multiple places on the panel.  It appears that 220v electrical arching across the wires led to melting of electrical components, but was not sufficient to trip the home (30A as code compliant) circuit breaker, nor enough to disable the unit.  Had I not been present, it more than likely would have continued until a fire started, which could have burned down my home with my pets within.
justification: The incident involved significant electrical damage and potential fire hazard, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
Rowenta Clothes Iron Model DW4060120V 50-60Hz 1700W  This is an approximately a 2 year old clothes iron used daily.  On the 22nd of December 2017 it was used as usual in the morning by turning the selector knob all the way to the right on high steam setting for cotton/linen.  The large dial was turn off (all the way to the left) as usual and I went about the day's business.  About 12 hours later at bedtime and while laying in bed with the lights off,  I have a small air fan blowing to circulate air. I noticed by sound an intermittent drop in speed sound on the little fan I was using.  Knowing that there is something in the bedroom's circuit drawing intermittent current that would cause the low fan speed to drop, my first impression was the Rowenta Iron. Knowing that this model iron has an 3 way automatic shut off I didn't at first think this is what was where the intermittent power was coming from and besides the indicator light was off on the Rowenta iron.    

I looked at everything that was plugged into the bedroom AC outlets and the only thing causing the intermittent power consumption was the Rowenta Iron but again it had an automatic shut off and I though this could not be it. 

I approached the iron, the indicator light was off but the iron was EXTREMELY HOT not only at the metal plate but the housing was almost too hot to touch as it caused some minor 1st degree burns to my right hand fingers.  The first thing I checked was the large dial and it was in the off position.  In the past, regardless of where the large dial was, this iron would always shut off automatically in about 8-10 min if not in use in an upright position as a safety measure.  Apparently this Rowenta model that was turned off in the morning via the large dial never shut off and the back up automatic shut off (shuts off automatically when no motion is detected over time) never engaged and "I would assume" this iron has a temperature sensor as a third safety backup that never engaged.  There is no doubt in my mind that this iron could of caused a fire as it was extremely over heated and sitting on a ironing board with a cloth cover. 

The only thing I could think of that would by-pass all these safety features is that there was a power outage the same day where three individual power surges in rapid succession occurred in a 30 second period.
justification: The incident caused minor 1st degree burns, indicating an injury occurred.

incident_description:
Occupant told front desk their A/C unit was sparking out of the vents. The front desk informed the occupants that they would have another room for them and they were sending maintenance up. He went into their room to assist them with switching rooms and noticed ÃÂa lot of smokeÃÂ coming from the window unit. He called the Chief Engineer as he realized this was more than a minor malfunction and closed the door behind him. He then ran to the electrical panel at the end of the hallway and threw the roomÃÂs breaker (it had not tripped). He returned to 510 where he met the chief engineer in the hallway. They opened the door and found the room charged with smoke and could see flames starting to climb the curtains. They closed the door and retrieved an ABC extinguisher from the hallway. They entered the room and extinguished the fire. They state the flames were coming from the vent side of the air conditioning unit.

However, these others had not led to a fire.
Before my injury I checked the consumer product recall webpage and was unable to find this LG air-conditioning unit product listed in their recalls. Upon my return to work I contacted LG and was told that this model was made for the [REDACTED] suite and their parent company. Their website does not show this model. When I informed the customer service agent of who I was and why I was calling she referred me to their internal investigator, [REDACTED], who was following up on this incident with the [REDACTED]. incident_description:
We installed a Carrier gas furnace (Model 58MV). In March it stopped working and after 6 service calls from 2 different Carrier service companies (and a replaced fan and motherboard), we were told that the problem is with a heat exchanger that has been known to fail and possibly lead to carbon monoxide poisoning. Here is one of many articles from HVAC companies about it:
https://www.aircoheating.ca/safety-notice-carrier-heat-exchangers/

When the technician came to our house, he turned off the gas on our unit because he suspected a leak. Carrier has not recalled this product despite the known issues and safety concerns.

While the heat exchangers are covered under warranty, it does not cover the repair, for which we received an estimate of $2300. To replace the unit would be $4,460.00+tax. The entire unit cost around $7,000. Without a recall and with the high cost of replacing this defective product, many people could result in harm due to carbon monoxide poisoning or worse. Please investigate this situation. Thank you.

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involves a known issue with a heat exchanger that could lead to carbon monoxide poisoning, but no actual injury or death has been reported in this case.

incident_description:
I purchased two SAMSONITE CONVERTER/ADAPTER PLUG KIT WITH POUCH (Item NO.: 495591073, http://shop.samsonite.com/exclusion-list-additional-sam25/samsonite-converter-adapter-plug-kit-with-pouch/495591073.html) on August 6th 2017 at Best Buy.

I lived in the US for three years and moved back to Germany in September 2017. I bought the converts to use it for some appliances I had purchased in the US. The product description states, that the adpater works with most travel products up to 1600 Watt.

I first used the adapter for an Air Bed (Insta-Bed Raised Air Mattress with Never Flat Pump). It ifrst worked fine and I was able to inflate the bed fully and also was able to add some air a few times. Also the built in never flat pump worked properly. But at some point there was a funny electric smell and the air bed pump stopped working. There is a fuse inside the samsonite adapter, but that one was perfectly OK. The indicator light on the adapter also still worked, but the air bed did not work at all anymore. 
To check if somehting is wrong with the converter I used it for my US shaver. The shaver basically blew up in my hand within a few seconds. I was not hurt, but I could clearly feel the impact. The fuse of the samsonite converter was still OK. I then checked the output of the converter with a Voltmeter and it showed about 230 Volts. This clearly indicated that the converter was broken as it should convert to 110 Volts. To compare it, I unpacked the second converter I had purchased and measured the output at that one. It gave me around 110 Volts.

I read some reviews on the Samsonite Homepage and there were customers that had similar issues. The converter simply does not work and can be dangerous in regards to fire or getting an electric shock.

Last week I sent a complaint E-Mail to costomer service at samsonite. No answer. Today I called them and the only thing they told me was, that I need to claim the product at Best Buy and there are no refunds for broken appliances that the converter was used for. I recommended them to take the product off the market, as it does not work and is dangerous. They want to get back to me within 48 hours. I already told them that I am very angry and will also file this saftey complaint.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning adapter that caused an appliance to blow up, but no injury was reported.
