incident_description:
For about 6 months in 2014, my wife and I smelled oil fumes in our house but we were unable to find the source. Service calls to clean and check the oil-burner furnace system failed to find any leak. The oil tank was a Roth Double-Wall Tank (DWT) that was installed in 2006 and still under its 10-year warranty. It is equipped with a ÃÂvisual leak indicatorÃÂ and it showed no leak. From July to December, my wife experienced a range of illness that caused her to seek medical treatments about 30 times. Her symptoms included frequent head and stomach pain, nausea, eye irritation, poor appetite and significant weight loss. The cause of these symptoms was unknown and all the treatments were ineffective.

On 12/8/2014, I finally discovered oil fumes were coming out of a corner at the top of the DWT. When it was reported to Roth, they alleged that the leak was caused by improper installation and denied the tank was defective. As an experimental physicist experienced in fluid handling systems, I investigated the cause of the leak and came to the conclusion that the design of the DWT is fundamentally flawed. Its inner plastic tank is prone to rupture and the leak indicator does nothing when it happens. This poses considerable health and safety hazards to every household where a Roth tank installed. The product should be recalled regardless of warranty period.

A summary of my experience with the DWT is given below and more details are given in the attached report.

************************
Roth markets the DWT for heating oil storage in residential homes and claims superiority over common steel tanks in both safety and durability. The extra protection is afforded by the two "completely sealed" tanks and a "highly visible optical leak alarm" that alerts the homeowner if oil leaks out of the inner tank into the wall space between the two tanks.  However, both of these safety claims are essentially false.  

The DWT uses an inner tank made of plastic to prevent corrosion. However, Roth is well aware that the oil weight causes the plastic tank to deform, which results in vertical movement of the pipe adapter at the top of the tank. Standard regulations require the external pipes be rigidly secured. Thus the movement of the adapter results in enormous stress on the plastic tank, making it susceptible to rupture.  Oil subsequently leaks into the space between the tanks.

The outer tank is made of steel and it is supposed to contain the oil when the inner tank fails. However, the ÃÂrolled seamsÃÂ of the steel tank are actually not sealed and they allow oil fumes to escape. This is a severe health and environmental hazard in residential homes, especially in the winter when all windows are closed.  The "leak indicator" is supposed to alert the owners to replace the tank promptly, but it actually does nothing until a substantial amount of oil has accumulated to float a buoy. In reality, the buoy does not float even when oil begins to drip out of the seams of the steel tank. So the leak indicator only gives the homeowner a false sense of security. Until an oil drip was observed, the dysfunctional alarm misleads people to look for leaks everywhere else but the tank itself. It took me six months to discover the DWT was the culprit of the oil fumes in the house. Service technicians were unable to find the cause. 

The Roth DWT carries a product warranty that is supposed to last ten years or more. When leakages were reported within the warranty period, the company alleged that they were caused by installers not following the instruction in the 2012 manual, even though the tanks were installed before 2012 when the supplied manuals gave no clue of the tank deformation problem. Specifically, the 2012 instruction included an unconventional pipe arrangement that was not followed even in the training video posted on RothÃÂs own site. The arrangement was claimed to relieve the stress caused by the intrinsic movement of the pipe adapter, but a simple mechanical analysis shows the claim to be false. 

Massachusetts regulations require oil tanks to be ÃÂsecurely supported by rigid noncombustible supports to prevent settling, sliding, or lifting.ÃÂ Since the DWTÃÂs inner plastic inner tank is known to have an intrinsic ÃÂsettlingÃÂ and ÃÂliftingÃÂ cycle in response to the filling and emptying of oil, as long as the external pipes are secured, the stress on the pipe adapter can cause internal rupture with no visible sign. Toxic fumes may exist in homes for many months before one realizes the tank has failed. The potentially serious ramifications should require a product recall regardless of warranty period.

The attached report describes the details of owners experience in dealing with the failures of Roth DWTs within the warranty period. It documents how Roth did not acknowledge the defects in their tanks or stand behind its warranty. In addition, by applying basic physics and common knowledge, the design flaws in the DWT are identified and analyzed. Simple remedies are also suggested.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (wife's illness requiring multiple medical treatments) and poses ongoing health hazards due to the flawed tank design.

incident_description:
11/2013:  The flooring was installed the consumer's master bedroom.

The consumer has always experienced hay fever, but after the flooring was install,  she began experiencing  sinus blockage and bloody nose symptoms at night.  The consumer does not have ventilation in her room, so it is closed up more often in the Winter.  The consumer was diagnosed with cancer in 12/2014, and had chemo radiation from March-June 2015 and August-September 2015. 

Mid April 2016, the consumer saw a news story on Dr. Oz about the flooring and started adding matters up.  The consumer had just finished a portion of radiation treatment.

4/18/2016:  The consumer was at her dentist and they noticed red spots on the back of her tongue, which gave them concern.  The dentist noted that the spots could be cancer related.

The consumer visited the firm's website, but according to the information listed on their site, her flooring is not included in the investigation.

The consumer completed cancer treatment in 2016 with targeted drug (Herceptin) from March 2015 - March 2016,
but was advised to see an Ear Nose & Throat Specialist about the spots on her tongue, if they persisted.  

She estimates that she had 279 square feet of the flooring in her home.
justification: The consumer experienced sinus blockage and bloody nose symptoms, which are injuries, and was later diagnosed with cancer, though a direct link to the flooring is not established.

incident_description:
I have a LG Clothes Washing Machine, model WT1101CW.  The unit had completed washing a small load of bedding at around 2 PM US CST.  The lid was left down after the load completed.  

I went into the laundry room around 8 PM US CST, and the washing machine was fine.

The door to the laundry room where the washing machine was closed shut when I left at 8 PM US CST.  When I woke up at 6 AM US CST, I went to the laundry room, and found the glass top of the washing machine to have shattered; there were spider web like cracks covering the entire glass area.  I put my hand on the glass, palm facing down, to see if the glass was some kind of laminated glass, a little piece of glass pierced my skin.  It was a minor cut.  When I opened the top, and then shut the top, the glass fell out from the middle of the glass area.  While the glass is safety glass, it is not like an automobile front windshield, and it does not have any laminate, tape, or adhesive to hold it together if it breaks.
justification: The incident resulted in a minor injury (a cut from broken glass), which classifies it as severity level 3. The occurrence likelihood is rated as rare (1) because spontaneous glass shattering in washing machines is not a common event.

T53 provided horizontal ventilation of the structure through open doors and windows via smoke ejector. Fire was reported as extinguished and confirmed via TIC. Once the structure was clear of smoke, pictures and an investigation were performed. When the investigation was confirmed complete, the dryer was removed to the outside of the structure and slight overhaul of the 2 walls the dryer sat on performed.

incident_description:
This is excerpts from a fire report:

C.  SUMMARY OF THE FIRE SCENE EXAMINATION

1.	On 03/25/2016 an initial examination of the fire scene was conducted by the Worcester Fire Department Fire Investigation Unit.  Lieutenant [REDACTED] was the investigator.  Entry to the fire scene was made by means of exigent circumstances, while the fire companies were still on scene for fire suppression.  The initial scene examination concluded on 03/25/2016 at approximately 18:43 hours.

2.	A systematic examination was initialed upon arrived.  External examination of the fire site revealed no smoke or fire damage.  Internal examination was conducted beginning in areas of least damage toward areas of heaviest damage which was all contained to the kitchen.  Examination of the fire scorched flooring, paint spray pattern, grease areas, uncommunicated areas of thermal damage under the cabinet and on the other side of the stove revealed no definitive cause.  Several ceiling tiles had fallen down, possibly resulting from the explosion.  The cabinet under the sink showed signs of a plumbing leak.  Many different items were stored under the sink. A paint spray can was found rusted and ruptured, and several other containers of cleaning supplies, pest poison, and other unknown chemicals appeared to be possibly leaking because of the water leak. Several ignition sources were located within proximity including electrical outlets, hot pans, and the open flame from the food cooking on the stove.  It could not be determined if there was a chemical reaction under the cabinet with leaking containers that caused the ignition and explosion because some items could not be identified.  The items that could be identified were logged and researched.  No persons smoked cigarettes in the home.  No circuit breakers were found to be tripped in the unit.   

III.   CONCLUSIONS

1.  	Based upon the information developed through the investigation, it is believed within a reasonable degree of investigative certainty that the origin of this flash fire was the failure and rupture of the paint can under the sink which allowed the flammable aerosol gases to escape, travel across the kitchen floor and ignite by the open flame of the stove top cooking and that the cause was accidental.

2.	An exemplar paint can was found at a local retailer and the MSDS was obtained.  According to the MSDS, the paint was made specifically for Walmart by Rust-Oleum as a low cost everyday paint.  The aerosol contained Acetone, Propane and Butane in mixtures ranging from 37.5% to 85%.  The explosive range is rated at 0.9% to 13.0%.  The can was not full according to [REDACTED] and it had been sitting in the same place for an unknown amount of time.  It cannot be determined if the can was compromised by a chemical reaction or from the water leak, or a combination of both.  

3.	 The first fuel ignited was the aerosol gases of the paint can.  The ignition was the piloted ignition of the open flame from the stove top burners.  The ignition sequence was the rupture and explosion of the paint can causing flammable gases to travel across the kitchen and make contact with the burner to create a flash fire.  The fire then scorched the wood cabinets and flooring near the sink as well as burning [REDACTED].  Other competent ignition sources located in the area of origin were ruled out as a cause. The minor pressure wave from the explosion caused several of the weak ceiling tiles to fall.
justification: The incident involved a flash fire and explosion causing damage but no mention of injuries or death.

incident_description:
This report is for a Kwikset Corporation keyed lockset used in homes and sold at various retail outlets.  The specific model being reported is the "Titan" series with the "Hancock" knob style. 

A standard door lockset will have several major parts, including a knob assembly on each side of the door.  Each knob assembly will contain the actual knob (that may contain a  key cylinder) and a stationary plate attached to the door.  This plate is sometimes called a "rose" or "anti-pry" plate.  This rose plate is typically manufactured with a rolled over edge to retain the knob.  

ok, here's the issue - On this model of kwikset locksets (and perhaps others), the rolled over edge  will begin to "unroll" on doors with daily usage.  In our case, its showing up on several locksets, and typically on the side of the door you pull to close.  When this happens, it leaves a VERY SHARP meal edge and poses a significant danger of fingers being sliced when normally operating the door.  In my case, I received a very deep finger cut similar to a knife cut.

This safety defect should be reported to the manufacturer.
justification: The incident resulted in a very deep finger cut, which qualifies as an injury, and the issue is reported on several locksets indicating a recurring problem.

incident_description: We purchased Morningstar Moso bamboo flooring from Lumber Liquidators in December 2014 and had it installed with one of their recommended installers.  The cost was about $10,000.  We recently had our air quality tested because of some unexplained health issues with myself and my children.  The formaldehyde level on our second floor and on the steps (where the flooring is installed) was 0.13 ppm.  The air quality expert said that was well above the 0.05ppm max that is recommended in residences.  In order to see if it was the flooring that was causing the increase, he took the meter to the garage, which was measuring 0 ppm.  We then took an extra board that was in the garage and placed the meter next to it.  The meter was immediately registering 0.12 ppm with just one board.  I contacted Lumber Liquidators since this is their brand of bamboo and was told that they are being investigated for their laminate flooring, but not the bamboo.  It also states on their website that they don't have any safety standards that they need to follow for bamboo.  The only recommendations that the air quality expert could give us (since we live in Florida & won't be able to keep the windows open for very long in the summer), is to buy a $1200 IQAir Multigas air purifier or remove the flooring.  We have decided to remove the flooring since there is no guarantee that the purifier will work and it is not a permanent solution.  The bamboo flooring from this company needs to be tested and this Lumber Liquidators needs to be held responsible.
justification: The incident involves unexplained health issues linked to high formaldehyde levels from the flooring, indicating injury (severity 3). The likelihood is high (4) as the flooring is already installed and emitting harmful levels.

The item is USB wall charger.  The description on Amazon reads:  iXCCÃÂ® Dual USB 4.8 Amp (24 Watt) SMART High Capacity [High Power] AC Travel Wall Charger.

The unit stopped charging.  When I removed it from the electrical outlet to investigate the negative and positive pins from the device stayed in the electrical outlet. 05/06/2014 (Approximate) - The consumer contacted the manufacturer's complaint hotline under the same case number as the medical hotline and explained in detail the incident he had with their air freshener. The representative he spoke to, [REDACTED], informed the consumer that they did not deem it necessary to send an inspector. He was advised to send the product in, photos and an estimate of the damages sustained. Less than a week afterwards, the consumer received a box from the manufacturer so that he send all they asked for back.

Approximately three days later, the consumer contacted the manufacturer and was informed that they had received everything he sent but that they could not provide him with an estimate for when he will receive any answers from them regarding his case.

When the pilot light problems continued even after installation of the replacement parts, your last customer representative said the problem may be with the utilities company and that we should ask the City to pressure test the gas flow. Once the City of Palo Alto turned off the gas to the water heater, I lost all faith in Rheem and had the water heater removed even though it still possesses a long-term warranty. Assuring the safety of my family pre-empts any warranty. Since the replacement parts did not resolve the problem and continued to put us at risk, I am demanding reimbursement of $453 that I paid to have parts installed in attempting to fix the inherently defective water heater.

[REDACTED]

incident_description:
I purchased 3 glass shower doors manufactured by Alumax through an authorized dealer/installer.  These doors were installed in 3 bathrooms in our home in early 2013.  Several months after installation, my 8 year old was getting out of the shower and there was a loud noise, then the shower door shattered all over her.  I was in the bathroom and witnessed this happen.  She was terrified, and had many small pieces of glass embedded in her skin that we needed to remove.  I called the installer who came to take a look.  He told me that the shower door had come out of its tracking (????) causing it to fall.  He stated that it was an extremely rare event for these doors to fall when I expressed concern about the safety (one quick internet search proves that this is absolutely not a rare event).  He supposedly contacted the manufacturer, and then replaced the shower door for us since we were within the 1 year warranty period.
Then, in December 2015, our cleaning person was cleaning in one of the other bathrooms.  She slid the door to the side to open it, heard a very loud noise and then had the glass door shatter over her.  She had to be taken to an urgent care center to have one of the larger pieces of glass removed from her arm.  Again, I contacted the installer to come take a look.  This time he told me that it appeared the door had slipped from its brackets.  He said the manufacturer had changed the installation procedure for theses doors (assuming to make them safer/more secure). After contacting the manufacturer, he told me that because the 1 year warranty period had expired, the manufacturer would not do anything, let alone address the safety of their product.  The installer said I could purchase a new shower door and he would install it in the "new" way.
So currently I am left with no shower door in one bathroom, and two extremely unsafe shower doors in my children's bathrooms.
justification: The incident resulted in injuries from glass shattering, with one case requiring urgent care, indicating a severity level of 3. The recurrence of similar incidents suggests an occurrence likelihood of 4 (likely).

incident_description:
The unit was installed by a licensed plumber. 

The consumer stated that there is a safety issue with his water heater. The water that comes out of the top of the heater to the faucet is extremely hot even at the lowest water temperature setting. 

The consumer stated he has the water heater set to the lowest temperature (115-120F). Initially when he purchased the unit, the water would come out at roughly 160F. Now, the water that comes out of the faucet is at about 182F. After purchasing this unit, the water at the faucet was never 120F even when set to the lowest temperature setting.

The consumer stated that highest setting the water heater can be set to is about 155F.

The consumer contacted the company multiple times over the past few years at 1-800-999-9515 in regards to the issue. In the past, the consumer was informed that the issue was with the controller. The consumer was sent the controller by the company covered under warranty. The consumer has replaced the controller about 4-5 times in the past 2-3 years. 

The consumer had a plumber come out for an inspection in Dec 2015 from [REDACTED]. The plumber informed the consumer that he has seen a lot of problems with these water heaters. The plumber said that the issue is with the controller. 

The consumer spoke to [REDACTED] at the company. She informed the consumer that he would have to have one of their plumbers come out for an inspection. The consumer would have to pay for the cost for an inspection. The consumer was informed that there is "heat stacking" issue with his unit. The consumer was informed, that this kind of thing can happen when the water heater is not used a lot. 
 
The consumer stated that the water temperature being measured at the bottom of the heater is what the controller is expecting to see and what the water heater is set to. However, the water temperature at the top of the heater is a lot hotter than what the temperature is set to. The consumer conducted his own tests to determine that information. 

The consumer stated that the controller is a resistance dependent device that measures the resistance of the thermister. The controller would turn on and off depending on what resistance it sees. The consumer took one of the older controllers and measured the resistance it was seeing from a 120F water in a bottle. The consumer received a number in ohms (about 1000 ohms). The consumer received the same resistance number at the controller that is installed in the unit. The consumer then checked the water temperature at the top of the heater and it came out to 180F. The consumer finally drained the heater and checked the temperature at the drain well and the water temperature was about 120F. 


The consumer noticed an issue with this heater from the time he purchased it. However, the issue has gotten much worse over the past 2-3 years.

The unit is still under parts warranty.
justification: The water heater is producing dangerously hot water, posing a burn risk, but no injury has been reported yet.

incident_description: My 8 year old son was finished taking his shower and went to slide open our glass framed double shower doors to get out when the door suddenly imploded.  The noise and our son screaming was heard by his father and I in the kitchen and we ran to investigate.  Our son stood soaking wet covered head to toe in small bits of glass and surrounding him were piles of glass chunks that were trapping him in the shower. The force of the implosion caused the bathroom floor also to be coated in glass with pieces landing as far as into the hallway.  After my husband carefully picked our son up and removed him to the other room I was able to gently remove the glass bits that were covering him and wash the rest off of him in the other bath. He sustained two minor cuts on his foot that I applied antibiotic ointment to.  However, he was psychologically traumatized by the incident and was weeping and shaking uncontrollablly from fear even hours later when he thought about it.  He swears now he will never use that shower again or any glass shower.  My husband vows no more glass showers.  The cleanup was ridiculous.  It took hours for us with two vacuums to get all the glass bits and pieces.  Many items in the shower had to be thrown away because of the film of glass covering them.  I too ended up with a small cut on my thumb from the cleanup.  The one door of the two that didn't break had the words Unitex tempered ANSIZ97.1-1984 16CFR  1201 11 SGCC-2575 1/4 U  there were no other identifying marks and the doors were in the house when we moved in 6 years ago and used regularly in a gentle manner.  I don't know how to contact the manufacturer since it's looks like they are located in china and I can't find a website.  I think these type of glass shower doors need to have a safety film that if broken keeps it from scattering glass or a warning label affixed permanently that this can happen.  We had no idea this could happen.  Surprisingly  his injuries were minor because my son jumped back into the corner got on his tippy toes and closed his eyes, but what if it was an elderly person who couldn't react as quickly.  Please do something about these doors to keep people safer!
justification: The son sustained minor cuts and psychological trauma, and the mother also got a small cut during cleanup, which qualifies as injury.

incident_description:
I purchased a "Neat Ice Kit (Double Mold) - Clear Ice Cube Mold" from Amazon.com for making clear ice. The way it works is that you freeze water in this special insulated mold. It makes a block of ice approximately 2" x 2" x 4"; it has clear ice in one end and cloudy ice in the other. The kit provides a steel chisel with a wooden mallet, intended to be used to break the block of ice into smaller pieces that would fit in a drinking glass. 

After using the chisel as directed to break off the clear portion of the ice (for the first time), I saw a very small dark object on the ice. Thinking my recently cleaned cutting board may have had something on it, I brushed it away with the many little pieces of ice. Then I noticed that there were seven new very small chipped areas on the sharp edge of the chisel. It looked like I had been cutting granite, instead of frozen water. Small pieces of steel had broken off and I only saw one of them. The other six pieces apparently got mixed in with the ice.

I don't want a product that inserts pieces of a steel chisel into the ice I put in my drinks. I will ask for a refund.

I'm not a doctor or scientist, and can't say for sure what the effects are of drinking a liquid with chips of steel chisel, but common sense tells me that this product, or at least the chisel, should be removed from the market until the problems can be solved. I should probably be writing the Consumer Products Safety Commission too.

Link to the item on Amazon:
http://www.amazon.com/Neat-Ice-Kit-Double-Mold/dp/B00O2CO93G/ref=cm_cr_pr_product_top?ie=UTF8
justification: The incident involves a product defect that could potentially lead to ingestion of metal chips, but no actual injury was reported.

incident_description:
Please see below letter that I emailed to the Corporate Secretary of the Dollar Tree. I have copied and pasted the letter into the body of this incident description. The email that I sent to the secretary also included 6 pictures of the fire damage caused by the Dollar Tree product. I have not received a response from Dollar Tree Corporate. I sent the email and pictures one week ago.

Corporate Secretary
Dollar Tree, Inc.
500 Volvo Parkway
Chesapeake, VA 23320
United States
 
[REDACTED]
RE: Aromatic Wax Warmer Purchased From Dollar Tree Store #2634
 
 
Attn. Merchandising Manager:
 
My husband, [REDACTED], purchased an aromatic wax warmer from a local Dollar Tree store in Tucson, Arizona. As the attached pictures depict, the small ceramic unit is meant to hold a tea light which when lit heats a scented wax cube. The warmer came with one cautionary sticker adhered to it. The sticker warned to fit a proportionately sized candle into the warmer. I am unable to provide the direct quote because the sticker has been peeled of.  However, I do recall that the product's only safety advisory was in reference to using a smaller candle, such a tea light; as opposed to a slightly larger candle, such as a votive.
 
The warmer was kept in our guest bathroom that is located in the front of our house. I recently lit a tea light in the lower portion of the warmer and placed one cube of "[REDACTED]" brand scented wax on the upper portion of the unit. Approximately one half of an hour later, I went to the back of our house to take a shower in our master bath.
 
Luckily, [REDACTED] was home that day. He was spending most of his time outside, however, he did make several trips in and out of the house. On the course of one of his trips, he thought that he smelled something burning. He came into the back bathroom to ask me if I had anything in the oven to which I replied no, I did not. Soon after, my husband came back and insisted that he smelled something burning. I thought it over again, and relayed that I was melting a wax cube in the warmer, however, this couldnÃÂt possibly be the source of his concern.
 
I never imagined that a tea light, contained within a ventilated ceramic warmer, had such hazardous potential. I have lit hundreds of tea lights with no incident. In rare circumstance, it has even been necessary for me to burn the candles straight from the plastic packaging, as they are in the metal casing (I was living in Southern Connecticut during the time that Hurricane Sandy hit).
 
Thank God that [REDACTED] went to investigate. When he looked in the front bathroom , he saw that a fire had began. [REDACTED] first instinct was to smother the fire, so he grabbed for a damp washcloth that happened to be lying on the opposite end of the counter. The moisture from the washcloth made the flames even mores uncontainable. It is common knowledge that in a kitchen fire, for example, to never add water to an oil fire. However, I certainly can see how scented wax wouldnÃÂt necessarily equate to an oil fire scenario. Especially when acting fast and on first instinct. Candles are made of wax and they donÃÂt burst into flames.
 
Again, I am so grateful that my husband was home and extinguished the fire before it managed to spread. His hand was burned in the process, but he refused a visit to the ER. Since the incident, [REDACTED] hand is nearly 100% healed. I don't know how long it would have taken me to realize that a fire was igniting due to the fact that I was taking a shower in the back of the house with the door closed.
 
In my opinion these wax heaters should not be sold to the public without some serious further consideration. Perhaps it is possible to redesign them, because I do not believe that they are safe as they are now. My guess is that reserve for the wax is too close to the flame of the candle. At the very least, the warmers should come with more precautionary warnings. For instance, I happen to be referring to them as "wax warmers." I am not sure what The Dollar Tree references them as, but if a consumer assumes that they are essential oil burners, that could be very dangerous. Even the old standby "never leave your candle unattended," is better than nothing. However, we all know that no one is going to sit around staring at their scented wax melt all day.   
 
Please note, that I did not take the enclosed pictures until after I began cleaning up the area where the wax warmer caught on fire. The area was covered with soot before I first began to clean it. I also opened the cabinet door after the fire was extinguished. You can see that the smoke from the flames was entering into the cabinet despite the cabinet door being closed. 
 
Thank you for your time,

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident resulted in a burn injury to the husband, though it did not require emergency medical attention.

incident_description:
RE: Failure of Samsung/Sears Aquajet rvt Top Loading Washer 
Mod. #WA456DRHDSU/AA; S/N Y6BP5AEC700398L; Mfg. Date 2012.7; Purchased on 11.17.12; Purchase Price, $699.99 plus 59.50 tax and $80 delivery and haul-away fee

Summary:  On January 14, 2016 my Samsung/Sears top loading washer failed, displaying an error code of ÃÂnF,ÃÂ (no fill as per Samsung Error Code taxonomy).  Water had discharged on the laundry room floor.  An internet search led me to the Samsung Service Bulletin addressing relocation of the drain pump (ASC20131127001, Nov. 27, 2013 RE WA400, WA422 & WA456 models) to prevent its support bracket from cracking and the pump detaching (falling off its mounting), thereby releasing water from the detached drain hose that becomes disconnected upon failure and severing its power leads.  This failure resulted in the main control board (PCB) arcing and melting.

Because the drain pump was mounted on the washer tub rather than on the machine frame, vibration induced fatigue results in fracture and parting of the support brackets at points of stress concentration, i.e., at the mounting screw tabs.  Moreover, the rubber bushings (a.k.a., ÃÂcushionsÃÂ as referred to by Samsung) fail from continual exposure to high cycle/amplitude vibration.  This is clearly a design defect.  Ironically, these machines  are marketed as ÃÂVRTÃÂ models, e.g., having ÃÂVibration Reduction Technology.ÃÂ

On February 22, 2013 Samsung issued its first Service Bulletin (ASC2013022001)
for the subject models entitled ÃÂDrain Pump Case Damage.ÃÂ  At that time, Samsung acknowledge damage to the drain pump case causing water leakage and called for replacement of the pump cover and mounting bushings.  Then, on November 27, 2013, Samsung issued a second Service Bulletin as mentioned above calling for relocating the drain pump.  As stated therein, this was done:
ÃÂ "To improve quality, we changed the position of the bottom of the TUB to the BASE"
ÃÂ "This improvement required us to change the ASSY GUIDE HOSE, ASSY HOSE DRAIN, and HOLDER WIRE SADDLE."

In fact, relocation of the drain pump is done to rectify a basic design flaw that created a dangerous situation to the consumer.  Nevertheless, to the best of my knowledge neither Samsung nor its product retailers, such as Sears, Lowes, etc., have ever issued a recall notice to consumers who bought these machines advising them of the immanent failure of the machineÃÂs drain pump during operations and the resulting risk of flooding and fire.  In my professional opinion as a fire safety expert, these machines ought to be recalled post-haste.

It should be noted that Samsung has a history of washing machine fires in both front loading and top loading machines.  In 2007 Samsung issued a recall for front loading machines due to electrical induced fires from water contact (CPSC Release #07-135, March 21, 2007.  More recently, a massive recall is underway in Australia and New Zealand for top loading machines.  More than 144,000 (AU) and 36,000 (NZ) Samsung top loading machines made between 2010 and 2013 are subject to recall due to a pervasive and serious fire hazard.  These machines reportedly have caused hundreds of fires; however, Samsung reportedly has refused to advertise the recall on Australian television.
justification: The incident involved a washing machine failure leading to water discharge and potential fire hazard, but no injury or death was reported.

I noted the machine had been warmer than normal before pumping bike tires on 1/9/2016 and accused the kids of playing with it.  I was able to wake everyone and escape injuries that night, but some other family may not be as lucky. 

This is my scenario that I will discuss with my insurance company. The air compressor began to spontaneously heat up over several days, melting the cord that I remember, was draped over the compressor motor. Once cord was fully melted, the arc occurred igniting the hot melted plastic on the unit.  The unit burned high enough to burn the many boxes of Christmas decorations store in the attic directly above.  Please add this information to any others you may have on the Porter-Cable Model #12236 and hopefully this is just a bad unit and isolated case.
justification: The incident involved a major house fire caused by an air compressor, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description: We purchased a Dyson AM04 fan/heater in April 2015. It was plugged into a wall outlet. My wife went to plug another device into the other receptacle and found that the fan cord was very hot and had scorched the outlet. It would have caused a fire if had been left plugged in.
justification: The incident involved a hot and scorched outlet, which could have caused a fire but did not result in injury or death.

incident_description: I recently purchased a gently used front loading washing machine.  I had absolutely NO idea that there was anything hiding inside of the rubber gasket.  I got it home, hooked it up and ran a cycle of laundry through the machine.  When I opened the door to remove the clothes, there was a very strong and distinct mildew/damp odor.  The clothes all were stinky and were not clean because of the smell.  I began examining the machine closer and saw residual water and soap bubbles in the gasket crease.  I used a towel and wiped the area out and the towel produced some dirt and stinky old soap residue.  I then got a flashlight and parted open the gasket crack to see what was in there and it was covered in black mold.  My entire family suffer from significant allergies to dust, pollen, mold and pet hair.  I am now unable to use this washing machine despite cleaning and bleaching and using powerful smell boosters in the machine to try to kill the mildew smell that the clothes have.
justification: The incident involves exposure to mold and mildew, which can exacerbate allergies but no direct injury is reported.

incident_description: There is a two-prong electrical connection between the hose hand and the wand. That connection put out enough heat the melt the plastic house surrounding one prong, blacken the prong and cause a short in the circuit completion.  Local repair center told me this is a fire hazard and I should not attempt to use the vacuum.  This is not an age or use issue, this is a built in defect.
justification: The incident involves a fire hazard due to a built-in defect causing overheating and a short circuit, but no injury or death is reported.

incident_description: Product: (DreamLine Visions 56-60x72-inch Frameless Sliding Shower Door - I do not see a serial number but on the remaining glass is stamped: Tempered  16CFR 1201-II  ANSI  Z97.1-2004   1/4UA  SGCC 3960) was purchased July 6, 2014 from Overstock.com and installed mid August, 2014. At 7:45am January 25, 2016 my husband stepped into the shower, closed the doors (the enclosure has two stationary panels on each side and two sliding panels that meet in the middle). After closing, the panel on the right side shattered and imploded on him. He had not turned the water on yet. He experienced some cuts (arm, thighs, abdomen, chest, feet) (none requiring suturing) and some glass in his right eye that came out with flushing (I am a nurse practitioner with 15 years of emergency department experience and I cared for him immediately). I took photos with him in place (in case information was required about the pattern in which the glass fell) and then gave him shoes to enable him to get out to safety. I removed glass from the anterior surface of his thighs, feet, arms, neck, face, and torso. He then showered in another bathroom and I swept up the glass into the corner of the shower to avoid further danger to us or our pets.
justification: The incident resulted in multiple cuts and glass in the eye, which constitutes an injury but no death or need for suturing.

incident_description: My husband and I were awoken at 1am this morning to a loud bang and then crackling (like popcorn) noise coming from our master bath. Upon entering the bathroom we noticed that the shower door had shattered all by itself leaving glass pieces everywhere. I have photos and a video of shower door but was unable to upload to your website. I can send them to you from my phone if needed
justification: The shower door shattered, causing an incident with no reported injuries.

incident_description:
I used the Humidifier last winter without issue. This year, I cleaned the unit as I normally did, filled the tank and set it up for use. It functioned but the output control knob did not seem to change the amount of vapor being produced. I assumed the switch was faulty, but it was outputting water vapor so I let it run. The next night, the Unit was working intermittently. I shut it off and did not use it. The next morning, I unplugged it and brought it downstairs to see if the switch was replaceable.

Upon opening the bottom of the housing, I could smell something had burned and the control circuit board was all burned and melted. I don't know how it did not start a fire or that I could not smell anything until the case was opened. It nearly melted a hole through the bottom of the case.
justification: The incident involved equipment damage and a potential fire hazard, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description: We were using a Lasko portable box fan. It was on low and was running on a wood floor overnight. The fan blades stopped running and the motor area started to smoke and get very hot. It burned some nearby paper and nearly started a house fire. Had I not happened to be awake at the time, it would have probably injured or killed both my wife and me, as well as our pets. This fan was in our bedroom next to our bed. The incident occurred within about 5 minutes of me getting up to go to the bathroom and get something to drink in the middle of the night and when I returned to bed. There was no smoke when I left the room, and when I returned the hallway and bedroom smelled of burning paper/active fire and there was a haze of smoke in the bedroom. The fan motor was about one foot away from a wall and heat vent, which were also very hot as a result of the fan smoking/burning. I woke up my wife and she ran the fan outside, which was very hot, even on the plastic handle, while it was smoking and threw it in the snow, ending the incident. We were operating this fan in a safe manner and have had box fans for years without problems. Aside from a very minor amounts of dust on the blades, the fan was clean and in good condition and only about three years old from our time of purchasing it. I have no doubt in my mind that had I not happened to be up, it would have caused a house fire and was on its way to doing so. We're not negligent or stupid when it comes to fire or household appliances. We operate things safely and have never had an issue like this with any other fan we've owned.
justification: The fan malfunction led to smoke and nearly caused a house fire, which could have resulted in injury or death if not for timely intervention.

incident_description: My son turned on our Heat Surge, electric heater, model #30000488, and walked out of the room. a few minutes later he walked back into the room and noticed a large amount of smoke and smell of something burning. He noticed that the heater's fire place was not lit up and unplugged the unit and carried it outside. when I got home I took the back off to see what happened and all the wires were melted together. It appeared that a connecter somehow came loose from the fan cage and rested against the metal on the side and started melting the inside wiring.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning heater causing smoke and melted wires, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description: Vivint Solar company Installed solar panels on our roof in 2012.We have had issues with the solar panels since the onset which causes snow and ice to avalanche off the roof all at once and has caused property damage twice since the installation. With the likely possibility of future personal injuries. They have thus far failed to remedy this issue since 2012. We have had two property damage claims against the company.Which they have paid out. But regardless they refuse to address the issue of the hazard that the panels cause. I am respectfully asking your agency for your help in this matter.

03/15/2015 (Approximate) - The consumer used the product once again and the same thing occurred; she kept being shocked by it. The consumer contacted the manufacturer and explained the situation. She was informed that the problem may be in the handle and so they would send her a replacement.

incident_description: I have recently learned that I am far from the only consumer who has experienced a premature failure of an indoor evaporator coil on a Goodman Manufacturing Co. heat pump/AC. Our unit was purchased in mid-2009. In sales literature, the company claimed that its coils had undergone rigorous testing:"Then, to ensure consistent comfort, every coil is tested three times to detect leaks, and not just the obvious kind. We test for the smallest possible leaks, so small they may only surrender one ounce in ten years. That way, you will never have to worry about costly refrigerant escaping or an unwanted service call to address leak-related system problems" (Goodman "AIR HANDLERS AND COILS brochure dated 11/07). Although the coil is under warranty, the labor and R410a refrigerant and refrigerant recovery parts have led to our being billed over $700. Twelve POUNDS of R410A had apparently bled out inside our home over who knows how long. The system would have been running inefficiently as a result, resulting in higher utility bills and excessive wear on the motor. Whether the leaking refrigerant was responsible I cannot say, but during the time we owned this heat pump I experienced heart arrythmia (multiple cardiac arrests), and lung issues that someone at Mayo Clinic believed looked like sarcoidosis in the lungs (sarcoidosis was later ruled out, I understand). Then came congestive heart failure and in 2014 a heart transplant. Please know that I'm only 62. Until my early 50s I was regularly bicycling to work -- about 14 miles round trip. I think I was in my 50s when I hiked up Pike's Peak on the Barr Trail, too. These health issues hit me out of the blue. My wife wasn't similarly affected, but I had retired early and had become basically a hermit within our home, so my exposure to indoor air pollutants would have been greater. Search Goodman coils on the internet and it won't take you long to find info on a class action lawsuit over these coils, or multitudes of complaints. Goodman has clearly known of the issue for years. But did Goodman or the local dealer who installed the unit let us know that this was something we should regularly check for so we could avoid spewing the refrigerant into the air, waste who knows how much electricity, or allow excessive wear and tear on the motor? Did Goodman recall the darned things or offer to cover the cost of labor and R410A replacement? Nope. We heard not one peep from them. The company may claim that the small leaks in the coils aren't harmful to one's health. Maybe that's true. But ask the company president and its directors to a confined room, haul in enough bottles of refrigerant so there is 10 pounds of refrigerant per person, open each bottle a crack and ask them to stay there until the bottles are empty. Think you'll get any takers? I hope you, or the FTC if you think that agency is a better fit, will hold their feet to the fire. From what I've read, there is no excuse for them to have allowed this to go on so long. You've got the power; please use it.
justification: The incident describes health issues (heart arrhythmia, lung issues) potentially linked to refrigerant exposure, warranting a severity level of 3. The high number of complaints and a class action lawsuit suggest the occurrence likelihood is likely (4).

incident_description: We bought a Feather River glass door from Home Depot. We had it professionally installed 3 months ago, walked in this morning to find it shattered, cracked from left to right, up and down, shards on the floor. I contacted both the seller and the manufacturer who wouldn't do anything about it but offer me a discount on another door, of which the price had gone up by about $80. I was very disappointed. I was told by both Feather River and Home Depot that we would be responsible for removing and trashing it.

incident_description:
We purchased a Samsung Top Loading washing (4.5 CU FT TL WASH WA45H7000AW) from Lowe's in September 2014. Last week, it exploded. The drum tore off the inside, the machine rotated around, and the top of the washing machine came off. The sides of the machine were bent. It made a loud grinding noise that shook the entire house and when we went to see what happened, it was still plugged in with 5 minutes left. Water was all over the floor. The risk to personal injury to myself, my pregnant wife, or my son was high. Luckily nobody was downstairs when this happened. 

We have been trying to get in touch with someone at Samsung to help and we continue to get non-specific answers, no call backs, or information that we will need to pay fees for labor, parts, diagnosis, etc. We took several pictures of the washing machine, which we can provide on request.
justification: The washing machine exploded causing significant damage but no injuries occurred, placing it at severity level 2. The likelihood is rated as rare given the specific circumstances described.

incident_description: While my 8 year old Fridgedaire Affinity dryer was being used on the normal, low heat setting, a loud noise came from the dryer (presumably from the drum motor coming to an abrupt stop). The control panel lights all began to flash on and off and the dryer made a loud buzzing sound. The laundry room began to fill with smoke and the first signs of fire could be observed behind the control panel. Eventually, the flames melted the front of the control panel, and flames began shooting out the front of the dryer. My husband turned off the breaker, unplug the dryer, and drag it out of the house before it could ignite anything else on fire. He then put out the fire with a fire extinguisher. The fire was electronic in nature and had nothing to do with any lint accumulation.
justification: The incident involved a fire and significant damage to the dryer, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

I simply grabbed the door handle to slide it closed when the door exploded.  Glass shards went everywhere including the ceiling and adjacent room.

incident_description:
Product purchased from Amazon on 12/9/2015 opened 1/12/2016 and found to be unsafe.

Product is a "Forney 58401 Electrical Receptacle, Pin-Type, Portable 50-Amp, 250-Volt " which is an inline (cord attached) NEMA 6-50R 3 pin 240V receptacle.

The design of this product is such that there is no cord anchorage to prevent any stress such as a child tugging on the cord resulting in the insulating cover coming away from the base of the product and exposing live terminals.  (There is cord anchorage but only to the cover.  The cover itself is not secured in any way to the base of the product and the base houses the electrical connections.)

https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B003X4338G/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o05_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1
justification: The product design flaw exposes live terminals if the cover is pulled away, posing a risk of electrical shock, but no actual incident or injury is reported.

incident_description: I used my Jacko portable jump starter on a regular basis because I worked in an automotive shop. I also used it to charge my phone when needed. I went to use it today, (1/14/16) and it was dead. I noticed that the side of it seemed to be pushed out a bit like the battery had expanded in it. When I got home I plugged it in, and the led light flickered and it began making a weird buzzing sound so I unplugged it and looked online what seemed to be going on.

incident_description:
10 years ago, I purchased a [REDACTED] coop and decided to put in new windows, "Tilt and Turns".  I was told they were German windows thought I am not sure this was accurate.
About 4 years ago, I was in my bedroom and one of the windows literally fell out of the frame and onto the bed.  I rolled over quickly and thank God.  The window weighs over 300 pounds and could have easily killed me.  I could not even lift it (and I am strong).  I have these windows throughout my apartment.  I called my window company, Skyline Windows, and they said they had never heard of this happening before.  They came to my apartment a day later and "repaired" it.  I assumed it was some sort of fluke but it scared me, because the window is massive and heavy (I would say it is 3 feet by 6 feet) and it must weigh over 300 pounds.
About 1-1/2 months ago I received a note from Skyline Windows about a safety recall.  The Safety Recall Notice refers to aluminum fittings on tilt-turn windows.  It describes the problem, "The window fittings can break.  This can cause the window to fall, posing an injury hazard to consumers".  The recall is dated November 28, 2012, but I have only been notified 1-1/2 months ago.  I immediately contacted the manufacturer, using both the email and phone number they offered.  I received an email from them basically stating that they will come out when they have a relevant number of consumers to make the trip worth their while.  I am concerned for my safety, as well as that of my pets in the apartment.  A month has passed and I they have not contacted me about scheduling an appointment.  I paid a lot of money for these windows, over $20K, but more importantly, there is a safety issue and I have already had an incident.  I hope you can help.
justification: The incident involved a heavy window falling, which could have caused severe injury or death, but no actual injury occurred. The recall notice and past incident indicate a likely recurrence.

incident_description:

The consumer stated that the explosion happened ten minutes after the heat in the home kicked on from 65 to 70 degrees.

incident_description: We purchased a Samsung model DV520AGP/XAA Gas Dryer in 2012. We had to store it until 12/30/2015. Upon installation and first use on 12/30/2015 the dryer caught fire due to an internal gas leak at the entry connection to the gas valve internal to the dryer chassis. The fire continued to burn after the dryer was shut off until we found the smoking unit in our garage and shut the gas and electricity off immediately. Thankfully we found it only 10-15 minute after the cycle had stopped and damage was limited to severe damage in the the interior of the dryer chassis, wiring and plastic parts. Samsung is taking no responsibility for the occurrence.

incident_description:
As with most phones and tablets, this tablet was sold with a wall charger. The wall charger we had was plugged into an outlet in my sons room right next to his bed. At some point in the night of 1/10/2016-1/11/2016 the charger came apart. The way it is assembled the wall socket plugs are mounted into a plastic piece and that is lightly glued into place. inside the charger unit the wall prongs slip into 2 metal loops where a power connection is made. This connection is maintained by the glued plastic and nothing else. When the glue fails, as was the case with ours the charger falls away from the prongs which remain plugged into the wall. The part of the prongs that would make contact with the loops are left exposed and charged with 100v of electricity. In my case it just came apart while removing the charger from the wall.
I have mentioned that nothing was used inside the charger where the prongs connect to the loops on the circuit board. If it had been soldered together this issue would not have ocured.
justification: The charger came apart, exposing live electrical parts, but no injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
I purchased and had installed Thermoblaster 32000 BTU Blue flame dual Fuel (Gas) heater in my garage this past weekend and found a issue with the unit that I believe is potentially extremely dangerous! This unit has 2 pilots one that is for natural gas and one for liquid propane. When the unit is started in the proper sequence for Natural Gas both pilots light and should stay on. The problem is when or if the Natural gas pilot goes off for what ever reason the LP gas pilot can stay and does stay lit. This allows the thermocouple to stay latched and in turn allows the main gas valve to open and for the gas to flow out. The problem is the LP pilot flame is smaller and located below the burner outlets as normally LP gas is heavier than air but because the unit is hooked up to natural gas which is lighter than air the gas rises quickly and does not ignite. In my case when the garage reached temperature the unit shut down and the natural gas pilot is going out constantly but the LP pilot stays lit. As stated this keeps the gas valve open and then the whole garage filled with gas to the point where we could smell it outside. I was very lucky that I went out to check on it when I did and that the gas did not build down to the point where the LP pilot could have ignited the gas. If it had I am sure it would have leveled my garage.I did speak to a couple of representatives at Thermoblaster at including the president and they recommended that the LP pilot be capped to prevent this scenario from happening and they even have procedure for doing this. I think this procedure would work but my concern is what if someone does not catch this issue in time. Someone or many could die using this product!
I was able to duplicate this issue a few times and have removed the heater and returned it to Lowes. I think it is also very important to mention that there are a couple of other reviews on the Lowes web site that indicate others have had the same or similar issues with this heater. They should be forced to remove the heater from the market until this safety defect is resolved. rous.
justification: The incident describes a potentially life-threatening gas leak scenario that could lead to an explosion, indicating a high severity risk of death.

incident_description: I have a Maytag washer and on November 18. 2015 while the machine was doing a small load of towels a loud bang. almost like an explosion, I went to the machine and noticed large amounts of smoke coming from around the tub. I shut of the breaker. I went back to the washer and heard another loud bang, and at that point flames shot up around the washer. The fire dept, came and the washer was still burning. If I was not in the area of the washer we would have lost our home. I contacted Maytag with no answer. I have had to purchase a new washer.
justification: The incident involved a washer catching fire, posing a significant risk, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description: I have a Benzomatic fire extinguisher and I had sitting on the kitchen counter  to find out how to dispose of it since it was old and one night it exploded. The bottom blew right off and the canister was split open. You could see where it hit the ceiling and bounced out into the family room. It knocked over and broke some canisters on the counter and blew the Easter basket that was sitting on the table beside of it out into the family room, breaking the basket and the DVDs in it.

incident_description: touchless faucet stopped working.  I thought it was the batteries.  When I went to replace them, it was very hot, so I disconnected the box and ran the faucet without it.
justification: The faucet malfunctioned and became very hot, posing a burn risk, but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
Our wipes warmer was empty and needing a new absorbent pad, so we decided to unplug it and clean it out as normal.

When carrying it to the sink, without the cord attached, I noticed some water leaking. After investigating further I found that the water was coming out around the power plug. There was about a half a cup of water in the bottom of it.

I didn't notice in the instructions if it was recommended to be plugged into a GFI plug for protection from electrical short circuits due to water inside of the electrical cavity, but I would do that if I were to buy another one.  

We have owned this product for a couple of years, and it has worked very well. But after finding the water coming out of the electrical plug-in we will not be using it any more.

There were no injuries or damage caused by this issue. Our little one will be disappointed to find only cold wipes until it is replaced.
justification: No injuries or damage occurred, but the presence of water near the electrical plug constitutes an incident.

incident_description:
I have been using various brands of steam mops for quite some time, [REDACTED] and my Haan  FS-20 which I had used for a few months, on a regular basis of about 2-3 times a month.   Upon pulling out the mop one day, I noticed that it kept tripping my circuit breaker whenever I would plug it into a GFI outlet.   Thinking that my house was just old or that I had a lot of other appliances connected to those outlets, I moved the mop to a regular outlet where I was luckily able to clean the floors.   

Upon doing further research online later to determine what the problem may be, I came across several reviews from other users that the inside corrodes causing the electrical components to malfunction.   I decided to take apart the bottom of my mop (of which coincidentally they use special screws that are not easy to get off.  Must be to just have users purchase a new one instead of trying to fix a broken mop??) to find that the entire inside of the mop was in fact corroded.  While there is a small O ring around the hole where the steam comes out, it is obviously not enough to keep water from getting inside the unit and therefore corroding all the interior components in due time.   In reading other complaints where others have been injured by either using this mop in bare feet where water gets left on the floor or touching the metal part of the mop, I'm glad to say that I did not encounter this of which is rare as living in Florida we are in bare feet a long portion of the year.

I feel that this is a major design flaw or negligence in the part of Haan to ensure that a device that they sell is not better sealed or protected from water and electrical components to come into contact with each other and cause not only a short life span or issues with the mop, but also potentially dangerous conditions for a user!    I would hope that the new Haan mops are much better made however in looking for a new steam mop currently, I am very hesitant to put my hard earned money out for another Haan if they can allow these things to occur.
justification: The incident describes a malfunctioning steam mop causing electrical issues but no injury or death, fitting severity level 2. The occurrence likelihood is 4 (likely) due to multiple user reports of similar issues.

incident_description: Whirlpool duet ht dryer caught fire, it started out with a liud screaming noise for about5 minutes then it went back to normal smoke blaze the back of the dryer, not sure what is going in. Cobtact whirlpool no answer yet.
justification: The dryer caught fire, which is an incident, but there is no mention of injury or death.

incident_description:
This water heater (AO Smith Pro Max: Model:  ECT 40 200 - Serial: 1006A011942) - has been malfunctioning for three months, most notably, producing a limited amount of hot water ÃÂ about 5 gallons.  After which the water has zero heat.  This behavior began with the upper breaker (on the AO Smith) frequently tripping from some overload.  Pressing the red button would restore heating, but this did not last more than a few days.  Eventually, the lower element stopped working totally, and only the top element was heating. 

Repairs comprised three visits from licensed plumbers.  The diagnosis ÃÂ after several long conversations with AO Smith technical support ÃÂ was defective thermostats.  Both heating elements were intact, as shown by testing.

Phase 1 ÃÂ Both upper and lower thermostats were replaced.  This did not work, as the heater again reverted to using only the upper element, and not the lower element.  The lower element was intact, but it simply did not heat.

Phase 2 ÃÂ Replaced just the upper thermostat, again.  During this repair, the plumber smelled ÃÂburningÃÂ coming from the water heater.  He warned me this is dangerous.  But it appeared that this repair worked.  But it only worked for one day, then again back to about 5 gallons of hot water.

The Fire ÃÂ On day 4 after the repair, the AO Smith unit had a complete burn-out of the lower control area (see photos).  This occurred during early morning, about 2:30 am, and fortunately our cat awoke [REDACTED] to turn-off the power before the fire spread to the whole house. The home owner went to the back yard to find the hot tub was on fire. He used a garden hose and home extinguisher to extinguish the flames. MPD unit on scene updated MFD units that the fire had been extinguished and response could be downgraded from emergent. As R-2  arrived on scene, white smoke was visible coming from the back yard, FF [REDACTED] and FF [REDACTED] proceeded to investigate. The hot tub was resting on a concrete pad bordered by a cedar fence on two sides. The hot tub unit was completely burned through the plastic paneling on the front and side and had extensive fire damage internally. No fire damage was sustained to the fencing or residence. E-2 arrived on scene and canceled other responding fire units. MFD then removed the hot tub cover and used the TIC and garden hose to eliminate hot spots. R-2 returned to service while E-2 remained on scene. MFD drained the hot tub of the water and moved the unit off of the concrete pad. [REDACTED] was called to investigate the incident. Property was then turned over to the home owner.

The fire investigation revealed that the hot tub was less then 2 years old. It was purchased through Paradise Spas and Motorsports in Minot, ND. A master electrician wired the hot tub. An electrician confirmed the hot tub was properly wired at the time of the fire. The fire originated inside of the heating element.
justification: The incident involved a fire in a hot tub with no injuries or deaths, and the fire was quickly extinguished without damage to the residence.

incident_description:
Was entertaining friends watching weekend bowl games.  As it was a bit chilly I brought out Kerosene heater to help keep guests warm.  When lit there was a fair amount of black smoke coming from the heater.  We waited a bit thinking it would burn off as it had not been used in a while.  The smoke got worse and started seeing flames shoot out the sides.  
At first I tried turning down the heater but nothing happened when I turned the knobs.  I then attempted to shut off the heater but the cut off valve fell off when pushed down (melted).  Flames got worse so moved the heater further away from guests and house.  
A friend grabbed fire extinguisher from house and we used on heater.  Flames went out but a few seconds later came back.  Then we sprayed again with fire extinguisher and same results.  
Finally moved further into the yard and watched as flames kept shooting out the top and sides.  We waited for the fuel to run out.  
As Kerosene heaters can be used indoors I am seriously concerned about these heaters.  
I purchased the heater in November of 2014.  Looking at the reviews for the heater on Amazon there are many, many complaints of the exact scenario I have outlined.  One reported major damage to home from the heater burning out of control and not able to shut off.
justification: The incident involved a kerosene heater malfunction leading to uncontrolled flames, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

I rushed into the room and found the fireplace off, white smoked swirling inside and an intense smell that smelled like electrical wires burning.  I rushed outside and turned the main gas line off.  I then turned the gas line off directly at the unit and unplugged the electrical source. 
This unit has never worked properly.  We reported it on numerous occasions before the recall and have reported delayed ignition after the recall.  Tonight our house almost blew up.  We are freaked out and very concerned.  What can we do to get an entirely different unit.  I can't trust this unit any longer.

incident_description:
I had a local contractor install spray foam insulation in the walls and roof for a portion of my home being remodeled.  The product is 1.6 PCF closed cell spray foam insulation supplied by Natural-Therm. Procedures for the installation outlined by the Center for the Polyurethanes Industry, American Chemistry Council / Spray Foam Coalition were not followed, including: 
1. occupants (my family) were not informed to vacate the premises during the installation 
2. the rooms being sprayed were not isolated from the rest of the home (plastic sheets, tape)
3. active ventilation (fans) of rooms being sprayed to exhaust fumes 
4. inadequate Personal Protective Equipment used during the installation

During the first day of the installation, family members had a reaction to the off-gassing/fumes and left the home - profusely runny nose, tightened throat, red/watering eyes.  One member continues to have this reaction whenever re-entering the home, even several weeks after the installation. I have had a qualitative test performed on the foam which indicates a very high level of isocyanate compound, indicating that the foam was not properly applied, and continues to off-gas.

My primary concern is that my home is no longer habitable by my family since the spray foam was installed.
justification: Family members experienced health reactions (runny nose, throat tightening, eye irritation) due to improper spray foam installation, indicating injury.

I called Kohler immediately describing the dangerous situation in our bathroom due to the spontaneous exploding shattering of a Kohler glass shower door.  They informed me, after talking to several reps, that they would replace the door.  They would not confirm if there were other similar complaints. They did however confirm that the replacement doors would be of the exact same material and composition because they do not feel it is a ÃÂdefect in the product or a faulty designÃÂ. incident_description:
the washer has a design flaw and keep breaking a part which holds the pump. it causes flooding in the house. (see details below). all the water washer takes goes directly underneath of the washer, as the tube never fills, it continues until you notice it. in my case it was soupy water and made me slip and fall on the ceramic tiles. it could happen to my children, we could get electrocuted.

I purchased a Samsung top loading washing machine about two years ago. Model Samsung WA456DRHDWR/AA-0000. The bracket that holds the drain pump to the drum got broken during a regular operation. It simply cracked/broke due to the strain on the bracket mounting points. In researching the issue looking for a replacement part what I discovered is that Samsung recognized that there was a design flaw in how the bracket was designed and did a redesign of this bracket. There is a technical bulletin describing the discontinuation of the old part and the replacement of the new. Do a Google search of ASC20130222001 dated 2/22/2013. This affects the WA400, WA422 and WA456 models.

The original bracket is part number DC63-01427A and is discontinued and out of stock everywhere.
The upgraded bracket is part number DC94-03523A and is discontinued and out of stock everywhere.
Samsung, later on 5/9/2013, recognized that this was still an issue and put out Bulletin # ASC20130509001, where they came out with a complete retrofit kit with new wires/hoses/brackets, etc. that moves the pump from being attached to the drum to being attached to the frame of the washing machine. Only problem with this is that they had made other design changes to these model numbers around 12/24/2012, you can tell if the machine is of the newer design due to a 01 being added to the end of the model number. The retrofit kit that moves the pump to the frame can only be done to machines made after that date or have the 01 at the end of the model number. Originally I thought my machines serial number meant that the retrofit kit would not work on my machine, but now I am not so sure due to some confusion of the affected serial numbers.

Regardless if my machine can take the retrofit kit, considering the acknowledged design flaws, and the multiple redesigns to attempt to correct this problem I approached Samsung that I was not comfortable that even if any of the possible repairs were done, old bracket/new bracket/retrofit, that it simply was delaying the inevitable failure of this part/assembly again. In my opinion this should be handled similar to how the Lemon Laws are done.
What I purchased had inherent design flaws with multiple attempts at redesign over a relativity short period of time. 

This product is UNSAFE. even you fix the part, it will still broke as the design flaw. i believe it must be recalled and samsung should either provide right fix or recall and replace all of them.
justification: The incident caused flooding and a slip-and-fall injury, indicating a severity level of 3. The design flaw and multiple failures suggest a high likelihood of recurrence.

The writer, a Fire and Explosive Investigator for the county, responded to a private residence in to investigate a report of a fire out. The owner contacted the county and indicated the baby monitor he used in his home nearly
caught the house on fire. This event occurred the previous day. They became aware of the problem when they
smelled an odor in babies room. Initially they were unable to identify the source but a family member touched the baby monitor power cord and found it to be very hot. They unplugged the device and one of the blades of the plug remained in the outlet. They isolated power to the outlet at the circuit breaker. No 911 was call was initiated. The writer met with a contractor who was working at the home. The baby monitor, the damaged outlet and wall outlet box had been removed by an electrician. The electrician had already installed a new wall outlet box and was preparing to install a new outlet; the wire connections were completed and pushed back into the box. The electrician indicated the wiring was not the cause of the fire.

The writer examined the items and determined the damage was not caused by a fire but from overheating. The
video camera was powered with a plug type transformer cord. One of the blade prongs was missing. The transformer case showed signs of heat damage around the missing prong. The plastic had melted away revealing the internal circuitry. The outlet cover and the outlet had damage that was consistent with the transformer being plugged in. The wall outlet box aslo showed signs of heat damage on the corner closest to the damaged prong.
justification: The incident involved overheating of a baby monitor, causing damage but no injury or fire, and was promptly addressed by the family and electrician.

incident_description: On September 5, 2015, I was out 4 wheeling with my wife.  I needed to use the winch which was connected on the front of my 4 wheeler to assist in righting the 4 wheeler.  I grabbed the hook with my right hand pointer and middle fingers.  Because I could not reach the winch button located near the handlebars, I asked my wife to let out the slack on the wench.  The switch is unmarked and unclear as to whether pressing it one way or the other will either release the hook/cable or will retract it towards the 4 wheeler.  My wife pressed the switch which instead of releasing the hook/cable, caused it suddenly to retract towards the 4 wheeler.  The winch is set up with 2 roller bars that appear to be barriers to prevent the hook on the end of the cable from going into the area where the winch cable is wound.  When the winch retracted after my wife pressed the switch, the purported roller bar protections in place to prevent the end of the hook from going past the rollers failed.  There was no safety switch associated with the cable near the hook, or the hook, to deactivate the winch.  Also, the rollers failed to stop the line-end of the hook.  The hook pulled through the winchÃÂs rollers and barriers taking my 2 fingers along with it and instantly cut off the middle finger on my right hand.  It happened so fast.  My pointer finger was smashed and my middle finger was cut off.  I was unable to remove my hand from between the rollers and reach the switch.  To try and free my hand, my wife again pressed the unmarked switch which further pulled the hook through the rollers which ripped off the rest of my pointer finger and left it hanging by a tendon.  There were 2 parts of my fingers on either side of the hook.  I yanked and stretched the tendon on my pointer finger so I could reach the button myself and pushed the switch and pulled on the back of the hook to get my fingers out of the winch.  My pointer finger was still connected by a tendon and my middle finder was missing.  I found my middle finger, put it in my pocket, jumped onto my wifeÃÂs 4 wheeler, and met the EMS at the road.  At a later date, I tried to loosen the hook from the winch with a hammer and the hook would not budge.  It appears the rollers and protections in place to prevent such an injury from happening failed on the winch.  The switch to engage the winch was not properly marked.  There were no proper warnings to advise consumers such as myself regarding those defects.
justification: The incident resulted in severe injuries, including the loss of fingers, which classifies it as a high-severity event. The likelihood is considered possible due to the described equipment failures and lack of safety measures.

incident_description:
(11/03/2015) The consumer stated that he was getting ready to put gas in the unit. He was not able to open the cap by hand. He had to use a Channel lock pliers to unscrew the cap. He drained the gas out of the unit into a glass jar. After draining the gas, he noticed water in the bottom of the glass jar. He remixed a brand new gallon of gasoline and put the mixture into the tank. He had to use the pliers to screw the cap back on. He noticed that the mixture was leaking from the vent hole in the cap. incident_description:

It should not have been on the shelve when the consumer bought it.  The next time the consumer spoke with her she told the consumer the gas pressure in WV was to high.
