incident_description:
Over the last 3 months we have had multiple activations of our smoke detectors. We have 7 installed throughout our home and 4 of 7 have went "activated" when no problems were present. I am a full-time firefighter so i clean and inspect these detectors regularly. I also change the batteries as directed. I contacted the company and advised them of this problem. They advised me that they were not aware of any problems with the detectors. They sent me 4 replacement detectors. Two days after receiving the replacement detectors, one of the new detectors they sent me activated. 

So, we have had 5 of our 7 detectors "actvate" when there was not problems within the home. I have found numerous reviews online on sites such as [REDACTED] where people are reporting the same problem. I have spoke to coworkers who have had this same kind of detector and they had the same problem. I am conserned for my families safety also, because at my fire department we hand out the exact same type of detector to the public and concerned that if the detector is activating they will just disconnect it and not have any detectors.
justification: The incident involves repeated false activations of smoke detectors with no actual harm or injury, but the issue is widespread and likely to recur based on multiple reports and similar experiences.

Approximately five minutes later, she came out to check on the generator and noticed there was a fuel circle with an approximate diameter of four feet. The consumer proceeded to turn off the generator immediately, as well as the gas lever. 

The consumer did not bother inspecting the unit to see where the leakage was from as she does not know much about these products. 

The consumer indicates this is the first time she ever used her generator, having started it on a few occasions before. The consumer states that the few times she started her generator, she turned it off immediately and therefore does not know if it leaked fuel then. 

02/02/2015 The consumer contacted the manufacturer and informed them what happened. The representative she spoke, [REDACTED], to informed her that she would be receiving an e-mail with instructions as to how to proceed fixing the unit. The representative offered to walk the consumer through the steps of finding out what is wrong but the consumer denied the offer.

The consumer checked her e-mail and came upon Carburetor Check Sheet, Fuel Flow Test and Carburetor Check Service Procedures, How to Cure a Carburetor that is Flooding Fuel. The consumer indicates that because she has no mechanical skills/ knowledge, she will have a family member follow the instructions to see if it would solve the issue. 

The consumer indicates that she paid approximately seven hundred dollars for her unit. The consumer has no injuries to report. The consumer does not plan on contacting the retailer. The consumer believes this product poses a safety hazard. 

Champion sent the consumer a new carborator.
justification: The incident involved a fuel leak but no injuries were reported, and the issue was addressed by the manufacturer.

incident_description:
While traveling abroad we used our Samsonite Dual-Wattage Converter (used to convert from US power to other countries like Italy, Spain, France) in our hotel room.  The product began to burn on fire, smoked, and melted down while attached to a wall outlet.  We were forced to evacuate the hotel room until the circuit breaker was tripped.  We then re-entered the room to noxious smoke and a smoldering converter stuck to the wall that was too hot to remove and touch.  Eventually the unit cooled and was removed.  We suffered hand burns when trying to originally remove it from the wall.  The unit is patently unsafe it seems.  We purchased a different unit from another brand while at the same hotel and used the same outlet and it worked without incident

Upon returning to the US we searched the internet for and explanation and found that all of these units had been recalled.  The number listed on the website for the recall is constantly busy and is never answered.  Being persistent we called the Customer Service for Samsonite where they representatives denied there being a recall, denied that I was entitled to remuneration, I asked for a refund which they refused.  The unit is 4-5 years old from what I can recall and it has no labeling or serial number or model number.  Then Samsonite said I was not eligible for a refund because it was purchased at Best Buy, then they tried to say they would replace it but I have no trust in the product as the fire and smoke was enough to tell me I should never buy or use another Samsonite product ever.  Next, after I explained to them that I am a lawyer and that consumer protection is something I take very seriously, they then wanted to open up a case and required much personal information I am not willing to give to such a poorly run company who put my life at risk and produced and put into the consumer chain such a dangerous product --- and then denies it.  

I want resolution and I want a refund.  The unit cost approximately $40 plus tax.  I also want them to be investigated and reprimanded for not servicing, under federal or state law mandates, the recall of a known hazardous product and denying claims.  They will never learn if there is no enforcement.  Please do what you can to protect us and families from these bad actors.
justification: The incident involved a fire, smoke, and hand burns, indicating injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is high (4) due to the product's recall status and the user's experience.

incident_description:
The consumer purchased the flooring from Lumber Liquidators in two parts (3/28/15 - $813.46
and 03/29/15 - $122.02). 

The consumer has the flooring installed in all three bedrooms and the hallway leading to the bedrooms.

The consumer went to purchase the flooring on 3/28/15 and inquired about the safety of the flooring with the store. The store informed her that the flooring was perfectly safe and that they have had it tested by multiple people. They informed her that it was a scam against the company to affect the stocks.

Two weeks after purchase, the retailer took the flooring off of the market. The consumer called the store but no one picked. She went into the store and asked how they would assist her since they took the flooring off the market when they informed her two week ago that the flooring was safe. They informed her that they have not recalled the flooring but only stopped its sale. They asked her to call their customer service line and request an air quality test kit.

The consumer contact customer service and was sent out the test kit. She tested the air quality for 24 hours in her children's room and sent it to an independent lab (Environmental Diagnostics Laboratory) on 5/17/15. The consumer received her test results her on 06/11/15. 

The results came back with .098 ppm formaldehyde levels in the air. The consumer stated that in the letter it explains that anything above .081 ppm can lead to sensory irritation and long term health effects.

The consumer stated that she and her husband have felt heath symptoms but cannot say for sure that those symptoms are caused by the flooring.

The consumer stated that she would like to have the floorings removed from her home. The consumer has 4 children and is worried that formaldehyde will cause them health hazards over time.

The consumer stated that she is not asking the retailer to provide her refund on the cost of installation but is expecting them to refund flooring material cost. The consumer stated that she trusted the company when they informed her that it was just a scam over stocks. She stated that they offered no help once the flooring was pulled off of the market.
justification: The consumer and her husband have experienced health symptoms, and the formaldehyde levels in the air exceed safe limits, indicating potential injury.

incident_description: I purchased a 3100 PSI pressure washer made by Power Stroke and sold at Costco. I read the manual as did my husband. We cleaned our deck. I wore shorts as it was 90 degrees out but did wear sturdy shoes. As I stepped backward with the wand, my calf made contact with the stationary machine. The piece that just out the farthest, on two sides, is the motor. It gave me a large (2 inch by 5 inch) second degree burn in the time it took to realize I was being burned. One second. The design is flawed. The most dangerous piece sticks out from the rest. It is at calf height for an adult, chest height for a toddler. This is meant for home use. The warning on the motor is the same color as the casing--silver--not noticeable. The manual makes no special mention of the burn danger, just lists it along with many other features. Not in a box, not in bold. I called the manufacturer and the man on the phone said their warnings are fine. That is an inappropriate response. I am a pediatrician. I take responsibility for my own injury, which is very painful one week later. But I am concerned about the many children who may come into contact with this due to the poor design and the adults as well. A large second degree burn in one second is too dangerous not to have better warnings and better housing around the motor. I have photos as well.
justification: The incident resulted in a second-degree burn, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The likelihood is rated as 4 (likely) due to the flawed design and inadequate warnings, increasing the risk for both adults and children.

incident_description:
The battery in my natural gas-powered backup generator exploded.  The service technician said that this has been happening to a number of other Kohler generators, both this model and other models.  The problem is that the controller module applies too large of a charging voltage to the battery causing it to overcharge and eventually explode when it tries to start the engine.  According to the service technician, Kohler is aware of this problem because they have made a new wiring harness with a built-in diode that limits the charging voltage to 13.5 volts.  This is supposed to compensate for the defectively designed controller module.

This battery explosion within the generator cabinet could damage the natural gas lines feeding the generator and could result in a much larger explosion and fire, resulting in major property damage and loss of life.

Kohler should not be treating this as a routine problem.  Kohler should be providing the new parts to its dealers ASAP and the dealers should be instructed to install them in every affected unit, also ASAP.
justification: The incident involves a battery explosion with potential for major property damage and loss of life, indicating a high severity level. The occurrence likelihood is high as the issue is known to affect multiple units and the manufacturer is aware.

incident_description:
On 06/23/15 the consumer's husband noticed a burn odor in his home and realized that it was coming from the basement. The consumer's husband opened the basement door and noticed a lot of smoke coming from the basement The consumer contacted the fire department, who arrived within 10 minutes. The consumer states the house sustained major smoke damages and the dehumidifier is completely burned. The consumer was told by the fire department that the dehumidifier was the cause of the fire. The fire department also told the consumer that the dehumidifier is affected by recall # 14-179 and the consumer should contact CPSC to file a report.

The consumer has contacted State Farm (Claim # [REDACTED]), her home insurance company and the consumer was told that the house damages were approximately $10, 000. The consumer has spoken with [REDACTED] who told the consumer that an insurance agent from State Farm plans to take the unit.

The dehumidifier remained in the basement and was used all day. There were no prior incidents.

The consumer has another dehumidifier which is affected by recall # 14-179. The dehumidifier is now turned off. The consumer has not had an incident and plans to contact the firm to request the recall remedy for both dehumidifier.

The submitter added the second dehumidifier was not on recall list, and they called Gree and they verified that it was not.  The submitter noted they bought the second one [dehumidifier] one year later. The submitter also added she e-mailed pictures of burnt unit on 6-29-2015 to clearinghouse@cpsc.gov.

incident_description: We purchased ASD Saver tub door ( glass shower doors) November 14, 2013 from Lowes, Bridgeport, WV .   They were installed on or about the same day.   On June 29, 2015, my children and my  husband was home, when my children heard a weird sound (a loud growling).  They perceived that it was the cats.  They then heard glass shattering.  They went and found the stationary glass door was partially shattered on the bathroom floor, with half still attached to the shower.  No one was near the bathroom with the glass shower door exploded.    We have children who use this shower daily and thankfully no one was in the shower when this occurred.  Very disappointed there are products especially glass shower doors that are able to explode.  We assumed these were safe to use around children and pets.
justification: The glass door shattered but no one was injured, indicating an incident without injury. The likelihood is unlikely as such events are not common.

incident_description:
About 2 weeks ago the concrete patio around my pool was repainted by a professional contractor using H&CÃÂ® Concrete Stain Solid Color Water-based (see http://www.hcconcrete.com/products/solid-color-stains/water-based-stain/) About a week after it was painted my young grandchildren spent the day swimming. When the patio got wet from water splashing on it from the kids getting in and out of the pool, the patio got very slippery. The children fell multiple times so we put wet towels around the pool to prevent them from falling. They were not running when they fell. 

The product is advertised for us around a pool and it had more than enough time to fully cure, yet it still dangerously slippery when wet. Lucky out grandchildren were not seriously hurt, but had they fallen differently there could have been a more serious injury.
justification: The children fell multiple times due to the slippery patio, indicating a clear incident with potential for injury, though none occurred.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that within six months to a year of purchasing the washer, he started having issues with the washer banging on the floor and hitting the nearby dryer. 

The consumer contacted the retailer in regards to the issues. The unit was under warranty through the retailer. The consumer was sent out a technician for inspection. The technician determined that a part (shock device) had to be replaced. The technician replaced the part during his visit. 

The consumer stated that the issue reoccurred about a month later.

The consumer contacted the retailer again for the issue. The consumer was sent out another technician who replaced the shock device part again. They informed him to lighten up the load. The consumer stated that the clothes did not completely dry. They informed him to put the load on dry-spin cycle if the clothes weren't completely dry.

The issue again reoccurred within 1-2 months. The consumer lived with the problem for a few years. The warranty on the unit had expired by then.

About a year to year and half ago, the consumer contacted an independent technician. The technician replaced the same shock device. The consumer stated that the technician also adjusted the pedestal so that the unit was balanced.The consumer also lightened up the wash load. This allowed the banging to become less. The consumer paid about $350 for repair. 

The consumer had the unit looked at again by a different independent technician from [REDACTED] (Snellville, GA) on 5/14/15. The technician tested the unit and took it back to his shop. The consumer was contacted to come into the shop on 05/16/15 to look at the unit. The technician showed the consumer that the rubber gasket appears to have been installed incorrectly by the manufacturer. That incorrect installation cause the bearing to throw off and cause issues with his unit. The consumer was notified that this was a manufacturer's defect.

The technician put in a rush order on the part to have it replaced. In the meantime, the consumer was provided a loaner washer while the repair work is being conducted. The consumer will be paying $350 for the part and labor.

The consumer had a separate 5 year retailer's warranty on the unit. The consumer stated that the retailer failed to inspect the unit properly while it was being repaired under warranty. The technicians that came out through the retailer never took the unit completely apart from the back to examine the issues.

The consumer's unit does not appear to be under any recalls.

The technician mention the rubber seal gasket may have been a manufacturer defect.  There was out of pocket expenses for necessary repairs.  This problem wasn't determined until after the consumer's extended warranty expired!  
Thank you,
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involves repeated mechanical failures and financial costs but no injuries or deaths.

incident_description: A 3-year-old boy died shortly after ingesting a poisonous substance, specifically Pro Par Brightener, a compound containing sulfuric acid, hydrofluoric acid and ethanol, that is used as an industrial aluminum and metal cleaner. The child gained access to the substance while the family vehicle  was stopped at a car wash. He and his 5-year-old brother were in their car seats in the back of the vehicle, while his parents were in the front. He worked his way out of his car seat and grabbed a 12 oz. plastic water bottle that was on the floor and where his father had stored the chemical substance. He drank approximately one third of its content and began to feel sick. When his parents realized what he had done they made the child drink water and called EMS for help. He was rushed to a hospital emergency room where he was treated but he was already unresponsive.
justification: The incident resulted in the death of a child due to ingestion of a poisonous substance, indicating the highest severity level. The occurrence likelihood is unlikely, as such incidents are rare but not impossible.

incident_description: One of the shower doors in our downstairs bathroom spontaneously shattered at 8:30 p.m. on June 25, 2015.  The shower doors were Kohler Fluence Frameless Sliding Shower Doors, which were 3 years-old and purchased in 2012 from Lowe's in New Carrollton, MD.  The shower doors were well-maintained (as this shower is only occasionally used).  We were sitting in the living room when we heard a large crash.  Thankfully no one was in the bathroom at the time or in the area immediately outside the bathroom where glass was also found.  As we have two small children, this was a very frightening occurrence--and one that we did not know was possible.  The glass from one of the shower doors literally exploded and shattered all over the bathroom floor.  In the process of cleaning up the glass, my husband experienced some small cuts.
justification: The incident caused small cuts during cleanup (injury), but no one was present during the shattering. Spontaneous glass breakage is uncommon.

incident_description:
I purchased the Samsung 4.5 cubic feet washing machine WA456DRHDWR/AA in 11/26/2012. It started leaking water within 90 days and had to be serviced once and then replaced with a new, replacement model of the same type. 

On 5/28/2015, the replacement washing machine started leaking in the same manner again. The machine was also gyrating wildly on the spin cycle and I was afraid that it might even tip over, such was the intensity of the gyrations. I have 2 baby daughters so this is a major concern. 

After reading hundreds to thousands of consumer complaints about this model on the internet, I'm shocked to learn that Samsung has not tried to recall this product. One of the many issues with this product is that the water pump is poorly designed in terms of materials & location, causing it fail often and put water all over the floor. If I had not caught the water coming out when it did, I would've suffered major water damage to my house. As it stands, the tile floor on which the WA456DRHDWR/AA had already suffered from waterlogging. 

I ask you to please investigate Samsung's WA456DRHDWR/AA and encourage them to do a product recall. This is an incredibly unsafe and unreliable product. Thank you.
justification: The incident involves a leaking washing machine causing water damage and potential safety hazards, but no injuries or deaths are reported.

incident_description:
The Flushmate III Pressure-Assisted Flushing System in the American Standard toilet in my apartment unit exploded. It shot parts of the porcelain tank into hallway. Part of the tank compressor landed 3-4 feet away.

The toilet was not in use at the time, no one was in the bathroom or hallway, and no injuries were sustained.  As we were present in an adjacent room, we were able to shut off the water almost immediately.  Other than the shattered porcelain toilet tank and destroyed pressure unit, no property damage occurred.  We needed to mop up the water and sweep up the porcelain shards.  The apartment maintenance team replaced the toilet tank and pressure unit very soon afterward.

It appears the unit was one of those covered under the earlier product recall (i.e. recall number 14-089 dated January 23, 2014 or  12-201 dated June 21, 2012).  Apartment building was built sometime between 2003 and 2004.  

I've lived in my apartment since March 2005 and the toilet's pressure unit had not been replaced during my residency.  There are roughly 100 units in my building and another 100 units in an adjacent building built a year prior to the building I live in.  Some units have 2 bathrooms.  Maintenance indicated they replaced a pressure unit in another apartment the week previous as the unit cracked, depressurized, and leaked water into the undamaged porcelain tank (i.e. that incident did not result in the porcelain tank rupturing).  Maintenance was not aware of the product recall.  I provided them the recall information.

Photos are available at: [REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved an explosion causing property damage but no injuries, fitting severity level 2. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) given the recall history and prior incidents in the building.

incident_description:
In August 2012 I purchased 7 Kidde Smoke Detectors, model PI2010, which were installed by an electrician in our home. Beginning Sept 2012 and continuing through today, 4 of the 7 detectors have failed. This product is wired into a ceiling fixture and has a battery backup. In each failure the product gives a false alarm and cannot be silenced until it is unplugged from the ceiling AND the battery is removed. The none of the detectors is in a dusty area. Vacuuming the sensor to remove dust does not solve the problem. 
     3 of the failed detectors were manufactured in May 2012. Kidde replace each of these 3 free of charge after the failure (1 in 2012, 1 in 2013, and 1 in 2014). They did not seem to be surprised or alarmed by these frequent failures. The fourth failure occurred this morning (6/22/2015) and it was one of the replacements, manufacture date May 2014. Even their replacement products are faulty!! I have no confidence this product is actually protecting our family from fire.
     The failure rate of this product is unacceptably high. From your website I see that I am not the first consumer to experience this problem. I would like to see this product recalled and I would like the company to refund the cost of all the detectors. (I will be contacting them to tell them this.)
justification: The incident involves frequent false alarms and product failures, but no injury or death has occurred.

incident_description:
I used  Arm & Hammer Carpet & Room Pet Fresh Odor Eliminator.

An hour or so after my son became sick...coughing and sneezing....I assumed it was allergies and never considered it might be the carpet freshener.

The next morning he woke up coughing, sneezing, runny nose and a bleeding nose.  I woke up with itchy painful eyes.

I determined it was the carpet cleaner...as after we left the house for a short time the symptoms disappeared. Reentering the apartment...we had problems again.

I did research and found that this product has been linked to animals getting sick as well as dying. It has put people in the hospital and has caused all kinds of problems.

At least 1 of the ingredients has been listed as toxic.
justification: The incident caused coughing, sneezing, runny nose, bleeding nose, and itchy painful eyes, indicating injury (severity 3). The product's known toxicity suggests occurrence is likely (4).

incident_description: I have five Nest Protect smoke detectors.  Three of the five have had false alarms for no reason at all.  I have had FOUR false alarms in total within the last year.  The latest false alarm happened while everyone was asleep.  There were no conditions present for any of the false alarms that would have triggered them.  All of the smoke detectors are less than two years old, and many have been recently replaced by Nest.  The false alarms keep happening.  Nest has refused to refund the price of these smoke detectors and insists on replacing them - but the false alarms are continuing.  My children have started to ignore the alarms because they happen so often.
justification: False alarms are occurring frequently without any actual danger, causing disruption and leading to ignored alarms, but no injuries or deaths have been reported.

incident_description:
The furnace was installed on 09/24/14. 

On 02/20/15, at 7:45am, all of the smoke alarms in the house went off. The consumer woke up to black smoke all over the house. The consumer opened up all of the windows and called the fire department. She ran outside to see if there was a fire. The consumer saw black smoke coming from the exhaust pipe of the furnace. The consumer ran into the house and turned off the furnace. She went back outside and saw that the smoke stopped.

The King George Fire Department came out by then. They inspected the house along with the consumer. They informed the consumer that the furnace exhaust pipe was iced over resulting in back exhaust.

The consumer contacted the installer on 02/20/15. The installer sent out two technicians the same day. They examined the issue and communicated their findings to the engineers at Thermopride (mfr). The consumer stated that the technicians were informed to remove the T-coupler (where the freezing took place).  The technicians made some other modifications/repairs but the consumer is not aware of those.

The consumer continued to use the furnace after that.

The consumer stated that in early April, the same technicians were sent over to her home to perform some repair work as instructed by Thermopride. They noticed that the heat exchanger was broken. In the absence of the heat exchanger, the technicians were unable to perform any work on the unit. They informed her to ask Thermopride for a new furnace instead of having it repaired so much.

The consumer contacted Thermopride. They put her through with the chief engineer, [REDACTED] . The consumer was informed by [REDACTED] that there were no replacement units available as of now. He stated that the company is not manufacturing these furnaces at the moment. The consumer was informed that the units would not be available until late summer/early fall 2015. The consumer asked [REDACTED] why the company stopped manufacturing the units. The consumer was informed that they have some fixes out for the ones that are installed already and they were waiting to see how the fix works. Depending on the results, the company would continue the manufacturing process.

The consumer informed the technicians of the information provided by Thermopride. The technicians contacted their lead, [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] set up a meeting on 04/09/15 at the consumerÃÂs house with other [REDACTED]  members and the territory manager for Thermopride [REDACTED] . 

In that meeting, [REDACTED] mentioned the issues that Thermopride was having with these oil furnaces. The consumerÃÂs understanding of the issues discussed at the meeting is as followed:
In total, 62 units were manufactured. Out of the 62 units, 12 units were field tested for several years. The remaining 50 units were sold and installed in the Northeast and Southern territory. [REDACTED]  indicated that around December 2014, Thermopride started receiving calls about the issue with back exhaust and ice. The manufacturing of the oil furnaces was stopped in March 2015.

The consumer asked [REDACTED] why the owners were not notified about the issues as soon as the company was made aware of them. The consumer was told that there were a lot of miscommunications on their end. [REDACTED]  indicated that the issue that occurred with her was the worst amongst the other reports the company received. 

The consumer was informed by [REDACTED] that he does not feel that the unit is safe and he would like to remove it from her home. At this point, the consumer realized that this is a larger failure that includes more than just her unit.

The consumer spoke to the risk manager, [REDACTED]  at Burnham Holdings (owner of Thermopride). She informed the consumer that she was unaware of any issues with Thermopride furnaces. 

The consumer also spoke to [REDACTED] at Thermopride [REDACTED]. He is a Safety Compliance Officer with the company. The consumer asked why notifications were not sent out to distributors/owners.  The consumer was informed that they did not feel the problem was substantial enough to send out notifications. The consumer stated that [REDACTED] hung up the phone on her.

On 04/20/15, an independent mechanical engineer ([REDACTED] ) was sent out by the consumerÃÂs home insurance company for inspection. He found problems and violations with installation of the unit. He observed that the exhaust pipe was in violation of code. He is going to be writing up a detailed report on his inspection. The consumer does not have a copy of the report yet.

Thermopride and [REDACTED] want to replace the consumerÃÂs furnace with a propane furnace. The consumer is not okay with having a propane furnace installed in her house. The consumer is also not eager to have the current furnace replaced as it serves as a proof of the issues that occurred.

The consumer stated that there are other consumers that have these units installed in their home with fixes that are being tested out on them. How the fixes will turn out will not be determined until the other consumers start their units. Thermopride tried to have her unit fixed accordingly as well in April 2015, but were unable to do so due to a broken heat exchanger.

The consumer stated that what frustrates her most in this case is that Thermopride was aware of the issues with this furnace. If the smoke alarms in her home had not gone off, she may not have been alive. The consumer believes that someone should have at least come out and conducted an inspection to make sure that her exhaust pipe was not freezing over. 

The consumer stated that all of the carpeting from the second floor and stairwell will have to be removed. The consumer also has to have other things (electronics, furniture, clothing) professionally cleaned. The consumer got the duct cleaned on 04/06/15. The consumer will also have to have the walls and the ceilings cleaned in the whole house. 

The soot that collected was oily. The consumer has to wait on a professional to come out and properly remove and clean the electronics.  The consumer was told by someone that the oil from the soot can cause problems with ÃÂallÃÂ of the electronics in her home and they may need to be cleaned professionally.  The consumer has retained filters for the furnace to show the amount of soot that was deposited.
justification: The incident involved significant smoke and potential fire hazard, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

I had to take the unit off the ceiling, unscrew the back cover and remove the batteries to get all alarms to stop.  I return the unit to Nest and they sent me a new one. incident_description:
In July 2015 I purchased a Juki TL 2200QVP Long Arm quilting machine with a Grace frame.  The Grace frame is subject to failure.  Note that the frame is intended to support a sewing machine that weighs in excess of 85 pounds and should operated on a sliding cradle system.  There are two incidents:
1.  The feet supporting the entire apparatus fell off.  This sent the heavy machine lurching forward while it was in operation at up to 700 stitches per minute as I operated it.  The sudden loss of balance and control created a very unsafe situation and the possibility of injury due to the startling and significant weight shift.  The Grace firm later sent new feet, secured by a bolt, to replace the defective parts.  Curiously, I visited a store just last week that had on display a new Juki like mine with the same frame.  The defective, old style feet were still being used.
2.  The plastic sleeve used to support the top bar on which the quilt backing is rolled is insecure and falls away from the frame at random times.  When I called Grace about the first issue, they asked me if there had been occasions of the top rail falling away from the frame.  At that time I had experienced no such problem.  That is no longer the case.  Again, it is unsafe to experience frame failure while operating a heavy, powerful industrial sewing machine.  The possibility of injury is apparent.  It disconcerts me that the Grace firm in Utah would continue to sell a product with defects that are know to them with disregard for consumer safety.
justification: The incident describes a hazardous situation with a high potential for injury due to equipment failure, but no actual injury is reported.

incident_description:
Caller ordered glass shower door December 3rd, 2014, it was delivered about one to two weeks later and had it installed by contractor who was remodeling her bathroom.    She had no problems with the shower door until May 29th, 2015 when her house guest stepped out of the shower after she turned the water off.
Once the house guest stepped out of the shower, the door shattered with one of the pieces of glass cutting her on her right hand.
The caller went to the retailer, spoke with [REDACTED] who checked with is supervisor then returned this callers phone and provided her with the manufacturer's contact information..
She spoke with the manufacturer  June 8th, 2015 and was advised that they would replace her shower door.
She is reporting this incident because she doesn't want just the shower door replaced, for safety sake she is asking for an entirely new replacement of frame, doors etc be provided at manufacturer expense with the manufacturer installing the product.
The manufacturer has advised her that the frame would only be replaced if the door shattering ruined the frame.
He informed her that these doors do not shatter on their own.

The house guest  treated her cut and did not require medical attention
justification: The house guest suffered a cut from shattered glass, which constitutes an injury, but did not require medical attention. The incident appears isolated, making recurrence unlikely.

incident_description:
My first indication of problem was after closing/ prior to move-in, when I pulled a vacuum cleaner plug from upstairs receptacle, and it appeared "wiggly".  Removing the plate revealed cracked plug (very evident from the picture, indicative of over 50 such outlets).  I replaced "on my own", thinking the seller's move-out may have bashed furniture into the plate (no damage to the plate itself).  Being an engineer, and prone to "situational awareness", this sensitized me to plugs, and subsequent plug-in/ plug-out on various outlets revealed the same problem.  I was prepared to replace several plugs, when an outside Electrician I hired (to rehang an 18' entry chandelier, replace timer switches on outside lites, and consolidate switches in bedroom and covering w/ blanking plate to gain more wall space for dresser), encountered cracked outlets AND switches (both 2 & 3-way) in the process of his work. He replaced the ones he worked on, but this sensitized me to the problem which I deemed epidemic, and I contacted Howard County Electrical Inspection, sidestepping original installing electrician, CECO (Catonsville Electric Co.), sub-contractor to Pulte-Builders (GC).  Their Chief Inspector, [REDACTED], came for a "look-see", and called CECO, who took an immediate interest.  They scheduled a work-session on Saturday (can you say: "overtime" -- such was their urgency to get this problem behind them) w/ 2 journeyman electricians, supervisor, and proprietor, replacing ALL outlets and selective switches (>30).  

I deem P&S/ Legrand negligent for not issuing a RECALL -- they were very aware of problem, linking it to 
manufacturing process deficiencies.  (think:  GM ignition key locks & Takata air bags) I flagged/ alerted other occupants in our development (45 units), most of which had replaced outlets on their own, deeming the occurrence "onezies".  Under P&S auspices, CECO was authorized to replace defective devices.  My angst is that when the journeymen electrician pulled out a switch/ outlet, and it appeared OK, the process of pushing it back into the J/B could have exacerbated the defective devices, and they cracked upon reinserting them.  I was pushing for TOTAL replacement, but other homeowners bragged they had only a few bad devices.  The ones not replaced are ticking time-bombs.  Subsequent alerts to Howard County Inspection & Fire Dept. met with deaf ears.  U.L. issued a case #, but claimed they didn't have jurisdiction to initiate a recall, instead recommending me kicking this up to Consumer Products Safety Commission (CPSC) ... you haven't heard the end of this yet.

During the Home Inspector's inspection, he diligently plugged his tester into numerous outlets (checking only for polarity), and wasn't sensitized to the cracked outlet problem.  Apparently all were sufficiently intact that they didn't register a fault, but had he wiggled them, or removed a sampling of wall plates looking for a problem, he would have made the discovery.
justification: The incident involves widespread defective electrical outlets and switches, posing a potential hazard, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description:
I attempted to open the dryer door for my LG DLEX3570W electric dryer after the drum had stopped rotating. I received a shock from the dryer door. It was not static electricity, it's a constant 120VAC

incident_description:
This is a Stanley Shop Vac Model: SL-18130 and could apply to many steel can vacuums

I have been an electrician for over 20 years and use all sorts of tools including vacuums to clean up all sorts of different materials in the past.  This one incident is pretty serious.  The voltage and arc generated could be, in my opinion, lethal. 

This electrical charge was repeated several times and observed open air arc was 25-45mm from another grounded appliance (furnace duct work).  The ignition coil on a car idling won't discharge an arc like this at 20mm.  The accompanying arc snap volume was quite alarming.

The material being cleaned up was 1950's vintage plaster and dust which settled over a hot air furnace.  In one respect, Tesla would have been pleased.

Ungrounded metal catch can will generate dangerous capacitive voltage depending on the material collected.  None of my test equipment had the range to measure voltage, current or joules. This information is based on my own experience (getting zapped) and then actually causing the situation to occur several times while observing the arc's behavior.

To sum this issue in a few words:  It doesn't matter how the electrics are protected.  Double insulated motors or grounded motors.  The point is the metal can was ungrounded and the materials being cleaned up caused a rare but dangerous situation.

Here's the thing.  National Electrical Code clearly states that all metal for any electrical device must be bonded to ground.  This is a safety issue.  Had this particular model simply put on any sort of ground to the can, the charge generated would have been safely discharged through the ground.

If I am not mistaken - Underwriters Lab also has rules for metal encased appliances - I.E. the use of a grounded power cord.  I test grounds on all 3 prong tools on job sites (as per OSHA).

This vacuum has a 3 prong cord (NEMA 5-15p) but the ground was never extended to the metal can.  

MY FIX: 16ga wire to a small copper strip positioned across the gasket.  When the vacuum lid is closed, the strip comes into contact with the can.  The copper strip under the seal provides an adequate ground path to discharge any stray or capacitive charges.

Such a fix should be used on any metal can shop vac, especially those used to collect WATER.  120v traveling through water could cause the metal can to become energized.  Why?  Some unsuspecting homeowner cleaning up water ... well, lets see ... water on the floor ... feet in the water ... metal can becomes full and stop float fails to work.  Water is drawn through the motor armature.  That situation is becoming dangerous.  I have had shut-off floats fail in the past during a flood water cleanup.

Some sort of mechanism should be developed to ensure the safety of metal can vacuums, especially any vacuum that could be involved with water. 

I hope this information is useful in preventing someone from getting injured or worse.

Thanks,
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a dangerous electrical situation with potential for lethal voltage and arc, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
Early on a Sunday morning we were awakened by the overwhelming odor of something burning. 

After searching the house we found the Soleus air dehumidifier powered by Gree model # SG-DEH-45-1  belching smoke. We immediately pulled the plug.  Had we not been home, I am not sure what would have happened. 

The unit in the basement was not operating but it was still smoking. We shut the breaker on the electrical panel off and pulled the plug on the unit, when we finally located the source of the smokey odor. 

We searched online and learned that the product had been recalled. We were unaware of the recall until the unit smoked.
justification: The incident involved a smoking dehumidifier but no injury or death occurred, and the likelihood is possible given the recall status and the event description.

incident_description: We were using a power adapter from Apple for iPhone, iPad, etc.  When removing the adapter from the outlet one of the metal prongs came out of the adapter and remained in the outlet but was unnoticed.  When plugging a different power cord into the outlet my mother-in-law's hand touched the metal prong from the Apple adapter and she was electrocuted.  This adapter had a green dot on it which I discovered (after doing some google research) was supposed to verify the adapter was safe and had been inspected by Apple engineers for this very concern after several customers complained of the same thing happening.  However, even these "green dot" adapters are not safe.
justification: The incident resulted in electrocution (injury), and similar occurrences have been reported, though not frequently.

incident_description: At approximately 7:00am, I experienced a catastrophic electrical failure at my home. I already had a "smart meter" (BGE; electric) in use at my house when I purchased it in April, 2013. As far as I know (and partisan investigators agreed), the electrical trunk line that attached to BGE's side of my smart meter was original, from the 1963 construction of the home. I was indisposed in the upstairs bathroom at the time. What I experienced was a radical cycling of power on & off over a period of perhaps a minute to a minute-and-a-half. During this time, I heard what sounded like a gun-fight going on downstairs. By the time I was able to get to the scene below, the inside utility room which houses my fuse panel, laundry, HVAC components & gas connection, the room was full of smoke that smelled heavily of electrical burning, but there was no fire evident (and no damage evident inside). Outside that room, on the exterior of the house, there was no notable conflagration continuing beyond the seat cushion of a chair that was near the smart meter and a spot of flame atop the Verizon FiOS terminal that was directly below the meter. I extinguished those flames myself in short order. The fire department was on scene within minutes, shortly followed by a BGE rep/technician who removed the smart meter and took it away immediately.
justification: The incident involved a catastrophic electrical failure with smoke and small flames, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

The explaination from Harbor freight was that the chargers will overcharge the battery (they are not smart chargers and will continue to over charge the battery. You should plug the battery charger in for no more than 4 hours whith the battery dead.  A little forgetfullness did and will overheat the transformer (exterior plastic distorted) and damage the battery.

I am an engineer and I feel that this battery/charger combination is inherently dangerous.  The product could easily cause a burn, and may be a fire hazard.

There was a lot of smoke and dripping plastic coming from the connection by the power head.

incident_description:
We purchased Vigo Industries' frameless shower (model number: VG6061CHCL36 in clear/chrome) in late 2007 or early 2008 and had it professionally installed. The product performed as expected until two days ago, when one of the fixed glass panels suddenly--and inexplicably--exploded as I stepped out of the shower.  The panel that broke had no weight on it and the shower door was closed.  It was the panel to which the shower door was attached with two metal hinges.  The door itself fell into the shower as a result of the panel explosion but did not break, and the other fixed panel remained intact.  Prior to the incident, there was nothing to indicate a potential issue with the shower: no chips, no cracks and nothing loose.

The exploded glass fell in sharp pieces as far as six feet across the bathroom and with significant force.  Having just stepped out of the shower, I was wearing nothing but a towel draped around my midsection, but fortunately had my back to the closed shower door.  I suffered numerous cuts across my shoulders and down the right side of my body, including my right arm, wrist, hand, leg and foot.  My hair was full of glass as well.  

After getting immediate assistance from my closest neighbor (who is a retired neurosurgeon), I ultimately was treated at an urgent care clinic.  Two cuts on the back of my right hand and wrist required a total of 13 stitches.  It took a nurse 90 minutes to pick glass shards out of my shoulders, upper back, arms, legs and feet.

I was lucky that I was not facing the shower and that I got no glass in my eyes.  And I was most fortunate that the flying glass did not hit an artery.  Likewise, I was lucky the door fell into the shower when its supporting panel exploded (rather than onto me, which would have pushed glass into my skin) and that the door did not shatter as well.
justification: The incident resulted in multiple injuries requiring medical treatment, but no fatalities. The sudden and inexplicable nature of the glass panel explosion suggests this is an unlikely event.

incident_description: I purchased a Cold Steel Pocket Bushman (which is a large folding pocket knife) online. The knife has a proprietary locking system unlike any other knife at the back of the handle which requires pulling a lanyard against spring tension to unlock. Upon receiving the knife it was very stiff out of the box. Although it is designed to be opened with one hand, it was so stiff that it required two hands to open it. When trying to unlock it, the lock was likewise extremely stiff. By pulling on the lanyard you are by design pulling a large sharp knife towards you which is unsafe. Because the lock was so tight, I gripped the handle tightly with one hand and pulled the lanyard with the other and somehow pulled the knife through my hand cutting the first digit of my index finger to the bone (and to a lesser degree my thumb.) I bled profusely and drove myself to the ER where I spent several hours and needed six stitches to close the cut. A few days later I went to a plastic surgeon (following the release instructions of the hospital) who determined that the digital nerve and tendon were severed. I had surgery several days later and was in a splint for 6 weeks and unable to work my profession as a cameraman. I have been in occupational therapy for the past few months and am slowly regaining feeling and some mobility. The medical costs and lost work has run into the thousands of dollars.
justification: The incident resulted in a severe injury requiring surgery, stitches, and long-term therapy, but no death occurred.

incident_description:
A Soleus Air dehumidifier overheated causing the plastic bottom of the unit to deform and discolor the carpet in my basement (I will try to attach pictures). I was very lucky that I went to check the water collection bucket or the dehumidifier could have caused a fire. On 14 May 2015 I called Soleus Air to report the issue, but I was instructed to call the Gree Recall Center. On the same day I notified the recall center of my issue, but they could only take a report and issue a reference number ([REDACTED) due to fact that my unit is not on the recall list. The following is the information for my dehumidifier:

Soleus Air
Model: GL-DEH-70F-2 L3
S/N: [REDACTED]
Made in China
Date Code: 0513

The recall center told me Soleus Air would contact me. After not hearing from Soleus Air, I contacted them on 20 May 2015. I was informed that Soleus Air knew nothing of the reference number, and that I should be hearing from the recall center. The only other option they said I had was to contact the Consumer Protection Safety Commission. On the same day, the recall center told me to wait a week or so for the reference number to be processed through their system. I contacted the recall center again on 1 June 2015, and was told to contact Soleus Air since the unit is not part of the recall.

It's pretty clear to me now that no one wants to take responsibility for an overheating dehumidifier that is not on the recall list. The unit is unsafe and should be added to the recall list as dangerous fire hazard.
justification: The dehumidifier overheated and caused property damage but no injury or death.

justification: The shower door shattered, causing glass to spread, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description:
I am a 56 year old single woman who began using Tilex Fresh Shower in my new shower where I moved a few weeks ago.
On Saturday, May 23, 2015, I was showering and put my foot on the seat of the stall shower to shave. When I switched legs, the leg I put down slipped as thought there were oil in the shower and I fell with such force that I gashed my head and have terrible bruises on my arm, hip and leg. I attended a family reunion just after that and my family could not believe the injuries I sustained.

I would like to send you pictures of these injuries. My nephews wife who is a nurse indicated that they stopped using this product for the same reason and, they have had injuries come in for falls like mine.

The next morning I could barely move my neck with the whip lash effects of this nasty fall. My arm remains bruised and sore and my head is scabbed.

This is an extremely dangerous product!
justification: The incident resulted in injuries including a gash, bruises, and whiplash, indicating a severity level of 3. The mention of similar injuries from others suggests the occurrence likelihood is high.

incident_description:
I have owned two Whirlpool "Energy Smart" electric water heaters over the past 10 years.  The electrical wiring that connects power to the electronic control circuit board has melted three times, twice on the first heater and once on the second, melting the cover, shorting it out, tripping circuit breakers, and disabling the units.  

The first heater, at about 4 years old, was replaced in 2011 after the circuit board twice malfunctioned and melted the electrical wires connecting the heater.  The newer heater, approximately 4 years old, has now also melted the electrical connections.  

New circuit boards have been the remedy offered by Whirlpool on each occasion.
justification: The incident involves repeated electrical malfunctions and wire melting, but no injuries or deaths are reported.

incident_description: Awoke this morning to find that one of the four glass panels in our shower had shattered. This particular panel is probably the most protected/shielded of any of the panels. It is a stationary panel (not a sliding door), and its outer side faces the side of a linen cabinet, and is therefore not exposed to impacts. No one was injured, as no one was in the bathroom at the time. The panel shattered overnight, sometime between 11pm and 7am.
justification: The glass panel shattered but no one was injured, making it an incident without injury.

incident_description:
This caller purchased hardwood flooring for her entire home in September 2014 from lumber retailer.

Around the end of October 2014 the mother, father and their four children began complaining of headaches, dizziness and nausea with the three smaller children also broke out in hives.

The three smaller children, the father and the mother began also having redness and irritation of their throats, congestion.

The mother and the three younger children began wheezing.

She humidified the furnace thinking it may help. 

The entire family has been to the doctors where the 18 yr old daughter, 8 yr old daughter, the 7 and 9 year old sons have been diagnosed with inflammation of the sinuses, and throat with redness and iritation. 
The 9 yr old had additional blood tests performed because proteins were found in his urine, body pains.

The 8 yr old has been chronic nose bleeds more than once a day since January 2015.

The father has been having severe chest tightness and pains but no heart problems have been diagnosed by any tests.  

Whenever the parents or the children are out of the home for a few days the symptoms each time begin to reverse.

The caller's have begun pulling the flooring out of their home.

They have returned the test kit to the laboratory but have not been able to retrieve results of any kind yet.
justification: Multiple family members experienced health issues including inflammation, nose bleeds, and chest pains, indicating injury.

incident_description: I purchased an Aqua Stone for home use. My understanding is the product is sold in Target, Costco and As Seen on TV. It is a clay stone non electric humidifier. I used this product for approximately 2 weeks, within one week of as instructed use it was covered in mold spores. I washed the stone and by the next day it had new mold growth. After some online research and finding numerous consumer complaints I contacted the Aqua Stone line. They tried to sell me another Aqua Stone to replace it! After pushing the issue and asking about the safety of using a product with mold on it or WHY it had mold on it or how it could be prevented, I was instructed by both the customer service rep and a supervisor that it was perfectly safe to keep using it with mold present and it was common. I asked if they had a quality control department and was put on hold and told that it was again perfectly safe to use it with mold present. I have coincidentally had respiratory irritation for the last two weeks. The product has been in my bedroom.
justification: The user experienced respiratory irritation likely linked to mold exposure from the product, indicating an injury (severity 3). The widespread consumer complaints suggest the issue is likely to occur (likelihood 4).

incident_description: I took out the Joy Mangano "My Little Steamer" on 10/1/14 to steam my 23 month old daughter's Halloween costume.  I noticed the steamer had corrosion since it had not been used in a while.  I followed the directions to clean the unit with half water/half vinegar & plugged the unit in as directed.  In the meantime, my daughter came in from outside & needed her bare feet cleaned since she ran outside with no shoes.  I picked her up & put her in the kitchen sink to wash her feet.  All of a sudden the steamer which was sitting at least 3 feet away started exploding like a water gun shooting hot scaulding water & vinegar at us.  My daughter immediately started screaming!!!  After unplugging the steamer & attending to my daughter I realized she had been burned.  I washed her leg with cold water & applied burn cream.  A few hours later this red spot on her leg began to bubble & blister.  I covered her leg with more cream & gave her ibuprofren for the pain because by then she was so worn out from crying that she fell asleep.  By the next morning my daughters skin was falling off her leg.  I immediately took her to the ER, once there they told us she had 2nd degree burns & she needed to see a burn center.  After having her skin peeled off her leg & creams & bandages applied day after day for over a month you can imagine that a now 2 year old is severely traumatized from this event.  After researching this product I have found so many complaints & others speaking about the steamer exploding.  They have even changed the steamers design.  I ask...why has this product not been recalled?  I just hope no one else has to go through the same thing.  I myself was 6 months pregnant & could have been burned severely.
justification: The incident resulted in second-degree burns to a child, indicating a severity level of 3 (Injury). The occurrence likelihood is 4 (likely) due to multiple complaints and a design change indicating a known issue.

incident_description: Purchased a Samsung top loading washing machine, model # WA45H7000AW at Lowe's on March 14, 2015.  On Thursday, May 21, 2015 at approximately 6:35 AM, there were two explosions from this machine that were felt across my entire house.  The first one I did not attribute to the cause of a washing machine as I never would have imagined that and thought it was some terrible thunder outside as I'd heard a weather prediction of that the previous day.  Just 5 minutes later, my daughter was in our kitchen which is on the other side of the wall from the laundry room and was able to tell us that the explosion sound we'd just heard again came from that room.  Upon inspection, we discovered our washer had indeed exploded not once, but twice!  Very unsafe!  We were so thankful no one had been in the room or that the damage to existing property wasn't worse.  The percussion blew containers of yard chemicals off of the wash sink (we'd recently been putting [REDACTED] in the yard to kill off weeds and used the slop sink to mix it), anyway those two jugs were blown off the counter and onto the floor.  There was a huge dent put into the side of our dryer and water and washing machine parts all over the floor.  I researched my model online as I'd only read previously reviews on the store's website which had been good and found another report on Amazon.com review of this same model also exploding.  Samsung needs to recall this item and find a fix to repair the issue before continuing to sell these dangerous items to the unsuspecting public at risk of property damage or injury to persons.
justification: The incident involved explosions causing property damage but no injuries, fitting severity level 2. The occurrence likelihood is rated 4 (likely) due to the report of another similar incident online.

incident_description: On April 26, 2015 around 10pm, I turned on my dryer to de-wrinkle some clothing, and then I left the laundry room in the basement and retuned upstairs.  About 2 minutes later the fire alarms started going off in the home.  When I got to the top of the stairs, I saw smoke crawling along the basement ceiling.  I turned into the laundry room, and saw flames coming out of the metal exhaust tube attached to the end of the dryer.   I grabbed the fire extinguisher in the basement and used it to put out the flames in the exhaust tube.  I touched the top of the dryer and it was very hot, so I did not open the door.  After evacuating the house, I called 911 to send the fire department.  When I was on the phone with the dispatcher, she asked me to look through a small back window in my laundry room so see if the fire had been put out.  At that time the smoke in the basement was very thick, but I could see flames shooting from the dryer.  The fire department put out the fire quickly, but we sustained smoke damage through the entire home and there was some damage to the basement laundry room.  After the fire I researched what the cause could have been online, and I found out that our dryer was involved in a class action lawsuit.  Electrolux settled the lawsuit, but has not recalled the dryer, even though they are aware of the issue of them catching fire from being made improperly.  I was never notified of the lawsuit, and just happened to find the information on our own, and I did verify that our model number: FGRB6600FS, and serial number: XD7141181, were involved in the class action lawsuit.  I am asking you to have these dryers recalled since Electrolux has failed to do so.  My brand is one of 5 brand included in the lawsuit.
justification: The incident involved a fire causing property damage but no injuries or deaths.

incident_description:
Fire on June 11,2013 at residence located W 131 S 8448 Eagles Way, Muskego, Wisconsin. Smoke and fire damage
exceeded $500,000. The fire was caused by an arcing incident within a dehumidifier. The dehumidifier was
examined and determined to be the cause of the fire. Attached is the Report of the two experts.
My law firm, Greg Cook Law, S.C. first became involved in this incident in late April. We gathered the information
and learned that similar dehumidifiers manufactured by the same company had been recalled for fire hazards. See
Release #01-130, 10-096 and 11-324.
This unit model number does not appear on any of the recalls. This unit is described in the report as one SIMILAR to
Model LHD459EL dehumidifier manufactured by LG.
My concern was that the engineers referred to manuals for models LHD30, LHD45EL, UD65EL, LD450EAL, and
LD451 EGL as well as the schematics for Model LDSOELY6 since the homeowner did not have any manuals in his
possession. Homeowner purchased unit in 2006-07 from a Home Depot, according to his recollection.
I suspect the other recalls involve similarly designed machines with almost identical wiring problems that were
found in this unit. Arcing was the reported cause in other fires and from what I could see it may have been a similar
defect.
The unit is in the custody of State Farm Mutual Fire Insurance company. We are trying to verify if the serial number
or other information can be gleaned from the unit.
justification: The incident involved a fire causing significant property damage but no reported injuries or fatalities.

incident_description:
On, 5/3/15, at about 2:45pm, [REDACTED] was shaking a new can of Rust-Oleum black spray paint. He shook it for about a minute and as he put his right hand on the lid to remove it, the can exploded in his hands.  

There was a loud explosion and the can burst open. The bottom portion of the can detached from the can, striking him on my chest, just below his throat causing a burn, his skin was cut and there was extreme swelling and bruising. His right thumb sustained a fracture as well.

I, [REDACTED], spouse to [REDACTED], took photos and after we cleaned the paint off of his skin, I transported him to PrimeCare. He received medical attention and was diagnosed with an abrasion to his anterior chest and a fracture of the metacarpal bones of his right hand. 
The paint got all over him, his clothes and several items in the area where he was standing. The marble from inside of the can was found in the area where he had been standing and the bottom of the can was later located in our neighbors back yard, about 30' from where he had been standing. There is a 6' block wall between our property. The lid and push button were never located.

The can was purchased less than 6 months ago at Home Depot and had been stored in a cabinet in the garage and the temperature in the garage was about 80 degrees. He removed it from the cabinet and walked outside to where the item was that he was going to paint. The can was never dropped nor did it make contact with anything while he was shaking it. A close examination of the can shows that the bottom blew out and the can separated at the seam. The can has the UPC# of 020066777982. We will be retaining all of the parts of the can.
justification: The incident resulted in a chest abrasion and a fractured thumb, requiring medical attention, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description:
Caller used a washing machine cleaner Saturday, April 18th, 2015 as she had a few times before this date to clean her washer.

On this particular day however he opened the foil package and emptied the pellets into the water filled washer but less that five minutes into the cycle the room then the house began filling with what smelled like a chlorine type chemical odor.

The odor remained very strong causing the caller and her husband to get their dog and go outside.

The caller began coughing uncontrollably.

Her husband returned into the home to obtain the caller's steroid medicine that she takes for her RSD.

She took the steroid and used a steroid nasal spry to open her pores and allow breathing.

They sat outside on their deck for approximately two hours then entered the home and her husband started the washer in an attempt to be rid of the odor.

The caller states that her husband had to run the washer eight times before the smell was gone.
She states that just reaching into the washer he felt a burning sensation on his forearms.

The caller contacted the manufacturer Monday, April 20th, 2015, she doesn't remember the name of the female representative she spoke with but she did ask for the lot number#  and barcode#.  The caller provided the lot number but the caller's throat began closing up just from the empty box from the washer cleaner.

The husband took over the phone call while the caller drove to an emergency clinic nearby and from the emergency clinic she was taken by ambulance to Lourdes Hospital in Binghamton, NY where she was diagnosed with an allergic reaction and as having difficulty breathing induced from (product named in this report).

She was transferred from the emergency room to the "Critical  Decisions" portion of the hospital and admitted overnight.

She was released Tuesday, April 21st, 2015 around 11:00AM with steroids and Benadryl.

Wednesday, April 22nd, 2015 around 9:00PM the ambulance was once again called to her home and she was taken again to Lourdes Emergency where she was kept five hours and treated 

On Friday, April 24th, 2015 she contacted the manufacturer again, spoke with [REDACTED] who once the caller provided her with an update did tell the consumer that an investigator may check into within a couple of weeks.

The caller is upset that this could consume weeks and no investigation would be put into action until that time.
The manufacturer also instructed her to mail the cleaner to them but she said that there is no way that
She is afraid that another consumer may be affected in a worse way if something isn't done quickly.
                                                                                              

Friday, April 24th, 2015 the caller kept a prior scheduled appointment with her physician, she was advised to continue the steroids.

Her diagnosis from this physician was allergic reaction, hospital discharge follow up.

The caller does still have two of the packets of this washing machine cleaner in her garage.
justification: The caller experienced an allergic reaction requiring hospitalization, indicating an injury (severity 3). The occurrence likelihood is rare (1) as this is an unusual reaction to a washing machine cleaner.

The first false alarm occurred when nobody was home.  The second false alarm occurred while my family was in another room.

Eventually someone is going to get hurt when they ignore a false alarm, or if they believe the alarm is real and run outside unprepared.  Smoke detectors should NOT have false alarms.  If nothing else, they end up scaring families and kids unnecessarily.
justification: False alarms have occurred multiple times without injury, but there is a risk of future harm if ignored.

Product: Space Heater
Brand: Comfort Zone
Model: CZ530WM 
Mfg date: 07/2014 
Dist by: Howard Berger Co. LLC.
Sold by: Wal-Mart
Country of origin: China
Purchase date: Winter 2014/15
Possible serial #: 67650-2/cz530wm/092414

Space heater had not been turned on or used for around one month, although it was left plugged in. The On/Off switch in the OFF position, thermostat set to the lowest setting, Hi 1500w/Low 1250w switch set to Hi, unit in standby/off mode, with only power running to the on off switch on the unit.  The room temperature was around 70 degrees Fahrenheit, so there was no attempt for the heater thermostat to activate due to temperature change.

With no indications of a problem, the male end of the units electrical cord shorted, made a buzzing sound, followed by a bright arc like an electric welder, the plug started blazing.  I pulled the cord causing the plug to release from the female receptacle, extinguished the flaming plug end without further damage to the house, myself or anyone else. The arc burned away one of the plug prongs, melted and burned the plug end leaving a burned out void where the prong would normally protrude out of the plastic. Luckily, this occurred while I was home, and awake, sitting 3 ft away, where I had a chance to take action. I'd hate to think what the outcome would have been had I not been able to intervene, or worse yet had I been asleep.
justification: The incident involved a fire hazard but no injury or death occurred due to timely intervention.

incident_description: I bought a QuickStrap 50 Water Heater Restraints manufactured by Hubbard Enterprises from Lowe's on 4/2/15. I checked the installation instructions which showed how to put the straps on the front of a water heater and attach the straps to wall studs behind the heater. I noted that those straps would prevent forward movement of a heater but would not stop backward movement of a heater unless the heater was in contact with a surface such as a wall behind the heater. I called customer support and was told that the consumer would have to build a spacer between the studs and the heater. When I asked why that information was not in the instructions I was told they could not put all that information in the instructions. Without that information a consumer would not know that in an emergency situation such as an earthquake, tornado or hurricane their hot water heater could be subject to backward motion that could result in property damage by water or fire and human harm or death. The lack of instructions concerning a required support for the back of a heater is misleading of the safety claims of the product and safety risk to consumers.
justification: The incident describes a potential safety risk due to inadequate instructions, which could lead to property damage or human harm in emergency situations.

incident_description: I purchase 5 Kidde Model P12040 smoke alarms and 2 Model [REDACTED] CO and smoke alarms for an addition I was putting on my house.  I had a professional electrician do all the wiring in my house.  Shortly after install I started having false alarms.  I knew they were false because I have one of each type still install from before the renovation and they were not going off.  As they would go off I would remove each one that caused the system to go off.  out of the 7 units only one had not gone off within a week.  I called kidde customer service to see what was going on.  They had me run all kinds of tests on my electrical system.  All came back as they should.  The final test was simple leaving them not hard wired and putting a battery in.  Of course one went off as I expected within 10 minutes.  A second was within 20 minutes.  Kidde said they would replace the two units, however they never arrived in the mail as they said.  After 6 months I still have not received assistance on any of the malfunctioning units.  I was forced to return them and buy another brand (first alert).  I have them now installed and do not have any false alarms, I have reached the conclusion that the issue lies in their product.  A consumer should not have to worry about whether a alarm is real or not.  Soon a person will ignore a alarm and it will bite them.
justification: False alarms from smoke detectors could lead to ignoring real alarms, posing a potential safety risk, but no actual injury or death occurred.

Product: Nest smoke detector
Model: NEST-97D8
Serial # 05CA02AC391300VG
Mfg date: 12/01/2013

During the evening of April 28, 2014, in Palm Springs, CA, our Nest smoke detector set off multiple false alarms for smoke.  We have a triple redundant smoke alarm system and none of the other types of detectors triggered.  We also did not smell any smoke at all.  The alarms triggered whether the windows were opened or closed with the AC on.

I called Nest customer support and they said they had other similar reports this evening.  They told us to remove the smoke detector from the wall and power source and to remove the batteries.  Nest is sending us a replacement detector.

Fortunately, we were at home at the time, as we are often away on travel.  If we had not been home we would have had to call the fire department.  False positives can also be hazardous if they occur when people are sleeping because people can be injured when responding to a false alarm when they are disoriented.

incident_description:
BACKGROUND:
I live in San Diego in a house that was newly constructed in 2009 with Open Energy OE-34 Watt integrated PV panels installed on the roof.  When the original safety recall was issued in 2011 (CPSC alert #12-725), I shut down my PV system for 16 months until the wiring clam-shell retrofit was performed in October 2012.  

The original manufacturer of the PV tiles was Open Energy and the distributor was Eagle Roofing.  Applied Solar LLC acquired Open Energy and in 2009 Applied Solar LLC declared bankruptcy and went out of business.

CONCERNS:
I have several ongoing concerns regarding these panels:

1. FIRE SAFETY:  I understand that there have been an additional two or three roof fires known to be caused by the OE34W panels even after the wiring clam shell retrofits were made.  I see the CPSC has a recent recall posted (#[REDACTED]) that's applicable to 240 "solar homes" with OE-34W panels built by [REDACTED] in [REDACTED] and [REDACTED], because of these fires.  [REDACTED] appears to be replacing these integrated PV systems with standard rack systems to eliminate the potential for any more roof fires. 

My question to the CPSC is, what makes the systems installed by [REDACTED] unique or different from any of the other OE-34 systems that were installed by other builders, including mine in San Diego?  Am I living in a house still at risk of a roof fire even with the safety retrofits done in 2012?

2. PERFORMANCE DEGRADATION and FIRE SAFETY:  It is clear to me that these Open Energy OE-34W (and presumably the OE-50W panels, as well) are grossly defective, either in design or through flaws in manufacturing.  Even ignoring the fire safety risks that triggered the 2011 and the 2014 [REDACTED] recalls, these PV panels degrade and fail prematurely. One of my neighbors, whose house was built one year before mine and has the exact same OE-34W panels, is getting just ~25% of his first year's output.  As an engineer, I have to wonder if this degradation process is related to the fire ignition mechanism?  Again I ask, are we living in houses at risk of bursting into flames on any given hot sunny day?

SPECIFIC QUESTIONS:
A. Did the [REDACTED] fires start because of short-circuits, panel de-lamination, cracks, or something else?  (What is the failure mechanism?)

B. Was a degradation in power output noted at the time or related to the roof fires? 

C. If the [REDACTED] fires weren't caused by a unique installation issue, what makes the SolarSave OE-34W panels on my house any different than the ones that were on the [REDACTED] houses?

I need answers to these questions so that I can decide on my own whether or not to remove these panels from my roof for fire safety reasons.  Or will it be OK to let them degrade to zero output in the next few years?  I have been unsuccessful in getting my builder, his contractors, sub-contractors, or even Wuxi-Suntech itself (the panel manufacturer) to help me or even to diagnose the specific problem(s), presumably because no one wants to assume financial responsibility.
