incident_description:
We have 12 Nest Protect smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in our home that we bought and installed at the end of 2013.  They are all interconnected with their wifi connection.  
A few months ago, we were awakened in the middle of the night by the alarms telling us there was a fire, and to get out!  There was no fire, no smoke, no nothing.  And there was not an immediate way to contact Nest for help.  The problem appeared to be emanating from one of the alarms that was telling us there was a fire there.  So, I removed it, and put it outside in my truck, and the next day was able to find a number for Nest, who told me to return it, and they would refund our money, as the alarms had just been taken off the market, so they couldn't give me a replacement.
But 2 nights ago, again in the middle of the night, all of them started repeatedly going off, and each telling us in turn that there was a fire in one location, then another, then another, and so on.  So, this time, I removed them all, and put them all in my truck, so we could try to get back to sleep.
I then had to go out and buy a whole new set of alarms of a competing brand, and install them.  So now, I have to return all of the Nest Protect alarms.  I am sorry to have to do this, because I really liked the concept, and its promise, especially the ability to let us know there was a problem via an app on our phone no matter where we happened to be.  But it appears that they are at present, unable to deliver on that promise.
justification: False alarms caused disruption and required replacement of devices, but no injury or damage occurred.

incident_description: We have a shower kit from American Bath Factory installed in our home built 2 1/2 years ago.  Yesterday, after my wife took a shower and left the room the glass door suddenly shattered to pieces.  The door was left pushed inward to the shower (to drip) and was directly under a running bath exhaust fan.  The sequence of events is really nothing new or different (this is typically how we use the shower and leave the door).  The hinges were still securely fastened to the wall and there were shattered glass fragments still inside the two hinges.  We are at a loss as to the sudden loss of our door.  After contacting American Bath Factory, I was told this event was unprecedented and that either a temperature change or impact to the edge of the glass would be required for the glass to break.
justification: The glass door shattered unexpectedly, but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
Lights dimmed briefly, then the circuit breaker blew.  Not being positive what blew the breaker, I disconnected a few things, turned off the lights and reset the breaker.  After about a minute, it blew again.  That time I saw a flash (the dehumidifier was near the breaker box) and I realized the dehumidifier was the cause.  I also detected a slight smell of heat/burnt wire insulation.

Since the unit was out of warranty, I decided to open it up to see if it was something as simple as a short in the power cord where it entered.  It wasn't.  What I found disturbed me and makes me concerned that the unit has been a potential fire hazard all along.

One of the wires running to the compressor had its insulation worn through, presumably due to vibration over time where it rested against a metal stud that holds a cover over the wiring where it enters the compressor.  Due to the arcing, the metal stud was mostly burnt through!  The insulation of that and the other wires going to the compressor also seemed hard/brittle from heat at the last couple inches before the compressor.  I can't say for sure whether it was from heat over a long period of time or heat from the short that blew the breaker, but typically insulation doesn't get stiff like that from one brief heating, and therefore I suspect the wires had been getting hot over time, which could also explain why the insulation wore through and allowed the short circuit.  (I would think this issue could have been avoided if it had been manufactured with better quality wire -- better insulation and/or heavier gauge wire, and some foam or heavy heatshrink insulation over the stud....or routing the wiring so it couldn't come into contact with the stud and wear.  Minimal cost at time of manufacturer.)

I immediately checked to see if the unit had been recalled, but it was not one of the models that are part of the current Danby / Gree recall.  I can't help but wonder, however, it the problem is similar to what happened in the recalled models.

I called the manufacturer, Danby, gave them this information, and then emailed the representative pictures of the burnt wiring.  The manufacturer's representative was very kind and interested in the issue, but said she could do nothing since the unit was out of warranty, but that she would forward the information and the pictures on to the appropriate people to look at the info from a safety issue.   

I have not heard back yet, but that was only yesterday.  In the mean time, I decided to file this report to serve as a warning to others to at least be on the lookout for the issue.

This appears to be something that can likely be repaired, and if done properly, repaired in a way that it won't happen again in the future, BUT as manufactured, I believe the dehumidifier to be unsafe, especially since dehumidifiers are often located in basements and areas that are generally unoccupied and therefore less likely to be noticed if giving off smoke, sparks, or a hot smell.
justification: The incident involved a potential fire hazard due to worn wiring and arcing, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
Welding goggles that I purchased failed, causing me to burn myself.

I was using a new pair of welding goggles that I purchased just the day before to do some brazing of copper tubing in my basement.

I had almost completed my braze, when I lifted up the shaded glass on the goggles (it's hinged) to inspect my braze, when suddenly the shaded glass fell from the goggles.  I was holding the lit torch in my right hand, and I operated the goggles with my left hand.  When the glass fell, I instinctively reached for it, causing the lit torch, with a large, multi-flame tip attachment, to come into direct contact with the back of my arm, causing a severe burn.  I almost dropped the lit torch.

I shut off the torch, removed the goggles, and then got a wet cloth on my burned arm.  I inspected the goggles and noticed that they appear to have a manufacturing defect which caused this problem to happen.

The frame that holds the shaded glass into the goggles is designed to allow the glass to be removed and replaced (possibly for different levels of shading?).  The glass is retained by a piece of springy wire that is supposed to hook into holes on the left and right at the top of the frame.  The hole on one side of that frame was defective.  Instead of a hole through the plastic, the back-side was missing, so it was just a dent.  As long as the shaded glass frame was down, it held the wire in place, but as soon as it was raised, the wire would spring out, thereby allowing the shaded glass to fall out.

Here is a link to the product at Lowe's:   http://www.lowes.com/pd_13867-47120-SGY-WELD14_0__?productId=50017000&Ntt=blue+hawk+welding&pl=1&currentURL=%3FNtt%3Dblue%2Bhawk%2Bwelding&facetInfo=
Product name: "Blue Hawk Black Welding Safety Glasses"
Item #: 13867
Product #: SGY-WELD14
justification: The incident resulted in a severe burn due to a manufacturing defect in the welding goggles, which is an injury but not fatal.

incident_description: Activated garage door opener (via remote) to close:  As the door closed, you could hear the door speed up and then slam onto the garage floor.  When I then tried to open the door via remote, the trolley moved along on the drive screw but the door did not lift.  Visual check showed that the  trolley had separated from the door linkage.  Further inspection showed that the "engagement" mechanism (actually a plastic bar) was not fully seated into the trolley.  This is because the cam on the emergency release handle pivot prevented the plastic bar from fully seating.  In order to continue to use the garage door, I have now fully re-seated the plastic bar into the trolley using a screw I have installed.  The emergency door handle and rope have been removed.  Note that no  wear was evident on the plastic bar.  I believe this is a very dangerous situation as the unexpected complete release of the door allows it to slam onto the garage floor possibly injuring someone.
justification: The incident involved a garage door slamming due to a mechanical failure, but no injury was reported. The likelihood is rated as possible (3) given the described mechanism failure.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that the cooking system comes on by itself.

The consumer stated that she always kept the unit plugged in but turned off. The consumer stated that recently, an error sign "Err" would come on.

One day, the consumer discovered that the unit's light was on. The consumer went to check on the unit and saw that it has stated on its own. The consumer stated that the unit was heated up. 

The consumer stated that they unplugged the unit and plugged it back it, to reset it. The consumer stated that the issues still exists.

The consumer stated that this  might have happened at least 6 times in the past 3 days.  

The consumer's husband contacted the manf. He was informed that the product is no longer covered under warranty. The manf informed him that they were not aware of such issues. The consumer's husband was informed that he can purchased an upgraded unit for $75. 

The consumer stated that the manf was not worried about the safety hazard of the unit. The manf did not ask to have the unit sent back for inspection. 

There are no recalls.
justification: The unit turning on by itself poses a potential safety hazard, but no injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
We recently purchased  a Duracell brand mini usb ac charger DU1673
 The product has 2 ends. One for the usb port and the other end plugs into the electrical outlet.  The end with the electrical plug detached from the device when my son unplugged it. Next, my 10 year old son got an electrical shock because he tried to pull out the piece of the charger that had detached and was still plugged into the wall outlet. We had to remove the piece stuck in our outlet and that is very unsafe. So basically the plug component that is suppsed to be fused to the charger device completely came off and remained in the electrical outlet.
justification: The incident resulted in an electrical shock to a child, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description: The glass sink on the bathroom vanity spontaneously combusted. It sounded like a huge explosion. The shards of glass flew 8 feet. There was no one in the bathroom at the time it exploded, and nothing fell on it. It was installed in March, 2013.
justification: The sink exploded but no one was injured, indicating an incident with no injury.

incident_description: Using a shark professional steam mop, models3601co. The housing became so hot you couldn't touch it and it began to smell of burning plastic. The front cover warped and separated from the rest of the housing.
justification: The steam mop became dangerously hot and emitted a burning smell, but no injury was reported.

incident_description: Dehumidifier running but different noise then usual.  Went to unit and noticed a burning smell and the air coming from the top vent very hot.  Back of unit also hot to the touch.  Pressed Off button with no response; unplugged unit.  Unit was in Normal mode with humidity set at 50% which allows the unit to cycle on and off automatically to maintain the humidity setting.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning dehumidifier with a burning smell and overheating, but no injury occurred.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that the handle slips out of the bucket grooves. 

The consumer stated that the handle has come off multiple times (at least 4-6) while she was carrying the bucket or taking it out. The consumer stated that one time, a full bucket fell on her right hand. The consumer was hurt. 

The consumer stated that she had to force the handle back into the bucket groove to fix it.

The consumer stated that she contacted the manf on 6/19/14. The consumer wanted the manf to replace the bucket with a new bucket where the handle does not come off. The consumer was informed that they would not offer that replacement since the issues is not covered under warranty. The consumer was informed that she can go and buy a new unit.

The consumer believes that the handle is not well designed. The consumer stated that she believes that this is a safety hazard.
justification: The consumer was hurt when the handle slipped, causing a full bucket to fall on her hand, indicating an injury.

incident_description:
vSpeed-Queen washer purchased 01/2011 - It had been checked by a service tech after it stopped working and wouldn't start again but while the tech was there the machine began working again although he said there was nothing wrong with it.

April 9th, 2014 this caller heard humming noise but couldn't figure out where it was coming from, a little while later she went to her utility room to check on the clothes she had in the washer and smelled a strong odor of burning electric.

She found also that the circuit breaker had tripped.

The caller checked the plug in area and it seemed fine, then she went to the breaker and tripped it back on to allow her clothes to complete the wash cycle. The washer only hummed: it would not run.

She contacted the retailer and informed them of the incident and that she had tripped the breaker back on but [REDACTED] who is the manager at Lipscombe Appliance, Inc. advised her to unplug the machine then he scheduled maintenance/service tech for April 11th, 2014.

The technician determined that this washer needed a timer and a motor but they did not have either part.

The caller asked if they had a new washer on their floor, the technician checked with the store, found that they did then caller purchased it and allowed the retailer to take the non working washer back.

The caller stated that the manufacturer had advised her that they would pay for the two parts for her washer but she had found a report submitted by another consumer who said her washer with the same model number had been repaired and then when she was using it she not only smelled burning but saw smoke and was shocked when she touched it.

The caller is reporting this incident to alert the public to the safety issues with this washer and have a recall generated by the manufacturer. 
She has contacted the Attorney General for Virginia.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning washer with electrical issues but no reported injuries or deaths, warranting a severity level of 2. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) given the described electrical problems and similar reports from other consumers.

incident_description: On Wednesday July 9th I purchased a Hudson backpack sprayer Model 13854. I came home read the instructions and connected the charger as instructed. On Thursday morning July 10th I prepared to use the sprayer. The light on the charger was green and I disconnected it. I moved the sprayer outside to fill it . Before filling it I decided to turn it on to make sure it worked. I pushed the on switch and it exploded. I called the 800 number and found that the person I talked to had no sense of urgency after I explained that the sprayer had exploded.  I was told to take pictures and return it and it would be replaced. I stated I did not want it. I was told to return it to the store I purchased it [REDACTED]I did and I received a refund. I was a GM trainer for twenty years and a Heavy Duty truck instructor for ten years before retiring. I believe that the sealed battery leaked Hydrogen gas while charging and an arc from the switch or wiring set off the explosion. I believe this product poses a risk that needs to be researched. What I do not understand is the lack of concern of the Hudson representative or the Manager for [REDACTED] when I stated the product exploded.
justification: The sprayer exploded, indicating a significant safety incident, but there was no mention of injury or death.

incident_description: I purchased a Whirlpool electric dryer several years ago.  Recently, the door switch stopped working.  I ordered the part and had an electrician out to replace it.  When he went to install the part he discovered that the switch had caught fire.  He said he would not repair the machine as he said this never should have happened and obviously the safety device did not work.  I have pictures I will send you if I am provided an email.  I was told we were very lucky the entire dryer did not catch on fire since the switch and surrounding area totally burned.
justification: The switch caught fire but no injury or death occurred, indicating a severity level of 2. The occurrence likelihood is rated as 2 (unlikely) since such incidents are not common but do happen occasionally.

incident_description: I washed my bedding on Saturday, July 12, 2014.  I put the items in between 7-8am.  I set the setting to "Bulky Bedding" on my washer and went about my day as usual.  I was the only one home at the time and was in the process of blow drying my hair when I heard a very loud boom and my house shook.  I turned the dryer off and looked outside and it was cloudy so I assumed that it may be thunder or I contributed it to large trucks going by my home since they are building many homes in my area.  I went back to getting ready for an appointment that I had.  Around 8:15 I went downstairs in my home and walked into my garage.  When I reached my car I heard the boom once again and sounded like a bomb.  I ran into my house and water was gushing on my floor from the washer and water spraying my whole laundry room.  The machine was spitting out all of its parts all over my floor and the top of the washer was blown off and hanging on sideways.  The machine was still running in full force banging into my walls and the dryer that it sat next too.  Danger was apparent at this point to I immediately contacted my husband on the phone as I was in severe panic mode since I could not reach the electrical outlet plug and the machine was out of control.  My husband contacted his father who lives 1 mile from me and he rushed over.  While I waited for his father I quickly thought that the power button was still lit up while the machine was ripping to shreds so I ran in the room and pushed it and it turned off.  My next concern was a fire since there was water everywhere and cords on the floor and the outlet completely wet.  I put on some gloves and climbed on top of the dryer to reach behind the washer and unplug the machine so that nothing more could come from this mess.  My father-in-law came over and helped me pull all the pieces out of my laundry room and into our garage where the unit currently sits. It was a sight we had never seen before and we were glad my kids were not in the room at the time.  Literally the screws, washers, metal rods, everything were thrown all over my floor.  Holes are in my walls, one hole in my floor, water leaked down to my basement.  I started researching on the internet and found this recall that I was never made aware of so I contacted the number you provided and a man is coming today to look at the damage.  I am grateful no one was hurt, but at the same time am FURIOUS that I was never contacted or informed about the recall.  They had all my information when I gave them my model number and serial number so why wasn't I ever contacted?  LG means Life's Good, well not in my home anymore....I am paranoid to have anything running if I have to leave the house now.  I am hoping this anxiety goes away.
justification: The incident caused significant property damage but no injuries, and such severe washer malfunctions are unlikely.

incident_description: We purchased a Whirlpool water heater in 2010. On July 12th, 2014, we noticed a burning smell in the house. The smell was coming from the energy smart control box located on top of the water heater. The box had overheated and had melted. Upon researching this issue, I found numerous complaints regarding this box overheating. Whirlpool was contacted and have agreed to ship a new control panel. Even though the water heater is under warranty, Whirlpool wants me to install the replacement part. I'm a little concerned that this is a known issue and no steps have been taken by Whirlpool to fix this problem. The results could have been serious had we not been home and awake.
justification: The incident caused a burning smell and melted control box, but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
This caller purchased her iron in March 2010 and had no problems with it until June 8th, 2014 when she was ironing a pair of pants after plugging in only a few seconds before ironing.
She had ironed one leg of the pants and was beginning the second leg when fire shot from where the cord connects into the iron and engulfed her left arm up to the elbow.
She screamed which alerted her husband who came running into the room, pulled the plug from the wall and rushed his wife into the bathroom.
Her arm from the hand to the elbow was black.
She continuously washed her left arm with anti bacterial soap and putting [REDACTED] then per a doctor's advice by phone she switched to [REDACTED] with pain re leif.
The caller was in pharmaceutical sales for years, she was aware that the main worry is infection whenever skin is burned and so is watching it carefully.
The skin of her arm is no longer black and is healing well.
She is reporting to inform the public of the burn danger with this product.

She contacted the manufacturer on June 10th, 2014 and June 11th, 2014 but has been trying not to return the iron to them because she is under the impression that a report was already filed with CPSC.  I found no report before this one.
She said that someone named [REDACTED] or [REDACTED] contacted her but I also found no one in the Virginia area who would have contacted her from CPSC by that name.
justification: The incident resulted in a burn injury to the arm, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is unlikely (2) as such incidents are not common but do happen occasionally with faulty appliances.

incident_description: I lost electrical power to a few of my electrical outlets. The circuit breaker was not blown but the GFCI stopped working correctly. I built this house in 2004 and since then this is the third GFCI that has failed. When I opened the units, I found the circuit boards to be poorly manufactured. I will try to include in this report a picture of the latest circuit board. I do not even know if these units would have found a Circuit Fault due to the faulty construction/manufacturing. Please report to Leviton that these units are poorly constructed and possibly dangerous as they might not have the ability to detect a Circuit Fault after years of use due to the faulty construction / manufacturing.
justification: The incident describes a recurring issue with faulty GFCI units that could potentially fail to detect circuit faults, but no injury or death has occurred.

incident_description:
Oxiclean laundry stain remover in spray form ...  purchased at any supermarket.  When used and it comes in contact with skin, it eats you up with so much irritation ... I took a picture of my hands to illustrate ... there are  no instruction to wear gloves when handling.  This product is dangerous ... am a sr. and the writing on the back of the spray bottle is so tiny I need a 10x magnifier to read.  I tried contacting the manufacturer online and their website is a display case and does not work.  I did print their complaint form and will fill it out and send it in by mail.  In the meantime, get this product spray off the shelves.  

This incident happened last week.
justification: The incident describes skin irritation from contact with the product, which qualifies as an injury. The likelihood is considered possible due to the product's widespread availability and lack of clear usage instructions.

incident_description:
Iron was in upright position, on ironing board, plugged in after brief use, and set on medium.  I walked away for about 5 minutes into the next room.  Then I smelled smoke and detector went off.  I found the iron on fire, with heavy smoke pouring out of both sides of the iron.  I was able to unplug it, grab it by the cord, and put in under the tub faucet to put the fire out.  

It smoked and spewed noxious fumes for at least two more minutes.  Filled most of upstairs of house with smoke.

If I hadn't walked back in, it would have caught the bedroom on fire.
justification: The incident involved a fire and heavy smoke but no injury or death, and such events are unlikely if proper precautions are taken.

incident_description:
Samsung Dryer Model DV448AEP / XAA

Our dryer had been making some thumping sounds, wasn't sure what was wrong until some clothes got "stuck" in the dryer and wouldn't come out.  The piece of clothing had become wedged in a crack in the drum.  The crack appears to have propogated along a weld seam line inward from the front of the drum, then at a curve in the drum surface it turned almost 90 degrees for a bit and then continued in a very jagged fashion with a very sharp edge.  I almost cut myself trying to free the clothing but was finally able to find a way to make the crack open a little to enable pulling it free.
I checked online and found several comments regarding the exact same problem in this and other Samsung dryer models, apparently both the stainless steel drums and other material drums, all having the same seam design and the pictures I saw showed almost identical fracturing of the seam, along the seam line from the outer edge then shifting at the curvature of the drum and continuing inward.
This appears to be a fairly common problem, whether it appears quickly, after about 18 months, or later as in our case (about 4 years old).  Clearly a design defect.
justification: The incident involved a design defect causing clothing to get stuck and a near-injury from sharp edges, but no actual injury occurred.

incident_description:
Milwaukee Tool Company random orbital sander model 6021-21 (5") has a on/off switch on the handle. This switch, when pressed for OFF apparently does not completely shut off the sander. The sander then restarts. 
While sanding some wood, I shut off the sander and placed it on top of a pile of wood over my head. The sander turned ON, spun around and fell off in front of me. I reached to catch the sander and received a deep laceration (to the bone) on my right thumb. Emergency care center sewed it back up with a large number of stitches. The laceration was deep enough to sever a number of nerves rendering the thumb partially insensitive and appears to be permanent damage.
I still use the tool and it will turn ON without warning about 50% of the time after being shut OFF.
justification: The incident resulted in a deep laceration with permanent nerve damage, which qualifies as an injury (severity 3). The sander restarts unexpectedly about 50% of the time, making the occurrence likelihood high (4).

incident_description:
I purchased 2 lasso tower heaters from Sams.  These heaters did not overheat, but when plugged into the electrical sockets proceeded to burn the socks and their plugs, so much so when shut off and unplugged they arched.  

I called lasso, and was told 1) they were out of warranty. and 2) that my plug MUST be faulty in the house.  When I explained that they both did the same thing, and that it was not 1 plug but multiple plugs, I was then told they must be industrial plugs.  I asked how a personal heater, sold at Sams for home use needed an industrial plug.  They continued to give excuses.
justification: The heaters caused electrical arcing and burned plugs, indicating a hazardous incident but no reported injury.

incident_description:
My 16 year old daughter was opened glass sliding door on bathtub after showering and the door exploded into pieces shattering and filing the tub with glass small pieces and covering the floor as well.

It was the inside door on a tub shower. It was purchased in 12/02/2012 from Home Depot. The manufacturer was Contract Wardrobe. The model number was #1050

She was cut on the right side of her nose near the bridge, close to her eyes that required 5 stitches at the emergency room.  She also had many smaller cuts on her hands, and leg. The doctor found tiny pieces of glass embedded in her forehead and checked all cuts and removed any small glass fragments.

Her right breast also had a small cut but butterfly tape was used to hold the cut together.
justification: The incident resulted in multiple injuries requiring medical attention, including stitches and glass removal, but no death occurred.

incident_description:
I purchased a whirlpool washer and dryer from Home Depot March 2013.
The red vent light continuously lit so I called for a service appointment in February 2014.
HD sent a technician who claimed the thermometer shorted. Installed a new one, and declared it 'tested good'.  
Next day. Red vent light lit again. I called for repair. HD sent out a new technician who looked at dryer and said I needed a new fuel gauge. He left without opening dryer. I asked that technician why the inner drum was all charcoal gray. His answer was "One of your children must have had a crayon in their pocket". This same technician came back 2 weeks later with part, opened dryer and said it didn't need a fuel gauge, it needed a conversion kit. Apparently, the dryer that was sold to me was for use in a natural gas setting, I have propane!  The technician demonstrated what had been occurring all these months;  large flames of FIRE running up the back of the dryer, each and every time I operated it. Thus the charcoal gray of the drum. Burn marks!!!

I complained to HD. They gave me the runaround, and sent me to 6 different people to speak to. I submitted a request for a replacement, which they declined. They are only offering to install a conversion kit, which is what the dryer SHOULD have had in it when delivered.

HD refuses to do anything but install the conversion kit into what is now a damaged dryer.

I have been without a dryer since February 2014.  I have a family of 4 and this has caused me MAJOR stress and inconvenience.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning dryer with potential fire hazards, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that the compartment where the liquid is supposed to go is covered in black mold.

The consumer stated that she has tried various methods to clean the product including cleaners that are meant to clean the mold. The consumer stated that the mold goes away but comes back.

The consumer stated that she started noticing this problem a month after purchase.

The consumer stated that her area is well ventilated. 

The consumer does not have sense of smell, so she does not know if the mold has odor. 

The consumer stated that she had to have the hose cleaned out twice (Nov 2011 and Feb 2014). The hose was clogged with paper towel that the consumer used to dry off the water from the tray. The consumer's kitchen and dining room flooded from the clogged hose in Feb 2014.

There are no recalls on this model.
justification: The incident involves persistent mold and flooding, but no reported injury or death.

incident_description:
Hoover Windtunnel Canister Cleaner
Model S3670
Series ZJ120
Serial No 090800015254

Does not appear on any recall list. I discovered today that it appeared to have similar problems as in

http://www.cpsc.gov/en/Recalls/2011/Hoover-Recalls-WindTunnel-Canister-Vacuums-Due-to-Fire-and-Shock-Hazards/

I can see spark in the electric cord below the place where the wand is plugged into the power nozzle.
justification: The description indicates sparks in the electric cord, posing a potential fire and shock hazard, but no injury or death is reported.

incident_description:
I was doing some maintenance on my car and had my air compressor sitting ready with the blow gun handle to help blow away any dirt/debris as I worked.  I head a loud pop, then a whoosh or air, then the air compressor turn on.  When I turned around to see what happened I noticed the plastic handle for the blow gun was sitting right behind me and the other part was still attached to the compressor hose leaking air.  The handle had shot off several feet to where I was working.  Luckily my young son wasn't helping me or it may have shot off and hit him.  When I went back to search to see if this had happened to others it seems that just about everyone is complaining in the reviews about the same issue:

http://www.harborfreight.com/pistol-grip-blow-gun-68259.html

If you read some of the reviews you'll notice an alarming trend that these often break and some may have already caused others injury.  It seems that the brass fitting where the air hose connects is merely pressed into the plastic housing of the handle with nothing but friction to hold it in place.  This is such a poorly designed/engineered tool that it should be pulled before someone gets seriously injured.
justification: The incident involved a tool failure that could have caused injury but did not, and reviews indicate this is a common issue.

incident_description: My Kenmore Oasis Elite washing machine began to experience unbalanced loads on EVERY load no matter the contents.  The machine has violently moved excessively causing damage to the washer, dryer and the floor.  Also I tried to stop it from moving into the dryer getting my hand hurt between the two units.
justification: The description reports physical injury ('getting my hand hurt') and repeated incidents ('EVERY load'), indicating both injury severity and high likelihood of recurrence.

incident_description: During routine routing the operator, [REDACTED], accidentally touched the router bit to the router power cord, partially cutting into the cord and was consequently shocked thru the handles. He dropped the router but was not otherwise injured and recovered without further incident.
justification: The operator was shocked but not seriously injured, indicating a moderate severity level. The incident was not rare but also not highly frequent.

incident_description: I purchased my current home in August 2009 from the original builder. The home was built in 2006. The roof is covered with Tamko Lamarite Slate Composite shingles. Over the past couple years, sections of shingles have started to crack and fall off the roof into my and my neighbors yard. These sections are typically up to a foot long by 7 to 8 inches wide. This does not appear to be an intallation issues since the cracks typically occur away from the nailed attachment area. When they break, they fall the 20 to 30 feet to the ground at a high rate of speed. Although they are not excessively heavy, their size, speed and configuration make it very dangerous to people below. My neighbor recently returned a section of one shingle that sailed into his yard. Given the number of children, including my own, who play in our yard - I'm very concerned about what would happen if the edge of shingle hit one of them. These shingles are thin and rigid with edges shaped like rough slate. I notified Tamko of the issue. They informed me that their  50 year warranty did not cover me since the builder lived in the house for three years while he was trying to sell it. Evidently the warranty cannot be transferred to a subsequent owner after two years - even if the house is bought directly from the Builder! Tamko has refused to consider any form of resolution. I have contacted a roofer about repairing the 10 to 12 shingles that have broken to date - and have been informed that other shingles are damaged and close to failure as well. I fear this condition will continue to get worse and continue for years unless properly addressed now. Given the cost of these shingles (~ $23,000 for just the shingles) - I had a higher expectation for quality and safety.
justification: The incident involves shingles falling at high speed, posing a danger to people below, especially children, though no injuries have been reported yet.

incident_description:
Our Harbor Breeze ceiling fan was installed by a professional electrician in September 2012 (purchased August 2012), but has not been used very often (it has maybe been on between 10 and 20 times total), because the nursery was not in use until our baby was born and sleeping in his own room, and the fan was not needed during the winter.  The fan/light is connected to a wall switch which controls the light, and the fan speed is controlled with a pull chain.  The fan and light have worked well since installation, with no noise or wobbling when the fan was in use.

Late in the evening on June 25, 2014, I went to my infant son's nursery to prepare the room for the night by turning on the monitor and turning on the fan.  Because my son had fallen asleep in another room, I went upstairs without him in my arms, which is normally not the case, so I could turn the light/fan on, then turn the light off with the pull chain to avoid waking him with the bright light.  With the light still on, I pulled the chain once for the fan, which put it at high speed.  After waiting a second, I pulled the chain again to reduce the fan to medium speed.  With the second pull, the fan, still spinning, can tumbling out of the ceiling onto my head.  I was able to protect my face from the spinning blades and light kit with my hand, and am so grateful I was not holding my son and that he was not in his crib to be hit by the falling debris.  

The fan stayed connected to the electric wires in the ceiling, but I was able to turn the wall switch off and eventually prop the ceiling fan on a ladder until an electrician could come to remove it.  We found the metal mounting bracket had snapped and a piece of it was on the floor.  Our electrician said he had never seen anything like it in 30 years.  I called the company and they said they would send a replacement part.  I asked if there were any recalls for this, as a newish fan should not have parts that break in such a dangerous way.  I was told no and that it is often because electricians use old mounting brackets when installing new fans.  I can attest this was NOT the case for us, as I was present for the installation and know all parts were new and from the fan box.  I told the customer services representative that we were lucky there were no more serious injuries than the very minor injury to my finger when deflecting the falling fan and encouraged them to investigate the mounting bracket.  To date, I have not been contacted for further information.
justification: The incident resulted in a minor injury to the finger when deflecting the falling fan, and the fan's mounting bracket failure is described as extremely rare by the electrician.

incident_description: I own the Shark Steam Pocket Mop and a few weeks ago it malfunctioned and the steam came out of  the side of the mop where it should NOT of come from, resulting in the burning of my hand. I also searched the internet and found several similar stories just like mine.
justification: The incident resulted in a hand burn, indicating an injury, and similar incidents have been reported online, suggesting it is likely to occur.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that she received a dehumidifier as a gift and approximately 2 years ago she started to experience problems with it. The consumer stated that she had it set on auto and decided to switch it to turn on and off for 4 hours and it started to overheat. The consumer stated that the unit was becoming extremely hot.  The consumer stated that the cord became really hot and the surge protector would trip when the dehumidifier would over heat. 

The consumer stated that no one was injured. 

The consumer stated that she believes that this product should be investigated due to the fire hazard that it poses to consumers. 

The consumer stated that she would be contacting the manufacturer to file a report.
justification: The incident involved overheating and a potential fire hazard, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description:
In November 2012, I replaced all 6 hard wired smoke alarms in my house with Kidde PI 2010. 

December 2013 one of the units alarm started sounding off.  Tried spraying with compressed air with no luck.  Amazon would not accept return so I purchased another unit.  In February 2014 other units started sounding their alarms with no specific cause.

I contacted Kidde, they then shipped out 6 replacement units plus a free shipping form.

This morning, July 1 one of the units started going off at 6AM.  I detached the unit from our bedroom ceiling.

I will again contact Kidde, but my concern is for the safety of my family and those who may just disconnect their alarms and not get around to replacing them.

Thank you,
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involves smoke alarms malfunctioning without causing injury or death, but poses a potential safety risk if not addressed.

incident_description:
This is regarding a Generac Guardian 10 Kw air-cooled standby generator model 040794 serial # 3210726 installed professionally 1/18/2001.  The battery exploded when the unit was attempting to start automatically for the weekly "exercise cycle" on 6/30/2014.  This has happened a total of 3 times.  The original, unbranded generic battery supplied by the installers exploded 5/19/2003.  I replaced it with a reputable name brand auto battery.  That lasted until I replaced it with another name-brand auto battery 7/7/2007.  That battery exploded 7/25/2010, and I replaced it with yet another, different name-brand auto battery.  That battery exploded 6/30/2014.  
When I reported the problem originally to Generac in 2003, Generac denied any responsibility (as did the installers) and  told me to pursue any complaint with the battery manufacturer, which of course I could not do since the original battery supplied by the installers was unbranded.
The subsequent 2 explosions have involved name brand auto batteries, and so I suspect there is NOT a battery problem but a design flaw in the battery charging circuit of the generator.  This causes  overcharging of the batteries, loss of electrolyte (boiling out), leading to exposure of the internal plates, and an internal arc under load when the unit attempts to start, leading to explosion of the hydrogen gas in the battery, destruction of the battery, showering of the internal generator cabinet and components with acid and battery case shrapnel.
This is a serious problem with the potential for serious injury (blindness, acid burns, shrapnel injury) if I had the cabinet open to manually start the engine (which I had just the week before) and of course the accelerated corrosion of the internal metallic components due to the acid.
I propose that Generac redesign and replace the battery charging circuit of the generator at their expense.
justification: The incident involves repeated battery explosions causing potential for serious injury, though no injuries are reported.

incident_description: General Electric Clothes Iron Model 898693 Series A2221DA Made for Walmart internal wiring burned through the back hard plastic cover of the iron (i.e., the base the iron when standing up, the back of the iron when ironing) with two exposed copper wires showing through the melted hard plastic. No damage to the exterior cord.  Did not trip home circuit breaker. No previous maintenance, disassembly, or other mistreatment of the iron occurred.
justification: The incident involved internal wiring burning through the plastic cover, exposing wires, but no injury or damage beyond the iron itself occurred.

incident_description: A recalled Homelite Pressure washer exploded striking left leg, causing blunt trauma, lacerations and broken bones.
justification: The pressure washer explosion caused blunt trauma, lacerations, and broken bones, indicating a significant injury.

incident_description:
03/29/2014- The consumer stated that the heater was located in her bathroom. Her husband set the heater in setting  number 5 or 6 prior to taking a shower. Approximately, 10 minutes later the consumer's husband heard a popping sound, he noticed a 3/4 inch wide 4 inch high flame emanating from the right side of the heater. Immediately, he turned it off and blew air towards the flame to extinguish it. After the flame was extinguished, the consumers shut the circuit breaker off, he contacted the contractor. The contractor indicated that the heater did not turn off by itself when the fire started.  The contractor removed the heater from the wall. No other injuries or property damage was reported.

incident_description:
My mother in law, age 84, has a Bryant T6 programmable thermostat in her home. She was able to enter the thermostat's SYSTEM CONFIGURATION MODE by pressing the FAN button for several seconds and then changed the configuration with an UP or DOWN arrow.  No technician level passcode was needed and no confirmation of changes was required. The thermostat automatically saved any change made...and also automatically saved any changes when the 3 minute timeout was reached.  
The changes to the SYSTEM CONFIGURATION were not reflected in the readout on the thermostat (in this incident the thermostat still reported being in Cooling Mode....but heat was actually being sent to the house).  In this example the thermostat did not have a maximum temperature to shut down the system....due to the thermostat being in cooling mode.

In plain English: My mother in law wanted to increase the fan speed...held down the fan button and pressed the UP arrow several times.  She had no idea that she had changed the output.  

The result:  She suffered a heart attack, was found unconscious on a floor, 911 was called, the police officer responding reported that the interior temperature was 95F/interior walls were hot/thermostat was in cooling mode...but house was heating up.    

The publicly available owner's manual does not mention System Configuration or specifically mention the FAN button as the access to System Configuration.  
The Byrant installer/technician manual clearly spells out System Configuration on pages 26-27 of that manual.

On June 5, 2014 the Lincoln NE Bryant Dealer answered a service call (I reported that my mother in law was hospitalized and the system was not functioning normally).  [REDACTED], the service manager, diagnosed the following:  "Found the configuration setting was on A/C instead of HP.  This is the first setting that can be changed if you accidentally enter configuration mode. Set to HP and checked operation it is working properly."
justification: The incident resulted in a heart attack and hospitalization due to incorrect thermostat configuration, indicating a severe outcome. The likelihood is unlikely as it requires specific user actions and lack of awareness.

incident_description: I own Samsung Washing Machine Model WA422PRHDWR/AA purchased 3/5/2013.  On 6/14/2014 it experienced a sudden failure of an assembly associated with the drain pump.  On this model and several other Samsungs from the 2012 and 2013 time frame the drain pump was attached to the drum in a plastic housing.  It appears this was a serious design flaw since the plastic housing is subject to intense stress and failure is inevitable.  Samsung came to recognize the flaw in early 2013 and relocated the drain pump assembly to the frame both in newer models and as a retrofit to the original design.  In my case the pump broke loose in the final 3 minutes of the final spin so only a gallon or so of water spilled out.  I have read other accounts of similar failures earlier on the wash or rinse cycle that resulted in enough water spillage to cause damage to flooring, walls and fixtures in excess of $17000.  I believe the failure mode of this flawed design is dangerous to consumers.   Water and electricity don't mix, and when the pump breaks loose water in the drum goes in many unsafe directions, both within the washing machine and within the consumers laundry room.  In addition to reports of damage to property there was at least one consumer who found subsequent black mold after making repairs.  I feel lucky I had no water damage, but I'm sure there is significant danger associated with this flawed design which will fail suddenly and catastrophically.  Samsung issued 2 Service Bulletins soon after the flaw was recognized by them.  Those Service Bulletins (Number ASC20130509001 and ASC20130222001) are now very difficult to find on the internet, presumably because the risk managers at Samsung want to hide any smoking guns.  I know CPSC's primary interest is consumer safety, and at first blush this flawed and defective design often will only result in inconvenience and cost to the consumer like it did in my case.  When my pump broke there was no injury and loss of life.  However, I believe with the suddenness of these failures and the mixing of water and electrical and electronic components it is inevitable there eventually will be reports of death or injury if there haven't been already.  I ask that you look into this and note the many similar accounts to mine that can be found on the internet.  I ask that you make Samsung come clean about this dangerous problem and protect the public by performing a recall to safely retrofit the flawed design.
justification: The incident describes a design flaw causing property damage but no reported injuries or deaths, with a high likelihood of occurrence based on multiple accounts.

incident_description:
During 2007-08 we undertook a substantial renovation of an early 19th Century House in Easton, Maryland on Maryland's Eastern Shore. In the process, during the summer of 2008, we paid our contractor (Accent General Contracting, Inc., a reputable General Contractor) $24,000 to arrange for and supervise the installation of high quality frameless glass shower enclosures and doors in all of our main baths -- the master bath on the second floor the guest bath on that floor and the third-floor bath. Accent and/or its sub-contractor selected Century products as being the most suitable. Last Sunday, May 4, 2014, my wife and I were having coffee in the dining room downstairs when we heard of massive explosion, followed by a very loud crash. The explosion sounded much like a hand grenade going off upstairs and the crash sounded like an armoire falling over onto the floor. After a moment of surprise and extreme puzzlement, I went upstairs expecting the worst and hoping for the best. I did not immediately see anything. Somewhat to my surprise, I did not see any sign of smoke or
explosion, and I did not smell anything like the residue of an explosion. After looking in the bedrooms and my study, I looked into the second floor guest bath and was shocked to see literally millions of shards of glass strewn over the floor both inside and outside the shower enclosure. My wife and I were truly thunderstruck. We wondered how a piece of glass could build up enough energy and force quite literally to blow itself to smithereens. We wondered what would happen if we or a guest or a grandchild had been in the shower when the door exploded. We did find the Century logo on the unexploded doors and panels and took a picture, a copy of which is attached. We also took the attached pictures of the second floor bath that shows the shards of glass everywhere. I also attach for your comparison some pictures of the master bath enclosure and also of the enclosure in the third-floor bath. It did not take us but a few minutes on the internet to discover that this problem has been floating around with Century products for more than a decade, since at least 2002. See this link. http://www.consumeraffairs.com/homeowners/century.html. In the circumstances, we expect Century to take responsibility directly or indirectly for arranging to swap out all of the potentially exploding glass in our bathrooms for similar doors and enclosures that are not capable of potentially fatal (and in any event unbelievably dangerous) spontaneous explosion.While the second floor bathroom is used only periodically, it is used by us, our children, our
grandchildren from time to time, as well as by visitors or house sitters. Given the potentially catastrophic nature of the injury that could be caused by the sort of spontaneous explosion, we have reported the entire incident to the CPSC (Consumer Product Safety Commission) in Washington, D.C, where I work as the Managing Partner of my D.C. law office. We have
left the affected bathroom completely intact so that the bathroom itself and the millions of shards of glass are just as we found them shortly after the explosion. The CPSC is sufficiently interested to send a person to our property early in the upcoming week to take pictures, to interview us, and otherwise to investigate the entire situation. Let me know if you
are interested in having a representative present. In any case, we will preserve the scene of the explosion for as long as might be practicable if you are interested in seeing it. We would very much like to know at your earliest convenience how you intend to proceed to repair the exploded door and also to replace any and all of the remaining doors and enclosures with glass that, perhaps like automobile windshield glass, contains a clear membrane or other protection that would prevent spontaneous explosion of the glass. We look forward to hearing from you. My contact details are set forth below.


Response:
Please accept my sincere apology on behalf of Century for this most unfortunate and upsetting experience that you had with your shower enclosure; we are thankful that no one was hurt. Century is regarded as one of the leading manufacturers in
the industry and produces thousands of shower and tub doors with minimal occurrence of glass breaking without obvious cause. The complaints which are mentioned in your letter are misleading and refer to [REDACTED], a manufacturer located on the west coast with no ties to Century Bathworks . Our doors are sold primarily in the Northeast and as far west
as Chicago, the majority of these complaints have taken place on the west coast. Our safety tempered glass is produced in accordance with accepted industry standards and we are confident that our products will perform as intended. Our enclosures are designed to function properly and efficiently with minimum maintenance. The enclosure that was sold to you was neither defective nor damaged and was manufactured to the specifications given. If you were to ask eight different people what causes spontaneous breakage of tempered glass you would get eight different answers. The various opinions and misconceptions about spontaneous breakage baffle many in the glass industry. The most commonly discussed is a nickel sulfide stone, this type of inclusion actually occurs very rarely. While nickel sulfide breaks are extremely rare itÃÂs still very helpful to understand; how spontaneous breakage due to nickel sulfide can sometimes occur. When glass goes through the tempering process, it becomes four to five times stronger than standard annealed glass, making it great from a safety perspective. However, nickel sulfide stones that can form during the production of float glass due to nickel contamination, can end up in the center tension zone of tempered glass. When that piece of tempered glass is later exposed to varying temperatures in its final installed position, this tiny stone may grow in size, and cause the glass to shatter for no apparent reason. While nickel sulfide stone is one potential reason for spontaneous glass breakage, there is almost always a more common explanation, such as glass edge or surface damage from handling and glazing, building or framing system movement. Given the length of time, six years of operating properly in your home we are led to believe that the glass had been compromised in some way causing stress and subsequently causing it to shatter. Century has been in business for over 50 years and we take pride in manufacturing a quality product using only the best material in our enclosures. As seen in the attached pictures, the glass broke into hundreds of small blunt particles which by design is excellent proof of a well tempered product. This is a foolproof characteristic of tempered glass which makes it an excellent product for safety glazing applications. For those applications, such as glass in doors, tub and shower enclosures and fixed glass in close proximity to a walking surface, fully tempered safety glass is required by building codes and ordinances. In closing, the glass used in a car windshield as you suggested cannot be used in a frameless shower door application. Edges cannot be highly polished, the plastic interlayer is visible and esthetically unattractive. The glass cannot be easily fabricated, i.e. handle holes and notches will cause glass to crack due to stress factors during the operation of the doors. As a courtesy, Century has agreed to replace the door and other glass which may have been damaged as a result of the door breaking with a minimal charge. If this is acceptable to you, please contact me.
justification: The incident involved a glass shower door exploding, causing significant damage but no injuries, and the manufacturer claims such occurrences are rare.

incident_description:
Generac Automatic standby generator 10 KW model 004916-0.  Generator start battery blew up, fortunately there was no collateral damage or injuries.

The cause of the explosion excessive charging voltage.  Lead acid batteries should charge at about 13.5 volts.  The charger on this unit provides 14 volts DC.   

When lead acid batteries were not sealed, this was not a huge problem, as water could be periodically added to low cells in order to compensate for slight overcharging.  Now because of current safety regulations, batteries are sealed and they will eventually explode if overcharged.

A search of the web shows that this is a common problem for some Generac  generators.
justification: The incident involved a battery explosion with no injuries or collateral damage, and it is described as a common problem for some Generac generators.

incident_description:
Caller purchased her hot tub spa March 19th, 2012 and had no problems with it until March 5th, 2014.
The tub is set at 98 degrees when not in use.

March 5th, 2014 the callers husband was preparing to get in the hot tub and set the water temperature from 98 to 101 degrees.

Once the hot tub read 101 degrees he got in,  turned the jets on but then got out within ten minutes stating that the water felt extremely hot.
The caller's husband had just returned from Florida so it was assumed that his body temperature was confused.

March 6th, 2014 the temperature was at 98, the caller's husband and son left this temperature at 98 and got into the hot tub.
Neither the husband or son was in the water any more than ten minutes before they got out and the husband stated again that it was extremely hot.

One cycle is 20 minutes before the hot tub shuts off, the husband normally goes in for two cycles and the son usually completes one cycle unless he is feeling exceptionally well, then he will complete two cycles.

After these two incidents the caller's husband purchased a standalone thermometer.
The thermometer read 108 after being in the tub for a few minutes but the temperature setting was at 98.

The owners manual for the hot tubs reads that the water should never reach over 104 and that any time the water temperature reaches 2 degrees above the set temperature that the circulation pump will stop working to reduce the temperature.

The caller states that this is a therapeutic tub and was purchased for the quality and functions that it produces because her husband has back issues and her son has cerebral palsy.
This is not a medical spa hot tub, was not purchased from a medical supply source but was purchased by the consumer for these purposes.

She believes that this rising in water temperature could be extremely dangerous

She contacted a contractor March 7th, 2014, he replaced the temperature sensor at callers expense at $98.20 after testing the water with the cover half off and obtaining a temperature of 107 with the setting at 98.

She will file reports to Consumer Protection regarding the company but is asking that this hot tub become recalled for the safety of the public.

There are no injuries being reported

She contacted the manufacturer on March 10th, 2014 and was advised by [REDACTED] that he was taking her information and would escalate it up then call her. 

March 17th, 2014 the caller contacted [REDACTED]  at the manufacturers because she had been advised she would receive  return call and she had not.

She spoke again with [REDACTED] who questioned her regarding the temperature fluctuation as well as the circulation  pump not stopping and he advised her that she is in the "Gray area" and that the hot tub would have turned off 112 degrees.

He offered her filters for the hot tub when she asked to be refunded after repeating that a 108 degree reading is
justification: No injuries were reported, but the hot tub's temperature malfunction poses a potential safety risk.

He was transported by ambulance to the hospital for open reduction internal fixation of left tibia fracture (fractured left tibia & fibula below the knee & left tibia above the ankle- he has a rod & three screws). In addition, he has numerous bumps and bruises as well as severe back pain which may be attributed to fractured ribs. He was discharged from the hospital on April 17, 2014. He is non-weight bearing for a minimum of 6 weeks postoperatively and unable to work.  The attic ladder is a Werner SS210 Mk 2 rated for 300 lbs. My husband weighs 235 pounds. The ladder folds into thirds up into the ceiling. The bottom third of the ladder complete broke away/off the ladder when the hinges broke while my husband was ascending the ladder. The hinges on the middle section of ladder broke as well; however it still hung precariously by two straps. I had a friend cut off the dangling middle section of the ladder so that no one would be further hurt by it.  From information obtained from the internet it appears that the pot metal hinges on this ladder are known to break; however no recall has been issued. These ladders are extremely dangerous and should have been recalled. 

I have photos of the defective product and my husband's injuries; however your website will not allow me to upload them.

incident_description:
I purchased a Ardisam E43 single-user auger in 2011 (Manufacture date of 2010, purchased August 2011) to dig several 3 foot deep post holes.  The "Viper" engine is powerful, but the controls for the engine are not robust.

Major:  Since initial purchase, the throttle has intermittently "stuck" in the full power position.  At first I could simply release and re-squeeze the throttle to unstick the mechanism.  During use in 2012, I had to switch off the unit with the electric "On/Off" switch to get the unit to stop.  After that experience the unit performed as before with mild stickling.  I cleaned the throttle at that time and periodically since then.  I serviced the auger to use it for the 2014 season.  I had previously stored the unit, but made sure the components were properly drained and/or lubricated for storage.  I re-lubricated the components, including cleaning the throttle, before fueling and attempting to start.  Upon starting the unit, the throttle stuck in the full power position and this time got away from me.  I ultimately had to knock the gas filler cap off with a sledge hammer while the unit spun on the ground.  The unit stopped when the fuel ran out.  

Minor:  After digging the first two holes, on the third hole the spring in the pull-start mechanism snapped.  I had to later order a replacement spring.  The second assembly also broke - this time the end of the spring assembly that attaches to the rope pull had broken.  I disassembled the mechanism and retied the rope to the end of the spring which I had to bend to catch the end of the rope.  The pull length was slightly shorter, but the mechanism has not broken since I made this modification.  

We have numerous power tools, including gas-fed units.  We have never experienced the issues we did with the Ardisam E43 auger.
justification: The throttle sticking in the full power position led to a dangerous situation requiring extreme measures to stop the unit, indicating potential for injury. The issue occurred multiple times, suggesting a possible likelihood.

incident_description:
I am writing to you to respectfully request your assistance in a matter that affects all New York State residents. I have worked as a surveyor for many years. In 2010 I became totally disabled due to COPD and am currently going through testing necessary for being put on the lung transplant list. I recently bought a container of [REDACTED]Marking Chalk and found a warning label on the container that concerned me in reference to my illness. I believe it is a contributing factor to my illness and in fact is what has caused my illness to progress as rapidly as it did. 
The [REDACTED] container states: "Wear appropriate safety items including eye goggles. Avoid inhalation of product as it contains silicone dioxide which may be injurious to your health. Keep out of reach of children. Warning: May cause lung, skin, or eye irritation. MSDS available upon request." 
From 2002 through 2010 I used a product called ProChalk manufactured by Keson Industries, Inc. located in Illinois. I have a container of Keson's chalk from when I was still working. The only caution on the container reads: "Red & Yellow chalks are permanent colors. There is no none way to remove them. Use accordingly." There is nothing on the label to indicate any possible health risks. I recently bought a new container of Keson's chalk with a redesigned label. The warning on this new label states: "Chalk can permanently color some surfaces. Please use accordingly. Keep out of reach of children. Always wear appropriate eye precaution. This product contains chemicals known to the State of California to cause cancer and other reproductive problems." 
There are no MSDS' (Material Safety Data Sheet) with the containers even when they are purchased by the case. I was able to obtain oneÃÂ dated January 1, 2013 by going on-line. There is no concentration listed of the principal components: Iron Oxide, Calcium Carbonate, and Silicon Dioxide. Under Health Hazard is a comment that "two of the ingredients, Calcium Carbonate and Iron Oxide contain crystalline silica at levels between .01 and 2%. There is some evidence that this material may be carcinogenic. Limit exposure to the lowest limit possible." Under Emergency First Aid Procedures for inhalation it states: "Remove victim from dust area to fresh air. Give artificial respiration if not breathing. Call a physician." 
Under Special Protection Information it states "Respiratory Protection: An approved NIOSH respiratory should be worn when TWA limits are exceeded. Ventilation: Use local ventilation to keep dust levels below recommended exposure limits. If exposure limits are exceeded, a NIOSH approved respirator for mineral dust should be worn. Protective clothing: Employees must wear gloves. Eye protection: Chemical safety goggles or safety glasses with splash guards." There is no mention of what the exposure limits are. TWA I have found out stands for Time Weighted Average Exposure-15 minutes. I used this product for well beyond that time frame sometimes for several hours at a time. Many days I came home with my clothing totally covered with the dust from the chalk. I was able to compare the MSDS from Keson Industries with one for marking chalk manufactured by [REDACTED] Products. While Keson's MSDS is only two pages, [REDACTED]'s MSDS is 10 pages long. The [REDACTED] MSDS was prepared December 11, 2007 and revised on July 29, 2010. Clearly the Keson MSDS should have the same information regarding the Crystalline Silica used in their product. [REDACTED]'s MSDS clearly states that a concentration of just .1 to 1.5% of Crystalline Silica is harmful. The Emergency Overview on the MSDS states: "Product Description: These products are colored, finely powdered, odorless chalks. Health Hazards: Inhalation of dusts from this product may irritate the respiratory system. Skin and eye contact may cause mechanical abrasion. These chalks contain Crystalline Silica, a known human carcinogen by inhalation." 
They have the labeling statement included on their MSDS: "CAUTION! MAY CAUSE EYE AND RESPIRATORY TRACT IRRITATION. CONTAINS CRYSTALLINE SILICA, WHICH IS A KNOWN HUMAN CARCINOGEN; CONTAINS CARBON BLACK, WHICH IS A KNOWN ANIMAL CARCINOGEN. INGESTION MAY BE HARMFUL. Avoid breathing dusts. Avoid contact with skin, eyes, and clothing. Keep container closed. Use with adequate ventilation. Prevent dust accumulation. Wash hands thoroughly after handling. Wear gloves, goggles, dust mask, and appropriate body protection during operations that can generate dust." 
Under Section 7 regarding Work Practices and Hygiene Practices the MSDS states in part: "As with all chemicals, avoid getting this product ON YOU or IN YOU. Wash thoroughly after handling this product. Do not eat, drink, smoke, or apply cosmetics while handling this product. Avoid breathing airborne dusts generated by this product. Use in a well-ventilated location. Ensure this substance is used with adequate ventilation and personal protective equipment (see sec 8 ... ). Avoid airborne dusts generated by this product. 
The respiratory protection required for concentrations up to 1.25 mg/m3 of Crystalline Silica is any powered air purifying respirator with a high efficiency particulate filter or any supplied air respirator operated in a continuous-flow mode. There is additional information under section 11 regarding toxicological information. Under inhalation in part it states : ... chronic exposure to concentrations of silicon dioxide fume may cause chronic obstructive lung disease. Inhalation of iron oxide fume or dust is cause of pulmonary roentgenographic appearance called siderosis, or an accumulation of iron that leads to reduced lung capacity. These products contain Crystalline Silica, which is a known human carcinogen. Chronic inhalation exposure to this material may cause silicosis, pulmonary fibrosis, bronchitis or present a hazard of cancer, due to the presence of Crystalline Silica." 
My next step was to access the Occupational safety and Health Administration (OSHA) website. OSHA's Hazard Communication standard (HCS) 29 CFR 1910.1200 specifically, section (f) requires that the chemical manufacturer, importer, or other responsible party to label, tag, or mark containers of hazardous chemicals leaving their workplaces with the following information: 
i) Identity of the hazardous chemical(s); 
ii) Appropriate hazard warnings, and 
iii) Name and address of the chemical manufacturer, importer, or other responsible party. The purpose of container labeling is to provide an immediate warning to users of the product of the hazards they may be exposed to and through the identity of the chemical(s) a link to more detailed information available through MSDS' and other sources. 
I was also able to review Appendix D to 1910.1200-Safety Data Sheets (Mandatory). A safety data sheet must contain information specified in Table D.l. I am only a layperson so I don't understand everything listed on this table. I do understand enough that it is very apparent that Keson's MSDS is lacking required information and their label is also severely lacking. If [REDACTED]'s MSDS and label was last updated in 2010 how can Keson's MSDS done in 2013 be missing such important information. 
I made a phone call to OSHA. The gentleman who I was connected to advised me that since I have been out of work over three years there was nothing OSHA could do for me. The gentleman refused to give me his name and when I requested to speak to a supervisor he stated "He is out to lunch." and terminated the call. I have always believed that New York State requires specific labeling on products sold in New York State even if they have been manufactured elsewhere. I am simply trying to find some assistance in correcting what I feel is an injustice to the people of New York and hopefully prevent any other individuals who use this products from developing the same illness' as I have. I have gone very quickly from being a contributing member of society to a totally disabled individual who has to have constant access to oxygen and is facing a double lung transplant. 
I look forward to hearing from you or one of your staff. Thank you in advance for taking your time to read my letter.
justification: The individual has suffered a severe injury (COPD) attributed to prolonged exposure to hazardous materials without adequate warning, leading to disability and the need for a lung transplant.

She contacted the manufacturer/retailer [REDACTED] at [REDACTED] and has surrendered the pillowcase, [REDACTED], charger and pillow to the retailer.

She will be attaching pictures to this report before returning.

There are no injuries to report

incident_description: We had a 2011 GE washing machine model #ptwn8050m0ww and I was washing a load and it went out of balance and instead of automatically stopping it kept going and the tub became unattached and destroyed the washing machine (everything in the inside is broken, the base of the washer is all dented out all the way around and the top is unattached now) and breaking our laundry doors and put two holes in the wall.
