incident_description:
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing this letter to you today to notify you of an almost tragic incident that happened in my home on December 12,2013. I did notify Consumer Reports and they suggested I also send you a copy to be aware of what happened. The Office of the Attorney General was also sent a copy of this letter.

On that date, I was awoken at 6:15am by my alarm clock. When I got up and then went into my kitchen I heard something talking. I went upstairs where there is no bedrooms only a family room to hear our [REDACTED] smoke/carbon monoxide detector warning of carbon monoxide. I was very puzzled on why it was going off and no other ones were in our home considering we have 5 carbon monoxide detectors in our home in
our living area. I figured it was a false alarm so I took another [REDACTED] carbon monoxide detector that was located in the same area and put it where the one going off was and there was nothing so I preceded to go back downstairs and about 2 minutes later that one started to go off. Now I am thinking it is not a false alarm. I called 911 immediately and got the family out. We have 2 first alert carbon monoxide detectors near our bedrooms right outside of our basement door and 1 going up to the family room that never went off
and then 2 [REDACTED] detectors in the family room that did go off which is the farthest point from the carbon monoxide problem.

When the fire department got there I explained what happened. They immediately went into the home down to our basement where our woodstove is. We only burn about 10 times a year if that because our primary source of heat is our pellet stove and electric heat. They were baffled on what went wrong because our stove, stovepipe, etc ... was perfect. We even bad the code enforcement officer there and a certified chimney inspector and they also do not know what happened. To this day, we still do not know what happened but as a parent I will never feel safe if our home again. This is the only place that I can keep my family safe and I was not able to do that.

The fire department found that we had lethal levels of carbon monoxide in our home. Our basement was 170, our first flour was 90 with 3 first alert carbon detectors that did not go off, and our second flour was 80 where the 2 [REDACTED] detectors went off.

We sleep with our bedroom door open due to our dogs that sleep in their but our boys rooms doors are open about 1/2 inch. When rescue got there they checked all of our carbon monoxide levels. My husband and myself were a leve 2. Our 15-year-old son was a 2 but our youngest son who is 11 was a level 9!!!! I asked rescue right away why he is a 9 and why and what does that mean? They said a 9 usually you are going into unconscious state and 12 usually means death. Right away they put him on oxygen for 1-1/2 hours to bring his levels down. Rescue remained outside of our home to do this. They said because he is so much smaller that he absorbed it faster and they breath faster being younger. My 11 year old and 15 year olds bedrooms are right next to each other. About 3 feet apart so I was baffled on how 1 son was so much higher than the other.

The same day I contacted Frist Alert to tell them of the issue. They took my information. They asked if I changed the batteries which I did on December 1st, 2013. I am very faithful on changing the batteries 2 times a year and I test them after I do this and also throughout the year. They offered to send me new detectors but I declined that offer. How could I put first alert into my home again when it failed when I needed them the most? Like I said earlier, it is the only place I can keep my family safe and thought I had control of it. I then contacted [REDACTED] to thank them for saving my families life. If it was not for them this could have been catastrophic to my family. A few days later I had a very nice man contact me from [REDACTED] and told me he was happy to hear that there alarms saved my families life. They thanked me for contacting them and they said they would like to offer to help us out and replace it with some of theirs. I thought that was very generous. They sent us a variation of 5 new ones. I still did not feel safe with this so I went out and purchased more. We now have 11 carbon monoxide detectors and 18 smoke detectors. You are probably thinking overkill but who would of thought having 5
carbon monoxide detectors would not be enough or for that matter having a brand that I can no longer trust and never will !!!! My home is only 1250 square feet so we had more than enough we thought for protection.

You might be wondering why I am just writing this letter. I should of done it awhile ago but it has been very hard for myself to get over this almost tragedy. I have had a lot of problems with stress, anxiety and sleeping problems. I cried for many days and still do at times thinking how thankful I am for my sons guardian angel that day. I cannot tell you what it feels like to be a mom and almost loss her son. My family is my world and I depended on First Alert to keep my family safe and it did not. [REDACTED] is the one I can count on. I am now doing better with each day but will never feel like safe in my home like I use to. We still use our pellet stove so the fear will always be there.

What my goal is to bring you aware of the issue with first alerts model that I feel needs to be recalled being model #SC05. These were new detectors that were purchased recently within the last 2 years but had older dates on them. You do not know the dates until you get home to open the packages. Also, the public was just made aware of the dates recently with the news. I feel all dates should be on the outside of the packages like
batteries have them. You should not have to get home to see the dates. I would like that to also be considered in the future on all fire/carbon monoxide detectors.

The models of carbon monoxide that did not go off are listed below. One of them was an older model and 2 of them were the newer ones with the same model. They are listed below.

7/21/2008- #3055574, Model #SCOS, Made in Mexico N04-3073-049

1/6/2011- #3055574, Model #SCOS, Made in Mexico N04-3073-054

Model #FCD3, Issue # A TS83285, Made in Mexico N04-3018-002

I am asking that you please check into this matter. The model # that concerns me is the SC05. The model FCD3 is an older model. I hope if anything good comes out of this almost tragedy is that other families will never have to go through what we have had to. I will unfortunately always live in fear as a result of this incident. How many other detectors out there are not providing the safety that we put our trust into.

I look forward to hearing back from you and what you are able to do for the families that put trust into First Alert. Thank you for your time and consideration into this matter.

Sincerely
justification: The incident involved lethal levels of carbon monoxide, with one child reaching a near-fatal level (9) and requiring oxygen treatment, indicating significant injury.

incident_description:
The Craftsman 10 inch Table Saw, MODEL 315.218050 failed while in use..  This is a home saw, and not used professionally.  I feel the failure was dangerous and that the switch is defective.  The switch is part 089110101701 and on replacement appeared to be cheaply made.

The issue is that the switch failed while in the on position preventing me from turning off the saw.  I had to go pull out the plug while the saw remained running.   This is dangerous.  The switch appeared to be cheaply made.

On an item such as a saw, any failure should shut the system down.
justification: The switch failure prevented the saw from being turned off, creating a dangerous situation, but no injury occurred.

incident_description:
Several weeks ago, I washed my clothes immediately after one of my housemates had used Clorox Greenworks 96%.  I ended up with significant inflammation on my back that looked like an allergic reaction, but didn't respond to antihistamines or other typical allergy treatments.  I made the mistake of not throwing out the detergent (but warning all of my housemates not to use it.)  On 4-26-2014, I washed my clothes again, apparently immediately after a houseguest had unknowningly used the greenworks detergent.

All of my skin that was exposed to clothing washed in that batch broke out, severely.  After several days, although OTC topical hydrocortisone had helped reduce the inflammation (it didn't react to antihistamines or other typical medications used to treat IgE mediated allergic reactions,) I ended up going to an urgent care clinic today after several of the lesions began to blister (including one on my penile head.)  They prescribed oral prednisone, a strong topical steroid, and [REDACTED] to deal with the pain of the blistering, and described it as a likely chemical burn.

I've began to follow up with Clorox but given that other anecdotal reports of similar reactions appear on the internet, decided it was a necessary thing to submit a report here as well. The exact product in question is Clorox Greenworks laundry detergent marked as 2x concentrated, in a 162 fluid ounce size. The UPC is 44600-30364.  It also has what I presume to be a batch number stamped above the Greenworks logo on the back which reads KC23041143.

I have previously suffered minor reactions to artificial dyes used in margarita mixes and suffered minor reactions to certain detergents when I was under 12 (more than 13 years ago,) but other than that have no record of allergies of this nature.
justification: The incident resulted in severe skin inflammation and blistering requiring medical treatment, indicating an injury.

incident_description: White Rodgers thermostat had to be replaced after the batteries corroded and shorted out the thermostat.  The device was registering the wrong room temperature causing the air conditioner to continue to run and not turn off.
justification: The incident involved equipment failure (thermostat malfunction) but no injury or death occurred, warranting a severity level of 2. The likelihood is possible (3) as battery corrosion leading to thermostat failure is a known but not extremely common issue.

incident_description: My American Standard heating and air unit motor caught fire the motor has been replaced a few years back bought unit in 2008 had motor go out this is the 3 one put in the first one just went out this one caught fire Thankfully fire stayed in unit and only smoke and elect fire smell came in house no one got hurt
justification: The motor caught fire but no one was injured, and the fire was contained within the unit.

incident_description: 3 years ago, we purchased a Sterling glass shower door with pebbled privacy glass from Lowe's Home Improvement store (model #1505D-36N).  We installed it in our new bathroom.  About 1 month after we installed it, we found that the glass from the entire door had shattered into hundreds of pieces everywhere in the bathroom.  There was no incident that caused the door to shatter, i.e. it was not caused by us.  We took the door back to Lowe's and they agreed to give us a replacement door.  We cleaned up the mess and reinstalled the door.  3 years later (today), I came home to find the door shattered once again.  This is more than a safety "concern", it is an outright dangerous product.  Luckily, no one was in the bathroom either time the door shattered so no one has been injured, but it definitely would have caused serious injury had someone been in the shower at the time.  We are now financially injured as we have to purchase a replacement door.  We will also have to clean up a significant mess and reinstall yet another door.  I do not want anyone else to be injured by such a clearly defective and unsafe product.
justification: The glass door shattered twice without causing injury, but poses a serious injury risk if someone is present during shattering.

incident_description:
I would like to report a faulty glue gun by the company AD TECH. The type is the Hi Temp, 40 Watt model.
     I need to use a glue gun for my work. This is the FOURTH  Ad Tech glue gun I've had that has shorted out and caught on fire, over a span of about 3 years. 
I leave the glue gun plugged in for about an hour at a time, and I always use the proper glue sticks. Nowhere on the package insert does it say how long of a time to leave the gun plugged in, so I assume this is alright. 
    After a few weeks of usage, I notice  a pattern. There is a black rubber piece inside the gun, which keeps the glue  stick away from the heating element inside. Over time, this piece begins to weaken, and when it finally breaks, the hot glue touches the inner heating element, which results in an electrical shortage. I have always been right next to the gun when this happens, and it trips the breaker every time, and I've noticed a burst of flame appear from the gun. 
     Whenever this happens, I always need to buy a replacement glue gun, and unfortunately, the nearest store only carries Ad Tech guns. This is why I've witnessed FOUR glue gun failures, because I'm stuck buying the same brand. The only other store that carries glue guns is one hour away. I would like to add that I have gone through probably 8-10 guns in the past 3 years, but not all of them resulted in an electrical shortage. Only four have done this, but the rest begin to have the same problems, with glue jamming, and I usually just throw them away before they finally break and catch fire. 
   These glue guns are a faulty, dangerous product, and I do believe they should be recalled.
justification: The glue gun has shorted out and caught fire multiple times, but no injuries have been reported.

incident_description:
Gas dryer, purchased in 2010, with significant gas smell when operating as well as a couple incidents of clothes scorching inside the dryer.

Make: LG
Model: DLG1320W
S/N: 905KWPV00296

I called LG around 4/25 to report the issue.  There was a recall in 2012 on this same dryer (http://www.cpsc.gov/en/Recalls/2012/LG-Electronics-and-Sears-Recall-Gas-Dryers-For-Repair-Due-to-Fire-Hazard/) However, LG support ran the s/n and reported that my dryer was not covered and that to fixing it would be up to me to pay for.  On 4/29, we had a repair man diagnose and fix the dryer, and the issue was due to a faulty gas valve not regulating/closing when it was supposed to (the same issue in the recall).  The repairman left the faulty gas valve with me in case I need to send it somewhere for investigation.

I can understand that as appliances age, there will be issues that need fixing. However, since we're dealing with Natural Gas in this case, appliances should not fail in regards to regulating gas as it could result in a catastrophic injury (or worse).
justification: The incident involved a faulty gas valve that could have led to a fire hazard, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description: I bought a Smartek USA handheld steamer, and the second time I used it, the switch malfunctioned...it seemed to melt to the point where I couldn't turn it on or off. I finally went to the ER where an x-ray was taken. A stainless steel wire from the grill brush (over 1/2 in long) was lodged in the soft tissue of my throat. I had to go into the OR and be put under general anaesthesia to have the foreign body removed immediately. From what the doctor said, they have seen this before and sometimes with much worse results such as a perforated bowel. I consider myself lucky that it happened to me and not to either of my young children and that I did not swallow the wire completely, potentially injuring me worse.

incident_description:
In mid-2012, we bought a new SAMSUNG top loading washer, model # WA400PJHDWR/AA (Ser. No. Y69Q5AEC703298R) from Lowes in Gainesville, FL for $666.85  Two weeks ago, while washing a load of clothes, we heard a loud clanging sound during the spin cycle, followed by a louder BANGING sound, after which water starting pouring out all over the floor of our utility room and adjoining family room.

We tilted the washer and saw that the drain pump assembly had broken loose from the bottom of the washing machine tub and had detached itself and the accompanying drain hose and was just dangling in mid-air.  The washing machine was now unusable.

I learned from a Lowes call center rep that there were many reports of this same problem with the WA400 model SAMSUNG washers, and that SAMSUNG had issued a RECALL for Lowes-owned store assets (washers still in stock at any Lowes store or warehouse).  However, SAMSUNG did not opt to issue a recall to the general public for the same problem, even though the Lowes rep was aware of 246 cases at that time (mine being #247), and that there were 155,000 affected washers. Also, some consumers had experienced "flooding damage" depending no what part of the cycle the machine was in and where it was located (luckily ours was downstairs and on ceramic tile and at the end of the spin cycle, but in some cases, washers were located upstairs or near hardwood flooring and there was significant flooding damage. Lowes did ask if this was the case for me.) 

So, it was a known defect, known by SAMSUNG and now Lowes.  Since the SAMSUNG washer only has a 1 year warranty, I learned I would be responsible for all repair costs, but not the parts. Armed with this information, I contacted Samsung Customer Service and filed a complaint, asking WHY they had not issued a RECALL of these known defective WA400 washers.  They DENIED that there were 155,000 defective washers, as I had learned from Lowes, or that there was a significant problem, but they offered to pay for the repair cost as a one time courtesy, which I accepted.

The washer was repaired today by the Samsung rep.   A whole new drain pump assembly, including the pump, bracket, hose and wiring harness were installed.  The new pump assembly does not attach to the bottom of the washing machine tub, as the original OEM part did.   I got a look at the SAMSUNG Service Bulletin that the technician had in his  possession, and it was number ASC20131127001 and it listed models WA400, WA422, and WA456 as all being affected by this problem.  So, this reassures me that the quantity of washers affected is quite large.

I have seen several complaints posted online about this same problem.  348 complaints on [REDACTED], and several on [REDACTED] and on LOWES.COM.  All say the same thing - that the drain pump breaks off and floods their home and they are stuck with the repair bill and potential damage to their home.   Electrocution is a possibility as well, as the wiring harness can also come loose when the pump breaks off, so if the washer were to flood an area and an unsuspecting homeowner were to step into the puddle created by the washer, he could possibly get electrocuted from 120 VAC.

I also found online reference to another SAMSUNG service bulletin ASC20130222001 dated June 6, 2013 that says the same thing as the one my technician had in hand.  I found this reference onlin here: [REDACTED].

I posted multiple times on the Samsung Home Appliance [REDACTED] page that they need to issue an IMMEDIATE RECALL of all of these affected units (models WA400, WA422, and WA456), as this problem is potentially hazardous to the property of the homeowner and to life safety.   However, Samsung seems to be handling this on a case-by-case basis.   I did read enough of the service bulletin, and learned from the appliance repair company, that this problem affects the 3 Samsung top loading washers models listed above, manufactured from Jan. 2012 - Dec. 2012.  The design was changed the 2nd week of Dec. 2012, I believe.  Our washer, like thousands of others was manufactured in July 2012, and purchased on Sept. 1 2012.  It is 17 months old.

PLEASE REVIEW THIS SITUATION AND CONTACT SAMSUNG.  My washer is now repaired, but the problem here is that there are THOUSANDS of other newer SAMSUNG washers out there that will very likely fall apart from regular normal use and can flood and damage the consumer's home.  Also, many consumers start a load of wash and then leave to go run errands (as we have done).  We were lucky - we were at home when ours broke apart and started flooding the floor.... Others might not be so lucky.

Ironically, Samsung's corporate model is this: "At Samsung, we follow a simple business philosophy: to devote our talent and technology to creating superior products and services that contribute to a better global society."   Where their washers are concerned, they have fallen far short of this mark!
justification: The incident describes property damage (flooding) and potential electrocution risk, but no actual injuries or deaths reported.

incident_description:
Our new Holmes Space Heater ...ModelHCH18l3M caught fire last night in our family room. It burned inside the unit and melted plastic on the bottom (rug) and in the units mid-section. Since we were there and  pulled the plug immediately, we prevented the fire from spreading. incident_description: I experienced a power outage and the generator came online and performed as it was supposed to.  At ~3am, they restored power, but the generator did not switch off. At the same time my smoke detectors all began to go off.  I went to investigate and found that the transfer switch (Part #C2237) had failed when the power was restored and ignited inside of the panel.  I had to remove the panel cover and put the fire out.  The switch seized in the "Generator on" position and I could not flip the power back to the house service line until the switch was removed.  I disconnected the main service and manually turned the generator to off and then went about removing the failed component.  I went to remove the first wire and it exploded off of the switch as soon as I applied pressure to separate it, this sent sparks and hot metal everywhere.  I was eventually able to remove the part and manually switch the power from the generator back to the main, but now I am left with the remnants of smoke damage in the basement, the failed part, a singed utility box, and several burnt/damaged wires.
justification: The incident involved a fire and equipment damage but no reported injuries, indicating an incident without injury. The likelihood is unlikely as such failures are not common but can occur under specific conditions.

incident_description:
The consumer smelled a plastic burning odor and started searching the house to see where it was coming from. He realized it was coming from the smoke detector. The consumer took the smoke detector down from the wall. The detector was very hot to the touch.  The consumer opened the smoke detectorÃÂs cover. The inside part of the cover was melting. The consumer took the battery out. The battery inside the smoke detector was a manufacturer's brand battery but it did not match the recommended battery specified in the smoke detectorÃÂs label.  The consumer said that the manufacturer's information recommends a specific model of battery, but the one in the smoke detector had a different model.

The consumer called the retailer and he was told that they would only replace the smoke detectors f90 days from date of purchase. The retailer's rep. (name unknown) did not say anything about the smoke detector melting.

On 04-14-2014, wife was using the steam mop and all of a sudden the mop quit working.  The body portion of the mop unit became very hot and stopped working.  I allowed it to cool down before inspecting the unit.  I found cracks on the plastic of the body unit amd some warping. I called customer service on 03-18-2014 regarding a solution t the problem. I asked them if there were any recalls on the unit that were caused from the overheating.  They answer "No".  I suggested to them that the unit nees to tbe redesigned or install a type of insulation in the plastic portion of the body including the water tank as to prvent cracking and electrical malfunction.

incident_description:
I had sent in a recalled air compressor produced by MAT Industries, LLC.  Please reference: https://www.cpsc.gov/en/Recalls/2014/Air-Compressors-Recalled-by-MAT-Industries/

Upon receiving the replacement compressor, I attempted to use it for the first time.  All had seemed well.  However, when I attempted to release the residual pressure in the tank, I received a severe blast of air in the eye.  It seems that the relief valve provided to release pressure when you are finished using the product is now pointed directly at the user (in this case, my face).  And has resulted in a dry contact and painful eye.  In the version before it was recalled, it was pointed away from me and there was no danger whatsoever.

I honestly feel this is a greater risk then the pre-recalled compressor.  You have to release the pressure after each use.  And now it's more dangerous.
justification: The user suffered a severe blast of air in the eye, causing pain and dry contact, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description:
In store 10 yrs. before purchase; receipt enclosed.  Frigidaire dehumidifier  purchased from retailer in 2009 with dom 1999 which takes it out of the dehumidifier recall.  The recall dates are 01/2007 through 09-2008.

The caller is having problems with his dehumidifier sparking where it plugs into the outlet and it would not shut off until he went to the circuit breaker and flipped it off.

Smells of electrical burn.  Unit hot.  Continues to run in off mode.

The caller is not sure how long this has been a safety issue but is sure that it has been at least a year.

He does not have the model number but he will enter it when he receives copy of this report.

There have been no injuries to report 

The caller reported this to the manufacturer March 30th, 2014. 

Gree says consumer can still use his unit; not affected by recall.

incident_description:
January 30, 2014, I purchased a new Juki TL 2010Q.  This new machine model comes with, not one, but 2 automatic thread cutters.  One thread cutter can be engaged by pushing a button on the sewing machine which is great.  However, the 2nd thread cutter is the problem.  This 2nd thread cutter switch is in the foot control (the foot pedal that is depressed to do the sewing).  When the heel  (bottom) of the foot controller is pressed, the thread cutter is engaged.  This is a dangerous feature.
     It is too easy to engage this foot controller accidentally by touching the foot controller when you are not sewing; for instance, moving or turning your fabric.  As long as your machine is in the "on" position, the thread cutter is active.  
     While we sew we may need to remove some thread from throat of machine.  There are many reasons our fingers could be near the needle while the machine IS operating.  We sew, we stop, adjust, we sew some more, etc.  Yes, we need to be cautious and keep our fingers away from needle while the machine is operating.  
     However, this automatic thread cutter in foot controller can be engaged while the machine IS NOT operating, those breaks in between, while we are adjusting our fabric as happened to me when I began to sew and was moving a thread out of the way.  The thread was not where it was suppose to be .  My foot (which was resting on the floor) somehow engaged the foot controller and the thread cutter was engaged.  Needle came down, caught and punctured the edge of my pinkie finger.  The needle has to go down into the hole that goes to bobbin in order for the thread to be cut.  The needle puncture my pinkie finger and actually took off a tiny bit of my finger.  Of course my finger bled and was sensitive for weeks.
     I have sewn professionally using industrial sewing machines.  I have owned and operated several domestic sewing machines of various brands.  I have never seen a feature on any machine, (not even an industrial serger) as dangerous as this thread cutter.  
      The threader cutter is too easy to engage by accident by the machine operator while the machine is idle.  When we stop stitching to do some adjusting of our fabric, turning it, whatever, our foot is still resting on the foot control.  The threader cutter switch can be engaged while we are just resting our foot.  This would be a dangerous machine for a CHILD or novice.  NO DOUBTS ABOUT IT!  
     Under WARNINGS, page 1, in the Juki manual, nothing is stated about the foot control thread cutter.  Juki does have caution statements in various pages of the manual .  Juki cautions to turn off power switch when changing the bobbin, threading the machine, changing the needle, and changing the pressure foot.  There is no warning on the foot control thread cutter, how easily it can be engaged. 
     The thread cutter on foot controller is not needed because you can push the other thread cutter button on machine itself; this is a conscious effort. 
     I am concerned that no one else gets injured and concerned about children also.  I contacted Juki online asking if there was a way to disengage the thread cutter on foot control.  The answer was "no". Also, the Juki rep. stated there have not been any other reported incidents of this problem.  
      Sincerely,
justification: The incident resulted in a finger injury, which classifies it as severity level 3. The occurrence likelihood is rated as 4 (likely) due to the ease of accidentally engaging the foot controller thread cutter.

incident_description:
Event: lint inside my dryer caught fire while the dryer was operating.
Reason:Traditional dryers have the heating unit up high and vertical in the back of the unit.    That 
design allows air pulled in to be heated to be relatively free from lint since it is up high. 
Also,the vertical  design does not allow lint to collect on or above the heating unit.
1) My dryer's design has the heater underneath the unit with the air pulling through the underside 
of the unit.  This is very unsafe as lint naturally collects at the ground level. Also,there are 
intake vents in the back that,if lint were to be pulled in, would again collect in the bottom of the unit and near the intake to the heaters.
2) The dryer has a horizontal heater covered by a metals haft. Lint can easily collect on top of  this, and when heated,catch fire. The metal shaft also has openings on the side which could allow  lint to pull in and be in direct contact with the heating coils. As lint collects in the bottom due  to gravity, a 'vacuum' effect occurs when the unit is operated, sucking air and lint into the open  horizontal shaft in the bottom of the unit directly across the heating element coils.
This happened on our unit within only a year or two of use. The dryer was turned on and immediately  smoke and burning smell was detected. Upon inspection it was found that lint collected inside the  bottom of the dryer caught fire.
justification: The incident involved a fire caused by lint in the dryer, but no injury or death was reported. The design flaw makes such incidents likely to occur.

incident_description: My Whirlpool Electric clothes dryer purchased in February 2011 does not turn off automatically as it is supposed to when on normal setting or when on setting which allows user to choose "more dry" options. I discovered this after I forgot I had loaded dryer and when I checked it 24 hours later, the dryer was still running and the machine and the clothes were extremely hot. The model number is:  WED4800XQ0   and the serial Number of my machine is :  M03905745

incident_description:

The manufacturer was not contacted as yet.  She is planning to return the burnt remains to the retailer.

incident_description: Four days ago my daughter was getting some things out of her shower at college and slipped on her bat mat and hit her cheek against the corner of the wall causing a concussion. Turns out she has a Microdry bath mat purchased from Bed Bath & Beyond. My daughter actually works at a BB&B and is going to look into this.

incident_description: I use this as a space heater in my son's bedroom. When I plugged it in tonight, it started to operate like normal. The temperature displayed and the fan waited until the temperature dropped and it had to turn on to heat the room. When the fan activated, I was in the room across the hallway. incident_description:

She stated that she called her dad and he advised her that the GE dehumidifiers were on recall. The consumer called CPSC and was advised that the unit was not involved in the recall.

incident_description:
I was using my Little Giant Ladder to take down some drapes. The ladder includes an Air Deck which is intended to hold onto when you are on the ladder.   While I was reaching to take down a drape the brackets holding the air deck shattered causing me to fall off the ladder into a window. Fortunately I was able to grab the window farm as I fell to avoid serious injury.  A few days later I saw the ladder on sale at a home show and the sales person said the ladder had been redesigned to change from plastic brackets to metal brackets because the company knew it was a problem.  When I reported it to the company they  required me to pay shipping to get a replacement part. The replacement part was totally redesigned.  The company, Little Giant knew they had a design defect but did nothing to notify consumers. I could have been seriously injured by falling off that ladder. The ladder with the plastic brackets is a risk to users.

Note: Incident occurred at prior home which I was in the process of selling. [REDACTED]

incident_description: This space heater would not shut off. I unplugged it and picked it up to get it out of the house. When picking it up, I heard a rattle in side. Thinking that this was the problem I took it apart to find that the counter weight that turns the unit off if tipped over was installed wit a clear plastic fitting that had melted and the weight had fallen off. buy using plastic that could melt instead of metal makes this unit a time bomb for fire or death!

It sent glass throughout the bathroom and sounded like a bomb going off.  We have a new home and the doors are not that old.  If someone was in the shower, bath or on the toilet it would have been a disaster.  We were slightly cut cleaning up the glass and mess.

incident_description: Our LG Waveforce washer destroyed itself after entering the spin cycle.  The with the exception of some electrical wires top assembly completely separated from the bottom section of the washer, the unit moved approximately 2-3 feet from the wall, rotated 90 degrees, the shell of the washer is bent, and the wall was damaged.  My wife and family were 10 feet away in another room.  They did not hear of it being out of balance before failing.

incident_description: My wife and I purchased the Prince Lionheart Wipe warmer premium model # 9002 with a white label on the bottom with the numbers 121106 from Buy Buy Baby. We have had it for about 5 months now and started experiencing problems with it about 2 weeks ago ( today is 03/29/14). I should say that when I set the warmer up for the first time I followed the instruction and made sure the warmer was away from potential hazards. I am a Professional Fire fighter and know that products like these have a potential to malfunction and cause issues. the issue began when my wife informed me that the heart shaped light on the front went out. I looked at the warmers power cord where it connects to the warmer to ensure that the cord hadn't worked its way out some how; it hadn't. I set the device back down and the light was on so we decided to continue to use it; keeping a cautious eye on it. We didn't have another issue with it until today when the light again went out. I tilted the wipe warmer towards me ( with plenty of slack in the cord) to look at the back again to see if the power cord came out. when I touched the cord it fell out of the power port and the cord adapter was covered in a wet black residue and the warmers power connector ( the piece that the power cord adapter fits over on the warmer) was still in the power cord adapter and it too was covered in the same residue. I immediately unplugged the cord from the wall and moved the warmer away from my son and his changing pad; as I moved it a reddish colored fluid ( rust colored) poured out of the power cord adapter hole on the warmer( approximately 3 mL) on to my carpet. I set it back down on the dresser/changing table and inspected the warmer both inside and out  for cracks, nicks, dents or dings and inspected the seal on the lid to make sure it was also intact, after I didn't find any of the afore mentioned I set it down on a section of my tile floor in my bathroom and immediately contacted the Prince lionheart Company and am waiting for their response.   Please make sure if you own one to watch out for any problems like I mentioned.

incident_description: I own a Lasko ceramic tower heater. I use it in my nursery to keep our infant daughter warm at night. The thermostat has ceased functioning. I went in the other night and the room was nearing 80 degrees and the heater was still running, even though the thermostat was set at 68. The digital readout said 71 at the time. I turned the unit off and set the thermostat to 66. Returning an hour or so later, the room was closer to 60 degrees. I reported this to the manufacturer and was told that this "did not sound like a defect."

incident_description:
Space heater (1-2 months old) was in use in an office. It suddenly began making an odd noise, so I looked at it. As I watched, it began putting out thick black smoke at the on/off knob. The knob was hot, so I yanked on the electrical cord to unplug it. The entire event was under 5 seconds (probably 3 seconds), but the on/off know was already hot! It was very sudden and I believe if I had not witnessed it, say I was in the bathroom, it could have caught anything nearby on fire. 

The unit put out a lot of smoke in a short time period that smelled stongly of chemical. In a confined space, that may be very dangerous. Our office is very open, so it was of no consequence to me.

Looking at reviews of this product (on Amazon, etc), there are several reports of smoking/melting  at the on/off knob and product failure. This product appears unusually dangerous.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that mold collects in the rubber gasket around the washer door.

incident_description:
My husband and I purchased a Dehumidifier from Lowe's on 3/19/2012 for $259.00 + Sales Tax.  The dehumidifier was a Soleus SG-DEH-70-2 / MD000121511000.  The unit ran for some time and then, while we were home, we smelled the unit burning.  We unplugged it and afterward, tried a few times to see if it would run.  It never did run again.  Due to problems locating a proper recycling/disposal facility, the unit stayed around our house.

Looking back on the incident, we should have notified you right away as it may have helped other people.

It was fortuitous that the unit never ran again and yet stayed around our house, as the recall was issued and we had to return the applicable parts for a refund.  We have just received our refund check for $202.50.  Although we are pleased to be refunded at least part of our costs, we are wondering why we were unable to submit our receipt and receive a refund of the purchase price.

There were a number of fortunate occurrences for our issue - our house, rescued animals, and 89 year old mother were harmed as a result of the dehumidifier's problems, we were home at the time of the problem, the unit stayed around due to our inability to find a proper facility, and we were able to receive almost 80% of our purchase price back.

We realize recalls are tough and thank you for your work on this issue.  If there is an option to submit our receipt, we will happily do so.

Thank you!
justification: The dehumidifier malfunctioned and emitted a burning smell, but no injuries or harm occurred to people or animals.

Approximately 2 weeks ago, I smelled a plastic burning odor emitting from the top of the heater while it was turned on. I turned off the unit for the evening after inspecting it.  The unit visually appeared to be ok.  On 03/20/2014, I turned the heater on a high level.  After approximately 45 minutes of being in use, I heard a fizzing noise, followed by a little pop with a spark emitting again from the top of the unit through the wire screen that protects the heating element.  Almost immediately, smoke started to come out from the unit in the area where the on/off switch is located.  I quickly unplugged the heater and removed it from the home as it continued to smoke.  After ensuring there was no further risk of fire, I again inspected the unit and took notice that the knob to the on/off switch had melted on the bottom side.

I have contacted Holmes to inform them of this product issue.  There have been multiple reports on the internet of this same issue occurring with this model heater.  Holmes has indicated to me that there currently is no active recall.  I feel that the chance for tragedy is extremely high with this unpredicatable unit.

Bad news: You better sit next to it and watch it at all times. One of my frisky cats knocked it over, face-down, and it did not shut off.
It got hot enough to scorch the vinyl kitchen floor tile and the much-heralded overheating sensor failed to work.
Had it been on carpet, etc., this thing could have started a fire that would have burned down the house!
Now we know why Target so kindly donated these units to Goodwill instead of destroying them. Thanks, Target.

incident_description:
LG Model 209PNVZ5D151, front loading washing machine, purchased in 2011.

When the door is open and the machine is Off, when you spin the drum with any force, the machine will turn on as if you touched the Start button.

The manufacturer recommends the door be left open when not in use to avoid mold and odors. The washing drum is only a few inches from the floor without an optional and expensive pedestal to raise it and is easily reached by a child.

I have found when unloading the washer and looking for clothes stuck to the side of the drum, that if turned with a relatively small amount of force the machine will turn on and only the Start button needs to be pushed after the door is closed.

My concern is a child spinning the drum with enough force to start the machine and then putting something or some other child in the drum, closing the door and pushing the Start button.

I don't think it is safe for a machine to be electronically on where moving a key part turns it fully on and engages all the electronics.  This is similar to old propeller bi-planes that had to be hand cranked to start by someone in front of the engine.  We all know losing an arm in the process in that instance was not unheard of.
justification: The incident describes a potential hazard where a child could start the machine by spinning the drum, posing a risk of injury if something or someone is placed inside. The severity is high due to the potential for injury, but the likelihood is moderate as it requires specific actions by a child.

incident_description:

incident_description:
A few years ago, I purchased a Ryobi 10 in. Table Saw, Model BTS21, SN X085002221, from Home Depot, the sole distributor of Ryobi products.  As you know, Ryobi is one of the brand names of One World Technologies, Inc., Anderson, SC.  This same company has an outstanding recall for  what is apparently a similar problem for a similar table saw marketed under the "Ridgid" brand name.

The saw has been used only occasionally and intermittently for perhaps a total operation time of less than 25 hours.  During the last two uses of a few minutes each, the saw was making a loud grinding noise and it was apparent that the blade was wobbling, as the kerf was over 1/4" wide, rather than the expected 1/8".  I installed a new blade, thinking the old blade might be warped, but the new blade made no difference.

I checked Home Depot's customer reviews and found a number of complaints about the gears stripping, requiring replacement of core motor components.  The primary gear is machined into the end of the motor shaft; the secondary gear is supported by a die-cast aluminum or zinc housing, which also supports a surprisingly very short arbor assembly.  If the gears should seize at full 5000 rpm because of damage and internal fragmenting,  the arbor assembly holding the 10" blade could explode out of the machine causing severe injury or death to the operator.

I contacted both Home Depot and Ryobi-One World Technologies about the problem but was greeted with total unconcern.  Home Depot, despite being the sole distributor of Ryobi products, said to contact Ryobi.  Ryobi said that the machine is past the 2-year warranty and so they will do nothing to repair or replace the machine.  They ignore the fact of "implied warranty" and that their product is extremely dangerous.

The number of complaints on Home Depot's website belie the fact that gear failure is a common occurrence with this tool.  Ryobi's parts distributor, Gardner, Inc., stocks over 40 complete motor assemblies and numerous armatures only (the shaft of which has the primary gear cut into it), indicating that such failures are common.   Failure of the gear train involving the arbor seems to be identical to that of the Ridgid R4511 which is subject to an ongoing recall.  The risks are the same with the Ridgid or the Ryobi, although it appears that the Ryobi has a high risk of failure with any blade, not just a dado assembly.
justification: The incident describes a dangerous malfunction with potential for severe injury or death, but no actual injury or death has occurred yet.

incident_description: Hoover Windtunnel Rewind T Series upright vacuum cleaner.  There is a hose on the back that detaches at one end for implement use.  Unfortunately, the beater bar on the main machine continues to rotate while the hose and implements are in use.  The hose is spring loaded as well so it is impossible to use the hose at any distance from the machine itself without pulling the machine toward the user.  I was down on the floor vacuuming dust underneath a piece of furniture and my hair got caught in the beater bar.  The power switch is at the top of the handle, which I could not reach with my hair caught in the bottom of there machine.  Luckily my husband was home to rescue me, but this is a very dangerous thing!  If it had been a necktie it could have been a strangulation incident.  Could have been catastrophic if it was a child.

incident_description: The Maytex Smart Rod shower ( Maytex Mills New york made in China) rod is made unreasonably for its intended use. It is supposed to be an unmounted curved shower rod. Yet, the weight of this rod is quite heavy compared to other unmounted straight rods and to add to the problem, it does not stay in place properly, probably a mixture of the weight and curve. It came down on my 6 year olds head and put her in the hospital. The product is dangerous and a real safety concern to consumers. A shower rod this heavy should be mounted or it should be made lighter weight if they are going to continue to sell it as an unmounted rod. If it had been a rusty rod that lacerated my child's this situation potentially could haven been deadly.
justification: The shower rod fell and injured a child, requiring hospitalization, which qualifies as an injury (severity 3). The description mentions multiple complaints about the product's instability and rusting, indicating a likely occurrence (4).

incident_description: We have electric baseboard heat in our basement.  In late 2011 we installed a Honeywell TL8230A1003 7 day programmable thermostat.  Today I went downstairs and realized that it was almost 80 degrees but the thermostat was set to 71 degrees and the radiator was hot.  I turned the thermostat off but the radiator after an hour did not cool down.  I switched to vacation mode and lower the heat to 65 degrees and the radiator did not cool down. I began to remove the back plate from the wall and the wires began to spark.  Once I pulled the wires out of the electrical box I noticed that all the wire nuts were burnt and melted.  After pulling the wires out of the box and making sure that nothing was touching the radiator soon there after began to cool down.

incident_description:
A Nest Protect smoke/fire/CO2 detector (the wired model) installed in our home had a major false alarm.  Our family was at home in the evening when a recorded voice from the device announced "There is smoke in the hallway."  We immediately went to check, and found no smoke in the hallway or in any other location.  The device could not be silenced, and soon the message escalated.  The device was now reporting a fire, and telling us that it was an emergency and that we needed to leave our house immediately.  It communicated with all other devices in our home, and loud alarms were sounding throughout our house -- all false, and all repeating every few minutes.  My husband removed the device from the ceiling and tried to silence it as I called Nest's customer service line.

Nest helped us silence the alarms. They told us they would replace the device -- the second that had failed in our home.  (The first reported a sensor that had failed, but created no false alarms.)  We called about both failed devices on the same day.  I learned that other consumers had experienced similar problems, and was told that engineers at Nest were examining faulty devices to find the source of the problem.  It is clear we are not the only people who have had problems with Nest Protect alarms.

We had purchased the device less than three months earlier.

Nest sent a replacement unit, which we installed.

There were no injuries.  But we were concerned that a new product -- one that is a fundamental home safety device -- would fail so quickly.

We purchased six units for our home.  This was the second of FOUR that have failed -- a failure rate of 66%.  An online search reveals that many other people have had similar problems with this product.

I am filing a separate incident report for each device. This is the third report of four.
justification: The incident involved a false alarm causing significant disruption but no injuries, and the description indicates a high likelihood of recurrence based on multiple device failures and similar reports from other consumers.

incident_description:
A Nest Protect Smoke + Carbon monoxide detector (the wired version) installed in our home had a false alarm, repeatedly warning of smoke where the was none.  I had to remove the device from the ceiling and remove the batteries from the device to end the alarm messages.

We had bought the device less than three months earlier.  Our home is about six years old, and we have never had another smoke alarm fail in this house.

After this unit failed, I called the manufacturer, which offered to replace the device.  A replacement arrived within a week.

This is the THIRD Nest Protect that has failed in our home, out of a total of six that we installed.  A total of four of the six have now failed.  We are very concerned about the failure rate -- 66% -- especially since the product is a fundamental home safety device.  While Nest has offered to replace each one without cost to us, I no longer trust the product and feel that a replacement of a flawed product is little better than keeping one that has already failed.  In fact, the fourth unit that failed in our home was a replacement for one of the first two that failed.

Of the four failures in our home, two were false alarms, and two were faulty sensors.  I have no doubt that we are far less safe with these units than we were with our old smoke and CO alarms - largely because I feel that I would not wholly trust a true alarm alerting me to a fire.  After the third unit failed, we asked Nest to refund our purchase price for all six devices, and they refused.  After our fourth failure, we asked again and they have promised to refund our money for all six devices.

We will now have to purchase new devices (from a company that is not Nest) to replace each of these.

My concern is that Nest rushed these products to market before the holidays, when they had not yet been fully tested.  If the overall failure rate is even a fraction of what it has been in our home, I feel strongly that these devices need to be recalled until the problems are resolved.

I have filed a separate incident report for each of our four failed devices.  This the fourth of four reports.

There are many reports of similar incidents online -- including many on Nest's own customer forum.
justification: The incident involves repeated false alarms and faulty sensors in safety devices, posing a potential risk but no actual injury or death.

While this was not a vent fire, need to alert current Whirlpool gas dryer owners to this for apparently it could have been preventable if Whirlpool would have alerted the owners to this potential by routinely cleanly out the dryer cabinet. This was our third dryer in almost 40 years of house ownership and this is the first fire incident. Oddly, I had purchased a vent clean out kit manufactured by [REDACTED] on Sunday to evaluate vent cleanliness. Within their instructions, it was noted to routinely clean out the inside of the cabinet only if the the home owner was proficient in gas dryer maintenance. Again, no mention of this process either in the CGW9250P dryer or the new WGD88HEAW2 model ower's instructions. I have enclosed a copy of my correspondence to Whirlpool and a copy of the pictures showing the damage. Anticipate that this could be useful to you and current owners to alert them to this unforeseen hazard. By the way, there was very little vent debris while using the [REDACTED] vent cleaner. However, it does work very well.

Thank you in advance for taking the time to read this letter. If you require additional information, kindly refer to the contact information in the letter head.


Best Regards

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a flash fire inside the dryer cabinet with no reported injuries or deaths, classifying it as an incident with no injury.

incident_description: We bought a forclosed home and bought a brand new heat pump unit to hook up.  This unit is about 2 years old. Recently we had an ice storm and lost power. Once we knew the power was off my husband turned off the breaker to the heat pump.  This would prevent the heat pump from running once power was restored. My husband new if power was restored and there was ice on the heat pump it may tear up something. Once power was restored 2 days later after the ice storm, the temperature in the house was 58 degrees.  In order to keep the heat strips from running because we didnt want to use so much electricity my husband turned the breaker on but we set the thermostat temperature to 59 degrees.  The heat pump only had to heat the house within 1 degree of the outside temperature.  This was on 14 February Valentines day of 2014. Once we heard the unit come on and felt air coming through the vents we assumed all was ok.  We left the thermostat set on 59 degrees and left the house to go out for Valentines day date night.  We left the house approximately at 5:30pm to go out. At that time the heat pump was functioning normal.  We got a call at approximately 10:30pm telling us our house was on fire and we needed to come home.  We rushed home to find our home fully engulfed in flames and most of it already gone.  They were not able to save anything in our home. We lost everything.  The fire chief filled out a fire report and has said the origin of the fire was "Heat Pump" and the possible cause is the Heat Pump Motor. The material ignited was "Flooring" - what we believe happened was the heat pump caught fire and when it blew the air through all the air vents it also blew the fire through the vents. The most/worst damage is right where the heat pump is located and the main trunk line sends the air. Once the flames were blown through the vents it started burning under neath the home. Once I got the fire report and knew that the cause was most likely the heat pump I was talking to some friends who did some research and sent me a link to a recall that Amana has on some of there units.  The website is http://www.recallowl.com/Consumer+Recalls/Household+Products/Goodman+Company+Recalls+Amana+Heating+and+Cooling+Units+Due+to+Fire+Hazard. When I researched on this website I seen where there were other fire hazards reported for certain models of Amana Heat pumps.  The exact model and serial number that I had is not listed, however maybe it should be. I seen that the manufacturer of the Amana heat pump was actually Goodman Company so I called the company and all I could do was leave a message.  I left a message saying I had a question about a recall and ask for them to return my call.  I did not receive a call back.
justification: The incident resulted in a house fire causing total loss of property, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description:
I have a LG DLG5966W gas dryer and there is a gas smell coming from the dryer vent when the dryer is running. In other words, a gas smell is present when the dryer is being used as it normally would be. The gas smell is primarily located where the vent enters the basement and where it exits the house. This problem was caused by opening the gas valve with no ignition source, which is the igniter coil. With no ignition source, the gas just enters the tub drum and then exits through the vent. The problem is described in the following YouTube video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mJqzwdBavfw. I contacted LG about the problem and they denied any existence of a problem and insisted I have a technician look at the dryer. I diagnosed and fixed the problem myself. The issue was caused by a faulty control board (part number: EBR36858802). I ordered a new control board from an internet supplier, which was clearly marked with revision two labels, and it fixed the issue.

This issue is quite dangerous and, as you can hopefully see, this problem is not uncommon. The danger of this issue and denial by LG about the problem prompted me to submit this complaint. Due to this issue being safety related, I hope there would be some sort of recall by LG or reimbursement for parts ordered to fix the problem.
justification: The incident involves a gas leak which is dangerous but no injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
I have a new Bosch 520 HN LP tankless water heater that we installed in September of 2013. We chose this water
heater because the vent and hook up were an exact fit for the 20 year old [REDACTED] tankless water heater originally
installed in our home. The Bosch water heater is designed such that the heat exchanger is placed near the vent of
the water heater. As such, it has flash frozen four times since it was installed (freezes very quickly). The latest
episode caused the tankless water heater to rupture the heat exchanger in two places, dumping water all over our
basement floor. During this time, the heater continued to operate continuously producing considerable noise, heat
and steam. Luckily for us, we were home at the time and heard the commotion in our basement. Otherwise, the
heater would have continued to pour water on the floor and run continuously.

I called Bosch before this incident to inquire about a backdraft preventer. They do not offer such a product for this
water heater and do not seem very concerned about the potential for problems. The service people suggested that
we contact an HVAC person to see if they could balance the house. As I mentioned, we had the previous tankless
water heater for years without incident. It would occasionally blow out the pilot light from down drafts. But, the
downdrafts were not a persistent problem and likely resulted from a rapid change in barometric pressure that
causes an imbalance between the outside and inside air. We were convinced that an HVAC person would not be
able to offer much in the way of solutions, particularly since the problem was so rare and episodic.
justification: The incident caused property damage (ruptured heat exchanger and water leakage) but no injury or death, and the problem is episodic but recurring.

incident_description:
I bought a Optimus 15Gal Warm Mist Humidifier White SKU: 1648407 online from www.bestbuy.com on Dec. 18,2013. Several days later it was delivered and I set it up two days later after reading the instruction booklet. It did put out a good amount of mist and was fairly quiet. I did notice that it had three lights on top, one for on/off, one for humidity, and one for refill. The humidity and refill light did not go on even when it was no longer producing steam and out of water, but otherwise it was working. Thought maybe it has to be completely dry for these lights to activate, but there was always residual water in the tray. I removed the water tower and steam tower looking for calcium deposits, but there were none, just a little brown sludge. 
I noticed a somewhat pungent, acrid smell from when I first started using it. I thought it was from the plastic and new parts and that the odor would go away. When I saw that it was out of water, I would refill it, or turn it to "off' and fill it a several hours later. The smell was irritating my sinuses and lungs. It caused shortness of breath that is still affecting me. On Jan. 26, 2014, I turned it off, waited 30 minutes and removed the two towers. The heating element was still very hot, and the "white" filter was brown and had a burnt smell. So I unplugged it to cut the electric power since obviously the on/off switch not turning off and stuck "on." I tried to remove the filter, but it was fused to the heating element. I soaked the filter in some vinegar water and finally able to remove it, but it looked brown and burnt, and found some brown stained calcium deposit on the projected heating element around which the wrap around filter goes with a [fastener] strip. By comparison, the [REDACTED] humidifier I bought at Best Buy at the same time still works well and never had an odor, and has no filter and the heating element is cleaned once a week or so with vinegar water depending on the amount of calcium deposit.
My complaint is that I think there is a design flaw in this humidifier and it is unsafe since it never turns off and out gasses fumes from the overheated filter. Perhaps the closely fitting filter is causing the overheating problem? It kind of frightened me that it could possibly have caused a fire and burned down my house. I don't know if it is the only one, or there might be thousands of malfunctioning units of this model, or similar units, out there endangering people. That is why I am reporting it. I contacted the manufacturer, who has not replied. I contacted Best Buy, and about an hour later I received a phone call asking me more questions and they were concerned and would give me a refund. They had UPS send me a return label that is good for ten days. Of course, once I send it back, it can no longer be examined, so I am wondering what to do.
Humidifier manufacturer: Optimus Enterprise, Inc., Customer Service Dept., 2201 E. Winston Road, Unit #J, Anaheim, CA 92806 Tel: 1-888- 672-5832 E-mail not listed in booklet, but found website through a search: www.optimusent.com
justification: The humidifier caused shortness of breath and sinus irritation, indicating an injury, and poses a potential fire hazard.

incident_description: Purchased SENGOKU CV-2230 kerosene heater to provide supplemental heat bduring recent cold weather. Had originally owned this type of heater back in the 80s-early 90s.  Used high quality 1-K kerosene and burned heater for a total of about 24 hours on 3 separate days. Flame and burner operation appeared to be perfect but after that time my apartment was was filled with uncombusted kerosene/ emissions product. I observed the combustion burner of this heater during actual operation and found the following; unlike the older [REDACTED] or [REDACTED] heaters, this heater had a combustion chamber screen diffuser with no catalytic activity during burning. The use of the catalytic combustion diffuser in the older heaters assured a combustion efficiency of greater than 99.9%. Not the cse with this heater. It is just a cheap imitation of the older efficient heaters. Also, this heater had both UL cert markings and NKHA (National Kerosene Heater Association) markings. Basis observed combustion performance, It is my belief that UL has not tested this item for performance in several years. Further, I have been unable to verify that there is even something known as the NKHA which is still in existence.
justification: The incident describes exposure to uncombusted kerosene emissions, which can cause health issues, warranting a severity level of 3. The likelihood is 'possible' as the issue occurred under specific conditions.

incident_description:
In Dec of 2009 I purchased a rug for our new home, an 8 ft round rug to put under the dining room table.  It was a SAFAVIEH rug - heritage,HG343A, green and gold,"handmade in India, 100%wool pile,child labor not used" on the label. I paid more than $700 for it.
The rug was lovely and fit the space perfectly, but from the start it had a whitish-yellow powder underneath it. We would vacuum the rug and under it, but the powder always came back. It was annoying but we didn't think anything else of it. This past Nov when we had our heating unit checked, the repairman said our furnace filter was dirty, and it had been in for only ten days.
When we changed it, I noticed it was loaded with the same gritty powder that was always under the rug. The rug had been producing more powder, but again, we didn't realize what could be consequences.  After Christmas, we took the rug out onto the driveway and washed it with the hose. The amount of powder flowing down the drive was astounding and it never quit. I decided to take the backing off and get to the actual rug fibers. In the burlap and gauze backing was a matted mess of what looked like ground sawdust,  We thought we could clean the rug with brushes, brooms and a heavy [REDACTED], and we removed masses of it,but the grit is fully embedded in the fabric.  We put it out on the deck and I sent an email telling the company. I got no answer for two weeks and then I wrote the company asking them to replace it with a "safe" rug as we had breathed the dust for four years. I got a call from [REDACTED], who said the latex backing on those rugs dries out and produces the powder and the only solution was to vacuum it up.  He said it was our fault and we had "ruined" the rug and the company had no responsibility. The rug is out on the deck, it still looks very nice, and it still is producing a large amount of residue. During this time, my husband did not experience any cardiac/respiratory problems. After the carpet was removed, he has been able to stay in our home without any further problems. My swollen eyes and blistered nostrils have also healed. incident_description:
Subject: Fire and Gas Leak in Goodman Furnace 

Brand: Goodman
Model Number: GSK130301BA
Serial Number: 1004125065
Install Date: 4-29-2010

About 7pm on January 24, 2014 my wife noticed that the furnace was not operating correctly and went into the attic to check on it.  The furnace had shown these symptoms many times in January and had been checked by professionals multiple times including earlier that day so we were not surprised that there was a problem.   When entering the attic she noticed that there was a natural gas smell and that the furnace was hot to the touch.  She shut off the electricity to the furnace and opened up the panel.  The flames coming out of the burners and it was damaging wires and other sensors inside the furnace.  I helped my wife shut off the gas valve into the furnace and the fire slowly burned its self out.  The fire department was notified and they sent some firefighters to check the furnace.

A short video of the fire was collected after we shut of the electricity and before we shut off the gas.  Please contact me to get a copy of the video.

The main symptoms leading up to the fire has been a roll out limit switch error corresponding to 6 flashes for the diagnostic light.  The furnace blower remains running all the time and the thermostat shuts off so the display is blank. The furnace was about 4 years old.  It had been serviced multiple times in November and January by Advanced Heating and Air in Knoxville TN. The technicians that serviced the unit have suggested many different causes for why the furnace entered that state. 

The day before the fire one technician came out to check the rollout limit error and to check for gas leaks because we had smelled gas in the attic and upstairs bed rooms.  The technician could not find a gas leak and said the furnace appeared to be operating correctly.  A new rollout switch was ordered.  He also smelled the gas and recommended having the gas lines to the house checked.

The day of the fire another technician came to check the gas lines and conduct a pressure test and found a very small leak near where the gas enters the furnace. The said leak was really small and probably was not the cause of the gas smell. That leak was repaired.

On Saturday, the day after the fire Advanced Heating and Air sent a technician to check the furnace.  He said he replicated the problem and that it was due to a sticky gas valve.  That gas valve had been replaced by the same company in November and was about 3 months old.  

I am concerned that multiple technicians have looked at this furnace and this problem seems to be very hard to diagnose.  Additionally two gas valves have failed in this relatively new furnace and the furnace has failed in a way that is a serious safety issue.  I am not convinced the technicians accurately diagnosed the problem and that replacing the gas valve AGAIN eliminates this safety problem.  I will be replacing the entire furnace and I am currently talking to American Home Shield to see if I can get it replaced under the home warrantee.  

Here are my notes and timeline on the recent service calls including a rollout limit switch error that occurred a year ago. 

Repair Date: Jan 2013	
Problem: Rollout Limit Circuit is Open (6 flashes)	
Solution: Adjusted Gas Flow?

Repair Date: Nov 1, 2013	
Problem: Furnace Lockout Due to Excessive Number of Ignition Retries (1 flash)	
Solution: Ordered Gas Valve

Repair Date: Nov 8, 2013	
Technician: [REDACTED]
Solution: Replaced Gas Valve

Repair Date: Jan 9, 2014	
Problem: Rollout Limit Circuit is Open (6 flashes) 
Technician: [REDACTED]	
Solution: No cause found. Possible problem with freezing condensation.

Repair Date: Jan 23, 2014
Problem: Rollout Limit Circuit is Open (6 flashes)/Smelled Gas Leak
Technician: [REDACTED]
Solution: Ordered Rollout Limit Switch / Furnace Operation Looked Fine / Could not find gas leak / Recommended house gas line check. 

Repair Date: Jan 24, 2014
Problem: House Gas Line Pressure Test
Technician: [REDACTED]
Solution: Very small leak found near connection to furnace and repaired.

Repair Date: Jan 24, 2014
Problem: 7pm - Symptoms consistent with Rollout Limit Circuit error. Gas smell. Top of furnace was very hot to the touch. Fire found in furnace burning wires and other components even after electricity was disconnected for 5-10 minutes.	
Electricity and Gas to furnace shut off by owner.  Damage appears limited to inside furnace.  Rural Metro Fire Department called to check that unit was shut off and safe.

Repair Date: Jan 25, 2014
Problem: Inspection of damage to furnace.	
Technician: [REDACTED]	
Solution: Was able to replicate fire conditions. Said fire was due to a sticky gas valveÃÂ.  Recommended replacing gas valve, rollout switches, and burnt wiring.
justification: The incident involved a fire and gas leak in the furnace, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

On January 26th, 2013, I was at my new house painting up
inside one of the skylight tunnels in the dinning room. My
wife was right next to me so that she could hand me paint
filled rollers and what ever else I might need while working
in the confined space.

I was using a 6' Werner FS106 fiberglass ladder, rated for
250 lbs, that was maybe a year old and is always stored in
my shop. I was on the fourth rung from the bottom. Due to
the confined area I was working in, there was no way
possible to be leaning hardly at all in any direction, so I
was centered over the ladder.

In a nut shell, all of a sudden the ladder dropped out from
under me and I fell out of the skylight tunnel and landed on
my right scapula on the hardwood floor. I ended up in the
emergency room with a small pneumothorax injury and spent
two days in the critical care center.

I went over to the house yesterday to look at everything.
Nothing has been moved since the accident and I am going
over today to get some photos. The right side rail was bent
in directly below the bottom rung about 45 degrees towards
the center of the ladder. The lateral support for the
bottom rung looks like it pushed up the bottom rung a good
3" in the middle. None of the fiberglass parts are torn
looking and I can not see any threads from fiberglass
tearing. Both side webs of the C channel side rail are
mushroomed outwards a lot. On the left hand side rail, you
can see a similar, but small, amount of deformation.
justification: The incident resulted in a pneumothorax injury requiring emergency care, indicating a severity level of 3 (Injury). The occurrence likelihood is 2 (unlikely) as ladder failures of this nature are not common but can happen under certain conditions.

incident_description: In 1996, I remodeled my house and installed two wood Kolbe & Kolbe casement windows (#KW14).  In November, 2013, the interior glass of one of the dual-glass windows cracked/shattered, leaving the exterior glass intact.  I contacted the manufacturer which said a vacuum had probably developed between the 2 pieces of glass, causing it to bow and then fail and that the company would replace it, although I would have to pay for installation. She had contacted the firm during the time they had Release #06-031.  She was informed that her model was not included in the recall.  However, she felt that this unit was safe to use after being advised by the firm.

12/3/13 The manufacturer was contacted and she was advised that the iron was out of warranty which only last for a year and she could not return the product.

Consumer feels that the product is a fire hazard and should be reported.

The product is not part of a recall.

I am sorry this letter  has been delayed. I was caught up in the holidays, and then I could not deliver it because I was snowed in.  I am writing this as an attachment to your form so that I can include more detailed and accurate information.

I purchased a Weller brand soldering iron 6 to 10 years ago. I'm not sure of the exact date.  I believe I purchased it from Warner Stained Glass Products of New Jersey. I'm not sure of that either because I have bought items from other stained glass suppliers. I have used Warner the most, however. Warner posted a recall on a couple of Weller soldering irons a couple of years ago, and I checked with Weller to see if mine was included.  Weller assured me that it was not, and mine was safe to use. Apex Tool Group of Apex North Carolina is the manufacturer of Weller brand soldering irons.

On December 2, 2013, I plugged my soldering iron in to warm up.  It was in its stand. I was not holding it. After about 2 minutes, there was a 'pop' and coming from the soldering iron handle were 3 to 4 inch flames and a lot of black smoke. I unplugged the unit and the flames stopped. The smoke continued a while longer, but then also stopped.  It really smelled.

When the soldering iron cooled, I looked at it closer. There is a flange directly behind the hot steel element and at the top of the handle.   It sticks out as if it is a way to have users stop moving their hands close to the heating element.  Well, there is a crack and opening in the flange material that was not there before this incident.   I believe this happened when I heard that 'pop', and it was through that opening that the flames and black smoke emerged.

On December 3, 2013, I called Weller Products and informed [REDACTED] of what happened.  I told them that the unit was old, but I believed it should die gracefully....like just not work.  I told them that I was not hurt, just scared.  But, if I had been holding the iron, I would probably have been burned.  I told them that I would mail them the unit for them to investigate what had happened. They gave me a return address, and I asked if they could send me a return shipping label or return my postage. They said that there was only a one-year warrantee on the product.  I said I was not asking for a warrantee because the product was 6-10 years old.

I was just asking for return postage because I really didn't  have to send it to them.  I thought that they would want to investigate.  They said that they had some products on the market that were about 20 years old, but my product was only warranted a year, and they refused to send me a return postage label or reimburse my postage for shipping it back to them.   I told them I contacted them a couple of years ago about the recall, but they said that was because some units sparked when they were unplugged....never any flames.  I assured them that this
incident did not involve sparks. It involved a 'pop', flames and black smoke.

That is when I called you.  I feel that there may be other soldering irons like this one that are in consumers' hands that could cause a fire or hurt someone if they were holding it. I believe it should be part of a recall.  I still have the unit and would be happy to send it to you.

Please let me know if you need additionalinformation.   You can contact me at [REDACTED]. [REDACTED]
