incident_description: The product was being used to maintain heat in a bedroom area of 500 sq. ft.  It was set to automatically adjust the flame height for the set room temperature.  It was set to the lowest blower speed with both front and back burner flames turned on.  3-5 days after installation the modulator stopped working and was replaced.  We then went on a vacation for one month, programming the room temperature at 70 degrees in smart mode to adjust flame height accordingly.  Upon our return the flame height was spreading across the top of the firebox about 5-7 inches. After about 20 minutes, we smelled strong smoke from another room, and ran into to find the QC888HB on fire internally and throwing mass amounts of smoke.  We quickly unplugged it and carefully got it outside.

I called Quality Craft, and their first reaction was that their are safeties on the unit and it can't catch on fire.  Their second reaction was to say the unit was out of warranty.  I explained that this is not a warranty issue - this is a product safety issue as my house was moments away from catching on fire.  They then asked for pictures, and after reviewing - offered to send me some internal electronic parts to replace inside the unit.

I stated I am not authorized or certified to repair appliances, and was dismayed that they were not interested in finding a root cause.  After much back and forth, they finally agreed to have me ship the unit back - but only after putting legal forms (liability waivers, releases, etc) in front of me.  

I told them before ever plugging in a Quality Craft unit again and placing my family at risk, I would need to understand why this happened in the first place, is it happening to other people, and lastly - I'm not releasing them if it catches on fire again.  Communication has since ceased.

I had purchased a First Alert 120V AC hardwired smoke & fire alarm (model 9120B) earlier this year.  I selected this model because it has a battery backup with an [REDACTED] 9V battery included.  The battery was in its swing-out battery compartment.  

In the User's Manual, it did not instruct how to properly install in the battery.  There were no markings on the alarm itself for where the battery's positive terminal should be place.  So, I left the battery in the same place in its swing-out battery compartment as it was when I purchased this alarm.  I pushed the door closed.  

Then, I noticed an opening under the swing-out battery compartment where I can see the battery's terminals.  They were touching only plastic.  

I opened the swing-out battery compartment, and noticed that part of the compartment covers one of the battery's terminals.  The battery is useless.  It does not connect to anything electrical.

There are no instructions in the User's Manual on how to install the battery, nor markings on the alarm itself on how to install the battery.  Having the battery in the alarm is false security, and in case the hardwiring fails, the alarm will not have any electricity because the battery won't be installed properly.  People depending on the battery backup could possibly die in the event of a fire.
justification: The incident describes a potential safety hazard due to improper battery installation instructions, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:

This past week I noticed a "shower" of tiny particles (later determined to be fiberglass) coming out of the ducts throughout the home. This was followed by small (1/16-1/4") particles of aluminum foil, paper and a black substance.

When the service technician arrived he determined that the fiberglass batts that lined the air handler had separated from the inner walls and had fallen into the fan - which in turn, chopped the fiberglass into little particles than then blew throughout the home.

I spoke to the manufacturer, Lennox, who denied that there was any sort of manufacturing defect. The technician commented that this was a not-uncommon occurence. He re lined the air handler with solid fiberglass "duct board".

I am not sure what the consequences of inhaling fiberglass dust, but I am sure it's not good for us (and our pets) to be breathing this material

incident_description:
I bought a "Commercial Electric" (brand name) Voltage Detector, model MS8903H form Home Depot.  Before using it, I read the User's Manual that accompanied the product.  I read the entire English part, looking for a clue to understanding how to safely use this product.  It is NOT POSSIBLE TO LEARN THE SAFE USE OF THIS PRODUCT by reading this document.  This is because the writing is such poor English, and what is conveyed assumes the user already has safe-working knowledge of the product.

The logo on this product is a C with a dash within the top and bottom parts of the C, so the C simultaneously resembles an E, followed by the words, Commercial Electric TM.  I have been to the CE site, and they have this disclaimer, in red, on their Contact Us page:
Please note that as the Commercial Electric Products Corporation, we are not affiliated with Home Depot or Commercial Electric which has consumer products sold at Home Depot.  We cannot provide any information regarding that company.

In the User's Manual document, a "Safety" symbol (an exclamation point surrounded by a triangle) refers the user to "the operating manual".  There is no reference to this: no web site, no page number if it means this document; this is a useless remark, and it concerns safety - a paramount concern when working with electricity!

Here is the first paragraph of the User's Manual (between === lines), verbatim, with matching punctuation, and line breaks:
===
GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS
This instrument complies with UL 61010-1, CAT. II
250V Product is only applicable to one-time use
Protection provided by the instrument will be
impaired if used in a manner not specified by the
manufacturer.Before measuring hazardous
voltages, first measure the voltage which is known
to determine if the equipment operate correctly.
===

This may be a good product, but if anyone wants to test a line to see if it is live, this document does not inform the user of a safe way to do this, and this is the PURPOSE OF THE PRODUCT.

This product is dangerous in anyone's hands.  I have done many electricity-oriented tasks in my  homes in the past 25 years.  I have checked out books from the library to learn the safe and proper ways to do the tasks I was interested in.  (I even had the library destroy one copy of a book that had important safety information torn out of it, because that page backed a useful reference table that someone wanted.)  I have used the same voltage tester for all these years, but have lost it.  National Electrical Code has changed, improving the safety and safe use of voltage testers (which excludes my lost one).  But this product is going to hurt or kill someone in too big a hurry to read and understand its safe use - and its safe use cannot be determined by reading this document.
justification: The product's poor manual could lead to unsafe use, posing a risk of injury or death when working with electricity.

incident_description:
At approximately 5:00am on 10/8/13, my wife and I were awakened by our fire alarm.  We jumped out of bed and immediately noticed the smell of electrical smoke.  After a quick look around the house, my wife identified the source as being our Cadet CEC163TW Com-Pak Energy Plus electric wall heater in the living room.  The top of the heater element was glowing red hot, and the cover grill fins had begun to melt.  I quickly ran into the basement and turned off the dedicated breaker for the heater.

The wall cavity above the heater felt really hot, and so we were worried that there may have been a fire smoldering inside the wall cavity.  We live in a rural area, and the volunteer fire department response time is not good.  So we monitored the temperature of the wall cavity for about 10-15 minutes and it slowly cooled off easing our fears of a house fire.  I believe that we were extremely fortunate that our house didnÃÂt burn down that morning.  If the heaterÃÂs breaker had been left on for just one or two more minutes, I believe there would have been a fire in the wall cavity that we would not have been able to put out.

HereÃÂs the disturbing partÃÂ.
Although the heaterÃÂs breaker was on (so we can monitor the temperature in the living room), THE HEATERÃÂS SWITCH WAS TURNED OFF!  We had not yet used the heater for this cold season, so the heater had been switched off since April 2013.  Why does a heater that is switched off, spontaneously start overheating?

I purchased 2 of these heaters on 10/8/12.  The other heater is installed in our kitchen (also wired 220 with its own dedicated breaker).  The heater in the living room had acted flaky before this incident.  About a dozen times over this past year, the heater has failed with a F8 code showing on the front display.  According to documentation, an F8 code is described as follows:   INTERNAL CONTROL FAULT  - Disconnect power, reconnect power.  If F8 code returns, replace heater assembly.  I called Cadet customer service about the F8 code, and received a brush-off response.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning heater that could have caused a fire, but no actual injury or death occurred.

Luckily I had closed the bathroom door before leaving town.  Bath, Kitchen, and Tile in Wilm. Delaware remodeled the bathroom about 5 years ago.  Kennett Square Glass Co. was responsible for putting the glass in the door.  Both companies are refusing to replace the door at no charge because they claim the warranty is for one year.  According to the internet and NBC and ABC News, this has happened many times.   [REDACTED] even recalled their shower doors.
justification: The incident involved shattered glass but no injury occurred, and the issue is known to happen based on news reports.

incident_description:
My family and I were at our camp on Hinckley lake.  The nights started to get cooler, so we plugged in our CALORE portable heater that I believe we purchased from Wal-Mart.  We placed it in the center of the living room.  The heater was on a medium setting, but does have a thermostat, so will turn of when temperature is reached.  My husband and I were in our room, and our children where in their bed/bunks.  I awoke from my husbands coughing, which at that time I smelled something horrible.  I woke him and we went in the other room.  The camp smelled very badly of burning plastic.  The heater was still running, but was MELTING.  It was partially charred, and misshapen.  We pulled the plug from the outlet.  Again, It was STILL running.  We awoke the kids and opened up all the windows.  The smell was disgusting.  We took kids to Dr.'s just to make sure they were fine from inhaling fumes from melting heater.  I have heater, and took pictures.  Could not find any information on company to notify them.  This was a very dangerous situation and could have been much worse if my husbands coughing from the smell did not awake us.

I hope this matter can be looked into.  Please contact me with any information.

Thank you,
[REDACTED]
justification: The heater malfunctioned and melted, releasing toxic fumes, but no injuries were reported as the family sought medical check-ups as a precaution.

incident_description: I puchased a "MaxAir" model 7500 tire pump from WalMart a little over one year ago.  It is made by Air Power America and advertised as rated up to 70 psi and for use with autombile tires.  Last week, on 10/3/13, I was attaching the pump to my car tire's air valve to put air in my car tire when the handle shot straight up and out of the base and struck me in the left cheek bone.  Luckily, I wear eye glasses and that protected my left eye.  My glasses were also partically struck by the handle.  I felt as if I had been punched in the face and my cheek was bruised and tender for a few days after.  The handle actually shot out of the body of the pump and detached from it, striking me in the face.  It is now broken and in two pieces.  I could have been seriously injured and if my 9 year old had been using it, he could have been killed.  If I had not been wearing glasses, I could have been blinded by the strike.  I could have lost a tooth had it hit me in the mouth.  My tire was only at about 30 psi, nowhere near the 70 psi max advertised rating.  I have e-mailed WalMart and Air Power America, which manufactured the tire pump but no reply yet.
justification: The incident resulted in a bruised and tender cheek, indicating an injury, but no long-term harm or death occurred.

incident_description:
Product Name: Universal Security Instruments MCND401B M Series Plug-In Carbon Monoxide and Natural Gas Alarm with 9-Volt Battery Backup

I purchased this item on May 1, 2013 to help us detect natural gas. I installed this item 3 feet away from the source which is the gas range. The product works ok when you press the test button but it never detected the natural gas that filled out our house yesterday.  The design is flawed and will never work when installed as designed which will give false sense of security to the consumer. 

I went home yesterday with the smell of natural gas inside my home. My Mother-In-Law who stayed with us for the day accidentally left the gas range open as she does not know to operate it properly. She said that she tried to heat up her lunch at around 12:pm but no fire comes out of the range. Instead of turning the range close, she turned it the other way which goes to the lowest setting. There was no fire produced so the Natural Gas escaped and fills the air in my house for more then 4 hours. I came in at around 4:20pm from work and smelled gas right away which my Mother-In-Law did not detect.  I check the range right away to see one of the switch was turned open. I closed the range, let everybody out the house and open all the doors and windows to ventilate my entire home. The 2nd floor I noticed has the stronger smell as compared to the 1st floor.  

This product always test OK every time I press the test button but failed on detecting a real natural gas.  I decided to test it again this time by letting the gas escape from the range for about 5 minutes with this one sitting about 2 inches from the source. Nothing happened so I tried to move his around the source but it did not detect anything. Next, I tried putting the product above the source so that the sensor if facing down as it was installed in the ceiling. The product detected the gas this time at a face down position. Well the problem is this product is a plug in type and will never work as designed. I checked online reviews of this product and most of the poor reviews have expressed the same thing while the 5 star reviewers gave it 5 star because of ease of use and/or that there is no false alarm. Well there will never be false alarm because it will never work.  Below is a video review of one of the buyer I found on Amazon. 

http://www.amazon.com/review/R2H1GI1AV9B2FY/ref=cm_cr_pr_viewpnt#R2H1GI1AV9B2FY

Please investigate this product and discontinue it if necessary. Families life depend on this product functioning properly.  No security is better than having false sense of security.  This product cannot be trusted.
justification: The incident involved a gas leak that was not detected by the alarm, posing a significant risk but no actual injury occurred.

incident_description:
Washing Machine Rear Counter Balance weight broke from its mounts , and caused damage to the belt and drum . 
This occurred shortly after a software change was made due to recall . 
I believe that the machine should have been inspected during the recall repairs , to preclude any other damage due to the instability of the drum . 
When the weight became unattached , it rubbed on the rear pulley , and created smoke , and heat due to friction . eventually the belt broke , but the motor pulley continued to rub on the belt , resulting in more smoke .

incident_description: We purchased a Frigidaire Gas Dryer Model FRG5714KWO three yrs ago and the dryer caught fire this week!  My husband heard a loud BOOM! from the laundry room and when he entered, the dryer was shooting flames from the bottom and sides and the laundry room was full of smoke.  He immediatley called 911 and the fire department arrived to extinguish the fire.  Our entire home was full of smoke and the charred dryer was removed by the fire department.  The firemen reported that the motor had caught fire and we were lucky that someone was home when the incident happened.  This model should be reported as a fire hazard and put on the recall list.  There are hundreds of complaints online about Frigidaire gas dryers catching fire.  No one should have to deal with the potential dangers of a dryer fire.

The blade guard is designed to drop down to cover the moving blade.  It failed to do so and stuck in the up position.  I brushed my left index finger against the blade the cut me severely.  I had to go to the hospital and was keep for two days and they had to cut my finger tip off at the first joint.

http://www.cpsc.gov/en/Recalls/2013/Gree-Recalls-12-Brands-of-Dehumidifiers/#remedy

... Mine did not catch fire before I unplugged it, but I *had* been noticing that it was running more continuously than the unit it replaced (which had itself been recalled), and that the tank-full cutoff switch did not seem to be working properly (which was not a problem in my case since I had it hooked to a drain hose, but which might be a secondary symptom of the same problem.)

incident_description:
I had a sears Kenmore dehumidifier that stopped working. I bought two new ones, Model # 251.50701011. Shortly after I bought the two new ones the old one that had stopped working (a different model) was recalled. Within a year of purchasing the two new ones one of them "burned out". I went down the basement and found one of them not working and the ground fault protector tripped. I reset the ground fault and turned it back on, sparks flew, smoke came out and my ground fault protector again tripped. I unplugged it and then unplugged second one.  

I suspected that these two had the same problem as the first one that was recalled. I saw in Consumer Reports that more dehumidifiers had been recalled and checked but they were not on the list. I believe that this model (# 251.50701011) has the same problem as the others and is subject to malfunctioning and causing a fire. I have disconnected my two and am not using them.

The serial numbers are: WNX4Y10001069
                            and: WNX4XC0001006
justification: The dehumidifier malfunctioned, causing sparks and smoke, but no injury or death occurred.

The consumer stated that their cabinet door, next to the bucket, in the kitchen was on fire. There was spontaneous combustion with the product and the sponge.

The consumer stated that the plastic bucket melted and left shards of the cabinet door. 

The consumer sent numerous emails to the online retailer where he purchased the product from, but they have not responded to any of his emails

The consumer stated that the product is meant to be used on the inside and outside of the car.

The consumer believes that the potential dangers of the product should be listed on the labeling.

There are no recalls on this product.
justification: The incident involved spontaneous combustion causing a fire, but there was no mention of injury or death.

incident_description: Purchased Rowenta clothes iron model DM 890, serial number 4106 approximately 5-7 years ago.  Iron is equipped with a plastic ball-and-socket type swivel strain relief for the electrical cord.  Iron started operating intermittently over the past year and eventually stopped working completely.  We purchased a new iron.  In my investigation of why the old iron stopped working, I removed the bottom plate where the cord enters the iron and saw that the inboard edge of the ball-and-socket strain relief had rubbed against the insulated electrical cord where the cord exits the ball-and-socket in the interior of the iron.  The exterior sheathing of the cord was worn completely through and continued to rub through one of the conductors, eventually severing the wire completely.   Although I believe the risk of electrical shock was minimal due to the plastic construction, the risk of fire was high, particularly as the copper conductors were severed (1750W iron), of if more than one conductor had worn at the same time.  We reported this to the company who seemed disinterested in the problem.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning iron with potential fire risk but no actual injury or death occurred.

Fortunately, we did not experience any negative effects from this dehumidifier, but I am glad we became aware of the problem before something did happen.

incident_description: I bought a Kidde Gas and Carbon Monoxide Alarm about a year ago, after we had had a natural gas leak.  The gas pipe outside broke, and the gas came into the house through the dryer vent.  There are not a lot of Natural Gas Alarms out there. Kidde is a good brand, so I bought their alarm.  Well, the gas pipe broke again recently, and the house filled with gas.  Thankfully, I have a good gas-sniffing nose, because the alarm registered 0 and did not even chirp once the entire time the gas was in the house.  I'm glad we were not out of town or sleeping.  The alarm was properly installed, plugged in, it had a working backup battery, and the test I performed afterwards was successful (the alarm is actually quite loud when it works).  I called Kidde and they sent me 2 more of the Gas and Carbon Monoxide Alarms.  I asked how I can be sure that these alarms will work in the event of another gas leak.  The answer was, "YOU CAN'T. YOU JUST HAVE TO RELY ON THE MONITOR. THEY ARE SUPPOSED TO WORK."  I don't feel any safer with the alarms.  I have no confidence that any of the Kidde gas alarms will function as they should in the event of a gas leak. The scary part is that we won't know if the alarm works until we have a gas leak.  We could die in our sleep or blow up the house with the flick of a light switch. Kidde is selling a safety product that carries no assurance of working when needed.
justification: The alarm failed to detect a gas leak, which could have led to serious injury or death, but no actual harm occurred this time.

incident_description: We have a Hampton Bay dehumidifier in our finished basement. September 15,2013 I awoke to a strange odor. When i opened the basement door I heard a strange popping noise. I woke my husband up and we attempted to investigate the basement but the light would not go on. We could see smoke filling the basement so we evacuated our home and called 911. Fire company searched our home top to bottom and finally found the problem. Our dehumidifier had a hole the size of an apple burnt in the front of the grill. The other grill pieces were melted. Around the controls there was scorching. The wiring pulled out with no effort. The entire cavity was black and burnt to a crisp. Fire company personnel removed the unit and took pictures to complete a report. They were unable to find this unit on the recall list but said they were documenting the incident. After removing the unit we found where the carpet was burnt in 5 different locations.
justification: The incident involved significant property damage and a fire hazard, but no injuries or deaths were reported.

incident_description:
[REDACTED]

August 15, 2013

U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission
4330 East West Highway
Bethesda, MD 20814

Re: questionable safety of Jacuzzi walk-in-tub marketed by FirstStreet- electrocution
hazard?

I am writing to bring to your attention questions that have arisen concerning the safety of the
Jacuzzi brand walk-in-tub that is being manufactured for and aggressively marketed by
F irstStreet.

It's a lengthy saga that brings me to this point, but to recap quickly, my 80 year-old mother
contracted, after a four-and-a-halfhigh pressure sales presentation in her home (complete with a
slick, polished Power Point presentation), with Beldon Home Solutions to install a Jacuzzi brand
walk-in tub within an existing barrier-free shower stall to replace a regular tub that had been
installed some years earlier.

Beldon botched the installation not once, but twice, leaving gaping holes underneath the unit that would have allowed water underneath. One Beldon employee even went so far, in an attempt to
convince her that their installation was acceptable, to claim that you could "hit these units with a fire hose and they'd be fine". The reality was quite the contrary.

Our first inkling of a problem came from the installer's admonition, after the first installation, to "not allow water to get on the front panel". The front panel ofthe unit was a problem from day one; it never lay flat to the front, leaving a noticeable gap that would easily allow water inside the unit.

We eventually came to find out that the unit should never have been recommended for my
mother's particular installation situation, but it was only after she had to pay to have it removed and we could see the inside of the unit (see attached photos) that the positioning of the electrical components and their susceptibility to water was made obvious.

I have questions as to whether this unit is sufficiently safe and the electrical components
are shielded from possible water exposure well enough to protect consumers. Jacuzzi claims
that the unit cannot be used as a shower stall, although they include a hand-held shower head in
the unit proper. They further caution not to allow water to get on the front panel. .. remember,
this is a TUB. Even someone gripping the side with a wet hand could end up with water
dripping down the front, into the panel. Someone with arthritic hands who can't grasp the shower head well, could easily overshoot the tub and water could drip down the side. And this is
a unit that is being heavily marketed for the elderly, including those with dementia and
Alzheimer's.

I've included pictures of the unit. I believe the design ofthe front panel of this unit is such
that it provides insufficient protection to prevent the electrical components from coming
into contact with water in the course of normal use of this unit.

Thanks for your attention to these concerns,

[REDACTED]
justification: The incident describes a potential electrocution hazard due to water exposure to electrical components in a walk-in tub, but no actual injury or death is reported.

My 81 year old Mother's Soleus Air SG DEH45-1 dehumidifier combusted -- smoke, no fire -- fire dept. was called and identified the dehumidifier as the source.  Massive smoke damage in the lower level storage room and smoke throughout entire home.  She cannot live there for 1-2 months (estimate $25,000 - $30,000 in damage) -- your recall was 5 days after her incident.  I looked it up on the internet at the time and saw that they had stopped selling the units due to smoke and fire but had not been recalled.  I am very upset with your agency that you allowed a dangerous product to exist without prior recall but fully knowing the danger.  She could have died if that happened during the night.  She left home that day at 4:30 PM for a church dinner and returned at 7:30 PM to a home filled with smoke.  You need to do a better job getting the information out on this recall -- people in general don't consider dehumidifiers to be a smoke/fire risk and leave them running continuously -- even while they are gone on vacation.  And -- people I talk to don't even know there is a lint filter that should be cleaned.  I talked to the fire dept. about doing local news and paper to warn of the risk.  This is serious.  Let's get the word out.
[REDACTED]
justification: The dehumidifier combusted causing smoke damage but no injury or death, and the incident suggests similar occurrences are likely given the product's history.

incident_description:
I purchased the Stealth central vacuum hose and power head kit manufactured/distributed by MD Manufacturing in Bakersfield, CA, in 2007. The kit included the electric power head and central vacuum hose with electric cord pigtail.
I have used this several times a week for the last 6 years- it had worked fine and without any problems until the
beginning of this week.
The unit worked great until earlier this week when electric sparks came out of the pistol grip handle where it
attached to the electric contacts in the power head wand. The unit started to flame until I shut the power switch off. The black plastic housing around the electric contacts in the pistol grip melted and left a melted plastic residue on the upright wand's electric contacts. The unit is now unusable and would be unsafe in any event.
I eMailed MD Manufacturing to let them know of this safety hazard and asked for the name of a person I should
contact. This was several days ago and, given the serious nature of th is problem, I think it is terrible that I have yet to hear back from them - even an acknowledgement of my eMail would have been nice.

I am attaching a photo of the pistol grip and the electric switch/contact assembly which show the burn marks.
justification: The incident involved electric sparks and flames, but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
I have had a 24 inch pedestal fan for 14 months which has been used only during tyhe summer months in my home.  about 5 Sep 2013 the fan was running in the bedroom and I was in an adjacent room when I head this loud noise and humming.  I found that the blade was off of the axel of the motor and tried its' best to enter the bedroom but was prevented by the fan's wire guard.  What happened was the blade broke loose from bracket which remained attached to the motor axel with a set screw.  Apparently the weld, or whatever method is used to attach the blade to the bracket, was defective.  Since the blade could not enter the room a small piece of the bracket did and could have injured someone if they had been close.

The fan has not been abused and was sitting on a level floor.

Utilitech fan, Item 0333662  sold by Lowes
justification: The fan blade detached but was contained by the wire guard, posing potential injury risk but no actual injury occurred.

incident_description: Harbor Breeze "Twin Breeze" ceiling fan model# HE-06114-3 item # 0275436 was turned on. After it was running about 1/2 hour we herd a loud noise and found one of the fan bracket broke and sent the blade into my wall above my bed.
justification: The fan blade broke and hit the wall, but there was no reported injury.

justification: Sparks and smoke indicate an incident, but there was no reported injury or death.

incident_description:
Smelled odor in basement.  Inspected dehumidifier and found it was blowing warm air but not condensing any water.  Removed water tank and found inside plastic very hot.  Immediately unplugged and took to garage.  Disassembled plastic panels.  Placed thermometer on compressor.  Read 275 degrees F.  This overheating compressor would have started a fire had we not noticed it.  WOW we dodged a bullet!

Condenser and evaporator were not plugged however drain line was half plugged with slime.  About 2 weeks ago drain line had totally plugged and lower part of evaporator was all froze.  Unclogged line and restarted, seemed to be working then.

The compressor says it is thermally protected, Guess NOT.  The contacts on the thermal protection device were probably stuck together because they were made of silver with impurities or not made of silver or even silver plate, or just too small for the amperage. If you don't want the unit to inspect it I will probably cut it apart to see what caused the failure.  Yeah you guessed it, I'm and engineer, and just have to know what would have probably burned down our house.
justification: The incident involved a dehumidifier overheating to a dangerous level, which could have caused a fire but was discovered and prevented in time, resulting in no injury or damage.

incident_description: Our dehumidifier caught fire in the middle of the night last night.  It was on a table and free of obstructions and had plenty of distance all around it.  Fortunately no one was injured and damage appears to minimal right now.  If we didn't have working smoke detectors or were not home we could have lost the entire house.
justification: The dehumidifier caught fire but no one was injured and damage was minimal.

incident_description:
In the late spring of 2008 we purchased a 70 qt Dehumidifier for drying out a flooded garage.  We had gotten 4"-8" of water on the floor during snow melt and after dewatering the shop used the humidifier to try to dry out the drywall on the walls.  We placed the unit in the middle of the shop floor and shut the doors and kept the unit operating 24 hours a day, checking on it often. After a week or so we were distracted by work and did not check it for a day or so.  Upon going into the garage we found a strong small of burned electrical parts and the unit was badly charred.  The paint had blistered off except for the very bottom of the unit, the bucket was a melted mass of plastic.  The unit was still plugged in and the breaker was not tripped.  We assumed the unit had overfilled, spilled and then shorted out the unit and caught fire.  We discarded the unit and aired out the garage by opening the door and turning on fans.  There was no other damage except for the humidifier which my late wife had purchased in Anchorage for about $300 and sent up to Kotzebue. 
We attributed the problem to our failing to check on the unit frequently enough and felt ourselves lucky that when the unit burned it was on a concrete floor and nothing else caught fire.  It was only upon reading about your recent recall notice that I looked and found the Owner's Manual for the Dehumidifier and found it on your recall list: Frigidaire Model FDB70R1. We cannot say with certainty that the unit malfunctioned which caused it to catch fire, but it does seem odd that the breaker did not trip and the unit failed within weeks of having been purchased.  We had otherwise maintained the unit properly, regularly draining it and cleaning the filter.
justification: The incident involved a dehumidifier catching fire, causing damage to the unit but no injuries or other property damage.

incident_description:
I have used my Whirlpool Model # AD40USR1 dehumidifier for a few years to control moisture in the air in my basement.  My Whirlpool dehumidifier is usually left on automatic mode and my husband and I empty it when it automatically shuts off due to the bin being full of water.  

Luckily we were home and hadn't gone to bed around 10pm the other night when our home began to fill with smoke.  I went to the basement, smoke filled the air and we determined that the problem was from the dehumidifier.  My husband was able to shut this unit off, unplug and drag it out of our basement door before it caused a fire.

I do not see this specific dehumidifier on any of the recent recall lists and am concerned for other consumers safety.  I shutter to think what may have happened to my home, or my husband and I had we gone to bed already.
justification: The incident involved smoke and potential fire risk, but no actual injury or death occurred, and the likelihood is unlikely as it was averted before causing harm.

incident_description: Fire. Dehumidifier was being used to reduce humidity in approx 780 square foot apt.

The consumer stated that she unplugged the vaporizer. The consumer stated that the plug was very hot. The consumer stated that the plug was so hot that it burned her hand.The consumer stated that the vaporizer had been on for about 20 to 30 minutes.

The father attempted to remove unit but the base erupted flames, he had to use a fire extinguisher to contain the fire.  This incident caused the area where the unit located to be burnt including carpet, padding etc.  There were no injuries.  Estimate property damages are $10,000.

incident_description:
I have an LG Model # WM2455HG purchased 01-26-2008 from Home Depot. I first noticed a few years ago it has been growing Black mold inside and all around the roof of the soap dispenser area I have kept cleaning it but it seems to have always returned. called LG about the issue on 9-11-2013 and they said they can replace the defective part ( so they did admit to me it was defective) but at my expence ??? Black mold continues to grow and no matter how i clean it it just keeps returning. Please Help with this matter
Thank you

incident_description: I purchased Tide Pods at Target after wearing the clothes I washed with the product I developed a severe rash on my thighs and under my breasts the itching was unbearable and was starting to blister after contacting my doctor I had an appt. on Friday the 30 then spent the entire afternoon being treated for a severe allergic reaction the only thing I had been using was the Tide Pods I was given a prescription for a cream that I have to apply twice a day for 10 days. I have not been able to any activities for over 2 weeks and the pain and itching are still very painful even with the cream.

incident_description: We have a Casablanca 84" Malibu Star ceiling fan in our home.  The fan was already installed in our home when we moved in in 2007.  The home was built in 2001.  On Monday, Sept 2, 2013, my husband and 2 young children were sitting in the living room under the fan when it suddenly fell from the ceiling that is 2 stories high, striking my 3 year old son in the head.  We took him immediately to the Urgent Care and then to follow up with his pediatrician.  He suffered a head contusion and abrasions on the hand and head.  I wanted to report this issue as it could have had a much worse outcome.  This ceiling fan could have caused serious injury or death.
justification: The ceiling fan fell and caused a head contusion and abrasions, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description:
Caller purchased a glass shower door around February 2010 and had no problems with it until June 30th, 2013 when her husband was stepping into the shower as he normally did when the glass on the left side of the glass door exploded with enough force to spread small shards of glass over the entire 5ft x 10ft bathroom. 
The glass cut the callers' husband and he also had a pierce of glass embedded in the middle of the sole of his left foot.

Caller contacted the manufacturer around July 5th, 2013.
The manufacturer advised caller to go to customer service at the retailers and if they had any problems with replacement being provided then have the retailer contact the manufacturer and they would approve replacement.
Caller followed these instructions and she states that there was no problem obtaining the replacement left side of the shower door.

The contractor came to callers' home on July 27th, 2013 to install the replacement left side of the door, he had both sides of the shower door off and as he picked up the right side it shattered in his hands.
Contractor was no injured.

Caller is reporting this door as a severe safety issue due the to damage these incidents could cause anyone but especially a child or an elderly person.
justification: The incident resulted in injury to the caller's husband, including cuts and a piece of glass embedded in his foot, warranting a severity level of 3. The occurrence likelihood is 3 (possible) as the issue happened twice but with no further reports of injury.

incident_description:
(08/11/2013) The consumer stated that he and his wife were in the garage where the circuit box is located. The consumer stated that his wife said that she heard something buzzing. His wife walked over to the box and didcovered that the buzzing was coming from the circuit panel. The consumer stated that he open the panel and saw that it was arcing. He turned the main breaker off and the arcing and sparking stopped. He pulled the panel out and saw that one of the circuit breakers had melted. The consumer stated that the panel box is ruined on the right side.

The consumer stated that he had the problem that was described in the recall rel#88-091. He stated that he was not notified of the recall.





(08/12/2013) The consumer stated that he contacted the manufacturer and described what happened. He stated that he was advised that his model was not in the recall. The consumer stated that he was told that his product was 26 years old.

I was using a Ryobi miter saw model TS1342L to cut a small 2x4 (about 4 inches long) at a 45-degree horizontal. I've owned this saw for several years and never had any issues with it.

The saw stopped suddenly and threw the wood out of my hands. It ricocheted off the wall twice and went through the window pane of a french door about 7 feet away.

I inspected the saw and the blade appears to have bent and gone through the housing.

The blade has been in place for at least a year, is relatively new, and is still securely attached.

There were no injuries and I immediately stopped using the saw.

incident_description:
The consumer stated that she was using her top loading washing machine and when it was on the spin cycle it started to shake excessively and move from where it was located. The consumer stated that she hit the ÃÂstopÃÂ button to turn it off.  The consumer stated that on the control panel it flashes error message ÃÂULÃÂ. She stated that the incident usually happened when she was washing towels and the machine was not over loaded. 

The consumer stated that when the machine was shaking it hit her left hip and she suffered a bruise. 

The consumer stated that she continued to use the washing machine and it continued to shake every time if gets to the spin the cycle. 

The manufacturer informed her that her model was not included on any recall and they referred her to the CPSC.

The consumer stated that her washer was experiencing the same hazard listed on release #13-073. The consumer stated that she believed that this product should be investigated due to the injury hazard and property damaged hazard. 

Consumer has 2 young children and she makes sure her laundry room door is closed so they don't get in there while the washer is running.  She's worried that the washer might hurt them when its on spin cycle.   The washer is very powerful when on spin cycle and very unsafe.

incident_description: I own an HXW2304 Staber washing machine. On July 5,2013 the machine was in the spin cycle when there was a loud boom. The lid was blown off and one of the four clothes guard flanges was driven through the bezel. Fortunately the flange did not get beyond the machine top. It could have killed someone had it hurtled through the air.  The force was such that the top was damaged. You can see the force of this by the bent angle iron used to hold the right corner of the top to the machine. My 85 year old mother in law was in the room only moments before the lid exploded off the machine. She could have been seriously injured. When I looked at what had happened I was astonished to find that each of the four clothes guards were only held on by two pop rivets. Based on the inertial forces generated during the spin cycle at the 175 Gs in Staber Industries specifications this method of attachment was grossly inadequate and presents a danger to users of these machines. This is a serious and potentially life threatening manufacturing defect and design flaw that has to be addressed.  I communicated with Staber Industries by phone and Email.  To date I have not received an acknowledgement or reply to the letter and photographs I was requested to send to Staber Industries.
justification: The incident involved a dangerous mechanical failure with potential for serious injury or death, but no actual injury occurred.

My Shop Vac model 4045AH caught fire.

We plugged our Shop Vac into a properly grounded 3-prong receptacle.  When we turned on the motor, it instantly began throwing orange sparks and caught fire internally.  We immediately unplugged it and took it outside.

Those few seconds of operation filled the room with a smoky electrical fire haze.  We vented the room for a while before closing the house back up.  The room smelled for two days, and the motor itself still smells of the electrical fire after three days.
justification: The incident involved a fire but no injuries were reported, only property damage and temporary discomfort from smoke.

incident_description:
I have the Generac GP5500 portable generator. My unit is experiencing the same float needle sticking issues reported on CPSC and many internet venues. The plating is flaking off the needle, same as in all the pictures of other people's units that I have seen. During a power outage last week, I found my running generator surrounded by a pool of fuel on the floor of my barn. I am amazed that everything did not go up in flames. My unit has under 20 hours on it and is about 2 weeks out of warranty. It has always been stored with the carb empty of fuel. I have also always used ethanol free premium Shell gasoline with Sta-Bil added. Generac has an obvious issue with a defective carburetor, specifically with the plating used on the float needle.

I have reported this issue to Generac via e-mail with no response so far.  If their response is consistent with others I have seen, they will deny the problem and blame it on dirty fuel. Dirty fuel does not cause a float needle to virtually weld itself into place, as was the case here. The plating process used on the float needle is defective and needs to be addressed by Generac before somebody is killed as a result.
justification: The incident involved a fuel leak that could have led to a fire, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
WE COULD HAVE ALL BEEN KILLED. URGENT AND IMMEDIATE ACTION ITEM

December 2012 I purchased a Cen-Tech 2000 W power inverter from Harbor Freight online. Here is a link: http://www.harborfreight.com/2000-watt-continuous4000-watt-peak-power-inverter-69662.html
Purpose was to provide 110 volt power to various small electric/electronic items on my boat, a 37' cutter rigged cruising sailboat. The item number is 69662. The unit connects to a 12 volt power supply and then can be switched on and supplies AC current via three conventional outlets.

After about four months of operation, the cooling fan suddenly malfunctioned. It ran all the time, even when the master switch was in "off" position, regardless of temperature. The proper behavior is for the fan to be activated only when a predetermined critical temperature is reached.

I called the supplier to report this malfunction and was told that the warranty was only for 90 days. In any case, we were sailing outside the US and would have had difficulty doing an exchange. I rewired the power supply lines with a switch so that I could turn off the fan when the unit was not in use and continued to use it in a limited way because it was cumbersome to go into the battery area to flip on and off the switch, and the fan made a noise all the time of course.

On August 24 2013 with my boat in a Marina in the SF Bay area, I turned on the inverter to charge a few electronic items and heard some pop pop poping noises. I moved closer to the inverter, and then saw sparking inside. In very short order the sparking turned to flames inside the unit; at the sight of the flames I quickly turned off the main power switch, grabbed a fire extinguisher, turned on a couple of fans in the salon and fled to the cockpit. The interior salon had filled with smoke. With the power off, the flames died out.

I am working with Harbor Freight to try to get the unit replaced. Had this happened offshore when all hands were topside, we could all easily have been killed by the fire that certainly would have erupted. 

I take good care of my boat and gear; #2 cable was used to connect the short, 4' run to our #2 battery bank which consists of two [REDACTED] deep cycle fully charged lead acid batteries. This is overkill for a 2000 watt unit. 

If this can happen on my boat, it can happen anywhere. I urge you to find and fix the problem before people die.

Thanks and feel free to call with any questions.
[REDACTED]
justification: The incident involved a fire hazard with potential for death, but no actual injuries or deaths occurred.

incident_description:
Fire in basement, only item that burned

incident_description: Last night one of the three identical ceiling fans that I have malfunctioned. A blade snapped off at the metal arm, causing a sharp heavy piece of fan to land on my child's bed. I have three of these fans and am now going to have to replace them because I am NOT going to put my children in danger of being sliced or bruised in the night. I contacted Lowes, who sent me to harbor breeze and then they sent me to litex fans who manufactures the product. They were very unresponsive and just wanted to send me replacement parts which would be identical to the one that snapped off and broke. I am not interested in replacing those parts with new ones because they have the potential to break that easily as well. I am confident the company will not report this as they acted as if it was not a big deal.
justification: A fan blade snapped off and landed on a child's bed, but no injury was reported. The likelihood is considered possible due to the incident occurring and the manufacturer's unresponsiveness.

incident_description:
Cleaned hot grill with the grill brush. A small bristle was left behind, but I didn't see it. Cooked food on the grill and the food picked up the bristle. I ate the food and the bristle was lodged in my throat. Required a trip to the emergency room to have it removed. 

When the brush is used on a hot grill, heat is conducted through the wire bristle to the plastic base. The plastic surrounded the bristle melts and releases the bristle.
justification: The incident resulted in a bristle being lodged in the throat, requiring emergency medical intervention, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description: Washing machine continues to go unbalanced.  Shakes violently and needs constant monitoring and manual intervention.
justification: The washing machine shakes violently but there is no mention of injury or death, only the need for monitoring and intervention.

incident_description:
Had a wall mounted electric heater in the bathroom (installed 20 years ago).

The unit had been running for about 10 minutes and it started glowing red inside.  Turning it off via the thermostat dial did not shut it off.  Smoke started coming out of the unit.  We called 911 and the fire department came and shut it off at the circuit breaker.

The unit had gotten so hot, it started to char the studs in the wall and they had started to smoke.  The fire department said that if they had gotten there 5 minutes later flames would have developed in the wall.

It appears that none of the protection devices inside the heater (thermal overload, etc.) worked.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning heater that caused smoke and potential fire hazard, but no injuries or deaths occurred.

incident_description: I injured my elbow on my Andersen sliding door while I was walking through the doorway.  Andersen designed their "reach out lock" to have a protruding, stationary, metal pin on the door frame.  Because the pin has no "give" to it, when I hit my elbow, the pin went right between my bones.  I did not seek medical attention but asked Andersen to start an insurance claim for me as I have psoriatic arthritis, and being I couldn't use my elbow for two days after the injury, I'm concerned about future arthritis in that elbow due to the injury.  Andersen sent a tech to my house to change the lock set to their newer design; which has a plastic, retractable, pin on the lock.  They would not admit that they changed the design due to the safety hazard the old design posed.  They also would not agree to recall the dangerous lock set either as I proposed to them. incident_description:
I was ironing with a Rowenta Professional Iron Model DE-811 Serie A.  I looked on the iron - I could not find any sort of other serial number or identifying number beyond this.

I was ironing as normal.  I smelled a burning smell.  A few seconds later, sparks began to fly from the base of the iron - where the cord connects to the iron.  The sparks turned to a small flame and began to burn the ironing board cover.  I quickly blew out the flames and then ran to the wall to unplug the iron.  

This all happened in a matter of seconds.  I shudder to think what would have happened had I left the room to hang up clothes or do something else.  It wouldn't have taken very long for the flames to have grown larger and could have easily begun to burn the room and perhaps the entire house down.  Really, this could have been catastrophic.  It wasn't like I had left the iron on and went to do other errands or chores.  I was standing there ironing and this happened.  Lucky thing.

I happened to mention this to my aunt who also has owned Rowenta irons.  She could not remember the model, but she also experienced the same thing.  She was ironing and the iron sparked and caught fire.  She quickly unplugged the iron and threw it away.  She said it happened in the exact same way - the base of the iron where the cord connects to the iron - began to spark and burn.

I have never filed such a report but this is a problem.  I worry for others who might have Rowenta irons.  This is very very dangerous.  I unfortunately do not have documentation for this iron.  It belonged to my mother.  She would have bought it from a retail store - but I'm not sure which store or when.

incident_description:
I purchased a new home completed in February 2012.  It has a Trane Products A/C system with a Heat Pump and Air Handler.  The Air Handler is a HyperionÃÂ XR - Model Number: GAM5A0C48M41SAA.

As with many similar systems in Florida, the Air Handler is located in the garage in an area built above the ceiling level.  To minimize the monthly maintenance, the system air filter is located inside the air handler unit, not at the return vents inside the house.

As stated on the Trane website, "Every Trane Air Handler is packed with high-quality components. Each helps ensure that time after time, your unit will provide total comfort your family can rely on. The HyperionÃÂ includes:
ÃÂ	Uniquely designed cabinet
ÃÂ	Fully enclosed insulation
ÃÂ	All-aluminum coil
ÃÂ	High-efficiency VorticaÃÂ blower motor (GAM5 models only)
ÃÂ	Unique modular design
ÃÂ	Electronic expansion valve metering device that is 400% more reliable than standard expansion valves
ÃÂ	Quick-turn fasteners
ÃÂ	ÃÂNo leakÃÂ drain pan made from rust-resistant composites and built with a gradual slope
ÃÂ	Heating options for either hydronic or electric heat
ÃÂ	Corrosion-resistant finish"

The problem is the combination of "Fully enclosed insulation" with inadequately designed "Quick-turn fasteners".

The cover which must be installed for the unit to run has two "Quick-turn fasteners" that are difficult to engage.  The cover plate seal must be collapsed for the fasteners to reach and catch to ensure fully enclosed insulation.

On May 30th of this year the HVAC service technician was finishing the reassembly of the unit after an issue with the thermal expansion valve.  He saw I had a filter and asked if I wanted him to change it.  Since the ladder needed to be moved, I said I would take care of it after he left.  I had changed the filter on a couple of other occasions.

I was having difficulty in engaging the fasteners so I increased the force pushing on the unit to collapse the seal.  The ladder I was on moved, then buckled and I fell approximately 10 feet onto the concrete floor.  The fall resulted in four broken ribs.  I was lucky.

I contacted Trane and received a very terse response.  Trane denies any responsibility and disagrees that there is any issue with the design of the fasteners.  If the fasteners were 1/2" longer they could engage without having to collapse the seal.  If the filter holding unit had a small door instead of the large cover plate, they could have different fasteners.  There are many inexpensive solutions to this issue.  The Trane representative told me to have the HVAC service technician change the filter once or twice a year even though the owner's manual states that the filters should be changed monthly.

For user safety, the cover plate needs to be redesigned or that type of installation must be avoided.  This should include existing units as well as new units prior to sale.
justification: The incident resulted in broken ribs from a fall, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The likelihood is rated as 3 (possible) given the described design flaw and the need for regular filter changes.

The gear on the drive shaft is metal and the gear on the agitator is plastic.  The plastic gear on the agitator was stripped.  I called the LG service man who had done the original software update.

After several adjustments were made, I installed 3 cable ties to secure the cable to the braces.  As I clipped the third cable tie, the stool suddenly collapsed.  The collapse was accompanied by a simultaneous pop or snap sound. Since my hands and arms were in front of me, they contacted the wall and assisted me in remaining upright, and on my feet.    My left foot was still on top of the collapsed stool surface, and my right foot contacted the patio. There were no major injuries; however, a slight sprain to the right ankle was noted.  Examination of the stool revealed the right end of the folding braces between the legs had failed, resulting in 2 pieces completely separating from the braces.  Several of the hinge points had unsnapped as a result of the collapse in conjunction with the users weight and subsequent contact with the concrete surface.  
Investigation and Analysis:  The concrete surface was clean, dry, level, and free of any obstructions.  The stool working surface was also clean and dry. Footwear consisted of [REDACTED] walking shoes, laced up, and in serviceable condition.  The shoes offered good traction in conjunction with the large traction dots on the stool working surface.   Closer examination of the broken parts of the stool did not indicate any fracture lines or cracks, but merely a shearing separation of the plastic at various points.   There are no visible markings, numbers or other data etched or embedded into the structure of this stool, indicating manufacture, style, or other significant information.  
Since I had retained my purchase receipt, but disposed of the cello wrapping and labels; I returned to Garden Ridge to conduct some fact finding, view and photo the labels, and inquire about the product.  I took photos of the product and labels. The merchandise return or exchange was addressed without favorable results.  While I acknowledge RidgesÃÂ policy of no returns/exchanges for broken items; the consumer is pretty much hung out to dry.   
According to the labeling; Home Collections is the distributor of the product, although the item is made in China.  A number HW-1265 appeared on a SKU label, and a SKU label for Garden Ridge for inventory control and pricing of $12.99.  In addition, the label indicates a rating of 265 lbs.  My current weight is 180 lbs on a bad day and has remained within 2% of that weight for the past 5 years. 
As an Occupational Safety and Health Manager for the U.S.A.F.  for 40 plus years; I have a responsibility and obligation to prevent mishaps, either before they occur or as a result of lessons learned.  I am submitting this information to the CPSC in hopes of preventing such future occurrences.  I have noted many step stool advisories and some recalls regarding stools of the same type configuration, but no exact matches for this particular product.  Attempts to contact Home Collections electronically have not been accomplished at this time.  Respectfully submitted,
[REDACTED]
Occupational safety and Heatlh Manager
justification: The incident resulted in a slight sprain to the right ankle, which qualifies as an injury (severity 3). The likelihood is unlikely (2) as the stool failure was due to a specific defect rather than a common occurrence.

incident_description:
I have a two year old self contained steam shower.  The shower product id is OW-217 sold by Luxury Spas, Inc. in Lorain, Ohio.   The shower, in the upstairs master bathroom, has two sliding tempered glass doors in the center of  the unit. On the morning of the day of the incident my wife and myself were downstairs in the house and no one was upstairs.  Suddenly were heard a loud thump as if something had exploded.  The right hand shower door had exploded showering glass bits inside the shower and all over the bathroom.  There was also pieces of glass and the metal door handle in the toilet, which is in front of and to the right of the shower.  This was not a case of something coming loose and the glass simply falling and breaking.  The door was securely fastened inside the shower by four rollers which were securely fastened to the door through holes in the glass. Two on top and two on the bottom.  The roller clamps were still closed and contained pieces of glass within them.  Even if the top clamps both came loose, the door would have fallen in the shower and could not have exploded outward as it did.  Luxury Spas has indicated they have no idea why this happened.

If anybody had been sitting on that toilet when the door disintegrated, they could have been severely injured.
justification: The incident involved an exploding shower door causing significant damage but no injuries, as no one was present at the time.

incident_description:

On July 28, 2013 this became a bigger issue for me as I tripped on the stability foot and broke a toe.  An minor emergency room visit was necessary to diagnose the broken toe and it was tape up. 
This caused considerable pain and I will be having to keep the toe taped up for several weeks and take care as the toe heals. 

The design of the Little Partners Learning Tower has safety feet that you assemble onto the tower when you put the tower together.  These safety feet extend beyond the bottoms of the tower into areas people walk around the tower.     
Many people in the two households have banged their feet into these extended feet many times, this time it resulted in a broken toe. 

Today I contacted Little Partners thru their web site: www.littlepartners.com explaining what was happening with these extended safety feet. [REDACTED] replied the following:
"Dear [REDACTED],
I am so sorry to hear about your toe, and I thank you for contacting us with your question.  Our product is not in recall.  As indicated in the assembly instructions, Part B is an optional part.  It was produced as an option for additional stability.  The Learning Tower has been tested and has met all safety standards both with and without this additional part.  Please feel free to remove the extra feet if they are not working well for your family.
justification: The incident resulted in a broken toe requiring medical attention, indicating an injury (severity 3). The description notes multiple instances of tripping, suggesting a likely occurrence (4).

incident_description:

We moved into our home in 2007. Previous owner had just redone kitchen, went high end on appliances not knowing they were going to have job transfer.

Recently Thermador downdraft fan stopped working properly. Figured it was out of warranty by now, I took a look to see if it was a switch I could replace - discovered it had a circuit board. I was shocked to see that the circuit board had started to melt along with the wires leading to it. I called Thermador, said I knew it must be out of warranty by now - but it seemed like a defect in manufacturing or design flaw and a fire hazard.

After many calls, Thermador reluctantly agreed to send someone at their expense to "diagnose". The technician informed me it happens all the time:. 

I maintain for the amount of money spent on this type of product one should expect it to last longer than five or six years, and of all the appliances I have ever owned, it is the only one that has ever had a part that melted and posed a fire hazard|. Thermador refuses to make good - "it is out of warranty" and it is "normal wear and tear".

I recorded my last conversation with Thermador! The audio, as well as pictures of the melted circuit board and wires and a video of it sparking and smoking can be found on you tube under the user [REDACTED]. I now have a stove in the middle of the kitchen with no ventilation;.
justification: The melted circuit board and sparking wires pose a fire hazard (Incident, No Injury), and the technician's statement that it 'happens all the time' suggests a likely occurrence.

incident_description:
Smoke detector mounted in basement area started to smoke and then went off.  My son went to pull the battery out and it was hot and then exploded in his hand.  The battery then caught the carpet on fire and the rest of the material was shot into the bathroom ruining the bath mat.  Luckily my son was not injured.  The battery is a FireX brand and the house was built in 2007 so the detectors all have mfg dates during that year.  I am well aware of the need to install the "right" type of battery in smoke detectors since the house we lived in in CA was built in 2000 and I had 3 detectors explode.  One also exploded in my hand and the only reason I was not injured was the connector part which shot out along with all the inside material was facing away from me.

How can it be that a smoke detector (a safety device!! Really!!) which has as it's only job to detect smoke and fire is very often the cause of the smoke and fire??  I am just glad in both cases we were home during these times otherwise it could have caused more damage or I would think even a house fire.

What is the CPSC doing about this??  I can find incident after incident on the web of these things exploding and causing damage and injury.  Supposedly this product was redesigned in 2000 but the issue is still occurring since this one was made in Aug of 2007.  I have told many people about these 2 incidents and that they must put in only certain types of 9V.  No one I have told has any idea that there are different 9V's and that, only in these stupid smoke detectors, that they have a microscopic message stating only to use certain brands and certain models of 9V batteries.  I guarantee if you ask 100 people on the street right now whether a 9V is a 9V that at least 99 will state yes.  The one who says no will be the one which has had a battery explode in a SMOKE DETECTOR!!
justification: The incident involved a smoke detector battery exploding and causing a small fire, but no injuries were reported.

incident_description:
Werner 6006 fiberglass stepladder failure
The morning of Friday July 12th 2013 was the beginning of a beautiful summer day. The temperature was somewhere in the upper seventies with virtually no wind. So I decided to trim the burning bushes on the south side of my house. I got out my Werner 6006 stepladder, set it up fully extended and on level ground in front of one of my bushes. With my electric trimmer in hand, I climbed several feet up the ladder and began trimming. I was almost done when I felt the ladder lean to my right. I responded by leaning to my left. However, the ladder continued to lean more and more to the right. The ladder went out from under me and I fell about 4 feet to the ground. I landed on my back and to the left of the ladder. I laid on the ground for several minutes as I worked to regain my normal breathing pattern. Once I felt able to do so, I made my way into the house and set on our couch. My wife came in and asked me what was wrong. See told me a looked white and very uncomfortable. I went to my doctor early the following week wear he sent me to the lab to be X-rayed. The results indicate that I have a fracture in my lower back. 
I closely inspected the ladder. What appears to have happened is that the right leg failed just above the bottom step. This failure allowed the right leg to buckle inward which caused the bottom step to buckle upward in the middle. The buckling of the bottom step pulled on the left leg causing it to buckle inward. This should have never happened. The ladder looked in good condition when I set it up and I never expected this kind of failure. The two main legs on this ladder are channelized fiberglass with the face being about 4 inches wide and the perpendicular being about 1 inch wide. I believe the fiberglass 1 inch perpendicular portions of the legs were not made strong enough to withstand the lateral forces that may be applied to it from normal use. I weighed about 200 pounds at the time of this accident and the ladder is rated at 250.
justification: The incident resulted in a fracture in the lower back, which qualifies as an injury (severity level 3). The ladder failure was unexpected given its apparent good condition and proper setup, making the occurrence likelihood rare (1).
