incident_description: I was using, only for the second time, a Black Cat Products electric pressure washer Model TW1303 on a sidewalk on the outside of my home.  It was approximately 65 degrees outside and sunny.  After approximately 2-3 minutes the pressure washer started to smell like it was getting hot.  I stopped using it and let it sit for about 5 minutes to cool down.  When I went to use it again, the motor made a loud humming noise and immediately began to smoke.  I released the handle and the motor smoked for another 3-4 minutes and is now completely non functional.  The GFCI switch never interrupted the circuit.  MCM International and RMM have several models which have recalled already.   This was a hazard and could have easily caught on fire if I had not immediately released the handle, thus stopping the unit.  This unit was manufactured in April of 2003 and should be added to the recall list.  The unit has always been stored inside in climate controled conditions and used exactly per the provided instructions.
justification: The pressure washer malfunctioned and smoked, posing a fire hazard, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
All propane stoves in RVs or mobile homes in the US are unsafe. They fail to incorporate Flame Failure Devices (also known as 100% safety shut offs or thermocouple protected burners) Inadvertent gas knob opening, flame failure and other foreseeable events that cause a gas knob to be in the on or open position, with no flame present. The propane gas then fills a relatively air tight, confined space with gas, and an explosion occurs due to innocent ignition sources. 
On November 29, 2009, someone was severely burned when his 2004 RV exploded. He later died as a result of the thermal burns he received in the explosion. The main burner of his Atwood stove top was found in the on position after the explosion. The burner is a 9,000 btu burner. The required LP gas detector was disconnected by an unknown person, probably because of nuisance alarms or battery draw.
The gas detector was older than the recommended life span of such gas detectors. No warnings are given about the shelf life of LP gas detectors.
The UK, Australia, and many other countries require flame failure devices on all RV stove tops. All boats and yachts in the US require Flame Failure Devices. The American Boat and Yacht Council started the process of requiring the life saving feature as far back as 1993. European countries have required them for years as well. This safety device, if required in the US could save lives here as well.
justification: The incident resulted in a death due to thermal burns from an explosion, indicating the highest severity level. The occurrence likelihood is rated as unlikely based on the provided frequency of 47 incidents out of 10,427.

incident_description:
i bought a set of glass shower doors manufactured by CW Door, Model 1050.  It was their cheapest model and the glass was thin, but tempered.  my contractor was reluctant to have me purchase it, but i didn't want to spend a lot of money. it didn't occur to me that there might be problems associated with a product being sold in a reputable store.

Model 1050 has two sliding glass doors that are over 5 feet tall.  after my contractor installed the doors on february 8, 2009, he suggested we wait a day or two.  after that, we used the shower several times, but it was a bit disconcerting because the doors slid on their tracks like ice skates on ice. the first couple of times the shower doors were used, you could hear a loud thump when the doors ran into the tiny plastic bumper mounted on the walls - the doors slid so quickly that it would hit the bumper hard and loud.  we learned to move the doors slowly and deliberately.  but on february 12, my daughter used the shower for the first time; when she slid open the door, there was a loud thump, and the door shattered and she was cut with tiny pieces of glass.

the manufacturer claims that the door was installed incorrectly; it's possible because one of the plastic bumpers was missing from the box and the contractor thought it would be okay to operate the doors with one bumper.  but it's also possible that the sliding action of the door makes it especially prone to constant impact.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (cuts from shattered glass), and the likelihood is possible given the described issues with the door's installation and operation.

incident_description:
I bought a Black & Decker NPP2018 Cordless Pole Saw last year at a special event sponsored by the Southern California Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD). Although I've had it for a number of months, today is the first time I've actually assembled and used it. This unit consists of a small chainsaw bar, chain and motor at one end of a long pole with the removable rechargable battery and trigger/switch at the other end. The three screw-together pole sections can be assembled with the center section omitted so as to make a shorter pole saw.

In order to operate the saw, a user would hold the pole with their left hand and hold the trigger grip with their right hand. They would then use their right thumb to press the "lock" button while squeezing the trigger with their right fingers. Once running, the lock button may be released. Upon releasing the trigger, the electric brake is supposed to stop the saw.

When I begin trimming trees in the back yard I started the saw according to the operating instructions, but when I released the trigger, the saw kept running. After pressing the lock button numerous times while squeezing and releasing the trigger I got the saw to stop. The first time this happened, I assumed my work glove had gotten caught in the trigger. The second time it happened I removed the glove and continued to use the saw. When it happened again, I realized the problem was with the trigger itself. I could feel the trigger returning to its un-squeezed position, but even when I completely removed my right hand from the trigger grip, the saw would keep running. Manipulating the lock and trigger finally got it to stop.
justification: The saw continued running after releasing the trigger, posing a potential hazard, but no injury occurred.

incident_description:
Late last October of 2009, I purchased two identical Honeywell/Kaz Quickheat Ceramic electric heaters for home use, and used them according to directions. They heat up to a certain point, then rapidly turn on and off - fan, heating element, and all, arcing and sparking. The packages warned of this potential, so I kept an eye on them. Please note there is no 'off' switch. These were unplugged when not in use.

The product in question is : http://www.kaz.com/kaz/heaters/products/honeywell-compact-quick-heat-ceramic-heater-hz-315/

After a few weeks of normal use, one of them reached its required temperature, then stopped pulsing off/on. A few minutes later, drawn by the smell of burning plastic, I discovered the temperature control knob assembly had ARC-WELDED itself in the position I'd left it. I had to unplug it, running full-blast, to keep it from starting a fire. I cut off the cord and got rid of it. 

Very cautious with the remaining heater after that, I used it in my bedroom for a few hours at a time, only when actually in the room, and only while awake. One afternoon, I accidentally dozed off and awoke to the same smell of burning plastic. The plastic knob was too hot - melted - and distorted as I touched it. I unplugged it from the wall and inspected it after it had cooled. Its thermostat control contacts had slagged-down and welded together as well. This one's cord was removed and was discarded also. 

Repairs under the manufacturer's warranty would have cost more than buying new heaters, and I did NOT want another product in my home from this manufacturer, however, I wish I would have kept one for investigation purposes.

I'm not sure if I grabbed two with the same problem and it's a rare coincidence, or if others have had this problem. If I had not been present to unplug these machines, I have little doubt they would have caused fires in my home. Perhaps they have caused fires - even deaths - in other homes where the purchasers are not as vigilant as I am.
justification: The incident involved potential fire hazards but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description: When air compressor was plugged in, sparks shot out from the motor area.
justification: Sparks from the motor area indicate an incident but no injury was reported.

incident_description:
Item involved:
Duracraft HEPA 200 Air Cleaner, Model DA-5020

We awoke in the middle of the night to a very strong, noxious smell throughout the house.  Our bedrooms are on the second floor of a two-story home.  After searching the home, I found that our HEPA filter unit in the basement was the source.  The internal fan was not turning.  I unplugged the filter unit and carried it outside.  I partially disassembled it and found that the motor was extremely hot and all plastic around it was severely melted.  I suspect that the device could have caught fire if it had been left unattended for much longer.  We've owned this device for about 9 years and it usually runs constantly.  We seldom turn it off.  We performed regular maintenance.  In fact, I had replaced the internal filter only a few days prior to this incident.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning air cleaner that could have caught fire, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description: I had this portable heater turned on and several hours later smelled an electrical odor.  I went to the unit and it was off.  The ground fault had popped.  I unplugged the unit and proceeded to inspect the interior housing of the switch and wires and found that they had melted.  The unit had gotten so hot that the black power wire was melted and the red wire was partially melted causing the unit to ground fault.
justification: The incident involved a portable heater malfunction causing melted wires and a ground fault, but no injury or death occurred.

incident_description: I was using my eureka The Boss Smart vac to vacuum the apartment. When I went to turn the vacuum off the switch would not work, it was also hot to the touch. I had to unplug the vacuum to shut it off. I opened the vacuum and found that the wires and connections to the rocker switch were all melted and frayed. If I had been vacuuming for much longer this no doubt would have started an electrical fire inside the vacuum. I had only been vacuuming for 5 to 10 minutes at the most if that. It's a small apartment, doesn't take long to do. I feel this is a dangerous fire hazard issue that needs to be addressed.
justification: The incident involved a malfunctioning vacuum that could have caused a fire, but no actual injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
I own a Harman Oakwood freestanding wood burning stove. It was professionally installed by a licensed dealer. This is my second year heating with the stove. The stove is a down draft design and requires the user to close a bypass damper to initiate clean burning. 

Once the clean burning stage has begun, there is a distinct smell of smoke in the house. It is enough to wake me up at night and I am two floors above the stove. I contacted the dealer who replaced a gasket. This did not help. I contacted the dealer again who said that they had problems with many Oakwoods smelling of smoke when in clean burn and advised me to place a pot of water on the top of the stove. This also did not help.

The stove is built with gaskets sealing the respective panels together instead of the traditional stove cement. Only a couple of these gaskets are replaceable by the dealer. The rest are "untouchable" according to my dealer. I suspect that there is a leak at one of these gaskets.

I believe my dealer is acting in good faith and we are trying to work out the problem. However, I do believe there is a design defect in the Harmon Oakwood and I would like you all to investigate it.

Thanks,
justification: The incident involves a persistent smoke smell but no reported injury or health impact, indicating a non-injury incident.
